“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, lines and also points.”
Written last, just after point, the same color(country) belongs to the points alone. Nothing splits the line, so one line joins the points of all five countries. A line joins its rows in x order, and here five rows share each year, so the line zigzags up and down at every year:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + point + color(country)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + line + point + color(col.country)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + point +
  color(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line, point,
  color(col.country))




gog: up to 5 rows of `line` share one value of `x(year)`, and nothing splits them, so they are joined in x order and the stroke zigzags inside that value. If you have several series, add `color(<field>)` or `group(<field>)`; for one value per `x`, summarize them with `line * mean`.




                                                                                              1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, a line and also points colored by country.”
gog prints a warning about the zigzag and suggests color(<field>) or group(<field>), although the sentence already has color(country). That color belongs to the points, so nothing splits the line.
The sentence read aloud under each plot also says which marks a channel reaches. “Color by country” names no mark, so it reaches every mark. “Points colored by country” reaches the points only.
With one mark, it makes no difference where you write a channel: data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) and data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) + point draw the same plot. This book writes the mark first, because the mark is what the sentence is about (The order of +). With several marks, write first what every mark shares. Then write each mark, followed by what belongs to that mark alone.
Order appears more than once in this grammar, and it does not mean the same thing every time. Which orders matter gathers all of it in one place: what you may reorder freely, what the engine refuses, and the two orders that change the picture with no warning. Encoding scope gives the rule for every kind of word.

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.8 The * operator: combining
A histogram is not in your table: the bands and their counts have to be computed before anything is drawn. * is how a sentence asks for that.
* attaches a transform to a mark. The mark is always on the left; the transform is on the right. Where two transforms follow one mark, either order draws the same plot. Write them in the order they happen: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each one.
bar * bin      # histogram
line * smooth  # smoothed trend line
zone * bin     # heatmap: the same `bin`, cutting both axes
The last line, zone * bin, shows the pattern: one transform means one thing, and the mark decides where it applies. In a histogram, each bar’s height shows the count, so one axis is used for the count and bin cuts only the other. A zone shows its count by color instead, so no axis is used for the count, and both axes are free for columns. In zone * bin + x(gdp) + y(life), bin cuts gdp into bands along the x axis and life into bands along the y axis. Each cell is where a gdp band meets a life band, and its color shows how many rows fall in that cell. Change the mark to bar and add space(), the 3-D cube, and the count becomes the height of a bar instead of a color. The 3-D histogram compares the two. When one of a zone’s positions is categorical, bin cuts only the other one, because a category is already divided into slots. The zone chapter’s mixed mesh draws one: life cut into bands, one row of cells per continent.
The six summaries (sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile) differ from bin in one way: they take the measurement from a column you name, instead of counting rows. One channel carries the measurement. On a bar it is the continuous axis: y for vertical bars, x for horizontal ones, and z in space(). On a zone it is color. A summary groups the rows by every position that does not carry the measurement, then reduces that channel’s column to one value inside each group. So zone * mean + x(a) + y(b) + color(v) averages v inside every cell two categories cross. Transforms draws all six from one column, so you can compare their answers.
See Operators for the full rules, and Transforms for each transform in detail.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.9 The | and / operators: faceting, or composing
text:
2.9 The | and / operators: faceting, or composing
Across the world, life expectancy rises with income. One scatter of 142 countries cannot show whether that holds inside each continent. A second question, how many countries each continent has, needs a plot of its own beside the first. Two operators put plots or panels in one figure: | puts them side by side, and / puts one above the other. Whether those are panels or whole plots is decided by what you write on the right.
With facet() on the right they split one plot into panels, one per category of the column it names:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# One panel per continent, side by side
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent))






                                                                0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                         0 20K 40K                                                                                 0 20K 40K                                                      0 20K 40K                               0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
Every panel shares one scale, which is what makes the panels comparable. Write free = TRUE inside a position, as in y(population, free = TRUE), and that axis is fitted to each panel’s own data instead. Use both operators together and the panels are laid out in rows and columns. See Faceting for the full rules.
With another plot on the right they make an arrangement: the two plots side by side or one above the other, each keeping its own coordinate space:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Two plots, side by side
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The parentheses keep each plot whole until | joins the two. Each language groups its operators in a fixed order, called precedence. Arithmetic does the same: it groups * before + and reads 2 + 3 * 4 as 2 + (3 * 4). In R and Python, | groups after +, so gog would draw this sentence without the parentheses. / groups before +, so without the parentheses gog would refuse the same two plots joined by /. In Julia, gog refuses both. So whenever this book composes plots, each plot goes inside its own parentheses. Parentheses in an arrangement shows what each language’s order does to an arrangement.
Composed plots share nothing by default. The arrangement decides which axis is aligned: x when one plot is above the other, y when they are side by side. If both plots name the same column on that axis and read it the same way, with the same scale and limits, they share it: one scale, one range of values, drawn once. Because of that rule, a marginal plot (a scatter with a small distribution drawn along each edge) needs no chart type of its own: it is several plots joined by | and /. See Composition.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.10 Scales: how a number becomes a position
text:
2.10 Scales: how a number becomes a position
Incomes in gapminder_2007 run from under 300 dollars to nearly 50,000. Most countries therefore crowd the left end of a linear axis, and a log scale spreads them out. A scale is written on the binding, the channel with its column in it (A first plot says why the same act is also called mapping). It is not a word of its own, because a scale belongs to one channel and means nothing without it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”
x_label() writes your own words under the axis in place of the column name. It is a label, not a scale, and Labels, below, covers all six.



Scale
What it does




linear
Equal steps for equal differences. The default


log
Equal steps for equal ratios, on x, y, z, color, size and opacity, with any base above 1


time
Positions dates and times, chosen from the column type: dates and date-times


category
One slot per distinct value, chosen from the column type: columns of text, and columns with a declared order


order
The order of the categories along an axis. You can also declare the order on the column: a factor in R, a pandas Categorical in Python, a CategoricalArray in Julia, ordered() in JavaScript



A scale is not a transform: it produces no new values, only different positions for the ones you have. Scales explains what happens when you use both, such as a log scale on bar * bin or bar * sum.
The same binding takes two more arguments, limits and tick_count. limits gives the range of values a channel covers, when you want a range other than the one in the data. tick_count says how many ticks an axis should have. Both describe the scale, so both are written where the scale is written. Three more say how the numbers on an axis or a legend are written: percent, short and decimals. Scales has all of them.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.11 Spaces: the surface a plot is drawn on
text:
2.11 Spaces: the surface a plot is drawn on
A space decides what a position means. Every plot so far has been drawn on the plane. That space is flat, and you never have to write it.







Space
Where the marks are drawn




flat
The plane: x across, y up. The default


space
The cube: x, y and z, projected onto the page, or the nodes a layout places in three directions


polar
The plane bent into a circle: one position becomes an angle, the other a radius


nest
Rectangles inside rectangles, each sized by its share of the one holding it


map
The earth flattened: longitude across, latitude up


globe
The earth as a sphere, seen from one side: marks are drawn only on the half that faces you


network
The space of a network: positions come from layout and their numbers mean nothing, so it draws no axes. Write space() in its place and the layout is computed in the cube instead



A plot is drawn in one space, and every layer of it uses that space. See Space, Polar, Nest, Map, Globe and Network.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.12 Settings: values you set rather than map
text:
2.12 Settings: values you set rather than map
Every channel above maps a column. color(continent) gives each continent a color, and a legend tells the reader which color is which.
Making every point one color maps no column. It needs no scale and no legend, so it is not a channel. That is style:







Setting
What it fixes




style(color = )
One color for the whole layer


style(opacity = )
One opacity, 0–1


style(size = )
Point radius, line stroke width, or a label’s font size


style(shape = )
One glyph for every point


style(pattern = )
The texture of a mark’s paint: a stroke pattern (solid/dashed/dotted/dotdash/longdash) or a fill texture (solid/hatch/crosshatch/stripes/grid/dots). Every mark but point, text and surface


palette( )
Which colors the color channel uses


theme( )
The page around the plot: grid, background, fonts, size





RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# map: color carries the continent, and a legend decodes it
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
Now the same points with one color and one opacity set for all of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# set: one color, no column mapped, no legend drawn
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.5)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.5))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.5)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "tomato", opacity: 0.5 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored tomato, with opacity 0.5.”
See Setting vs mapping for the full rules.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.13 Labels: the words on the plot
text:
2.13 Labels: the words on the plot
An axis carries the name of the column bound to it. A label replaces that name when the column name is not what a reader should see.



Label
What it names




title
The plot


subtitle
What the plot shows, in a smaller line under the title


caption
Where the numbers came from, in a line at the bottom


x_label y_label z_label
One axis each



title(), subtitle() and caption() add words of their own rather than replacing a column’s name. Without them, a plot cannot say what it is about or where its numbers came from. The title is a bold line above the plot. The subtitle is a smaller, lighter line under it, for what the plot shows, such as which countries and which year. The caption is in the same small size as the tick labels, at the bottom of the picture, lined up with the left side of the panel. It is for the source of the numbers:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + title("People in richer countries live longer") +
  subtitle("Life expectancy against GDP per person, 142 countries, 2007") +
  caption("Source: Gapminder Foundation")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + title("People in richer countries live longer") +
  subtitle("Life expectancy against GDP per person, 142 countries, 2007") +
  caption("Source: Gapminder Foundation"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + title("People in richer countries live longer") +
  subtitle("Life expectancy against GDP per person, 142 countries, 2007") +
  caption("Source: Gapminder Foundation")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent),
  title("People in richer countries live longer"),
  subtitle("Life expectancy against GDP per person, 142 countries, 2007"),
  caption("Source: Gapminder Foundation"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  People in richer countries live longer Life expectancy against GDP per person, 142 countries, 2007 Source: Gapminder Foundation Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
Each of the three makes the panel shorter by the height of its line. At the default size of 800 by 600 pixels, the three together take about 60 pixels.

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.14 Facets: one panel per category
When one plot shows too many groups to compare, a facet gives each group a panel of its own.







Facet
What it cuts




facet
Splits one plot into panels, one per category of the column it names



A facet is written on the right of | or /, which is why you have already seen it drawn in the operator section: … | facet(continent). See Faceting.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.15 Selections: choosing rows in a drawn plot
text:
2.15 Selections: choosing rows in a drawn plot
A plot that is already on the screen can still answer a question, if you can select part of it.



Selection
What it does




brush
Dims the rows you did not pick, and removes none of them



A selection is the only kind that acts on a plot after it is drawn. Dragging changes what you see. It never changes the sentence, so running the sentence again gives you the selection it names, not the one you dragged. See Selection.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.16 Names the host language already uses
text:
2.16 Names the host language already uses
Every word in the kernel is an ordinary English word, and many ordinary words already name something else. mean names a statistic in every language that has one. data, order, range, text and box all name something in R before gog is loaded. That is a consequence of choosing plain names rather than a sign that something has gone wrong, and in ordinary code almost nothing changes.
When a word is both gog’s and the language’s own, the language decides which one your call reaches. gog does not change that, and each language decides differently, so the answer is different in each one:








Language
What the language does
To reach the other one




R
Twenty kernel words collide with R names. Eight are objects, and a call skips them; twelve are functions, and those mask R’s own
base::order(x), stats::density(x)


Python
A star-import rebinds six builtins, because Python has no rule that protects them
from builtins import sum


Julia
Two modules exporting one name is an error, never a silent choice
Base.sum([1, 2, 3])


JavaScript
Nothing happens, because no name reaches your scope unless you import it
nothing to do



R’s case is the one to understand. Twenty kernel words collide with R names, but only five of them can give you a wrong result with no message: data, box, title, order and palette. The other fifteen are safe, for two different reasons.
Eight of the twenty are plain objects, not functions. Most marks take no argument, and neither does a statistic like mean or max. When R evaluates a call, it looks for a function of that name and skips any name whose value is not a function. So base R still answers mean(c(1, 2, 3)), and sapply(df, mean) works for the same reason. When gog loads, R prints a message listing the names gog masks. It lists only the twelve functions, because an ordinary call can reach only a function.
The other twelve take arguments, so they are functions, and they do mask R’s own. Once gog loads, range(0.25, 0.75) is gog’s range transform, the band between two quantiles; to reach base R’s, write base::range(). Suppose you forget and write range(heights) to get the smallest and largest values of a vector. The call reaches gog’s range(), which takes two numbers between 0 and 1, not a vector, so it refuses the call and names the base R function you meant, base::range(). Seven of the twelve functions catch a mistake this way. The other five cannot. data(mtcars), meant to load R’s example dataset, is also correct gog that names a plot’s table, so gog answers it and cannot warn you. box(), title("..."), order(key) and palette("Set1") are the same. A refusal needs a mistake the engine can detect, and none of these calls contains one.
There is no way to remove the collision without losing something. Prefixing the vocabulary, gog_mean and gog_range, would remove the reason for the vocabulary: a reader who has to learn a prefix learns every word twice, and none of the words is English any more. Renaming order to sort_by would take away a word every reader already knows. So the words stay, and the few places that need a qualified name write one.
Each binding chapter carries three things for its language: the full list of collisions, that language’s rule from the table above as code you can run, and the few calls the rule does not cover. In R there are five such calls, and they fail for two reasons. Three hand a word to one function that passes it to a second, the way aggregate(v ~ g, df, mean) passes mean on. Two use the word as a value rather than calling it, as do.call(sum, list(x)) does. See R, Python, Julia and JavaScript.

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.17 In short
The kernel has eleven kinds of word: five build a plot, and six refine or arrange one. The minimum sentence is a table, a mark, and that mark’s required positions. A sentence gog cannot draw is refused, and the refusal says what to write instead. Most of +’s order is free, with two exceptions: the first mark is drawn at the bottom, and a channel applies to every layer only when it comes before every mark (Encoding scope).

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.18 What comes next
The kernel is the whole vocabulary, but knowing the words is not yet using them easily. Reading practice gives you ten plots written in these words, and Writing practice leaves the writing to you.

Can you say what a plot will look like from its sentence alone? The last chapter gave you the vocabulary, and this one practices reading with it. Ten plots follow, ending in a cube. For each one, read the sentence aloud before looking at the picture, then check the picture against what you said. The sentence read aloud is given under each plot. Try to say it yourself first.

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold.” A bar measures an amount from zero, so the amount needs a continuous axis and the category takes the other one. The bindings put countries on x and gold on y. There is no transform here. bar draws the numbers exactly as the table gives them.

title: 3  Reading practice
text:
3.2 The same bars, horizontal
A medal table is usually printed as a list, with the leader at the top. The same five counts can be read that way. medals already lists the countries by gold, and the first row is drawn at the top, so the leader comes first.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(gold) + y(country)


data(medals) + bar + x(col.gold) + y(col.country)

“Given the medals: bars, x is gold, y is country.” Put the category on the vertical axis and the amount on the horizontal one, and the bars become horizontal. There is no “horizontal bar” atom, and no argument that turns the bars. The sentence already says which axis holds the category, so the orientation follows from the bindings.

The first two plots drew five counts that were already in the table. Often a table holds only measurements, and no counts.
Do petal lengths gather around one typical value, or do they separate into groups? One column, petal length, answers that, and it comes from a new table. iris_flowers holds one row per flower: three measurements (sepal length, sepal width and petal length), and the species the flower belongs to.

title: 3  Reading practice
section: 3.5 One strip of dots per continent
text:
3.5 One strip of dots per continent
The density curve in plot four reduced 142 countries to one shape. Do the continents differ in life expectancy, and how widely do the countries inside each one vary? Both answers are visible when every country is shown.

text:
3.8 Three species on one axis
Plot three showed two peaks in petal length, and the table has three species. How do three species make two peaks?

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species.” The left peak is setosa alone. The right peak is versicolor and virginica together, because their petal lengths overlap. All three histograms use the same bin edges, and each species has bars only in the bins its own values fall into. title: 3  Reading practice
text:
3.9 One panel per continent
Richer countries live longer across the world as a whole, as the first chapter showed. Is that also true inside each continent?


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), across(col.continent))






                                                              1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                       1K 10K                                                                               1K 10K                                                    1K 10K                             1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.” Inside every continent except Oceania, which has only two countries here, life expectancy also rises with income. The rise is clearest in Europe and Asia and least clear in Africa, where the points are most scattered. The | operator splits the plot into panels side by side, one panel per category. All the panels share one pair of scales, so they can be compared; free = TRUE on a position fits that axis to each panel instead (Faceting). As in the first chapter, scale = "log" spreads out the poorer countries, which would otherwise be pressed together at the left edge.

“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal length, color by species.” Drawing in three dimensions needs no other package and no other mark. z is one more position channel, and the same sentence without z(petal_length) would draw a flat scatter. In the web edition the cube turns with a drag: drag right and the side facing you moves right, drag down and it tips down to show you the top. Every angle hides some points and shows others, so turn the cube more than once.

title: 3  Reading practice
text:
3.11 What you just did
Those ten plots used thirteen words: data, bar, point, line, bin, density, mean, x, y, z, color, facet, and the scale log. Every plot reads in the same order: data, mark, positions, then any refinements. A transform joined the mark and a facet came last, exactly where the first chapter put them. The same color split the bars and lines, and colored the points. The same * attached bin, mean and density, which derived counts, means and densities. Each word meant the same thing in every plot that used it.

title: 3  Reading practice
text:
3.12 What comes next
Every sentence here was already written, so nothing asked you to choose a mark. Writing practice reverses that: it starts from a question and asks you to write the sentence.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.1 Which continents live longest?
How does a question about your data turn into a sentence? Reading was recognition; writing is recall. Psychologists use those two words for two kinds of remembering. Recognition starts from something in front of you, and asks only whether you have seen it before. That is what Reading practice did: it gave you finished sentences and asked what they say. Recall starts from nothing in front of you: you produce the answer yourself. It is the harder of the two, and it is what writing a sentence asks of you.
From here on, this chapter asks you to recall. Three worked examples come first. The first two show the method you will use: start with the minimum sentence, look, refine. The third asks you to write the whole sentence at once. Five questions follow, each answered by a sentence you met in Reading practice. For each, write your sentence before you look at the printed one, then check it. Last comes the other half of writing: what happens when a sentence is wrong, and what a refusal tells you to do next.
This is the first of the three worked examples. Before reading on, try to write the sentence that answers the question above: which mark, which transform, which positions? Then build it one step at a time. Start with the minimum sentence, the smallest one that shows the data:

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life.” The plot shows how each continent’s countries spread, but the question asked for a comparison of typical values, and this one shows every country. Swap point for bar, and attach the transform mean with *; everything else stays:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.” Now there is one bar per continent, as tall as the mean life expectancy of its countries.
Bars are easiest to compare when they are sorted, with the largest first. A categorical column can carry a fixed order, declared when the table is built (Declaring the order of categories). The order you want here depends on the means the plot has just computed, so the table cannot carry it. The sentence has to ask for it: order(life) sorts the axis by the bars’ values for life, here the means, and desc = TRUE puts the largest first:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  order(col.life, desc = True))

  order(:life, desc = true)

4.3 Where is the world’s wealth, and its health?
The first two questions were each about one measurement. This one is about two, income and life expectancy, and they fill both positions. Someone reading the plot also wants to know how many people live in each country. A first plot built this sentence, without size, step by step. data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + size(col.population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + size(:population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), size(col.population),
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007"))

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.5 When gog says no
Every sentence so far was correct. The other half of writing is what happens when one is not.
You will write wrong sentences. Everyone does. gog promises that a wrong sentence is refused with a message that says how to fix it, never drawn with the wrong part quietly removed. Here are five refusals that new users see most often.
Forgetting to bind the table. A sentence starts with data(), which names the table:

gapminder_2007 + point + x(gdp) + y(life)

Error:
! gog: a plot starts with `data()`, which names the table — columns are bare names and the nearest named table wins, so the name matters. Write `data(gapminder_2007) + point + ...`.


The message above is R’s. Python, Julia and JavaScript give the same advice, each writing a column the way that language does.
Quoting a column name, a habit from other packages. The refusal names the fix:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x("gdp"), y("life"))




Error:
! gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*: `x(gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.


That message is R’s too. Python and JavaScript name the fix x(col.gdp), and Julia names it x(:gdp).
Mapping a channel to a column of the wrong type. size needs a continuous column, because it shows an amount, and continent is a categorical column, so the message suggests color or shape instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + size(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  size(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `size(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `size` on `point` needs a continuous (numeric) column. Use `color` or `shape` to distinguish categories.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Forgetting the column a summary reads. The refusal names the missing y, because mean must be told which column to average:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bar * mean` needs `y()`, because `mean` averages the column named there, and none is set. Add `y(<column>)` with that column. To count the rows in each slot instead, write `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Binning a category. bin divides a continuous axis into intervals, and the refusal names count, the transform that tallies rows per category:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bin` cuts a continuous axis into intervals, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows per category, `count` is the transform that does it: `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Each message names the rule and the fix. No wrong plot was drawn, and no binding was dropped to complete one. Read any refusal outside this list the same way.
The last three refusals end with a second option: set GOG_STRICT=0 and draw the plot anyway. The first two are caught by the language’s package before the engine sees the sentence, so there is nothing to draw. GOG_STRICT is an environment variable, and Drawing it anyway shows which refusals GOG_STRICT affects, with the one line that sets it in each language. For now, make the fix the message asks for. At this stage, reading a refusal and making its fix is the practice.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.6 The morning checkpoint
That is the whole method: start with the minimum sentence, look, refine, and read the refusal when one comes. If you have read this part from the start, check yourself against the three skills A morning promised:

Read any gog sentence aloud before looking at its plot.
Given a question (distribution? comparison? relationship? change over time?), write a sentence that answers it.
Predict whether gog will draw a sentence or refuse it, and roughly what the refusal will say.

If you can do most of that, you have done what Part I set out to teach. You can read the next part in order, or go directly to the cookbook and answer your own questions, following a link back whenever a recipe uses a word you want explained.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.7 What comes next
Part I taught how a sentence is built. It did not show everything a single word can do; Part II gives each kind of word chapters of its own. Its first chapter, Data, covers the table every sentence starts from: the shape gog needs, and how gog reads each column’s type.

title: The letters
text:
After stating its system in brief, the 1446 book explained the letters one class at a time: the initial consonants, the vowels, the final consonants. Each class was explained by the same method.
Part I stated gog’s whole system in brief. This part then explains gog’s letters one class at a time, as the 1446 book did. The marks are the initial consonants: the visible forms, such as a dot, a bar or a line. A mark draws nothing until a position places it. The positions are the vowels: x, y and z. Only edge takes none of them: a layout transform computes its positions instead. Each position has a scale, which decides where a number, a category or a date falls on its axis. The refining channels are the final consonants: color, size, shape, pattern, opacity. Each is optional, and when it is mapped to a column, it gets a legend that shows which value each color, size, shape, pattern or opacity stands for.
Three channels belong to none of these classes: group, label and play. On a line, group makes the same split as color: one line per category. But every line is drawn alike, so group gets no legend. It separates the lines, but nothing on the plot shows how. label gives each text mark the words it draws, rather than refining the mark. play splits the rows into frames and plays them in order, the way a facet splits them into panels. Its chapter is in Part III, The sentences.
The Data chapter opens this part with the table every sentence starts from, because nothing can be drawn until a table is named. The book’s data follows, saying where this book’s own tables come from and how to load one in any of the four languages. Then come the letters themselves. Choosing a mark opens them, and then each mark has a chapter of its own, fourteen in a row from point to edge. After the marks, the Scales chapter covers the scales of the positions x, y and z, and the Channels and legends chapter covers the final consonants and their legends. The Setting vs mapping chapter shows the difference between a column you map and a constant you set. The Transforms chapter closes the part: a transform derives new values from your columns, such as counts, means or a smooth curve. Transforms take more practice than any other kind of word. They are also what let you ask questions of a table instead of only drawing it. The better you know them, the better you can use gog, so read that chapter without hurrying.
Every mark chapter follows the same template, just as the 1446 book explained each letter class by the same method. It says what the mark draws, what it requires and what refines it. It then closes with four sections that have the same names in every chapter: Transforms it takes, which draws every transform the mark takes, What you can set, What it refuses and What comes next. A short summary, In short, may come between the last two. That sameness is deliberate: it is the No Exceptions law applied to this book’s structure. Learning the second mark is faster than learning the first. By the fifth you know which section answers which question, and you can read only the one you need.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.1 Binding a table
Where does a plot get its data? Every sentence starts by naming a table, and every column named after it is looked up in that table. This chapter covers the two ways to name one, data() and query(), the shape the table must have, and the order of categories that a column can carry with it.
Most of the time the table is already in memory. You read it from a file, such as a CSV file, with your language’s usual tools (readr in R or pandas in Python, for example), and data() names it. Column names after that are bare words: no quotes, no table prefix, no indexing.
The first example uses gapminder_2007, one of the book’s tables. It holds 142 countries in 2007, one row per country, with each country’s continent, GDP per person (gdp), life expectancy (life) and population (population):

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
gog looks up gdp and life inside the gapminder_2007 table automatically. This is the Bind-Once Law: name the table once, then use columns freely.
gapminder_2007 here is an ordinary table in memory, whatever your language calls one: a data frame in R, a dict of columns or a pandas DataFrame in Python. In Julia it is a named tuple of columns or a DataFrame, and in JavaScript an object of columns or an array of rows. You do not register the table or convert it to a special type first. Part VI, The host language, shows how each language builds one. The R chapter also lists the twenty names that gog and base R both use. For the eleven that are functions, it shows how to call base R’s version, such as base::order().
When you write data(gapminder_2007), gog receives the table’s values and also keeps its name, gapminder_2007. The name matters as soon as a plot has more than one table. Each layer looks up its bare column names in one of those tables, and gog finds that table by its name. Leave data() out and the table arrives with no name, so gog refuses and tells you what to write:
gapminder_2007 + point + x(gdp) + y(life)

Error:
! gog: a plot starts with `data()`, which names the table — columns are bare names and the nearest named table wins, so the name matters. Write `data(gapminder_2007) + point + ...`.
The message above is R’s. gog gives the same advice for a sentence with no data at all, point + x(gdp) with nothing before it. Each language’s package writes this advice with its own way of naming a column.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.2 The table has to be tidy
text:
5.2 The table has to be tidy
Every table in this book has the same shape. Each row is one observation, and each column is one variable. That shape has a name, tidy data (Wickham, 2014), and gog assumes it in every sentence you write.
The reason is the rule that defines a channel in Grammar: a channel maps a column to a visual property, so anything you want to map has to be a column. Suppose you record sales for two regions, and you give each region a column of its own:

                   north = c(120, 135, 128, 152, 168),
                   south = c( 90, 101, 140, 133, 155))


wide = {
    "year": [2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023],
    "north": [120, 135, 128, 152, 168],
    "south": [90, 101, 140, 133, 155],
}


wide = (
    year = 2019:2023,
    north = [120, 135, 128, 152, 168],
    south = [90, 101, 140, 133, 155],
)


const wide = {
  year: [2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023],
  north: [120, 135, 128, 152, 168],
  south: [90, 101, 140, 133, 155],
};

The message names two problems: there is no column called sales, and no column called region. It asks you to check the spelling, but the spelling is not the problem. Your two regions are column names, not values in a column. Your sales numbers are in two columns instead of one. The sentence asks for columns the table does not have, so gog draws nothing.
The same numbers, one row per observation, look like this:

                   region = rep(c("north", "south"), each = 5),

“Given the long table: lines, x is year, y is sales, color by region.”
gog never reshapes a table, and no transform turns columns into rows. You do that work before you write the sentence, in the language you are already using. R has tidyr::pivot_longer(). Python has pandas.melt(). Julia has DataFrames.stack(). JavaScript has no standard table library, so you write a short loop instead.
On the shape of the table, gog asks no more than ggplot2 does. ggplot2 does not reshape tables either, and it refuses the wide table above just as gog does. gog asks more in one place: ggplot2 lets you calculate a value while you map it, so aes(x = log(gdp)) works there. gog does not allow that, because a channel takes a column name and nothing else. Some of those calculations are already part of the grammar. A log axis is one of them, written x(gdp, scale = "log"). For anything else, add the column to your table first. So a tidy table is not enough on its own. Every column your sentence names has to be in the table already.
This book does not teach you how to tidy data, and it should not, because there is a better book for it. Read R for Data Science by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Garrett Grolemund (Wickham et al., 2023), which is free online at https://r4ds.hadley.nz/. Its chapter on data tidying is the one that matters here. If the shape of your data is not settled yet, read that chapter before you read this one.

168







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Both layers read from "actuals"
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  point


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  point)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + point


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, point)






                                             2019 2020 2021 2022 2023   120 130 140 150 160 170  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line and also points.”
A forecast continues a history of past values, and the two usually arrive as separate tables. You want both on one pair of axes. forecast holds the three years still to come:



forecast: all 3 rows


year
sales




2024
180


2025
195


2026
210





A data() that appears between two marks overrides the table for the layer that follows it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# line uses "actuals"; point uses "forecast"
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + data(forecast) + point


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, data(forecast),
  point)






                                       2020 2022 2024 2026   120 140 160 180 200  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line; then given the forecast: points.”
The rule: the first data() is the plot’s table, and each later data() applies to the mark written directly after it. A mark with no data() of its own reads the plot’s table. The refusal at the start of this chapter holds for the second table too: write + data(forecast), not + forecast.
Two things follow from the rule for a later data(). gog tells you about the first, but not about the second.
A data() at the end of a sentence has no mark after it, so its table would never be drawn. gog refuses the sentence rather than leave that table out of the plot without telling you:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  point +
  data(forecast)


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  point +
  data(forecast))


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + point + data(forecast)


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, point,
  data(forecast))




Error:
! gog: `data(forecast)` ends the sentence, so no mark comes after it to read its table. A later `data()` gives its table to the mark written directly after it: write that mark next, as in `+ data(forecast) + point`, or remove `data(forecast)`.


The message names the table and gives two ways to fix the sentence: write a mark after the data(), or remove the data().
Second, a later data() applies only to the one mark written directly after it. The mark after that one reads the plot’s table again:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# line reads actuals. point reads forecast. area reads actuals again.
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point +
  area


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point +
  area)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + data(forecast) + point +
  area


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, data(forecast),
  point, area)






                                      2020 2022 2024 2026   0 100 200  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line; then given the forecast: points; then given the actuals again: an area.”
The two tables cover different years, so you can see which table each mark draws from. actuals runs from 2019 to 2023, and forecast from 2024 to 2026. The area and the line are both on the left. The points are alone on the right. To draw two marks from the second table, write data() before each of them.
The one-mark rule fits what a second table is usually for. The axes come from the first table, and a later table adds an annotation: a threshold, a band, a note, a forecast. An annotation is one mark, so a data() that reaches one mark is enough. In this book, a table added after the first one is usually an annotation of this kind. The fan chart also draws one mark from its second table, but its tables come in the opposite order from the plot above. Its forecast takes three marks, so naming the forecast first means writing its data() once instead of three times. The observed values, one line, come second.
The sentence above is correct, and it still reads badly. area is written on the line of code just below data(forecast), so it looks like part of the forecast. Only the rule tells you that area draws from actuals. The same sentence is easier to read when each mark is written next to the table it draws from. Drawn again, it is the same picture:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line + area +
  data(forecast) + point


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line + area +
  data(forecast) + point)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + area + data(forecast) +
  point


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, area, data(forecast),
  point)






                                      2020 2022 2024 2026   0 100 200  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line and also an area; then given the forecast: points.”
This is style, not grammar. Both spellings are legal, and both draw the same plot. The order of area and point has changed, and here that changes nothing. The two tables share no year, so neither mark is drawn over the other. gog will never refuse either spelling, because legal is not the same as clear (Law 8). Two sentences can mean the same thing and still be very different to read. Which one you write is your choice.
So group the marks by the table they read. Keep each extra data() on the same line as the mark it applies to, and keep the marks that read the plot’s table together. Every line is then one table and the marks that read it, and no mark is written under a table it does not read. The rest of this book follows that layout.
The first data() is written differently. It applies to every mark below it, so it takes a line of its own. A later data() applies to one mark only, so it shares that mark’s line of code. Alone on a line, it would seem to apply to every mark below it. That is why, in the code above, data(actuals) has a line of its own and data(forecast) shares its line with point.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.4 When the second table names its columns differently
text:
5.4 When the second table names its columns differently
The plot above was the easy case: actuals and forecast both call their columns year and sales, so one pair of positions written at the front served both layers.
Plots often carry a note at a chosen point, and the note comes from a small table of its own. That table’s column names rarely match the first table’s. The milestones table marks two points on the income axis:



milestones: all 2 rows


at
value
note




10000
72
less steep from here


40000
80
almost flat here





Its columns are at, value and note. None of those names appear in gapminder_2007, shown in Binding a table, whose columns are gdp and life. A layer may name its own columns, and the axis does not change:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(milestones) + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note) +
  style(size = 20, color = "red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(milestones) + text + x(col.at) + y(col.value) + label(col.note) +
  style(size = 20, color = "red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(milestones) +
  text + x(:at) + y(:value) + label(:note) +
  style(size = 20, color = "red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(milestones), text, x(col.at), y(col.value), label(col.note),
  style({ size: 20, color: "red" }))






                                                                                                                                                                  less steep from here almost flat here                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given the milestones: text, x is at, y is value, label by note.”
There is still one x axis and one y axis, one scale each, one set of ticks. Only the names differ, because the two tables were written by different people for different reasons.
The last word, style(), sets how the notes look: their size and their color. A value written in style() is fixed, the same for every row, and no column decides it. Setting vs mapping explains the difference between setting a value this way and mapping a column.
What the two tables share is the measurement: an axis stands for one measurement. at holds income and value holds years of life, the same two quantities gdp and life hold. A table whose numbers mean something else does not belong on these axes, whatever its columns are called. If you put sales figures on an income axis, gog draws the plot without an error, but nothing it shows is true. Matching names are not the test. Matching meanings are.
The same test says when a second table does not belong in the plot at all. A layer is drawn on the axes that come from the first table, so its values must measure what those axes measure. Values that measure something else need their own axes, and a second pair of axes means a second plot. Put that plot beside the first one instead. Composition shows how, with | and /.
A layer that names no position of its own reads the axis that is already there. That is why the earlier plot worked with the positions written once at the front.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.5 A table in a database
data() is the first of the two ways to name a table. This section shows the second, for a table kept in a database.
Not every table fits on one computer. Most of the data used at work is kept in a database. A warehouse, a database built to keep all of a company’s records, can hold billions of rows. gog draws from those tables with one word, query(), written where data() would be. It sends your SQL and receives the rows the database returns.
Nothing else in the sentence changes:
data(orders)                          + bar + x(status)
query(connection, "SELECT ...")       + bar + x(status)
The SQL is written only inside query(), as a string; nothing after it is SQL. After it, the columns are still bare names. The marks, channels, transforms and operators are the ones you have already learned. You are not writing a second language for databases. You are naming the rows a different way.
Here is a real database. The code below builds a small one in memory, so it needs no server and no password:

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "countries", gapminder_2007)

Now the sentence. The connection is the only new part:

query(con, "SELECT gdp, life, continent FROM countries WHERE gdp > 5000") +
  point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)



                                                                                                             10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Asia 





“Given the query: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
The plot is an ordinary scatterplot. The database chose which rows to send, and gog drew them from a table of rows, as it does for every other sentence in this book.
A query and a loaded table produce the same picture, byte for byte, when they hold the same rows. The tests of all four packages check exactly that. So query() is never a different way of drawing; it is a different way of finding the rows to draw.

5.5.1 Three things to know
You open the connection yourself. gog never opens one, and it never stores a password. You connect with whatever your language already uses, and hand the open connection to query(). That also means gog adds no database driver to your install. Someone who never writes SQL never installs one.
The query runs when the plot is drawn, not when the sentence is written. Writing query(con, "...") asks the database nothing. The sentence is a specification, exactly like every other sentence in this book, and the engine draws a plot from it later. gog sends your SQL exactly as you wrote it.
Every language reaches a different set of databases. The word is the same in all four. What differs is the connection you hand it, because each language has its own database convention. Your language’s chapter says which: R, Python, Julia, JavaScript.


5.5.2 How much data comes back
query() brings every row the query returns to the computer running gog. The database does the selecting. Your machine does the drawing. Know that before you run this against a large table.
For most tables it does not matter. A few thousand rows arrive quickly, so write the simple query and stop there. Selecting the columns you need and letting gog do the rest is the normal case, and the example above is exactly that.
As a rough guide, the number of rows starts to matter at about a hundred thousand. Above that, moving the rows costs more time than drawing them. A warehouse table can hold billions, and SELECT * FROM that_table would try to bring all of them to you.
The way to avoid it is already familiar to anyone who works with a warehouse: summarize in SQL, then draw the summary. This works because a plot is nearly always a summary anyway. A bar chart of a billion orders shows only a few bars, and a database can produce those bars far more cheaply than your laptop can.

query(con, "SELECT continent, COUNT(*) AS countries
            FROM countries GROUP BY continent") +
  bar + x(continent) + y(countries)



                               Africa Americas Asia Europe Oceania   0 20 40  Countries Continent





“Given the query: bars, x is continent, y is countries.”
The database did the counting and sent back five rows. Without the count, SELECT continent FROM countries would have sent all 142. The bars are the same ones bar * count would draw from the loaded table.


5.5.3 Two directions, and which one suits you
If you write the summary in SQL, you may ask whether the whole plot could be written in SQL too. There is another way to give SQL users a grammar of graphics. Posit’s ggsql (Posit Software, PBC, 2026) adds visual clauses to SQL itself: you write VISUALIZE, DRAW and SCALE inside the query, and the database returns a picture.
It has two strengths. Its clauses read like SQL, so someone who writes SQL all day stays in the language they already think in, and no other language, such as R or Python, is needed at all. And it runs the whole pipeline in the database, one query per layer, so a bar chart of ten billion rows fetches only the bar heights. On that second point ggsql does something gog does not. gog brings the rows to you, so on a large table you write the summary in SQL yourself, as the count above did.
If you write only SQL, ggsql is probably the better choice. gog would first ask you to learn R, Python, Julia or JavaScript, which is a real cost for someone who uses none of them.
gog does the opposite. ggsql puts the grammar inside the database; gog keeps the grammar outside it and brings the rows to the grammar. So one sentence draws a table in memory, a table in Postgres or a table in a data warehouse, in any of the four languages, and the sentence is the same in every case.
Which of the two to use depends on how you work:








If you work
Choose
Why




Only in SQL
ggsql
No other language to install, and the syntax is the SQL you already use


Across several languages
gog
One grammar covers all four languages, and tables in a database too

title: 5  Data
text:
5.6 Declaring the order of categories
Wherever the table comes from, some of its categories have an order that a column of plain text does not record. Low, Medium and High have an order every reader knows. A plot that draws them in any other order makes the reader sort them. A column of plain text has no order of its own, so gog draws its categories in the order the rows happen to arrive:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


severity <- data.frame(
  level = c("High", "Low", "Medium"),
  count = c(30.0, 10.0, 20.0)
)

data(severity) + bar + x(level) + y(count) +
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in")


severity = {
  "level": ["High", "Low", "Medium"],
  "count": [30.0, 10.0, 20.0],
}
(data(severity) + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count) +
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in"))


severity = (
  level = ["High", "Low", "Medium"],
  count = [30, 10, 20],
)
data(severity) + bar + x(:level) + y(:count) +
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in")


const severity = {
  level: ["High", "Low", "Medium"],
  count: [30, 10, 20],
};
plot(data(severity), bar, x(col.level), y(col.count),
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in"))






                             High Low Medium   0 10 20 30  Text column: the order the rows came in Count Level





“Given the severity table: bars, x is level, y is count.”
That order is almost never the one you mean. Declare the order you mean, where you build the table, with the type your language or its table package already has for categories. In R that type is a factor. In Python it is a pandas Categorical or a polars Enum, and in Julia a CategoricalArray. JavaScript has no such type, so gog supplies one function for it, ordered(). Each of these pairs the column’s values with the order its categories go in, and everything after it reads the same in all four languages:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


severity <- data.frame(
  level = factor(c("High", "Low", "Medium"), levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
  count = c(30.0, 10.0, 20.0)
)

data(severity) + bar + x(level) + y(count) +
  title("Declared: the order you asked for")


import pandas as pd

severity = {
  "level": pd.Categorical(["High", "Low", "Medium"], categories=["Low", "Medium", "High"]),
  "count": [30.0, 10.0, 20.0],
}
(data(severity) + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count) +
  title("Declared: the order you asked for"))


using CategoricalArrays
severity = (
  level = CategoricalArray(["High", "Low", "Medium"]; levels = ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),
  count = [30, 10, 20],
)
data(severity) + bar + x(:level) + y(:count) +
  title("Declared: the order you asked for")


const severity = {
  level: ordered(["High", "Low", "Medium"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),
  count: [30, 10, 20],
};
plot(data(severity), bar, x(col.level), y(col.count),
  title("Declared: the order you asked for"))






                             Low Medium High   0 10 20 30  Declared: the order you asked for Count Level





“Given the severity table: bars, x is level, y is count.”
The order goes with the column, so every part of the plot agrees: the axis, the color assignment, and the legend all read in the same order. The next plot is there only to show the legend. Its x and y are both count, so the points form a diagonal line.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(severity) + point + x(count) + y(count) + color(level) +
  title("The legend follows the same order")


(data(severity) + point + x(col.count) + y(col.count) + color(col.level) +
  title("The legend follows the same order"))


data(severity) + point + x(:count) + y(:count) + color(:level) +
  title("The legend follows the same order")


plot(data(severity), point, x(col.count), y(col.count), color(col.level),
  title("The legend follows the same order"))






                                      10 15 20 25 30   10 15 20 25 30  The legend follows the same order Count Count  Level    Low  Medium  High 





“Given the severity table: points, x is count, y is count, color by level.”
The declared order stays even when gog does the counting for you. The first of the eight tickets below is High, but the axis of bar * count still shows Low, Medium, High. count makes one row per level, and the levels belong to the column, so the axis keeps their order, not the order of the rows:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


tickets <- data.frame(
  level = factor(
    c("High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"),
    levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
  )
)

data(tickets) + bar * count + x(level) +
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis")


import pandas as pd

tickets = {"level": pd.Categorical(["High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"], categories=["Low", "Medium", "High"])}
(data(tickets) + bar * count + x(col.level) +
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis"))


using CategoricalArrays
tickets = (level = CategoricalArray(["High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"]; levels = ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),)
data(tickets) + bar * count + x(:level) +
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis")


const tickets = { level: ordered(["High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]) };
plot(data(tickets), layer(bar, count), x(col.level),
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis"))






                              Low Medium High   0 1 2 3 4  bar * count: the levels still order the axis Count Level





“Given the tickets: bars derived by count, x is level.”
In R, the list of levels can mean two things. factor(x, levels = ...) says only which order the categories appear in. Adding ordered = TRUE says more: that Low really is less than High. gog draws the categories in the listed order either way. Most people list levels only to set the order on the page, and a plot needs nothing more than that.
gog reads the declaration from the column, in all four languages. It does not change the table, and it offers no function of its own for this where the language already has a type. A pandas Categorical can be a column of a DataFrame or of a plain dict of lists, and the Python tab above shows the second.
Two rules apply:

Levels set the order. The data sets which categories appear. A level with no rows in the data gets no bar and no slot on the axis. For example, if the levels are Low, Medium and High and no row is Medium, the axis shows only Low and High. A Medium slot would hold a label and no bar, and an empty slot like that is harder to read than a shorter axis. A value in the data that the levels do not mention is drawn after the listed ones, because gog drops no value itself. But only JavaScript’s ordered() passes such a value on to gog. R’s factor() and a pandas Categorical turn it into a missing value before gog sees it, so the row is dropped, and a polars Enum or a Julia CategoricalArray stops with an error. In those three languages, list every value you want drawn.
order() in the plot wins. The levels came with the table, so they apply to every plot drawn from it. order() is written in this one plot, so it applies here, and the more specific instruction wins. Name another column in order(), one that holds numbers, and the categories are ordered by its values instead. That is how you sort by value:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(severity) + bar + x(level) + y(count) + order(count, desc = TRUE) +
  title("order() overrides the levels")


(data(severity) + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count) + order(col.count, desc = True) +
  title("order() overrides the levels"))


data(severity) + bar + x(:level) + y(:count) +
  order(:count, desc = true) + title("order() overrides the levels")


plot(data(severity), bar, x(col.level), y(col.count),
  order(col.count, { desc: true }), title("order() overrides the levels"))






                             High Medium Low   0 10 20 30  order() overrides the levels Count Level





“Given the severity table: bars, x is level, y is count, ordered by count, largest first.”
order() can also name the categorical column itself, as in order(level). That asks for the column’s own order. For a column of plain text, that order is alphabetical. For a column with declared levels, it is the declared order. desc = TRUE reverses whichever applies. So a declared order cannot be turned alphabetical from inside the plot. To change it, change the levels where the table was built, in the language you are already using. The declaration belongs to the table, and so does the change.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.7 Missing values
A declared order is something you choose. Missing values are something you do not choose. Real data has gaps, and survey tables are usually missing many values. A row with no value in a column the plot maps cannot be placed, so gog drops it and says how many, rather than changing the count without telling you:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


patchy <- data.frame(
  weight = c(3.1, 4.2, NA, 5.8, 6.0, NA, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5),
  batch  = c("A", "A", "B", "B", NA, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B")
)
data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(weight) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("Two rows have no weight")


patchy = {
  "weight": [3.1, 4.2, None, 5.8, 6.0, None, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5],
  "batch": ["A", "A", "B", "B", None, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
}
(data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(col.weight) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("Two rows have no weight"))


patchy = (
  weight = [3.1, 4.2, missing, 5.8, 6, missing, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5],
  batch = ["A", "A", "B", "B", missing, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
)
data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(:weight) + x_label("Weight") +
  title("Two rows have no weight")


const patchy = {
  weight: [3.1, 4.2, null, 5.8, 6, null, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5],
  batch: ["A", "A", "B", "B", null, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
};
plot(data(patchy), layer(bar, bin), x(col.weight), x_label("Weight"),
  title("Two rows have no weight"))




gog: dropped 2 rows of `patchy` with a missing value in `weight` — a row with no value in a column the plot maps cannot be placed, and it is left out of every layer drawn from `patchy`. To keep those rows in a layer that does not map `weight`, give that layer a table of its own.




                                    3.5 4.0 4.5 5.0 5.5   0 1 2 3  Two rows have no weight Count Weight





“Given the patchy table: bars derived by bin, x is weight.”
Only the columns the plot maps decide which rows are dropped. This plot maps weight, so the message names weight, and the two rows with no weight are left out. The table also has one row with no batch. The plot never reads batch, so that row stays in the histogram. Bind batch to color, and the same row is dropped as well, because it now has no color to take. Three rows are left out in all, two with no weight and one with no batch, and the message names both columns:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(weight) + color(batch) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped")


(data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(col.weight) + color(col.batch) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped"))


data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(:weight) + color(:batch) +
  x_label("Weight") +
  title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped")


plot(data(patchy), layer(bar, bin), x(col.weight), color(col.batch),
  x_label("Weight"),
  title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped"))




gog: dropped 3 rows of `patchy` with a missing value in `batch` or `weight` — a row with no value in a column the plot maps cannot be placed, and it is left out of every layer drawn from `patchy`. To keep those rows in a layer that does not map any of them, give that layer a table of its own.




                                       3.5 4.0 4.5 5.0 5.5   0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0  One more column mapped, one more row dropped Count Weight  Batch    A  B 





“Given the patchy table: bars derived by bin, x is weight, color by batch.”
So a missing value in a column the plot never reads changes nothing. A missing value in a column the plot maps always drops the row, and the message says which column.
A mark that joins its rows into one stroke breaks where a row was dropped for a missing measurement. A line, an area and a step outline break where y is missing, and a path breaks where x or y is missing. They do not join the rows on either side of the gap, because nothing was measured between them. A row with no x has no place along a line, so the line goes on without it. monthly has no value for June:

monthly <- data.frame(
  month  = 1:12,
  visits = c(42, 45, 51, 58, 63, NA, 71, 69, 60, 52, 47, 44)
)
data(monthly) + line + point + x(month) + y(visits) +
  title("June was not recorded")

gog: dropped 1 row of `monthly` with a missing value in `visits` — a row with no value in a column the plot maps cannot be placed, and it is left out of every layer drawn from `monthly`. To keep those rows in a layer that does not map `visits`, give that layer a table of its own.




                                                2 4 6 8 10 12   50 60 70  June was not recorded Visits Month





“Given the monthly table: a line and also points, x is month, y is visits.”
The line stops at May and starts again at July, and the message still says that one row was dropped. A row that is missing some other mapped value, such as the column that gives its color, has no line to break, so it is only dropped.
An infinite value, such as the one a computer returns for the logarithm of 0, is not a missing value, so gog does not drop its row. No scale can place it either, so gog refuses the plot when a column the plot maps holds one. If you want such a row left out, write a missing value in its place, the way your language writes one: NA in R, None in Python, missing in Julia and null in JavaScript. The R chapter shows the message in Two kinds of value gog refuses.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.8 Special characters and other writing systems
text:
5.8 Special characters and other writing systems
The people who built a table chose its names, and a plot has to print them unchanged. Category names, titles and axis labels you write are drawn exactly as you wrote them. A plot is drawn as an SVG file, which is a picture written as text. Three characters have a special meaning inside one: &, < and >. gog writes them in the form the file needs, so they print as themselves, and a name like R&D needs no special handling. The plot below puts all three into its names and its title:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


special <- data.frame(
  firm  = c("R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"),
  spend = c(10, 25, 15)
)
data(special) + bar + x(firm) + y(spend) + title("Q3 <spend> & forecast")


special = {
  "firm": ["R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"],
  "spend": [10, 25, 15],
}
data(special) + bar + x(col.firm) + y(col.spend) + title("Q3 <spend> & forecast")


special = (
  firm = ["R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"],
  spend = [10, 25, 15],
)
data(special) + bar + x(:firm) + y(:spend) +
  title("Q3 <spend> & forecast")


const special = {
  firm: ["R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"],
  spend: [10, 25, 15],
};
plot(data(special), bar, x(col.firm), y(col.spend),
  title("Q3 <spend> & forecast"))






                           R&D Sales & Ops <10% unit   0 10 20  Q3 <spend> & forecast Spend Firm





“Given the special table: bars, x is firm, y is spend.”
A name in a table can also hold a control character, an invisible character such as U+0001, which is Unicode character number 1. An SVG file cannot hold one, so gog draws U+FFFD, the replacement character, in its place. The file then still opens.
Many tables are not written in Latin letters at all. gog reads their column names as written, with no renaming first. A name in another writing system can be a bare column name as well as a label. The table below is in Korean. Its name, 지역별, means by region. Its two columns are 지역 (region) and 값 (value). The three rows are the cities 서울 (Seoul), 부산 (Busan) and 대구 (Daegu). The plot title, 한국 지역별 값, means value by region, Korea.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


지역별 <- data.frame(
  지역 = c("서울", "부산", "대구"),
  값   = c(10, 25, 15)
)
data(지역별) + bar + x(지역) + y(값) + title("한국 지역별 값")


지역별 = {
  "지역": ["서울", "부산", "대구"],
  "값": [10, 25, 15],
}
data(지역별) + bar + x(col.지역) + y(col.값) + title("한국 지역별 값")


지역별 = (
  지역 = ["서울", "부산", "대구"],
  값 = [10, 25, 15],
)
data(지역별) + bar + x(:지역) + y(:값) + title("한국 지역별 값")


const 지역별 = {
  지역: ["서울", "부산", "대구"],
  값: [10, 25, 15],
};
plot(data(지역별), bar, x(col.지역), y(col.값), title("한국 지역별 값"))






                           서울 부산 대구   0 10 20  한국 지역별 값 값 지역





“Given the 지역별 table: bars, x is 지역, y is 값.”
A label’s width is measured from its characters, and a Korean or Chinese character is about twice as wide as a Latin one, so these labels get the margin they need and no more.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.9 In short
The first data() names the plot’s table; a later data() applies to the mark after it. gog refuses a sentence that names columns the table does not have; it never reshapes the table. query() is written where data() would be. A missing value drops its row only when the plot maps that column. A declared order goes with the column onto the axis and the legend; order() changes it for one plot, and the levels change it for every plot.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.10 What comes next
This chapter says what gog needs from your own table, and nothing about the tables in this book. The book’s data names them, says where they come from, and shows how to read one in your own language.




Posit Software, PBC. (2026). Ggsql: A SQL extension for declarative data visualisation based on the grammar of graphics (Versions 0.3.0 (alpha)). https://ggsql.org/


Wickham, H. (2014). Tidy data. Journal of Statistical Software, 59(10), 1–23. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10
