title: 6  The book’s data
text:
6.1 Reading a table
Where do gapminder_2007, medals and winds come from, and how do you get them?
Data was about a table of your own. This chapter is about the shared tables that the book’s examples draw from, listed in full under The tables. They are published beside the book as CSV files, one per table, so you can run any example in this book yourself. Each file has a fixed address:
gapminder_2007.csv holds the 142 countries drawn in the chapter A first plot. medals.csv holds the medal counts drawn in Reading practice, and winds.csv holds the wind observations drawn in Polar.
Reading one takes a single call, gog_table(), which is part of the gog package in all four languages. Nothing else needs to be installed.
gog_table() is a convenience: a quick way to read the book’s tables from the book’s website. It is not a tool for reading or preparing data, and you do not have to use it. A table you read yourself, with readr in R, pandas in Python or any other reader you already use, works the same in data(). Reading a table says what to check when you do.
To run the first chapter’s plot yourself, you need its table loaded in R, Python, Julia or JavaScript. One line fetches it. gog_table() reads any of these tables by name:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


gapminder_2007 <- gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)


gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


const gapminder_2007 = await gog_table("gapminder_2007");
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life));
0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
Those four calls draw the same picture, because the table is the same file and the engine is the same program.
A CSV file stores every value as text, so gog_table() converts each column when it reads the file. A column becomes numbers when every value in it is a number. An empty cell or NA counts as a missing value, not as text, so a column of numbers with gaps still becomes numbers. Every other column stays text. This rule gives the right type for most columns. It gives the wrong type for a label written as a number, and for a date, which stays text. The text argument keeps a column as text. Ten columns in these tables need it, and Labels that look like numbers, below, explains which and why. gog_table() decides types this way so that the book’s examples run with nothing else installed. If you already use readr, pandas or another reader, set each column’s type there, where you can see and control it.
Why does a graphics package carry a table reader at all? R reads a CSV in one call, and Python and Julia in a few lines. JavaScript has no CSV reader in its standard library, and the work takes dozens of lines there, because a CSV reader cannot simply split each line on commas. Six countries in gapminder_2007.csv have a comma in the name, "Congo, Dem. Rep." among them, so that split gives those rows seven fields, while the header has six. Nobody should have to paste dozens of lines of parsing before drawing, so each package carries gog_table() instead.
Each package fetches the file with what its language already has: R’s read.csv(), urllib in Python, Downloads in Julia and fetch in JavaScript.
Read a file with a CSV reader of your own, and the rest of this chapter still applies, because data() takes any table already in memory. You then do two things yourself. First, check each column’s type: your CSV reader decides it, so the ten columns listed in Labels that look like numbers need whatever that reader offers for keeping a column as text. Second, declare the category order, because a CSV never records one. You declare it with factor() in R, a pandas Categorical in Python, a CategoricalArray in Julia, and ordered() in JavaScript. gog_table() does not declare the order either, so after it, too, you declare the order yourself. Three things a CSV cannot record covers both, and dates as well.
Reading a different table is the same call with a different name: gog_table("winds"), gog_table("medals"). gog_table() refuses a misspelled name, and its message suggests the nearest published name, or points to the list under The tables.

title: 6  The book’s data
section: 6.2 Three things a CSV cannot record
text:
6.2 Three things a CSV cannot record
A CSV records the values in a column, and never says what kind of column it is. Three kinds of information are therefore lost when the file is written. You restore them when you read the file. Each one changes the plot: the order of the categories, whether an axis has one slot per value, and whether an axis is a calendar. This chapter explains each one.
Restoring them is data preparation, and the tools you already use for your data do it best: readr and factor() in R, pandas in Python, CSV.jl and CategoricalArrays in Julia. This chapter shows how the book’s own tables get them only because gog_table() exists to read those tables quickly. For your own data, do this work with those tools, before the table reaches data().

6.2.1 A declared order
The eight compass points have a fixed order, and a plot of them reads correctly only when its axis keeps that order. The winds table records one wind observation per row:



winds: first 5 of 264 rows


direction
bearing
speed
season




N
19.612260

11.0

N
349.709737
13.8

N
2.602499
7.4

N
338.210715
3.7
Summer





The direction column of winds holds the eight compass points. Their order is N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW, clockwise from north. The Data chapter shows how a declared order sets the axis, the color assignment and the legend. A CSV cannot record that declaration. gog_table("winds") therefore reads direction as plain text, so you declare the order yourself after reading the file.
Until you declare an order, gog places the categories in the order they first appear in the rows. The winds file lists its rows in compass order, so a plot of direction made without the declaration reads correctly. Sort the rows by speed, and the axis shows S, N, NE, NW, SE, E, SW, W. The plot still draws, and nothing on it shows that the compass is in the wrong order.
The example below reads the table, sorts it by speed so that the rows are no longer in compass order, and then declares the compass order:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


winds <- gog_table("winds")
# `base::order`, because gog's `order()` masks it
winds <- winds[base::order(winds$speed), ]
compass <- c("N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW")
winds$direction <- factor(winds$direction, levels = compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction)


import pandas as pd

winds = gog_table("winds")
by_speed = sorted(enumerate(winds["speed"]), key=lambda pair: pair[1])
winds = {name: [column[i] for i, _ in by_speed]
         for name, column in winds.items()}
compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
winds["direction"] = pd.Categorical(winds["direction"], categories=compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction)


using CategoricalArrays

winds = gog_table("winds")
by_speed = sortperm(winds["speed"])
winds = Dict{String,Any}(name => column[by_speed] for (name, column) in winds)
compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
winds["direction"] = CategoricalArray(winds["direction"]; levels = compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction)


const winds = await gog_table("winds");
const by_speed = winds.speed.map((_, i) => i)
  .sort((a, b) => winds.speed[a] - winds.speed[b]);
for (const name in winds) winds[name] = by_speed.map((i) => winds[name][i]);
const compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"];
winds.direction = ordered(winds.direction, compass);

plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction));









                                      N NE E SE S SW W NW   0 20 40 60  Count Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction.”
The rows are in speed order, and the axis still reads N to NW. The declared order decides the axis, not the order of the rows. A declared order is also kept when the plot is drawn in another space, such as a circle. The polar chapter draws these same counts of winds per direction as a wind rose, and the change is one word. Add polar(), and the axis is drawn as a circle, with N at the top and the rest clockwise from it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction) + polar()


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction), polar())






                            N NE E SE S SW W NW   20 40 60  Count Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction, in polar.”
The polar chapter explains that plot. The circle starts at the first category and runs clockwise through the rest, so the compass reads correctly in the flat plot and in the circle.
The example sorts the rows only to take them out of compass order, so that you can see the declaration still works. The sort does not change the plot, so in your own code you need only the declaration.

A file that already lists its values in order still needs the declaration. Without it, the plot keeps that order only until you sort the rows, as the example above did. It is also lost when a sentence uses order(), which sorts undeclared text alphabetically. (Given a column of numbers, order() sorts by size instead; the labels in this list are text, so they are sorted alphabetically.) On the unsorted winds file, order(direction) puts the compass points in the order E, N, NE, NW, S, SE, SW, W. For most columns in this list, alphabetical order is also wrong: 10th comes before 1st, 10 comes before 2, and Ambient comes before Folk. The next section shows what happens to census without its declaration.


6.2.2 Labels that look like numbers
The second thing a CSV cannot record is which columns are text. Ten columns in these tables hold labels written as numbers, and gog_table() reads each of them as numbers unless you name it in the text argument. Eight of their tables are in the list above. The other two are new: eras holds the outline of every country, with its life expectancy in 1957 and 2007. ohio_turnout holds the share of each Ohio county’s citizens who voted in three elections. Each of these values is a name, not a quantity. The 0 in census names the youngest age band; it does not measure anything. sessions shows a second problem: a number cannot keep a leading zero, so gog_table() reads 01 as 1. These two problems are the reason gog_table() takes a text argument:

const census = await gog_table("census", ["age"]);
const sessions = await gog_table("sessions", ["session"]);
const candles = await gog_table("candles", ["session"]);
const gm_eras = await gog_table("gm_eras", ["era"]);
const gm_twelve_ends = await gog_table("gm_twelve_ends", ["year"]);
const ohio_turnout = await gog_table("ohio_turnout", ["election"]);
const eras = await gog_table("eras", ["era"]);
const gm_four = await gog_table("gm_four", ["period"]);
const thermal_moments = await gog_table("thermal_moments", ["moment"]);

Without the text argument, age becomes numbers. A point or a line then places the bands along a continuous axis from 0 to 85, with ticks at 0, 20, 40, 60 and 80. No band gets its own slot. The plot still looks reasonable, so nothing tells you the axis is wrong. With age read as numbers, the engine also refuses the population pyramid’s sentence in Many groups, because it sorts the bands with order(), and order() needs a categorical axis. When age is read as text, it still needs its declared order. Without the declaration, order() sorts the bands alphabetically, one character at a time. The band 5 is then drawn between 45 and 50.
Each call above names one column, and a text argument can name more than one. gm_eras holds the same values in two columns: year as a number, era as a label. The calls above name only era, so year stays a number. To read the year as a label too, name both columns in one text argument:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


gm_eras <- gog_table("gm_eras", text = c("year", "era"))


gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text=("year", "era"))


gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text = ["year", "era"])


const gm_eras = await gog_table("gm_eras", ["year", "era"]);





Each language writes more than one name in its own way. R puts them inside c(), Python inside parentheses, and Julia and JavaScript inside square brackets. In Python, one name can also be written alone, as in text="age". Inside parentheses it needs a trailing comma, as in ("age",), and two names do not. In Julia and JavaScript, the second name is added inside the brackets, after a comma.
Only census, sessions, candles, gm_eras, gm_twelve_ends, ohio_turnout, eras, gm_four, thermal_moments and storm_seasons need a text argument; no other shared table does.


6.2.3 A date
The third thing a CSV cannot record is which columns are dates. Six tables have a column of dates: day in four of them (six_weeks, revenue, sessions and candles), at in monitoring, and week in quakes_2011. gog_table() returns each of these columns as text, so the axis gets one slot per date instead of a calendar axis. After reading, convert the column to your language’s date or timestamp type. In R, that is as.Date() for six_weeks, revenue, sessions, candles and quakes_2011. monitoring also records the hour, so it takes as.POSIXct(). In JavaScript, write a time after each date, so that it is midnight in local time: six_weeks.day.map((d) => new Date(d + "T00:00")). For monitoring, which has a time already, replace the space with a T: new Date(t.replace(" ", "T")). The JavaScript chapter explains why. Scales shows the calendar axis you get.

Some tables hold real data and some were made for this book. The tables whose names begin with gapminder or gm hold figures from the Gapminder Foundation, which released them into the public domain. So do asia_2007, recent, three_continents and two_readings. continents_2007, continent_means, life_ranges and world_median are computed from those figures. population_spikes, filled, eras and enclave join them to world_borders, the country outlines described below. iris_flowers, iris_measurements, iris_predicted, petals, petal_stars, maunga_whau, peak, band, relief, nyc_horizon, quakes_fiji and titanic are reshaped from tables included with R, and carry R’s own license. nightingale is Florence Nightingale’s table of the British army’s deaths in the Crimean War, 1854 to 1856. It comes from the HistData package, under the same license as R’s tables. lung_survival and lung_at_risk come from R’s survival package, under that package’s own license. world_borders is Natural Earth’s public-domain outline of the countries. cyclones and storm_seasons are US government records: the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s storms of hurricane strength, 1980 to 2025, as tracks and as counts. So are quakes_2011, us_counties and ohio_turnout: the US Geological Survey’s earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more in 2011, the Census Bureau’s counties of the 48 states between Canada and Mexico, with their poverty rates in 2023, and the share of each Ohio county’s citizens who voted in 2016, 2020 and 2024, from the Election Assistance Commission and the Census Bureau. Everything else was made for this book, each table to show one thing; census is two plausible city profiles, not a real census. The terms for each are in data/LICENSE.md.

title: 6  The book’s data
text:
6.4 What comes next
A table holds the rows, and says nothing about how they look on the page. Choosing a mark shows how to pick the mark that draws them. There are fourteen, and your question and your columns decide which one fits.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.1 One variable
Which visible form should your data take? A mark is that visible form: a dot, a bar, a line. Choosing the mark is the first decision in every plot. The types of your variables narrow the choice, and the question you are asking picks among the marks that remain.
There are fourteen marks, and they are not a list to learn before you draw. This chapter helps you with the choice: it shows which mark answers which question and draws the common cases. Each mark then has a chapter of its own, with examples. The tables in Quick reference are for later, when you are working with your own data and want the row that fits.
If you have used ggplot2, a mark is similar to a geom, but the two differ in one way. Many geoms compute a statistic before they draw. geom_histogram() bins your data and then draws bars. geom_smooth() fits a curve and then draws a line. A mark never does that. A mark is only the shape, and the statistic is a separate word: a histogram is bar * bin, a trend line is line * smooth. A geom tends to name a chart. A mark names a shape.
Each column of your data is one variable, and gog reads its type from the data. There are two types:
Most plots in this chapter draw from the gapminder_2007 table. It holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007. Among its columns are life expectancy (life), GDP per person (gdp) and continent (continent). The book’s data describes it and every other table in the book. The chapters on each mark draw from gapminder_2007 too, so many of their plots will look familiar. That is on purpose: when you already know the table, and often the plot, you can see what each new word changes.
With one variable there is one question: how are its values spread out? The answer depends on whether the column is continuous or categorical.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.1.1 Continuous variable
Are the life expectancies of the 142 countries close to one value, or spread across a wide range? You can cut a continuous column into bands, or estimate a smooth curve over it. bin cuts the column into bands and counts the rows in each. bar * bin draws one bar per band, which is the histogram:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# How is life expectancy distributed? → histogram
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Distribution: bar * bin")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Distribution: bar * bin"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Distribution: bar * bin")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("Distribution: bar * bin"))






                                       50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Distribution: bar * bin Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life.”
The height of each bar depends on where the band edges fall, so two neighboring bars can differ sharply for that reason alone. Those jumps can hide the overall shape, such as whether the values have one peak or two. A smooth curve shows the same spread without them. density estimates that curve over the same column, and line * density draws it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Smooth shape of the distribution → density curve
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Density: line * density")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Density: line * density"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Density: line * density")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("Density: line * density"))






                               40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  Density: line * density Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life.”
A density curve is an estimate, not a count. It is harder to relate back to the rows than a histogram, and it assumes the values are continuous, smooth and unbounded, which is not true of every column (Wickham, 2016). When you are not sure the curve fits your data, draw the histogram too.


7.1.2 Categorical variable
A categorical column cannot be cut into bands, so the same question becomes: how often does each category occur? count tallies the rows in each category, and bar * count draws one bar per category:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# How many countries per continent? → frequency bar
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  title("Frequency: bar * count")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  title("Frequency: bar * count"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  title("Frequency: bar * count")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  title("Frequency: bar * count"))






                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Frequency: bar * count Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”
A count does not say what part of the whole each continent is. proportion is the same tally as a share of the whole, so the heights of the bars add up to 1:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# What share of countries per continent? → proportion bar
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  title("Shares: bar * proportion")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  title("Shares: bar * proportion"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("Shares: bar * proportion")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("Shares: bar * proportion"))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  Shares: bar * proportion Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent.”
Africa’s bar reaches about 0.37, a little above the 0.3 tick: Africa holds 52 of the 142 countries, more than a third of them.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.2 Two variables
With two variables, the pair of column types narrows the choice, and your question picks among the marks that remain.

7.2.1 Continuous × Continuous
Both variables are continuous, so the questions are about how the two are related, and how one changes as the other grows. Do people in richer countries live longer? point draws one dot per row. The shape the dots make together shows the answer before any line is added:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Is there a relationship? → scatter
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Relationship: point")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Relationship: point"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Relationship: point")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Relationship: point"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Relationship: point Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
Often the overall direction of the points matters more than any one country. As GDP goes up, does life expectancy go up too? smooth fits a trend line through the points, and line * smooth draws it over the scatter. color(continent) is written right after point, so it colors only the points, and one line is fitted to all of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Smooth the relationship → fitted trend line
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Trend: point + line * smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Trend: point + line * smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth + x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Trend: point + line * smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Trend: point + line * smooth"))






                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Trend: point + line * smooth Life expectancy GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
A question about two continuous columns is not always about a relationship. When one column is time and the other an amount, the question can be how much there was. The actuals table holds one sales figure for each year from 2019 to 2023:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# How much, not just where → filled area
data(actuals) + area + x(year) + y(sales) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Quantity: area")


(data(actuals) + area + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Quantity: area"))


data(actuals) + area + x(:year) + y(:sales) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Quantity: area")


plot(data(actuals), area, x(col.year), y(col.sales), y_label("Sales"),
  title("Quantity: area"))






                                 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023   0 50 100 150  Quantity: area Sales Year





“Given the actuals: an area, x is year, y is sales.”
line and area draw the same boundary and give it different meanings. A line says where the value was; an area says how much there was, so it fills to zero and the filled region is the quantity. Choose area when zero is a true baseline for your variable, and line when it is not. Sales of zero mean that nothing was sold, so zero is a true baseline and area fits. A temperature in degrees Celsius has no true zero: 0 °C is where water freezes, not the absence of heat. The filled region between zero and the curve would not measure any real amount, so line is the better choice.
Sometimes each x has a spread to show, not one value. ribbon fills between a low boundary and a high one, and the range transform supplies that pair. ribbon * range fills between the minimum and the maximum at each x. Give range two quantiles, as in ribbon * range(0.25, 0.75), and the ribbon fills between those instead. Here they are the 25th and the 75th percentiles, which hold the middle half of the values. The Ribbon chapter draws a band with a line of means inside it, and a nested percentile bands made with quantiles.
When the order of the rows is what you want to show, path connects them in that order. line sorts its points by x before it joins them. path does not, so the stroke can move left as well as right, cross itself, or return to where it started. That is the connected scatterplot: the two axes carry measurements, and the joining line shows the order in time. The gapminder_asia table holds five Asian countries (China, India, Indonesia, Japan and the Republic of Korea, written Korea, Rep.), measured every five years from 1952 to 2007, in order of year within each country:

# The reading order is the table's → path
data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Route: path (the arrow points to 2007)")

  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Route: path (the arrow points to 2007)"))

  style(arrow = "end") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Route: path (the arrow points to 2007)")

  color(col.country), style({ arrow: "end" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Route: path (the arrow points to 2007)"))

“Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow end.”
Layered over any of the marks above, rule draws a straight stroke at one value on one axis. It has two forms. By default each rule reaches across the whole panel, which makes a threshold line. With style(reach = "edge"), each rule is a short stroke at the edge of the panel instead, one for each row of the table. Together those strokes are a rug, and they show where the values of the rows lie along that axis.
Do the countries with a life expectancy below 60, 70 or 80 years tend to be the poorer ones? And where along the income axis are most countries? The life_bands table holds three threshold values of life expectancy, each with a name:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# One position, the panel supplies the other → rule
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Threshold and rug: rule")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(col.gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(col.band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Threshold and rug: rule"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + rule + x(:gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(:band) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Threshold and rug: rule")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), rule, x(col.gdp), style({ reach: "edge" }),
  data(life_bands), rule, color(col.band), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Threshold and rug: rule"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Threshold and rug: rule Life expectancy GDP per person  Band    Low  Middle  High 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp, with reach edge, and also rules from the life bands, colored by band.”
The rug’s rule names x(gdp) even though the points already named it. That second x(gdp) does not add an axis. Every layer shares the plot’s one x and one y. A rule marks a value on one axis, so it has to say which axis. The rug’s rule reads gapminder_2007, which holds both gdp and life, so either column could place it. Without x(gdp), gog refuses rather than guessing; the Rule chapter shows the refusal. The three rules from life_bands need no position. That table holds life and no gdp, so life is the only column that can place them. The plot puts life on the y axis, so each of the three rules goes across the panel at its value.
text is also layered over other marks: it writes a label from a column at each position where point would draw a dot.
zone shades a rectangle, usually behind the other marks. gog draws the layers in the order they are written, so write the zone first, and the marks written after it are drawn on top. The bounds transform names the columns that hold the edges of the rectangle. When the categories are on x, zone * bounds(lower, upper) takes the bottom and top of the rectangle from the columns lower and upper; when the categories are on y, the pair bounds x instead, as in the schedule. zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) takes its left and right from the columns start and end. On an axis that gets no pair of columns, the rectangle spans the whole panel. Write zone * bin instead, and bin cuts the panel into a grid of cells and counts the rows in each, and the same mark shades the cells: the heatmap.


7.2.2 Categorical × Continuous
One axis groups, the other measures. The natural question is how the measurement differs across groups. mean reduces each group to one value, its average. bar * mean draws one bar per group, and the bar’s height is that value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Mean value per group → bar
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Group summary: bar * mean")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Group summary: bar * mean"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Group summary: bar * mean")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Group summary: bar * mean"))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Group summary: bar * mean Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
A mean hides how far apart the countries inside one continent are. Sometimes that spread is what you want to see. Replace bar * mean with point, and it draws every country in its continent’s slot, the space on the x axis that belongs to that continent:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# All individual points per group → strip plot
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)"))






                                                                                                                                                                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Strip plot: point (one dot per country) Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life.”
Nothing is summarized: each dot is one country, placed by its continent and its life expectancy. Dots for countries with similar life expectancies overlap, so a crowded slot hides two things: how many dots it holds, and how they are spread.
The mean and the spread can be shown in one plot. A second layer, point * mean, draws each continent’s mean over its countries. Here x() and y() are written once, before the first mark, so both layers use them (one axis, and which column each layer reads):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Every point and the mean per group → strip plot with means
data(gapminder_2007) + x(continent) + y(life) +
  point + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  point * mean + style(color = "black", size = 7) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot with means: point, then point * mean")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  point + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  point * mean + style(color = "black", size = 7) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot with means: point, then point * mean"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:continent) + y(:life) + point +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + point * mean +
  style(color = "black", size = 7) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot with means: point, then point * mean")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.continent), y(col.life), point,
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), layer(point, mean),
  style({ color: "black", size: 7 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Strip plot with means: point, then point * mean"))






                                                                                                                                                                                        Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Strip plot with means: point, then point * mean Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: x is continent, y is life, points and also points derived by mean.”
Each black dot is a continent’s mean, and the lighter dots are its countries. Africa’s mean is about 55, and its countries range from about 40 to 76. Oceania has only two countries, so its mean lies between two dots that almost touch.
There are three ways to draw a crowded group more clearly, and each shows something different. For the shape of each group rather than every point, write box + x(continent) + y(life). box draws a box between the quartiles, a line at the median, whiskers, and outliers as separate dots. ribbon * density draws the whole estimated distribution that the box summarizes: the violin plot. When every point matters but the points overlap, point * jitter spreads them sideways: the jittered strip plot.
The question is not always which group is highest. It can be how the value changes from one group to the next. line, area, step and ribbon accept a category on x too. They join one summary per group instead of drawing a bar on each, and the result is a profile:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# One value per group, joined → profile
data(gapminder_2007) + x(continent) + y(life) +
  line * mean + point * mean +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Profile: line * mean")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  line * mean + point * mean +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Profile: line * mean"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:continent) + y(:life) + line * mean +
  point * mean + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Profile: line * mean")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  layer(line, mean), layer(point, mean), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Profile: line * mean"))






                                      Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  Profile: line * mean Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: x is continent, y is life, a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean.”
A bar compares one group with another; a profile traces a change across the groups. A profile needs more care than a bar, because its segments cross parts of the panel where nothing was measured. Use it when the categories have an order, such as a rating scale or size groups from smallest to largest. Continents have no order, so that advice says not to draw this plot. gog draws it anyway. gog refuses a sentence that has no meaning, such as cutting a category into bands. It never refuses a sentence only because it may be a poor choice. Whether a profile suits your categories is your decision (Law 8).
line is not the only mark that draws a profile. area fills under the same boundary, step holds each value flat until the next category, and ribbon * range fills the spread as a band. Add polar() to the same line * mean profile, and the axis of categories bends into a circle: that is the radar chart, drawn in Polar.

7.3.1 Swapping x and y
Long category names, such as country names, are easier to read on the vertical axis than along the bottom. In the first table, each row with a categorical x and a continuous y whose mark is drawn in a slot also works with the two axes swapped. bar, box, interval, point and the violin (ribbon * density) are all drawn in a slot on one axis and measure along the other. The column types decide which axis holds the slots: the one with the categorical column. Swapping the two positions therefore draws the same plot horizontally.
Here is a box plot with life on x and continent on y. Nothing else is needed:

“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is life, y is continent.”
The continents are listed down the left side, and each box lies along the x axis.
Some plotting libraries use a separate word for a horizontal chart, such as matplotlib’s barh(). gog needs no such word, because it reads the orientation from the axis that carries the categories.
line, step, area and a ribbon drawn as a band are read along a domain, the axis the mark runs along, and they turn by the rule a bar follows. A category is always their domain, so a category on y turns them down the page, as The profile, turned shows. Their two columns are often both numbers, though, and then no column type can say which one is the domain, so the domain is x. The line chapter shows what a swap of two continuous columns draws, and what to write when such a domain must be the vertical axis.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.4 Mark families
The mark list looks like a set to memorize, one entry at a time. It is not. The fourteen basic consonants of Hangeul (한글) are not fourteen unrelated shapes either. The letters are featural: most of them are another letter with a single feature changed. ㅋ (k) is ㄱ (g) with one stroke added, so learning ㄱ teaches you most of ㅋ.
The marks are built the same way. The marks in the table below come in families of two, and the two marks of a family have the same rules for every channel: x, y, color, size and the rest. If one mark requires, accepts or refuses a channel, the other mark does the same. They differ in the geometry they draw:








Family
Same rules for every channel
They differ in




area and ribbon
✓
area closes its region on the baseline; ribbon closes it on a second data boundary


line and step
✓
line slopes from one value to the next; step holds each value until it changes



Once you know one mark of a family, the other is quick to learn. It follows the same rules for every channel, so you already know those. The grid of marks and channels in Combinations shows this: the two marks of a family have identical rows there. What is left to learn is the shape the second mark draws. One more thing differs: ribbon and interval need a transform, such as range or bounds, to supply their two ends, and gog refuses them without one.
When does gog add a mark? Only for a shape that no existing mark can draw. step was added because “hold the value until it changes” is such a shape: no channel, transform or setting can say it. A thick line was not added as a mark, because style(size = ) already says it. A new chart is never the reason. A histogram, a radar chart and a population pyramid are built from marks that already exist. A new word is spelled with the letters you have, and a new chart is written with the marks you have. The families make the marks quick to learn, but gog never adds a mark only to complete a family.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.5 Unpronounceable combinations
Just as some letter combinations cannot be pronounced, some pairs of a transform and a column type have no meaning. gog refuses each one and draws nothing.
bin, density and smooth all work along a continuous axis, so the column on that axis must be continuous. A category on that axis is refused, and each refusal names the sentence to use for a category instead:








Combination
Problem
Use instead




bar * bin + x(category)
bin cuts a continuous axis into bands
bar * count + x(category)


bar * density + x(category)
density estimates a continuous distribution
bar * proportion + x(category)


point * smooth + x(category)
smooth fits a curve along a continuous axis
bar * mean + x(category) + y(value)



All three appear as refusals in where bin, density and smooth cannot be used; the table above is this page’s summary of them.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.6 What comes next
Choosing the mark is the first decision in a plot, not the last one. Point opens the fourteen chapters that follow, each describing one mark: its channels, its transforms, its settings and its refusals.




Wickham, H. (2016). ggplot2: Elegant graphics for data analysis (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-24277-4

title: 8  Point
text:
8.1 Basic usage
How does one measurement change as another changes? point draws one glyph, a small symbol, at the (x, y) position of each row. The glyph is a dot unless you choose another.
The plot it makes is the scatterplot, and it was invented later than the other basic charts. William Playfair published the line chart and the bar chart in 1786 (Playfair, 1786), and the pie chart in 1801 (Playfair, 1801). The first scatterplot came in 1833, about thirty years after the pie chart: historians usually name John Herschel as the first person to plot one measured column against another. He plotted the position of a double star against the year, then drew a smooth curve through the dots so the trend could be seen (Friendly & Denis, 2005). Other names for the same picture are scatter diagram and scattergram. When size maps a third column, the same plot is called the bubble chart.
None of those chart names is a word in gog, and that is deliberate. point is a mark, not a chart. point + x(gdp) + y(life) is a scatterplot, and point + x(continent) + y(life) is a strip plot. The mark is the same in both. The chart name belongs to the whole sentence, not to any word in the vocabulary. That is why the names are listed in an appendix, Chart names, instead of in the kernel.
Do people in richer countries live longer? The gapminder_2007 table can answer that. It holds one row per country in 2007, with the country’s gdp, its life expectancy life, its continent and its population. The book’s data says where the table comes from. Most examples in this chapter start from the smallest sentence that draws a point: the table, the mark, and its two positions.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.2 The dot as a default
Write point and you get a dot. Calling it the dot mark is accurate whenever no shape is mapped or set. But the dot is only a default, and you can change it. A point is a glyph at a position, and shape replaces the dot with one of the seven glyphs gog draws, a different one for each category of a column. Shape below names the seven, says which category gets which, and what to do with more than seven.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + shape(continent) +
  title("The glyph is not always a dot")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + shape(col.continent) +
  title("The glyph is not always a dot"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + shape(:continent) +
  title("The glyph is not always a dot")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  shape(col.continent), title("The glyph is not always a dot"))

To draw every point with the same glyph instead, set one with style(). The seven are circle, square, triangle, diamond, cross, star and wye, and Shape draws each of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(shape = "triangle") +
  title("One glyph for every point")

  title("One glyph for every point"))

  style(shape = "triangle") + title("One glyph for every point")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ shape: "triangle" }), title("One glyph for every point"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, with shape triangle.”

A text mark draws the value of a column, chosen with label. Put both on one plot and each row is located by a dot and named by its label.

title: 8  Point
section: 8.3 A categorical x: the strip plot
text:
8.3 A categorical x: the strip plot
Every plot so far has put a measurement on x, but x also accepts a categorical column. Each category gets its own slot on the axis, and every row is drawn in its category’s slot. You see the whole distribution rather than a summary of it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("One dot per country"))






                                                                                                                                                                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  One dot per country Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life.”
Every mark places a categorical column this way, bar included. Compare the strip plot with bar * mean, which reduces each group to one number:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("The same data, summarized"))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  The same data, summarized Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
mean is not the bar’s own transform. Other marks take it too, and each draws the same means in its own way:



Mark derived by mean
What it draws




point * mean
one dot at each mean


line * mean
the means joined into a profile


area * mean
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * mean
each mean held flat until the next category


bar * mean
one bar per category, the plot above



median, sum, min and max can replace mean in every row of that table. So can quantile, which needs a probability: quantile(0.9) is the value nine tenths of each group falls below. The statistic decides the number, and the mark decides how it is drawn.
The strip plot shows Africa’s spread and its overlap with Asia; the bar chart shows neither. The strip plot has one weakness: every point in a category is on the same vertical line. Where many countries have close values, their dots cover each other, and you cannot see how many there are. There are four ways to show the overlapping points.
The first way is to make each point partly transparent with one setting, style(opacity = 0.6), so overlap reads as a darker area. The horizontal strip plot in Either axis below is drawn this way. The second way is point * jitter. It moves overlapping points sideways along the categorical axis, and never changes their measured value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same dots, spread sideways"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  The same dots, spread sideways Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life.”
Every dot keeps its life expectancy, so its height has not changed. Only its place inside its continent’s slot has changed, and that place means nothing: the dot still reads as its continent. jitter moves a dot only along the categorical axis, inside its slot, and never along the measured axis. By default jitter moves a dot at most 0.2 of a slot from its category’s center. The number in jitter() multiplies that default, so jitter(0.5) spreads the dots half as wide (How much to spread). In a scatterplot both axes are measurements, so a moved dot would show a value the data does not hold. gog never draws a point at a value that was not measured, not even to keep points from covering each other. So it refuses point * jitter when x and y are both continuous, as What it refuses shows.
The third way, point * dodge, also moves points sideways within their slot. Unlike jitter, it moves each point only as far as it must to touch no other point:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, set apart until none touch")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, set apart until none touch"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same dots, set apart until none touch")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same dots, set apart until none touch"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  The same dots, set apart until none touch Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life.”
With 142 countries, no dot covers another, and every dot keeps its life expectancy. Where many countries have close values, the dots spread wide, so the outline of each group shows the shape of its distribution, one dot per country. This plot is the beeswarm (Eklund & Trimble, 2021). When a slot is too crowded to hold its dots, gog draws the extra ones at the slot’s edge, on top of one another, and a warning says how many overlap. It never moves them into the next continent’s slot. When a slot is full, add style(opacity = ) as well: the dots drawn over one another at the slot’s edge then show as a darker band, so you can see where they overlap.
The fourth way is to count the overlapping points instead of separating them. point * bin * stack cuts the measured column into bins and piles one dot per row above each bin, which is the dot plot (Wilkinson, 1999). It shows one distribution, with the measure on x; | facet(continent) draws one for each continent. The cookbook draws it with thirty rows, where every row is still visible. Choose among the four ways by what you want the reader to see. Opacity, jitter and dodge keep the spread: on the measured axis, every dot stays where its value was measured. Opacity leaves every dot in its place, and with dodge no dot covers another unless its slot is full. bin * stack gives the count: how many rows fall in each bin. The result looks like a bar chart, but each row is still its own dot.

8.3.1 Either axis: a horizontal strip
gog decides a plot’s direction from which axis holds which column: the axis that carries the category sets it, for a point exactly as for a bar. So the category can be on y instead of x, and the strips run horizontally. The countries and the distributions are the same, and each continent’s dots now run from left to right:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(life) + y(continent) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) + x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  style({ opacity: 0.6 }), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same distributions, lying down"))






                                                                                                                                                                                 40 50 60 70 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  The same distributions, lying down Continent Life expectancy





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is life, y is continent, with opacity 0.6.”
If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip(), there is no such word here. Swapping the columns on x and y was the whole change, the same way you swap the two arguments of matplotlib’s scatter(). Use the horizontal form when the category names are too long for the bottom axis. It also helps when there are many categories, since names listed down the left side are easier to read than names crowded along the bottom.
The same holds for the ways of setting dots apart: with the category on y, point * jitter and point * dodge spread the dots up and down instead of sideways. Here is the beeswarm lying down:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The beeswarm, lying down")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The beeswarm, lying down"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The beeswarm, lying down")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, dodge), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The beeswarm, lying down"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by dodge, x is life, y is continent.”
With one row per category, the horizontal strip is the Cleveland dot plot (Cleveland, 1984). It shares a name with the dot plot above but is a different chart: there each dot is one row in a bin, and here each dot is one category’s value. Comparing categories draws it for twelve countries.
A point derived by count can be horizontal too. point * count counts the rows in each category and draws one point for each. With the category on y, that is a Cleveland dot plot of the counts:

  title("How many countries each continent holds")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + y(col.continent) + x_label("Countries") +
  title("How many countries each continent holds"))

  x_label("Countries") + title("How many countries each continent holds")

  x_label("Countries"), title("How many countries each continent holds"))

Africa holds the most countries, 52, and Oceania the fewest, 2. Three other transforms also compute a number from the one column you name. bin counts the rows in each range of a measured column, and proportion gives each category’s share of the rows. density estimates, as a smooth curve, where a measured column’s values are most common. On a point, as on a bar, the computed number goes on the axis you left empty. Name the column on y, and the count, share or density is drawn along x.

title: 8  Point

8.4 Color
In the scatterplot of gdp against life, every dot looks the same, so you cannot see which continent each country is in. Bind color to a categorical column to color points by group. gog assigns a distinct color from a 20-color palette automatically.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
Most African countries are at the lower left, and most European countries at the upper right. gog adds a color legend whenever you map a column to color.

8.4.1 Splitting without color
Sometimes another layer already uses color, such as boxes colored by era. The points should then be split by era too, without being painted. color does two things at once: it splits the points into groups, and it paints each group. group does only the first. On points, a split needs something that works on each group. A statistic computes one value for each group, such as each era’s mean. dodge sets the groups side by side within each category’s slot. Without either, a point layer draws one dot for each row, so splitting the rows changes nothing, and gog refuses the sentence (What it refuses). With dodge or a statistic, group(era) splits the points by era, and another layer shows which era is which: the colored boxes in the first plot below, the colored lines in the second. “Given the gapminder eras: boxes derived by dodge, colored by era, and also points derived by dodge, grouped by era, with size 2.5, x is continent, y is life.”
A channel written after a mark belongs to that mark alone, so color(era) colors only the boxes and group(era) splits only the points. The positions are the exception: x and y come after point, and the boxes use them too, because every mark shares the axes (Which marks a channel reaches). Without group(era), each continent’s dots would form one beeswarm in the middle of its slot, between its two boxes. style(size = 2.5) draws smaller dots, so more of them fit in each half of a crowded slot.
A statistic is split the same way. point * mean + group(era) computes one mean for each era within each continent. Here colored lines join each era’s means across the continents, and black dots mark the means themselves:

  point * mean + group(era) + style(color = "black") +
  x(continent) + y(life)

  point * mean + group(col.era) + style(color = "black") +
  x(col.continent) + y(col.life))

  style(color = "black") + x(:continent) + y(:life)

  group(col.era), style({ color: "black" }), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))

“Given the gapminder eras: lines derived by mean, colored by era, and also points derived by mean, grouped by era, colored black, x is continent, y is life.”
Without group(era), point * mean would compute one mean for each continent from both eras, and each dot would be between the two lines.
These plots use only two layers each, but combining more layers the same way shows more about the data in one plot. Each layer adds one more view of the same rows: Three layers instead of one mark draws each species’ full range, its middle half and its median as three layers.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.5 Shape
Which glyph does each category get, and what happens when there are more categories than glyphs? shape maps a categorical column to one of seven glyphs. In order, they are the circle, the square, the triangle, the diamond, the cross, the star and the wye, which looks like the letter Y. The categories are ordered by where each first appears in the table, or by the order you declare. The first category gets the circle, the second the square, and so on. Here is the whole set, in the order gog assigns them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


glyphs <- data.frame(
  glyph = c("circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross", "star", "wye"),
  row   = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)
)
data(glyphs) + point + x(glyph) + y(row) + shape(glyph) +
  style(size = 8) + x_label("") + y_label("") +
  title("The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned")


glyphs = {
  "glyph": ["circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross", "star", "wye"],
  "row": [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
}
(data(glyphs) + point + x(col.glyph) + y(col.row) + shape(col.glyph) +
  style(size = 8) + x_label("") + y_label("") +
  title("The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned"))


glyphs = (
  glyph = ["circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross", "star", "wye"],
  row = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
)
data(glyphs) + point + x(:glyph) + y(:row) + shape(:glyph) +
  style(size = 8) + x_label("") + y_label("") +
  title("The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned")


const glyphs = {
  glyph: ["circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross", "star", "wye"],
  row: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1],
};
plot(data(glyphs), point, x(col.glyph), y(col.row), shape(col.glyph),
  style({ size: 8 }), x_label(""), y_label(""),
  title("The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned"))






                                          circle square triangle diamond cross star wye   0 1 2  The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned  Glyph    circle  square  triangle  diamond  cross  star  wye 





“Given the glyphs table: points, x is glyph, y is row, shape by glyph, with size 8.”
Asia comes first in the gapminder table, so Asia is the circle, and every continent legend in this chapter lists Asia first. Seven is the whole set gog draws. Map shape to a column with more than seven categories and the eighth category gets the circle again, so two categories share a glyph and look the same. gog says so when that happens, naming the number of categories and the seven glyphs, and the plot still draws.                                                                              protein fat carbs fiber iron   0 10 20 30 40 50  Eight foods, seven glyphs Amount per 100g Nutrient  Food    salmon  rice  almonds  lentils  chicken  spinach  beans  oats 





“Given the nutrients: points, x is nutrient, y is amount, shape by food.”
Oats is the eighth food in the table, so its points are circles, the glyph salmon already has. Nothing in the picture shows which circles are salmon and which are oats, so the message counts the foods and the glyphs for you. The book has four ways to draw more than seven groups:

color, whose default palette has 20 colors, as Color above does with the continents.
One panel per category with facet, folded into rows so the panels stay wide: Folding a long line of panels.
The name on the point instead of a glyph: a text layer with label, the labeled scatter, and repel when the names overlap. Of the four, only this one can name each of a hundred categories. In the web edition, a brush dims the labels outside the selection, so only the selected names stay readable. A text layer that uses repel is not dimmed: the brush leaves its labels as they are.
Every category in one pale color, and the few that matter drawn again on top, in a second layer: What settings are for.

When a table has two categorical columns, map shape to the one with fewer categories. continent has five, and seven glyphs are enough for five. country has 142, so it goes on a label or a facet instead.
shape works best when it repeats the column on color. Some readers cannot see the difference between colors, and a black-and-white printout removes it. The glyphs still separate the groups where the colors cannot:

  color(continent) + shape(continent)

  color(col.continent) + shape(col.continent))

  shape(:continent)

  color(col.continent), shape(col.continent))

Each continent now differs in two ways, so either one alone still separates the groups.

  color(continent) + size(population)

  color(col.continent) + size(col.population))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  size(:population)

8.7 Opacity
opacity is a setting, as the horizontal strip plot above showed, and it is also a channel: a larger value in a continuous column gives a more opaque point.   opacity(:population, scale = "log") +
  title("Opacity: population, on a log scale")

  opacity(col.population, { scale: "log" }),

8.8 All channels at once
A table often has more columns to show than two positions can hold. The color, shape and size channels can show the others, and all three can be on one plot at once. Here continent is mapped to both color and shape, so the groups stay separate in black-and-white printing, and population is mapped to size:

  color(continent) +
  shape(continent) +
  size(population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) +
  shape(col.continent) +
  size(col.population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  shape(:continent) + size(:population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population")

  color(col.continent), shape(col.continent), size(col.population),
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population"))

This one plot shows four columns: gdp and life by position, continent by color and glyph, and population by size.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.9 Transforms it takes
With transforms, a mark can draw plots it cannot draw alone, such as a histogram, a trend line or a running total. Learning which transforms each mark takes is not easy, and some pairs do not behave the way you might first expect. gog makes this easier with one rule: each transform has one meaning, and every mark that takes it applies that meaning in the same way (No Exceptions). So once you understand a transform on one mark, you already know most of what it does on another. Every mark chapter has this section, starting with this one.
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a point takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
bin, count, density, proportion
—


Summaries
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile
—


Fitted lines
smooth, straight
—


Running total
cumulative
—


Pairs: a low and a high
—
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds


Collision modifiers
dodge, stack, jitter
repel


Layouts of a whole picture
layout
partition, flow, cluster



The plots below show every transform a point takes. Some of these transforms appeared earlier in this chapter. They are shown again here so that all of a point’s transforms are in one place. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change.
Counting. count and proportion tally the rows at each value of x, on a category or a number. bin and density work on a number. bin counts the rows in each interval, and density estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty. The top two plots put continent on x, and the plot below them puts life:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(continent) + title("point * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("point * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin + x(life) + title("point * bin"))


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(col.continent) + title("point * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * proportion + x(col.continent) +
     title("point * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin + x(col.life) + title("point * bin")))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(:continent) +
  title("point * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("point * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin + x(:life) + title("point * bin"))


below(beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count),
  x(col.continent), title("point * count")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("point * proportion"))),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, bin), x(col.life),
  title("point * bin")))






                                           Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 10 20 30 40 50  point * count Count Continent


                                     Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  point * proportion Proportion Continent


                                     50 60 70 80   10 20 30  point * bin Count Life






“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by count, x is continent, beside points derived by proportion, x is continent; above points derived by bin, x is life.”
The density is drawn in a figure of its own. In one figure with the bin plot, the two would share one life axis that covers only the range of the rows, and the density’s tails would be cut off (A plot cut by a shared axis). The curve is computed at 256 places unless you set places. The plots below leave it at 256 and set it to 32:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * density + x(life) +
   title("point * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * density(places = 32) + x(life) +
     title("point * density(places = 32)"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point * density + x(col.life) +
   title("point * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * density(places = 32) + x(col.life) +
     title("point * density(places = 32)")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * density + x(:life) +
  title("point * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * density(places = 32) + x(:life) +
  title("point * density(places = 32)"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, density), x(col.life),
  title("point * density: 256 places, the default")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, density({ places: 32 })),
  x(col.life), title("point * density(places = 32)")))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  point * density: 256 places, the default Density Life


                                                              40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  point * density(places = 32) Density Life






“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by density, x is life, beside points derived by density at 32 places, x is life.”
At 256 places the dots overlap into a thick line wherever the curve is flat, and they separate only where it is steep. At 32, every dot can be seen on its own.
Look at the y axis of the five plots above, from point * count to point * density(places = 32). None of the five sentences writes y(), yet each y axis has a name: Count, Proportion, Count, Density and Density. The table has no column by those names. Each transform writes one, and y draws it. count and bin write count, the number of rows at each value or in each interval. proportion writes proportion, each count’s share of all the rows. density writes density, the height of the estimated curve. The axis is labeled with the column’s name, capitalized, as The name on a measure axis explains.
Summaries. The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of x to one value, so they need a number on y. sum reads population, because only an amount has a total that means something. The other five read life. They give the mean, the median, the largest and the smallest value, and quantile(0.9) gives the value that nine tenths of the rows fall below:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
    title("point * sum")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("point * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * median + x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("point * median"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point * max + x(continent) + y(life) +
      title("point * max")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point * min + x(continent) + y(life) +
        title("point * min")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point * quantile(0.9) + x(continent) + y(life) +
        title("point * quantile(0.9)")))


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point * sum + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
    title("point * sum")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +

Collision modifiers. Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another. dodge sets groups side by side within a category’s slot, and gives each group its own part of the slot. The parts are left and right when the category is on x, and up and down when it is on y. On a point it also moves each point within its group’s part, only as far as it must to touch no other point. Layouts. Some tables record relations rather than measurements. In an edge table, each row says that one name is related to another. No column gives a name a position on x, y or z, yet the relations still have to be drawn. So the layout transform computes a position for each name, and places the two names of each row near each other. It needs two columns of names and the network space, network(). The positions mean nothing as quantities, so network() draws no axes. A point draws a dot at each name’s position, and edge draws a stroke for each row, as the Edge chapter shows. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, which interval, ribbon, line and step take. partition, flow and cluster lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which zone, ribbon and path draw. repel moves text labels off each other.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.10 What you can set
A setting changes how every point looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a point’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(shape = )
circle, square, triangle, diamond, cross, star, wye


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels



A point takes six settings, and it is the only mark that can set shape. Every glyph except the cross is filled with color, so a point is also one of the marks that draw a border. size is the radius in pixels, and border_color and border_size give that border its own color and width.
A point layer can take several settings at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue",
        border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue",
        border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue", border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ shape: "diamond", size: 7, color: "steelblue",
  border_color: "navy", border_size: 1.5 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("A shape, a size, and a border"))
