“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored steelblue, with shape diamond, size 7, border color navy and border size 1.5.”
Where two diamonds overlap, the navy border shows where one ends and the next begins. That is what a border is for where many points crowd together. A cross has no fill to outline, so border_color and border_size change nothing on that glyph.
A border can also be the whole point. Set the fill color to "none" and give the border a color, and each point is drawn hollow: an outline with no fill. A hollow point can be partly transparent as well. opacity fades what color paints, and color = "none" paints nothing, so gog refuses opacity on a hollow point. Put the transparency in the border’s color instead. In "#4682b44d", the first six hex digits are steelblue, and the last two, 4d, make the outline 30% opaque. Transparency in a hex value shows how to find those two digits for any opacity. Here are all 1,704 rows of gm_all again, the table the Opacity section drew at one opacity:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent")

  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 3) +

  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 3) +
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent")


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "none", border_color: "#4682b44d", size: 3 }),
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent"))

“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored none, with border color #4682b44d and size 3.”
Where hollow points overlap, every outline stays visible, and where many pile up, the outlines add up to a darker area. The plot shows each point and the crowding at once. Neither this nor opacity moves a point off its measured value, which is why they, and not jitter, are the answers for a crowded scatterplot. On a categorical axis, jitter and dodge move points apart instead, as the strip plot showed.
pattern is not on the list. It sets the texture of a stroke or of a fill, and a glyph is neither. To separate groups by glyph, a point uses shape instead, and What it refuses shows the refusal.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.11 What it refuses
Five refusals follow, each with its reason: a category on size, any pattern, jitter or dodge on a scatterplot, opacity on a hollow point, and group on points with no statistic and no dodge.
size shows an amount, so it needs a continuous column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + size(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  size(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `size(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `size` on `point` needs a continuous (numeric) column. Use `color` or `shape` to distinguish categories.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


continent is a categorical column. Its values are names, not amounts, and a larger dot would claim an order the data does not have. The message suggests color or shape instead: each continent gets its own color or glyph.
The second refusal is about texture. pattern sets the texture of a stroke or of a fill, and a point is a glyph, which is neither:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(pattern = "dashed")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(pattern = "dashed")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(pattern = "dashed")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ pattern: "dashed" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = )` sets a stroke pattern or a fill texture, and a `point` is neither a stroke nor a fill — a point's form is set by `shape`, a text's by its content. The strokes (`line`/`step`/`interval`/`path`/`rule`/`edge`) take a stroke pattern; the fills (`area`/`bar`/`box`/`ribbon`/`zone`) a fill texture.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names shape, which chooses a point’s glyph.
The third refusal is jitter on a scatterplot. In a strip plot, jitter moves a dot sideways inside its continent’s slot. A place inside a slot has no scale, so the move changes nothing a reader could measure. In a scatterplot both axes are continuous, and every place on them is a value. A jittered dot would be drawn at a gdp and a life expectancy that are not in the table. Two countries with the same values would no longer look the same, and a reader who reads a dot against the axes would read a number that was never measured. So gog refuses:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `point * jitter` spreads points sideways within a category's slot, but here both `x` and `y` are continuous — there is no slot to spread within, and nudging a measured value would misplace it. For overplotting on two continuous axes, `style(opacity = )` reveals density without moving any point off its value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


This is a design rule, not a missing feature. Every dot is drawn at the values in its row. gog never draws a point at a value that was not measured, not even to keep points from covering each other, so jitter never moves a dot along a measured axis. ggplot2’s geom_jitter() moves points along both axes by a small random amount, and gog does not. To show overlapping points in a scatterplot, keep every point at its value and change how it is drawn. style(opacity = ), which the message suggests, makes overlap read as a darker area, as in the plot of every gapminder year under Opacity. A hollow point, an outline with no fill, keeps every point visible where points overlap, as the same table shows under What you can set.
point * dodge is refused on a scatterplot for the same reason. It moves a dot only within a category’s slot, and a scatterplot has no slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, dodge), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `point * dodge` sets points apart inside a category's slot and moves them along the categorical axis only, but here neither `x` nor `y` is categorical — there is no slot to swarm in, and moving a measured value would misplace it. For overplotting on two continuous axes, `style(opacity = )` reveals density without moving any point off its value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message again suggests style(opacity = ).
The fourth refusal is opacity on a hollow point. opacity fades what color paints, and color = "none" paints nothing, so there is nothing for it to fade:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "none", border_color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.3 }))




Error:
! gog: `style(opacity = 0.3)` fades what `color` paints, and `color = "none"` paints nothing, so there is nothing here for it to fade. A border is drawn in its own color, so its transparency goes there: `style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d")` draws a steelblue outline at 30%.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests border_color = "#4682b44d" instead. In "#4682b44d" the transparency is part of the border’s own color, as in the hollow points under What you can set.
The fifth refusal is group on points with no statistic and no dodge. On a line, group cuts one stroke into several. Points are not joined into a stroke, and each row is already its own point, so splitting the rows by continent would change nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + group(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + group(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + group(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  group(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `group` on a `point` needs `dodge` or a statistic to act on, and on this plot neither helps: `dodge` needs a categorical axis, and a statistic over `gdp` would summarize one row at a time. Each row is already its own point, so splitting the rows by `continent` would change nothing. To show the groups, map `continent` to `color` or `shape`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


gog accepts group on points only when a statistic or dodge is joined to them, as in Splitting without color. A scatterplot has no categorical axis for dodge to use, so the message offers the two channels that show the groups: map continent to color or shape instead.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.12 In short
A point is a glyph at a position. The point mark draws one per row, unless a transform such as mean summarizes the rows first. It is the only mark that maps shape, because it is the only mark that picks its glyph from a fixed set. There are seven glyphs, and an eighth category gets the circle again.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.13 What comes next
The point mark draws each row as a separate glyph, and nothing joins one row to the next. When one column puts the rows in order, such as years, the change from one value to the next often matters most. Line joins the rows into one stroke that shows whether the value rose or fell.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.1 Basic usage
How did one value change over time? line sorts the rows by x, from smallest to largest, and draws one stroke through their (x, y) points in that order, the x order. The stroke is straight pieces laid end to end, each joining one row’s point to the next, with nothing smoothed between them.

The gapminder_asia table holds China, India, Indonesia, Japan and South Korea (Korea, Rep. in the table), with one row for each country every five years from 1952 to 2007.                                1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year
“Given gapminder Asia: a line, x is year, y is life.”
The stroke looks wrong, but gog drew exactly what the sentence asks for. All five countries have a row for each year, so the one stroke passes through five values at every year. The vertical segments are where it joins the five countries inside one year, before it continues to the next year. That is exactly what a line does when nothing splits the rows: it draws one series, a single stroke in x order. Above the plot, gog prints a message that names what to add: a color or a group for several series, or line * mean for one value at each year. That value is the average life expectancy of the five countries in that year, so the line shows how their average changed over the years. Multiple series, two sections below, draws the same table as five lines, one per country.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.2 Automatic sorting by x
The rows of a table can be in any order: a file may be sorted by name, or by nothing at all. line sorts its own vertices, the points it joins, by x, so the order of the rows does not matter. The scrambled table holds five years and a life expectancy for each, listed out of order on purpose. The line still runs from left to right:



scrambled: all 5 rows


year
life




1992

52

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(scrambled) + line + x(year) + y(life)


data(scrambled) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life)


data(scrambled) + line + x(:year) + y(:life)


plot(data(scrambled), line, x(col.year), y(col.life))






                                 1960 1970 1980 1990 2000   55 60 65 70  Life Year





“Given scrambled: a line, x is year, y is life.”
That sorting is part of what the mark means. It is not an extra step that the engine performs for you. A line says this value changed along this axis, and an axis has one direction, so there is only one order the vertices could be joined in.
path is the mark that does the opposite. It joins the rows in the order your table holds them, which is what draws a route or a loop. Here is the scrambled table drawn both ways, with a point at each row:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(scrambled) + line + point + x(year) + y(life) + title("line")) |
  (data(scrambled) + path + point + x(year) + y(life) + title("path"))


((data(scrambled) + line + point + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + title("line")) |
  (data(scrambled) + path + point + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + title("path")))


(data(scrambled) + line + point + x(:year) + y(:life) + title("line")) |
  (data(scrambled) + path + point + x(:year) + y(:life) + title("path"))


beside(plot(data(scrambled), line, point, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  title("line")),
  plot(data(scrambled), path, point, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  title("path")))






                                           1960 1970 1980 1990 2000   55 60 65 70  line Life Year


                                     1960 1970 1980 1990 2000    path Year






“Given scrambled: a line, and also points, x is year, y is life, beside a path, and also points, x is year, y is life.”
The line joins the five points from left to right. The path starts at 1992, the first row, and goes to 1962, 2002, 1972 and 1982 in turn, so it runs back and forth and crosses itself. So choosing between the two is choosing whether the order of your rows carries meaning. With line the row order cannot carry meaning; with path the row order sets the whole shape.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.3 Multiple series
The chapter’s first plot drew one stroke through all five countries, and gog asked for a color or a group. Here is the same table with color(country) added in the upper plot and group(country) in the lower one. Both split the single stroke into a line per country:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
   title("color(country)")) /
  (data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
     title("group(country)"))


((data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
   title("color(country)")) /
  (data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
     title("group(country)")))


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:country) +
  title("color(country)")) /
  (data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  title("group(country)"))


below(plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  color(col.country), title("color(country)")),
  plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), title("group(country)")))






                                    40 50 60 70 80  color(country) Life  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 


                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  group(country) Life Year






“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country, above lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country.”
Each unique value in country becomes a separate line in both. color does two things at once. It splits the rows into one line per country, and it paints each line its own color, with a legend, so you can tell which line belongs to which country. group does only the first: the lines in the lower plot are split, all in one color, and no legend is drawn. Use it when the overall pattern of the lines matters and the name of each line does not, as in the Many groups recipe.

title: 9  Line
section: 9.4 Layering a line over other marks
text:
9.4 Layering a line over other marks
A line shows the trend and hides where the measurements were. A dot at each row shows them again, which is why line and point are so often combined. Where you write color decides which of the two it colors. Written before the marks, it belongs to the plot, so both layers use it. Written after a mark, it belongs to that mark alone (Which marks a channel reaches). The three plots below show each place. Outside the outer parentheses, theme(height = 900) sets the height of the whole figure, so each of the three plots has room:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) + line + point +
    title("color(country) before the marks")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + color(country) + point +
      title("color(country) after line")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + group(country) + point +
      color(country) + title("color(country) after point"))) +
  theme(height = 900)


(((data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) + line + point +
    title("color(country) before the marks")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + line + color(col.country) + point +
      title("color(country) after line")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + line + group(col.country) + point +
      color(col.country) + title("color(country) after point"))) +
  theme(height = 900))


((data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:country) + line +
  point + title("color(country) before the marks")) /
  (data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + color(:country) +
  point + title("color(country) after line")) /
  (data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  point + color(:country) + title("color(country) after point"))) +
  theme(height = 900)


below(below(plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  color(col.country), line, point,
  title("color(country) before the marks")),
  plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  color(col.country), point, title("color(country) after line"))),
  plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), point, color(col.country),
  title("color(country) after point")), theme({ height: 900 }))






                                                                                                   40 50 60 70 80  color(country) before the marks Life  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 


                                                                                                 40 50 60 70 80  color(country) after line Life  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 


                                                                                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  color(country) after point Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 






“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, lines and also points, above x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also points, above x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, and also points colored by country.”
In the top plot, the lines and the points share one color per country. In the middle plot, color(country) follows line, so only the lines are colored. In the bottom plot, it follows point, so it splits and colors only the points. The line is split by group(country), written after line, which splits without coloring. A layer that takes no color is drawn in dark gray whenever the plot has a color legend, so it cannot be mistaken for a country (Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped).
The bottom plot uses color and group together, and it shows what each one is for:



Channel
Splits the rows

Draws a legend

So write color on the layer that should show which country is which, and group on any other layer that has to be split the same way. Here the points carry the colors and the legend. The line is split by group, so it does not zigzag through all five countries, as the chapter’s first plot did.

9.4.1 Giving each layer its own appearance
You do not have to map a column to color at all. Sometimes you want one color for the lines and another for the points, chosen by you rather than read from the data. That is a setting, written style(color = ), and no legend appears. group(country) still keeps one line per country: it splits without coloring. A style() applies only to the nearest mark before it, so each layer can be styled on its own:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  point + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line + group(col.country) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  point + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  style(color = "steelblue") + point +
  style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "steelblue" }), point,
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 3 }),
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer"))






                                                                                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Blue line, red points: styled per layer Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, colored steelblue, and also points, colored firebrick, with size 3.”
A channel can belong to the whole plot or to one layer. Written before any mark, it belongs to the plot and reaches every layer, as color(country) did above. Written after a mark, it belongs to that mark alone, like style(), so each layer can map a different column. The whole rule, for every atom, is one table in Encoding scope:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line  + color(country) +
  point + size(population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line  + color(col.country) +
  point + size(col.population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + color(:country) +
  point + size(:population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  color(col.country), point, size(col.population),
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points"))






                                                                                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Color on the lines, size on the points Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep.   Population    20.9M  669.8M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also points sized by population.”
Each layer maps its own column here: color(country) reaches only the lines, and size(population) only the points.

title: 9  Line
section: 9.5 A category on the domain: the profile
text:
9.5 A category on the domain: the profile
In Point, swapping the two bindings turned a strip plot on its side. Whether a swap turns a line depends on its columns, because a line’s two axes have two different jobs. One is the domain, the axis the line is read along. The other is the measure, the quantity it traces.
A bar draws horizontally when you swap its bindings, because the axis that holds its categorical column is the axis that holds the slots. A line reads its domain the same way when it has a categorical column: the category is always the domain. But a line’s two columns are usually both numbers, such as year and life, and then nothing in the columns says which one to read along. So with two numbers, the domain is always x. The quarterly table, despite its name, holds one sales figure for each year. With the years on x, the line is the plot you expect:



quarterly: first 5 of 19 rows


year
sales




2005

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + line + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years")


(data(quarterly) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years"))


data(quarterly) + line + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years")


plot(data(quarterly), line, x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years"))






                                 2005 2010 2015 2020   100 120 140 160 180  Years on x: sales read along the years Sales Year





“Given quarterly: a line, x is year, y is sales.”
Sales climbed for most of the years. They fell in 2008 and 2009, and again in 2020, and rose again after each fall. Swap the two bindings and the line still sorts along x, which is now sales. The stroke starts at 2009, the year with the lowest sales. Later it climbs from 2012 to 2020 and drops back to 2013, because 2020’s sales fall between those of 2012 and 2013. tick_count = 20 on the year axis gives it a tick for every year, so each one can be read (tick_count):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + line + x(sales) + y(year, tick_count = 20) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x")


(data(quarterly) + line + x(col.sales) + y(col.year, tick_count = 20) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x"))


data(quarterly) + line + x(:sales) + y(:year, tick_count = 20) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x")


plot(data(quarterly), line, x(col.sales), y(col.year, { tick_count: 20 }),
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x"))






                                                               100 120 140 160 180   2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023  The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x Year Sales





“Given quarterly: a line, x is sales, y is year with 20 ticks.”
The zigzag seems to show a value that rose and fell many times. It does not. Each segment joins a year to the year with the next higher sales, not to the next year, so the rises and falls come from the sorting. Only the overall slope is real, and only because sales were mostly higher in later years.
So the swap has two outcomes. When both columns are numbers, the line still sorts along x, and the swap draws a different picture, as above. When one column is a category, the swap moves it to y, and the line is read down the page, as The profile, turned shows below.
Sometimes a continuous domain has to run up the page, as depth does in a plot of ocean temperature, or as the years do here. Then write path instead. A path joins the rows in the order the table holds them. The quarterly table is sorted by year, so the path runs up the page from the first year to the last. That is the vertical series the line could not draw:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + path + x(sales) + y(year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order")


(data(quarterly) + path + x(col.sales) + y(col.year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order"))


data(quarterly) + path + x(:sales) + y(:year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order")


plot(data(quarterly), path, x(col.sales), y(col.year),
  title("The same rows, joined in table order"))






                                 100 120 140 160 180   2005 2010 2015 2020  The same rows, joined in table order Year Sales





“Given quarterly: a path, x is sales, y is year.”
Now put a category on the domain. Connecting one summary per category is the profile plot. The gapminder_2007 table holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007, with its continent, life expectancy, population and GDP per person:

data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +

(data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +

                                      Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  line * mean + x(continent): one value per category, joined Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
The mean transform is what makes the profile readable. Without it, a line connects all 142 rows across five category slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(continent) + y(life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), line, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a line, x is continent, y is life.”
No reader can follow that. Inside each slot the stroke runs up and down through every country, and between slots it joins the last country of one slot to the first country of the next. gog prints a message in your session when several rows of one line share an x value. In Africa, 52 countries share one slot. mean leaves exactly one point per category, so the stroke joins five summaries instead of 142 rows.
Does the connection mean anything? That depends on your data. Nothing was measured between Africa and the Americas, and the segment is still drawn there. If you read only the vertices, the segments help you compare the five heights. If you read the segments themselves, they claim a change that never happened. gog draws what you wrote. You decide whether your data supports the connection. When it does not, keep the mean and change the mark to bar. A bar is in its own slot and claims nothing between one slot and the next. An ordered category, such as a grade, a clothing size or a survey scale, suits a line when its order is declared, because then the line has a direction to follow. Without a declared order, gog places the categories in the order they first appear in the rows (Declaring the order of categories). Two years stored as text, in a declared order, are such a category. One line for each country, from its value in the first year to its value in the second, is the slope chart (Comparing categories).
Continents have no order, but a straight axis must still put one of them first and another last. A circle has no first or last place. Drop the point layer and add polar(), and the same profile is drawn around a circle. That is the radar chart, and it needs no new atom:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), polar(), title("line * mean + polar(): the radar"))






                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  line * mean + polar(): the radar Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, in polar.”
Look at the segment from Oceania back to Asia. On the flat profile the line has two ends, because a straight axis has two ends. In the circle the five categories are spread around the whole ring, so the last one is beside the first and the line closes. No atom was added to close the ring. A categorical angular axis wraps around the circle, so a line drawn along it closes into a ring. The Polar chapter covers this in full.

9.5.1 The profile, turned
Long category names, or many categories, are easier to read down the left side of a plot than along the bottom, as the horizontal strip showed for points. A profile can turn the same way. Put the category on y and the number on x, and the category is still the domain: the line joins one value per category, read from top to bottom.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("line * mean + y(continent): the profile, turned")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("line * mean + y(continent): the profile, turned"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(:life) +
  y(:continent) + x_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("line * mean + y(continent): the profile, turned")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, mean), layer(point, mean),
  x(col.life), y(col.continent), x_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("line * mean + y(continent): the profile, turned"))






                                      60 70 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  line * mean + y(continent): the profile, turned Continent Mean life expectancy





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean, x is life, y is continent.”
The five means are the ones in the profile above, and only the direction changed. Asia, the first continent in the table, is at the top, and mean now groups the rows by y. step, area and ribbon turn the same way, because a category is their domain too, on either axis.
A category on y turns a line even when you want the line to follow x. With a rank stored as text, such as "1st", on y and the year on x, the line is read down the ranks, not along the years. Why not line? shows those lines above the bump chart that path draws instead.
A profile does not need a summary. Each line can instead follow one thing measured several times, such as one flower through its four measurements, and group names the column that says which rows belong to it.
You may know the iris data as a wide table: 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species, with one row for each flower. Its species is in one column, and its four measurements (sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width) are in four more. In that table the measurements are column names, not values in a column, so x cannot read them.
A profile needs a long table instead, with one row for each measurement of each flower: measurement holds the name, and cm the value in centimeters. In the wide table, a row was a flower. In the long table each flower has four rows, and the flower column says which four belong together. You reshape a table, turning its columns into rows, in the language you already use, as The table has to be tidy explains. iris_measurements is that long table, 150 flowers in 600 rows:

So in the upper plot, color(species) alone makes three lines. Each runs up and down through the values of 50 flowers at every measurement, then jumps to the next measurement. In the lower plot, group(flower) gives each flower its own line, and color still colors it by species:

    style(opacity = 0.4) + title("color(species) alone: three lines")) /
   (data(iris_measurements) + line + x(col.measurement) + y(col.cm) + color(col.species) +
      group(col.flower) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
      title("color(species) + group(flower): 150 lines"))) +

title: 9  Line
text:
9.6 Smoothed trend line
People in richer countries tend to live longer. The relationship between gdp and life is positive: as one rises, the other tends to rise as well. Sometimes the direction of a relationship is all a reader needs to know. Combine line with the smooth transform to draw a trend line fitted through all the rows instead of the rows themselves:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth))






                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
The point layer keeps every country visible, and smooth reduces the same rows to one fitted curve. Only the line layer carries the transform, so the points are untouched.
smooth does not average the rows at each x value. The mean transform does that, and line * mean draws it. In Basic usage, five countries share each year, so their average means something. Here each country has its own gdp, so the average at each x would be the row itself. smooth computes the curve at 100 evenly spaced places along x instead. At each place, it fits a straight line through the 75% of the rows whose x is nearest to that place. Nearer rows get more weight in that fit. Each fit gives one value at its place, and the line joins those values (smooth has the details).
smooth is not only for line. Four other marks take it too, and each draws the same fitted curve in its own way:



Mark derived by smooth
What it draws




point * smooth
one dot at each fitted value


area * smooth
the curve filled to the baseline


bar * smooth
one thin bar at each fitted value


step * smooth
the curve as a staircase


line * smooth
the fitted curve above

title: 9  Line
text:
9.7 A running total
A line can show how a quantity adds up over time. The cumulative transform adds each year’s value to the years before it, so the line passes through the total so far. The quarterly table, shown in A category on the domain, holds one year of sales in each row:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + line * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("Sales so far, since 2005")


(data(quarterly) + line * cumulative + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  title("Sales so far, since 2005"))


data(quarterly) + line * cumulative + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  title("Sales so far, since 2005")


plot(data(quarterly), layer(line, cumulative), x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  title("Sales so far, since 2005"))






                             2005 2010 2015 2020   0 1K 2K  Sales so far, since 2005 Cumulative Year





“Given quarterly: a line derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales.”
The line ends at 2,595, the sales of all 19 years. It always rises, because the sales of every year are positive. The rise from one year to the next is the sales of the later year. So the flattest piece is the one that ends at 2009, when sales fell to 88. With color or group, each line adds up its own rows.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.8 Two boundaries from a pair
Sometimes the answer at each x is two values rather than one: a lowest and a highest, or the spread around a mean. Most transforms compute one value per x. A pair transform gives it two, a low and a high. A line then draws both boundaries as two separate lines, not one zigzag joining them. A ribbon takes the same pair and fills the band between the two boundaries; a line draws only the boundaries. There are six pair transforms: range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band and bounds. The gapminder_asia table, shown in Basic usage, holds five countries. Here are the lowest and the highest life expectancy among them in each year, drawn as two lines:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(line, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines"))






                                1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines Life expectancy Year





“Given gapminder Asia: a line derived by range, x is year, y is life.”
Add style(pattern = "dashed") for the dashed band often used in published figures. That plot is in Ribbon, which shows the same pair filled and then as two dashed edges.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.9 Stroke width and opacity
You may want thicker lines for a slide, or fainter ones where many lines cross. A line takes one width and one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. style() sets them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ size: 4, opacity: 0.45 }),
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer"))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  One width, one opacity, for the whole layer Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, with size 4 and opacity 0.45.”
A mapped color is different: it can change along one line. gog draws that line as short segments, one color each, so the color changes at every vertex. A width could change at every vertex in the same way, and some libraries draw that. gog does not: it keeps one width and one opacity for the whole layer. Mapping gdp to size is refused, and the message says to set one width with style(size = ):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) + size(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) + size(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  size(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), size(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `size` cannot be bound to `line` — a line takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `gdp` mapping and set it with `style(size = )`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Mapping the same column to color is allowed. Each country’s line changes color along its length, and the legend is a ramp rather than one color per country:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  color(gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Each country's line, colored by its income")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  color(col.gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Each country's line, colored by its income"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  color(:gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each country's line, colored by its income")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), color(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  palette("viridis"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Each country's line, colored by its income"))






                                                                                     1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Each country's line, colored by its income Life expectancy Year  Gdp            31.7K 3560.4 400.4 





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, color by gdp on a log scale, with the viridis palette.”
Read one country’s line from left to right and you see two variables. The height is how long people live, and the color is how rich the country was then. The width is the same along every line; only the color changes. group still splits the mark into one line per country; color carries the second variable, income. A categorical color splits and colors at the same time, as Multiple series showed above.
palette() chooses the colors a mapping uses. "viridis" is a ramp, and the named palettes and what each is for are in Palettes.
Two questions look alike and are not the same: “Does this mark have this property?” and “Can a column be mapped here?” For a line’s width, the first answer is yes and the second is no. For its color, both answers are yes. Setting vs mapping uses a line as its clearest case.
Setting one pale color on a layer is the usual way to make another layer easier to see:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line + group(col.country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + line * smooth +
  style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, smooth),
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 3 }),
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red"))






                                      1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Every country in gray, the trend in red Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, colored lightgray, and also a line derived by smooth, colored firebrick, with size 3.”
Each layer here carries its own style(). A style() applies only to the nearest mark before it, and to no other mark. The first one colors the five country lines light gray, and the second colors and thickens only the trend. The first one does not reach the trend: without the second, the trend would be drawn in the default blue. Unlike a channel, style() cannot belong to the whole plot. Written before any mark, it is refused, because it has no mark to style. In style and the layer it follows, only the points have a style(), and the trend line keeps its default color.

9.10 Each country and its continent’s mean or median
The plot above draws five countries and one trend. The gm_all table holds 142 countries, measured every five years from 1952 to 2007. In one panel, 142 gray lines are too many to read. One trend through all of them would also hide how the continents differ. So draw one panel for each continent, with its countries in gray and their mean as one blue line.
The sentence below has two line layers. The first draws one gray line for each country, as above. The second is line * mean. In each year, mean averages the values of the countries, so it leaves one value per year, and the line joins those values. | facet(continent) splits the whole plot into one panel per continent. Every layer is split the same way, so the blue line in each panel is the mean of that continent’s countries. Faceting explains the operator in full.

“Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, and also a line derived by mean, split into panel columns by continent.”
The blue line is the continent’s mean, and the gray lines show how far each country was from it. Every continent’s mean rose over the whole period, but Africa’s stopped rising for fifteen years. It rose from 39 years in 1952 to 53 in 1987, and in 2002 it was still 53. In 22 of Africa’s 52 countries, life expectancy was lower in 2002 than in 1987. In Zimbabwe it fell from 62 years to 40. The table has only two countries in Oceania, Australia and New Zealand, so the blue line almost covers their two gray lines.
smooth summarizes the same rows another way. Instead of averaging the countries in each year, it fits a curve to each continent’s rows, as Smoothed trend line describes:

  style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, smooth),
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 3 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),

  across(col.continent))

“Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, and also a line derived by smooth, split into panel columns by continent.”
In four of the five panels, the red curve has nearly the same shape as the blue line in the previous plot, because those means rise at a nearly steady rate. In Africa they differ. The mean line stops rising after 1987 and falls a little in 2002. The red curve only rises more slowly, so it hides the stop. The mean line passes through each of the 12 yearly averages, so it shows every change of direction. Each point of the smooth curve is fitted from the rows of the nine nearest of the 12 years. Those nine years cover a period of 40 years, so a stop of 15 years becomes a gentle bend.
Use mean when you want the average at each x value, with every change in it. It needs many rows at each value, as here, where every country has a row for each year. Use smooth when you want the general direction, or when no two rows share an x value, as in Smoothed trend line.
Income is a second way to compare the continents. The two layers of the mean plot can draw GDP per person, with two changes to the sentence. The first change is the scale. GDP per person runs from a few hundred dollars to more than a hundred thousand, so the next plot draws it on a log scale. On this scale each labeled tick is ten times the one below it, so the poorer countries are not crowded together at the bottom.
The second change is the summary. gog computes mean in dollars, and only then places the result on the log axis (The measured value keeps its own units). In dollars, one very rich country can raise the mean far above most of the others. In 1952, Kuwait’s GDP per person was 108,382 dollars, and Asia’s mean was 5,195. Sorted from poorest to richest, the middle one of Asia’s 33 countries had 1,207, less than a quarter of the mean. In the Asia panel, a mean line would therefore run above most of the gray lines. The median is that middle value, and sorting the countries gives the same order in dollars as in logarithms. So line * median has half of the gray lines above it and half below, on a log axis too:

  y_label("GDP per person") +

  y_label("GDP per person") +
  title("GDP per person on five continents") | facet(col.continent))

  group(:country) + style(color = "lightgray") + line * median +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 3) + y_label("GDP per person") +
  title("GDP per person on five continents") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gm_all), x(col.year), y(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, median),
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 3 }), y_label("GDP per person"),
  title("GDP per person on five continents"), across(col.continent))

“Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is gdp on a log scale, lines grouped by country, and also a line derived by median, split into panel columns by continent.”
The medians grew at very different rates. Europe’s rose from 5,142 dollars in 1952 to 28,054 in 2007, more than five times its 1952 value. Africa’s rose from 987 dollars to 1,452, less than one and a half times its 1952 value. In 2002 it was lower than in 1972.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.11 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a line takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
bin, count, density, proportion
—


Summaries
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile
—


Fitted lines
smooth, straight
—


Running total
cumulative
—


Pairs: a low and a high
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds
—


Collision modifiers
—
dodge, stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
—
partition, flow, layout, cluster



The plots below show every transform a line takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change.
Counting. count and proportion tally the rows at each value of x, on a category or a number. bin and density work on a number. bin counts the rows in each interval, and density estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty, and the line joins the results in order along x. With bin, the stroke passes through the center of each bin, and the plot is called a frequency polygon. The top two plots put continent on x, and the plot below them puts life:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + line * count + x(continent) + title("line * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("line * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * bin + x(life) + title("line * bin"))


(((data(gapminder_2007) + line * count + x(col.continent) + title("line * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * proportion + x(col.continent) +
     title("line * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * bin + x(col.life) + title("line * bin")))


((data(gapminder_2007) + line * count + x(:continent) +
  title("line * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("line * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * bin + x(:life) + title("line * bin"))

  x(col.continent), title("line * count")),

Look at the y axis of the four plots above, from line * count to line * density. None of the four sentences writes y(), yet each y axis has a name: Count, Proportion, Count and Density. The table has no column by those names. Each transform writes one, and y draws it. count and bin write count, the number of rows at each value or in each interval. proportion writes proportion, each count’s share of all the rows. density writes density, the height of the estimated curve. The axis is labeled with the column’s name, capitalized, as The name on a measure axis explains.
The two plots on top have the same shape, because each proportion is a count divided by 142, the number of countries. In those two plots, read only the vertices. Nothing was measured between two continents, as A category on the domain explains.

Fitted lines. smooth and straight need a number on each axis. They fit a line to the rows, each placed at its x and its y. smooth follows the shape of the data, and straight is the least-squares line. Each fit gives a value at evenly spaced places along x, 100 unless you set places, and the line joins those values into one stroke. Smoothed trend line draws smooth over the countries and says how it fits, and Each country and its continent’s mean or median compares it with mean.

Some reports use a 99% interval, or lines two standard deviations from the mean. Write the number in parentheses after the transform’s name. confidence takes the confidence level, a number greater than 0 and less than 1, so 0.95 rather than 95. A line refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as bar and point. A line is a thin stroke, so two lines that meet cross instead. To pile one series on another, use stack with area. repel moves only text labels. partition, flow and cluster lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which zone, ribbon and path draw. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.12 What you can set
A setting changes how the stroke looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a line’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash, longdash



A line is a stroke, so size sets its width and pattern sets whether it is solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash or longdash. A setting gives the whole layer one value. A channel reads a column instead, so what is drawn follows the data.
Two of the four settings in the list above, color and pattern, are also channels. color(country) draws one color per country. A mapped pattern gives each series its own stroke pattern instead. pattern has five values for a stroke, including solid. gog assigns them in the order the categories first appear in the table, and this plot shows that order:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


stroke_patterns <- data.frame(
  stroke_pattern = c("solid", "solid", "dashed", "dashed", "dotted", "dotted",
                     "dotdash", "dotdash", "longdash", "longdash"),
  at             = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2),
  level          = c(5, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1)
)
data(stroke_patterns) + line + x(at) + y(level) + pattern(stroke_pattern) +
  style(size = 2) + x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The five stroke patterns")


stroke_patterns = {

  "level": [5, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1],
}

  style(size = 2) + x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The five stroke patterns"))

  level = [5, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1],
)

Of the four, only color can be mapped to a continuous column, and the color then changes along a single line. Stroke width and opacity shows this after a refused size.

Each property takes its value from one source: a column, or you. Here color reads a column, and size and pattern are set, so no property is given a value twice. Ask for both on one property and gog refuses, rather than dropping one in silence. Setting vs mapping shows the refusal.
A transform’s own arguments are neither a mapping nor a setting. They change what is computed, not how it is drawn. line * density(adjust = 1.5) widens the bandwidth, so the curve is smoother than the default one. Choosing the bandwidth draws a density line twice as smooth. The Transforms chapter lists what each transform takes.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

9.13 What it refuses
A line takes only the stroke patterns. "hatch" is a fill texture, and a line has no area to fill.

Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = "hatch")` is not a stroke pattern. Use "solid" (the default), "dashed", "dotted", "dotdash", "longdash".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The refusal lists the five values pattern does take on a stroke. Five more refusals follow from this chapter’s rules. The first is a turned profile in polar(). Bent into a circle, its measure would run around the circle and its categories out along the radius, which is not the radar. The message says that a profile turned that way does not bend into polar(), and it writes the radar’s sentence instead, with the category on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(life) + y(continent) + polar()


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) + polar()

  y(col.continent), polar())




Error:
! gog: `line` is read down `y` here, because `y(continent)` is categorical, and a profile turned that way does not bend into `polar()`. Put the category on `x`: `line * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + polar()` is the radar.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The second is a category on both axes. A line traces a value across its categories, so one axis must hold a continuous column, and with categories on both there is nothing to trace:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(continent) + y(country)

Each continent is now a series that holds one mean, so nothing would be drawn, and gog refuses the sentence. A split from color, group, pattern, facet or play is refused in the same way, when it leaves one position in every series and no other layer draws. When only some series hold one position, gog draws the others and prints a message naming the ones it left out. Add point with the line’s transform, such as point * mean, and those positions are drawn as well, as in Layering a line over other marks.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.14 In short
A categorical color, a group or a mapped pattern splits the rows into one line per category. Each line needs at least two positions. Without a split, one stroke joins every row. A line sorts along its domain, so row order means nothing to it. A category is the domain on either axis, and with two numbers the domain is x. A line takes one width and one opacity for the whole layer, and only color changes along it.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.15 What comes next
You read a line by comparing its values with each other, so its axis need not reach zero. Bar measures from zero instead, so one bar’s length has a meaning by itself.

title: 10  Bar
text:
10.1 Basic usage
How large is each category? bar draws a rectangle from the baseline (zero) to the value for each row. Bars are vertical when the categories are on x and horizontal when they are on y; see Horizontal bars.
The bar chart exists because William Playfair had too little data. His Commercial and Political Atlas of 1786 drew England’s imports and exports as two curves across thirty years (Playfair, 1786). For Scotland he had a single year, and no curve can show one year. So he drew a bar for each of Scotland’s trading partners instead, and wrote that the result was a weaker picture than a curve, because it showed no change over time. The form he apologized for became the one everyone knows.
Two names for it are still in use, and they name opposite orientations. Much of the business world, Excel included, calls this a column chart when the bars are vertical, and uses bar chart only when they are horizontal. gog has one bar, and its direction comes from whichever axis carries the category. A third name, histogram, belongs to a different plot drawn with the same mark. Karl Pearson introduced the word in the 1890s (Pearson, 1895) for the picture of a distribution. Its bars cover intervals cut from a continuous axis, and neighboring bars touch. In gog that plot is bar * bin, shown in Histogram below.
Which country won the most gold medals? Most examples in this chapter start from the smallest sentence that draws a bar: a source, the mark, and its two positions. The medals table holds one row for each of five countries, and each row gives the number of Olympic gold, silver and bronze medals that country won. The book’s data describes it and every other table in the book.

10.2 Color
Every bar is the same color until you map a column to color. With a color for each bar, a reader can find one country quickly and match it to the same country in another plot, as long as that plot also colors by country. Bind color to the column that is already on x, and color fills each bar with a distinct color:

  color(country)

  color(col.country))

title: 10  Bar
text:
10.3 Ordering bars
In what order should the bars appear? A reader looking for the largest value wants it first. A reader looking for one name wants the names in alphabetical order. order() controls the sequence of categories along whichever axis carries them: x on a vertical plot, y on a horizontal one. You can sort on the categorical column itself, on the measured column, or on a third column of numbers. After bar * count, you can also sort on the count. Naming the categorical column asks for that column’s own order. Here that is alphabetical, because order() sorts plain text such as country from A to Z. A column with a declared order uses that order instead.
Default, data order (rows as they appear in the table) is the order of the plot in Basic usage.
By value, descending, tallest bar first, the usual order for a ranking:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: largest first")

  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  title("Gold medals: largest first"))

  title("Gold medals: largest first")


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), title("Gold medals: largest first"))

title: 10  Bar
text:
10.4 Duplicate categories
A table often holds several rows for one category, one per event or one per year. The question is still how large each category is in total. Without a transform, bar draws one bar per row, and rows that share a category share a slot. This table has two rows each for USA and GBR:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


medals_dup <- data.frame(
  country = c("USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"),
  gold    = c(10, 5, 8, 4, 6)
)
data(medals_dup) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform")


medals_dup = {
  "country": ["USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"],
  "gold": [10, 5, 8, 4, 6],
}
(data(medals_dup) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform"))


medals_dup = (
  country = ["USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"],
  gold = [10, 5, 8, 4, 6],
)
data(medals_dup) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform")


const medals_dup = {
  country: ["USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"],
  gold: [10, 5, 8, 4, 6],
};
plot(data(medals_dup), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform"))






                                   USA GBR JPN   0 2 4 6 8 10  Duplicate rows: no transform Gold Country





“Given the medals dup table: bars, x is country, y is gold.”
Every bar grows from zero, so the shorter ones are drawn inside the tallest. USA has rows of 10 and 5, and its bar reads 10 rather than 15. Each bar is drawn slightly translucent, so the color is darker where two bars overlap. For USA, that darker band ends at 5, where the shorter bar stops. That band is the only sign that a category has extra rows. When two rows hold the same value, the two bars cover each other exactly. The whole bar is then darker than a bar of one row, and no band shows, so the darker color is the only sign.
Use the sum transform to total the values per category first:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) + title("Totals: bar * sum")


(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) + title("Totals: bar * sum"))


data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + title("Totals: bar * sum")


plot(data(medals_dup), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), title("Totals: bar * sum"))






                            USA GBR JPN   0 5 10 15  Totals: bar * sum Gold Country





“Given the medals dup table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”
sum gives one number for each category. It reads every row that shares a category and totals them. USA’s 10 and 5 become 15, and GBR’s 8 and 4 become 12. Five rows become three bars, one for each country, and the darker band is gone.
count, from Ordering bars, also draws one bar for each category, but it measures something else. sum adds up the values in a column, here gold on y. count counts the rows in each category and reads no column. It writes its count on y itself, so y(gold) is refused (What it refuses). On this table it gives USA 2, GBR 2 and JPN 1, the number of rows for each country:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
   title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(country) +
     title("bar * count: rows counted"))


((data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
   title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(col.country) +
     title("bar * count: rows counted")))


(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(:country) +
  title("bar * count: rows counted"))


beside(plot(data(medals_dup), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country),
  y(col.gold), title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")),
  plot(data(medals_dup), layer(bar, count), x(col.country),
  title("bar * count: rows counted")))

                              USA GBR JPN   0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0  bar * count: rows counted Count Country






“Given the medals dup table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, beside bars derived by count, x is country.”
Use sum when you ask how much each category holds in total, such as gold medals or sales. Use count when you ask how many rows each category has, such as the countries of each continent.

title: 10  Bar
text:
10.5 Negative values
A bar can also point the other way, when a value is below zero, such as the profit of a quarter that lost money. Every bar starts at zero. That rule made the duplicate bars overlap, and it is also why a negative bar points down. So you write nothing extra for a negative value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


balance <- data.frame(quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
                      profit  = c(12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0))
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero")


balance = {
  "quarter": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  "profit": [12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0],
}
(data(balance) + bar + x(col.quarter) + y(col.profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero"))


balance = (
  quarter = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit = [12, -5, 8, -2],
)
data(balance) + bar + x(:quarter) + y(:profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero")


const balance = {
  quarter: ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit: [12, -5, 8, -2],
};
plot(data(balance), bar, x(col.quarter), y(col.profit),
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero"))






                               Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4   -5 0 5 10  Negative values grow downward from zero Profit Quarter





“Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit.”
To color the losses and the profits differently, you need a column that says which is which, because gog does not decide which bars are losses. Map that column with color, and let palette() say which colors the mapping uses. The table below sets the column’s values by hand. In practice you compute it from profit with one condition. Above zero is a profit, and anything else is a loss.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


balance <- data.frame(
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
  profit  = c(12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0),
  result  = factor(c("profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"),
                   levels = c("loss", "profit"))
)
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) + color(result) +
  palette(c("firebrick", "seagreen")) +
  title("Red below zero, green above")


import pandas as pd

balance = {
  "quarter": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  "profit": [12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0],
  "result": pd.Categorical(["profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"], categories=["loss", "profit"]),
}
(data(balance) + bar + x(col.quarter) + y(col.profit) + color(col.result) +
  palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]) +
  title("Red below zero, green above"))


using CategoricalArrays
balance = (
  quarter = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit = [12, -5, 8, -2],
  result = CategoricalArray(["profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"]; levels = ["loss", "profit"]),
)
data(balance) + bar + x(:quarter) + y(:profit) + color(:result) +
  palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]) +
  title("Red below zero, green above")


const balance = {
  quarter: ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit: [12, -5, 8, -2],
  result: ordered(["profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"], ["loss", "profit"]),

  palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]),

“Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit, color by result, with a palette of firebrick and seagreen.”
palette() assigns its colors in category order, and that is why result carries a declared order here instead of being plain text. palette() does not sort plain text, and order() does not move its colors: it assigns them in the order the values first appear in the table. The first row here is a profit, so the palette would give firebrick to the profits. Declaring the order as loss, then profit, gives firebrick to the losses, and the legend lists them in that order. The colors then stay with their results, even if next year’s table starts with a loss. R spells that with a factor’s levels, Python with a pandas Categorical, Julia with a CategoricalArray, and JavaScript with ordered(). This is the same mechanism as Declaring the order of categories.
Red for loss and green for profit is one common convention. It is also the hardest pair to separate for red-green color blindness, the most common kind. Texture solves that and keeps the colors, by giving each result its own texture as well as its own color. Texture below draws these bars that way, and Will it read in gray? in the cookbook applies the same idea to other plots.

10.6 Horizontal bars
Sometimes the bars should be horizontal. The category names may be too long for the bottom axis. Or there may be many categories, and a tall list of horizontal bars reads more easily than a crowded row of vertical ones. Swap the bindings, and put the categories on y and the measure on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(gold) + y(country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars")


(data(medals) + bar + x(col.gold) + y(col.country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars"))


data(medals) + bar + x(:gold) + y(:country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars")


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.gold), y(col.country),
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars"))






                                   0 10 20 30 40   Germany Russia Great Britain China USA  Categories on y: horizontal bars Country Gold





“Given the medals: bars, x is gold, y is country.”
If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip() or matplotlib’s barh(), gog has no such word, because it would be a second way to say one thing. gog takes the orientation from the bindings. The axis with the number is the one the bars grow along, so their length is read on it. The axis with the category is the one the bars are placed on, one slot each. Nothing else changes: order, transforms such as sum and bin, color and style() all behave as they do on vertical bars.
Horizontal bars help most when the category names are long. On a vertical axis each label is written across the page, so it does not have to fit inside one slot. The departments table holds the number of people (headcount) in each of five departments of one company. The department names are long:

order means the same thing in both orientations: the first category in sort order takes the first slot. Descending puts the largest bar leftmost on a vertical plot and topmost on a horizontal one.
Only one pair of columns says nothing about orientation: two columns of plain numbers, such as year and sales. gog has one rule for that case: it measures the column on y and draws vertical bars. So x(year) + y(sales) gives vertical bars. Swapping the two bindings does not make the bars horizontal. x(sales) + y(year) also gives vertical bars. 10.7 Texture
The profit and loss bars in Negative values are red and green, the pair hardest to distinguish for a reader with red-green color blindness. Give each result its own texture as well, and that reader can separate the bars without seeing color at all.
A bar’s fill can carry a texture: lines or dots repeated across the bar, in the bar’s color. You set it with style(pattern = ). A texture does not need color, so a hatched bar chart stays legible in grayscale or in a black-and-white print:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color")


(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color"))


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color")


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  style({ pattern: "hatch" }), title("A hatched bar reads without color"))






                                    USA China Great Britain Russia Germany   0 10 20 30 40  A hatched bar reads without color Gold Country





“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, with pattern hatch.”
style(pattern = ) gives every bar in the layer the same texture. To give each category its own texture, map a column with the pattern() channel, which does for texture what shape() does for glyphs. The plot below maps the texture column with pattern(). Each bar then shows one of the six fill textures, in this order: "solid" (the default, a plain fill), "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid" and "dots":

  texture = c("solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"),
  height  = c(6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1)
)

  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures")

  "texture": ["solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"],
  "height": [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
}
(data(textures) + bar + x(col.texture) + y(col.height) + pattern(col.texture) +
  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures"))

  texture = ["solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"],
  height = [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
)
data(textures) + bar + x(:texture) + y(:height) + pattern(:texture) +
  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures")

  texture: ["solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"],
  height: [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
};

The style chapter shows them beside the stroke patterns a line takes, because style(pattern = ) is one name whose values depend on the shape: fill textures on a fill, stroke patterns on a stroke.
