Line shows the same refusal for line.

title: 11  Area
text:
11.11 In short
An area reads a category as its domain, on either axis, as a bar does, so a category on y turns it down the page. With two numbers its domain is x. density reads a category on either axis as the slot its curve is drawn in. opacity belongs to the layer, and color to each region. Its extent comes from its x, its y and its baseline, so size is refused both ways.

title: 11  Area
text:
11.12 What comes next
An area’s top edge runs straight from one value to the next, so it shows the value changing steadily in between. Step shows instead that each value held until the next one, and then jumped.

title: 12  Step
text:
12.1 A step function
How do you draw a value that holds until it jumps? step draws it as a staircase. A line slopes straight from one point to the next. A step holds each value until it changes, then jumps. The flat part runs from one observation to the next, and the jump is where the value changes. That is the right shape for anything that does not change between observations: a cumulative count, a survival probability, an interest rate. step takes the same channels as line, and only the path drawn between two points differs.
Several professions draw this shape, each under its own name, and step draws each of these plots from a table that holds its values. Statisticians draw the empirical cumulative distribution function (the empirical CDF) with it. Medical researchers draw the survival curve, the Kaplan–Meier estimate (Kaplan & Meier, 1958), which drops at each observed death. Reliability engineers draw the same staircase for parts rather than patients, and call it a failure plot. Analysts in finance draw the step chart of a rate that holds until someone changes it. A cumulative count rises and a survival probability falls, and step draws both as this one staircase.
What share of European countries have a life expectancy at or below 75 years, or 80, or any value you choose? The empirical CDF answers all of those questions at once. It is a step function: flat between observations, with a jump at each one. The gm_europe_cdf table holds one row for each of the 30 European countries in 2007: its life expectancy, and the share of countries at or below it. Each country’s share is its rank by life expectancy divided by 30: the lowest has 1/30, about 0.033, and the highest has 1. The table already holds the shares, so step needs no transform: give it an x and a y, and it draws the curve:

The step is exact: between two countries no country is added, so the share does not change.
The cumulative transform computes the same shares from the countries themselves, in three steps. On a continuous axis, count tallies the rows at each distinct value. cumulative adds those tallies up from left to right, so at 75 years the running total is 8 countries. share = TRUE then divides each running total by the last one, the 30 countries. So 8 becomes 8/30, about 0.27, and the curve ends at 1. Without share = TRUE, the axis would count countries, from 0 to 30. The gm_europe table holds the same 30 countries, with no share column:

title: 12  Step
text:
12.4 A category on the domain
Every x so far has been a number. How does the mean life expectancy compare across continents? A step will draw that plot, but a bar is the better mark for it, as the step drawn below shows. A step reads one axis as its domain, the axis it runs along, and the other as its measure, the quantity it traces. A category is always the domain, so here the domain is x. A category on the domain gets one slot per value, an equal stretch of the axis for each continent, as in Line. The staircase holds each continent’s mean from the center of its slot to the center of the next one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + step * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("step * mean + x(continent): the five means as a staircase")

  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("step * mean + x(continent): the five means as a staircase"))


data(gapminder_2007) + step * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("step * mean + x(continent): the five means as a staircase")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(step, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("step * mean + x(continent): the five means as a staircase"))






                               Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  step * mean + x(continent): the five means as a staircase Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a step outline derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
Africa is lowest at 54.8 years and Oceania highest at 80.7. Oceania, the last slot, has no next slot, so its mean is only the top of the last jump. The five slots run in the order the continents first appear in the table. That order means nothing, so the rise and fall across the slots is not a trend.
Every flat part of a step is at one of the five means. A line slopes from one category to the next, so between them it passes through heights that are no continent’s mean.
That does not make it the right mark for this plot. A flat part claims that the value held across the part of the axis under it. A policy rate does hold between two dates, as A value that holds until it changes showed. Between two continents there is no value to hold, so the flat part there says nothing about the data. One summary value per category is what a bar draws: keep the mean and change the mark. Each bar is in its own slot, joined to nothing.
Other marks take the same mean, and only the shape changes:







Mark derived by mean
Shape

one bar per category, each in its own slot

one dot at each mean

the means joined into a profile


area * mean
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * mean
each mean held flat until the next category, the plot above



gog draws this step and prints no warning. It never refuses a sentence only because another mark would show the data better, so the choice of mark is yours (Law 8).

title: 12  Step

12.6 Stroke width and opacity
The three outlines above are thin, and where two of them run along the same bin edge, the one drawn last covers the other. A thicker stroke is easier to see, and a little transparency lets the covered stroke show through. Like line, a step is a single stroke per series, so on a step size and opacity cannot be mapped to a column; they are settings for the whole stroke:

  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("A thicker, more transparent outline")

  style(size = 2.5, opacity = 0.7) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("A thicker, more transparent outline"))

  style(size = 2.5, opacity = 0.7) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A thicker, more transparent outline")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(step, bin), x(col.petal_length),
  color(col.species), style({ size: 2.5, opacity: 0.7 }),
  x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("A thicker, more transparent outline"))

“Given the iris flowers: step outlines derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species, with size 2.5 and opacity 0.7.”
size sets the stroke width. opacity makes the whole staircase more transparent. Both are set, never mapped, exactly as on a line; Setting vs mapping explains the difference.
A mapped color is different: it is the one property that can change along a single staircase. A width and a stroke pattern (solid, dashed, dotted and others) belong to the whole stroke. A stroke pattern can still change from one series to the next, as it does for a line, but never along one series. A color belongs to each place on the stroke instead, so a column can change it from one row to the next. 12.7 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a step takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
bin, count, density, proportion

Summaries

—

smooth, straight

cumulative

range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds
—


Collision modifiers
—

Layouts of a whole picture
—
partition, flow, layout, cluster



The plots below show every transform a step takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change.
Counting. count and proportion tally the rows at each value of x, on a category or a number. bin and density work on a number. bin counts the rows in each interval, and density estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty. The top two plots put continent on x, and the plot below them puts life. With continent on x, the staircase holds each count from the center of one slot to the center of the next. A step refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. These are the same transforms a line refuses. The collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as bar and point. A step is a thin stroke, so two staircases that meet cross instead. A step is also read by its height, and a stack would raise each staircase by the ones below it, so its height would no longer be its own value. To pile one series on another, use stack with area, whose filled bands show what each series adds. repel moves only text labels. partition, flow and cluster lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which zone, ribbon and path draw. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 12  Step
text:
12.9 What it refuses
A step refuses four kinds of sentence: a mapped size or opacity, a fill texture, a category on both axes, and a split that leaves one position in every series. A step is one connected stroke with no filled interior, and the first two refusals follow from that. The third comes from the value a step traces, and the fourth from a series that holds a single position. A step also refuses two more sentences a line refuses, for the same reasons: a turned profile in polar(), and a step drawn over horizontal bars. The Line chapter shows both.
One stroke has one width, the same at every place along it. So no column can make the staircase wider in one place than in another. The gapminder_asia table, shown in Stroke width and opacity, holds five Asian countries:

The fourth is shared by line, area, ribbon and path. A staircase needs at least two positions in each series. A plot in which every series holds one would draw nothing, so gog refuses it, as Line shows.
A color mapped to a column is not refused: it is the one property that can change along a single staircase, as Stroke width and opacity shows.

title: 12  Step
text:
12.10 In short
A step holds each value until it changes, so between two observations it draws no value that was not in the data. It takes the same channels and settings as a line: width and opacity belong to the whole stroke, and only color varies along it. With color, group or a mapped pattern it draws one staircase per category, and with bin it draws a histogram as an outline instead of as bars.

title: 12  Step
text:
12.11 What comes next
Each staircase has one value at each x. Interval spans two values at every position instead, from a low one to a high one.




Kaplan, E. L., & Meier, P. (1958). Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 53(282), 457–481. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1958.10501452

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.1 A range per group
How far does each group reach, from its lowest value to its highest? interval draws a whisker for each group: a span from a low value to a high one, with a short line across each end called a cap. When the statistic behind the whisker has a center, such as the mean inside a confidence interval, a dot marks that center. interval is the mark that draws error bars and min–max ranges. A bar measures from a baseline up to a value. An interval has no baseline, so it needs both a low value and a high value before it can draw. Whiskers are vertical when the categories are on x and horizontal when they are on y; see Horizontal whiskers.
The name can mislead. You met range, confidence, deviation and bounds in the Line and Step chapters, and in statistics an interval is something computed, such as a confidence interval. So interval sounds like one more of those transforms. It is not a transform: interval is a mark, and it computes nothing. A transform computes a low and a high, and interval draws a whisker between them, just as line and step draw the same pair as two strokes.
Almost everyone calls this an error bar, and that name does not say what the whisker measures. Three different quantities are drawn as the same picture: the mean plus and minus one standard deviation, the mean plus and minus one standard error, and a confidence interval (CI) for the mean. On the iris data in this chapter, the standard deviation whisker is about three and a half times as long as the 95% confidence interval. Nothing in the drawing says which one it is, and a reader without a caption cannot know.
gog makes the sentence name the statistic instead. interval * deviation spans one standard deviation on each side of the mean. interval * confidence(0.95) spans a 95% confidence interval, and the level is written in the sentence. A standard error has no transform of its own: compute its two ends yourself, and interval * bounds(lower, upper) reads them from two columns. interval * range, drawn first below, spans the lowest value to the highest. The mark is the same whisker in all of them; what differs is the transform, and the transform is written down. That is the law Explicit Over Implicit, applied to one mark. The name error bar never says which statistic was drawn. A written sentence has to say it.
How far do the petal lengths of each species reach, from the shortest to the longest? The iris_flowers table holds 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species, measured in centimeters. One whisker per species answers the question, and a whisker needs a low value and a high value to span. Both come from a transform; Why interval needs a transform explains why. range reduces y to its minimum and maximum within each x group, and interval spans between them:

interval * range is written the same way as bar * mean. The difference is what the transform returns: mean returns one number per group, and range returns two. So you do not write a low and a high yourself. You write one column, petal_length on y, and the transform computes the low and the high from it. These two values are the extents, and the mark spans them.
range does not belong to interval alone. Three other marks take the same low and high values, and only the shape changes:
range is one of the six pair transforms you met in Two boundaries from a pair, which supply a low value and a high value where most transforms supply a single number. The other five are confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band and bounds, and every mark in that table takes all six. smooth_band and straight_band fit a curve of y against x, so they need a continuous column on both axes. With a category on x, as in every interval in this chapter, they are refused.

A box draws a similar summary in one mark, five numbers (the median, the two quartiles and the two whisker ends), and you cannot remove one of them.   title("Petal length per species, drawn in three layers"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range, and also intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, and also points derived by median, x is species, y is petal length.”
The gray whisker is the full range, the thick blue whisker is the middle half, and the gold dot is the median. The order of the layers decides what stays visible. A later layer is drawn over an earlier one, so the median is written last. Move it to the front of the sentence and the blue whisker draws over it, and almost none of the dot is left. If you have used ggplot2, this is the rule you already know: a geom added later draws on top. The dot is set opaque as well, since a point is slightly translucent by default.
The three layers name the three statistics they draw. A box plot draws similar information and names none of it, and its whiskers end in a different place. The Box chapter draws a box beside these three layers and shows where.
Because each statistic is its own layer, you can change one and leave the others as they are. Widen the blue whisker to range(0.1, 0.9) and the plot reports a different statistic, with the same marks. Drop the gray layer and the y axis is scaled to the blue whisker rather than to the extremes. Add a fourth layer with another pair of quantiles, range(0.1, 0.9), and the whiskers nest, each wider range drawn thinner and paler around the narrower one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) +
  interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
  interval * range(0.1, 0.9) + style(color = "lightsteelblue", size = 4) +
  interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
  point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
  x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Nested ranges: all, the middle 80%, the middle half")


(data(iris_flowers) +
  interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
  interval * range(0.1, 0.9) + style(color = "lightsteelblue", size = 4) +
  interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
  point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
  x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Nested ranges: all, the middle 80%, the middle half"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
  interval * range(0.1, 0.9) + style(color = "lightsteelblue", size = 4) +
  interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
  point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
  x(:species) + y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Nested ranges: all, the middle 80%, the middle half")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range),
  style({ color: "darkgray" }), layer(interval, range(0.1, 0.9)),
  style({ color: "lightsteelblue", size: 4 }),
  layer(interval, range(0.25, 0.75)),
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 8 }), layer(point, median),
  style({ color: "gold", size: 5, opacity: 1 }), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Nested ranges: all, the middle 80%, the middle half"))






                                                              setosa versicolor virginica   2 4 6  Nested ranges: all, the middle 80%, the middle half Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range, and also intervals derived by range from 0.1 to 0.9, and also intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, and also points derived by median, x is species, y is petal length.”
Read each species from the inside out: the middle half, the middle 80%, then every flower. The Ribbon chapter draws the same nested ranges as bands along a continuous axis. A box is still the shorter sentence when you want the median, the quartiles, the whiskers and the outlier rule together. How much to summarize draws one table in four ways, from every row to one value for each group, and says what each way loses.

title: 13  Interval
section: 13.4 A confidence interval, with a center
text:
13.4 A confidence interval, with a center
How precisely do fifty flowers estimate the average petal length of their species? That is a different question from how far the flowers spread, and it needs a different statistic. range shows the full spread. For the uncertainty of the mean, use confidence. It computes a t-interval for each group’s mean. That is the confidence interval named at the start of this chapter, and it widens when the group is small. confidence also keeps the mean as the center of the span, and the mark draws a dot there. A whisker with a dot at its center is a pointrange.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("95% CI of mean petal length"))






                                        setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5  95% CI of mean petal length Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length.”
The level is confidence’s only argument: a number greater than 0 and less than 1, so 0.95 rather than 95. It is 0.95 when you leave it out. A higher level draws a longer whisker, so confidence(0.99) is longer than confidence(0.95). The interval is always a t-interval. For a z-interval, a bootstrap interval, or an interval built from a model’s standard errors, compute the low and the high yourself, put them in two columns, and draw them with bounds.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.5 The spread of the data
How far is a typical flower from the average of its species? That is a question about the spread of the data, not about how well the average is known. The opening of this chapter named three quantities: a standard deviation, a standard error and a confidence interval. confidence draws the confidence interval. The standard deviation has a transform of its own, deviation:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, deviation), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))






                                          setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5 6  Mean petal length, with one standard deviation Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length.”
deviation with no argument reaches one standard deviation on each side of the mean. deviation(2) reaches two, so that whisker is four standard deviations long. Like confidence, it computes a mean as its center, so it draws a pointrange rather than a bare error bar, a whisker with no dot.
The standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the group size. confidence already computes it and draws the interval built from it, which is what a reader of the plot needs, so gog has no transform that draws the standard error alone. gog computes only a few intervals itself, and draws any other interval from two columns you computed before the plot. To draw one standard error on each side of the mean, compute the mean minus the standard error and the mean plus it, put them in two columns, and draw them with bounds.
deviation and confidence look alike and answer different questions. The two plots below both name petal_length on y, so they share that scale, drawn once down the left. Composition explains when two plots share a scale. Here are the two statistics on the same fifty flowers per species:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
   y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Spread of the data")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
     title("Uncertainty of the mean"))


((data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
   y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Spread of the data")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
     title("Uncertainty of the mean")))


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Spread of the data")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + title("Uncertainty of the mean"))


beside(plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, deviation),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Spread of the data")),
  plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), title("Uncertainty of the mean")))






                                            setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5 6  Spread of the data Petal length (cm) Species


                                     setosa versicolor virginica    Uncertainty of the mean Species






“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length, beside intervals derived by confidence, x is species, y is petal length.”
The whiskers on the right are less than a third as long, and the data is identical. The ratio is the same in all three species. The two statistics do not contradict each other. deviation describes how far the flowers are from their average, and measuring more of them does not make that whisker shorter. confidence describes how precisely the average itself is known. More flowers make its whisker shorter: four times as many flowers make it about half as long. So the ratio between the two whiskers comes from the group size. With six or fewer flowers per species, the confidence whisker is the longer one, because a t-interval widens when the group is small.
So choose the statistic by asking which caption you would write under the plot. “A versicolor petal is usually within half a centimeter of its species average” describes the left panel. “The average versicolor petal is 4.26 cm, and its 95% confidence interval reaches 0.13 cm on either side” describes the right one. Reporting one and meaning the other is the mistake the name error bar allows, and the reason gog requires the statistic in the sentence.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.6 Why interval needs a transform
Every sentence so far has named a transform. A mark needs one when it draws a number that nothing else supplies. A bar needs no transform, because the grammar already supplies its baseline: zero. bar + x(species) + y(petal_length) draws. An interval has no such default. A low and a high are two numbers, and a plain y() supplies one. So the shortest sentence that draws an interval is the mark, its positions, and a pair transform. Law 7, the minimum syllable, says a mark draws only with every position it needs, and an interval needs two numbers where y() gives one. Ask for an interval without a transform and the engine refuses the sentence rather than drawing an empty panel. What it refuses shows that refusal.
A whisker needs a low and a high, and there are two ways to give it them. One is two more channels, one for each: ggplot2 does this with its ymin and ymax aesthetics. But only a few marks would use those two channels, and a box plot would then need five, one for each of its numbers. gog takes the other way: a pair transform computes the two extents, as mean computes one value per group, so the channel vocabulary does not grow. ribbon reads the same low and high values, and box computes its five numbers inside the mark. The pair transform bounds(lower, upper) takes a low and a high you already have as two columns of the table, and Horizontal whiskers draws a coefficient plot with it.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.7 Horizontal whiskers
Whiskers turn horizontal for the reasons bars do: the names are long, or there are many of them. A tall list of horizontal whiskers is then easier to read than a crowded row of vertical ones. An interval takes its orientation from the bindings, the way a bar and a box do. Put the categories on y and the measured column on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(petal_length) + y(species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.petal_length) + y(col.species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:petal_length) +
  y(:species) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.petal_length), y(col.species), x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  y_label("Species"), title("The same 95% CI, horizontal"))






                                        2 3 4 5   virginica versicolor setosa  The same 95% CI, horizontal Species Petal length (cm)





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is petal length, y is species.”
The caps turn too, since a cap always crosses the span at its end, and the center dot stays at the center. The sections after this one work the same way on horizontal whiskers. color, dodge, caps, center and pattern, all introduced below, behave the same whichever axis carries the categories.
This is the usual shape for a coefficient plot: one line of the plot for each term of a model, read from top to bottom. The numbers in such a plot are usually computed when the model is fitted, not from raw observations. That is what bounds is for: it reads two columns you already have as the low and the high, and computes nothing. The coefs table was made for this book. It holds one row for each term of a model of log wage, and lo and hi are the ends of each term’s 95% confidence interval. The term column goes on y. bounds supplies the values for the other axis, so there is no x() to write:

  x_label("Effect on log wage") +
  title("A coefficient plot, from bounds you already have")


(data(coefs) + interval * bounds(col.lo, col.hi) + y(col.term) +
  x_label("Effect on log wage") +
  title("A coefficient plot, from bounds you already have"))


data(coefs) + interval * bounds(:lo, :hi) + y(:term) +
  x_label("Effect on log wage") +
  title("A coefficient plot, from bounds you already have")


plot(data(coefs), layer(interval, bounds(col.lo, col.hi)), y(col.term),
  x_label("Effect on log wage"),
  title("A coefficient plot, from bounds you already have"))

“Given the coefs table: intervals from lo to hi, y is term.”
The two Region whiskers, North and South, run from a negative low to a positive high. Each one includes zero, so at the 95% level each effect could be negative, zero or positive.
An interval needs a number to span, so two categorical axes are refused, as they are on a bar and a box. What it refuses shows that refusal.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.8 Splitting by color
With color, a reader can see which whisker is which without reading the axis. color splits an interval into one whisker per group, the same categorical split line and bar make. The statistic is computed inside each group, so every group gets its own whisker. Here color repeats the species already on x, so each species gets its own hue, and one legend names them all:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  color(species) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species"))






                                        setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5  95% CI of mean petal length, by species Petal length (cm) Species  Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length, color by species.”
Mapping a second category to color puts several whiskers on the same category of x, one for each color, and they overlap. dodge sets them side by side instead. It is the collision modifier that sets grouped bars side by side, and it moves whiskers the same way. Written in the other order, interval * dodge * range draws the same plot. After the mark, transforms can be written in any order (one fixed place, and one free order). This book still writes range first, so the sentence reads in the order of the work: range finds each whisker’s two ends, and dodge sets the whiskers side by side.
Oceania’s 1957 whisker looks like a single cap. The table has only two countries there, Australia and New Zealand. In 1957 their life expectancies were within a tenth of a year of each other. That span is shorter than a pixel, so the two caps draw on top of each other. In 2007 the two countries were a year apart, and the caps separate.
color on an interval takes a categorical column and splits the interval into groups, so each whisker has one color. range replaces your rows with a low and a high value for each group, so no row of your table is left to give a whisker a width or an opacity.   style(color = "tomato", size = 2.5) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A heavier, one-color range"))

  style(color = "tomato", size = 2.5) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("A heavier, one-color range")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), style({ color: "tomato", size: 2.5 }),
  x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("A heavier, one-color range"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range, x is species, y is petal length, colored tomato, with size 2.5.”
Every whisker is drawn in tomato and 2.5 pixels wide, whatever its species.

  layer(interval, bounds(col.lowest, col.highest)), x(col.continent),

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.10 Caps, or a linerange
The caps are the short lines across each end of a whisker. They are decoration rather than data, because they only mark where a whisker stops. A crowded plot is often easier to read without them. So whether to draw them is a setting. style(caps = FALSE) removes them, and a whisker with no caps is a linerange. caps = TRUE, the default, keeps the capped error bar. Here is the confidence interval from Splitting by color with its caps off:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  color(species) + style(caps = FALSE) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) + style(caps = False) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + style(caps = false) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  style({ caps: false }), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length, color by species, with caps off.”
caps belongs to the two marks that draw whiskers, interval and box. On any other mark, style(caps = ) is refused, and the message says what to use instead. A bar’s border_size is refused on a line the same way. caps combines with all six pair transforms. So the error bar, the linerange and the pointrange are all the same mark. A whisker with caps and no dot is a bare error bar. One with no caps is a linerange, and one with a dot at its center is a pointrange. Whether there is a dot depends on the transform, and whether there are caps depends on the caps setting.
A linerange from zero to each value, with a point layer marking the value, is the lollipop chart. A linerange between one category’s two values, such as a country in two years, with a point at each end, is the dumbbell chart. Comparing categories draws both.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.11 Hiding the center dot
Whether a center exists is decided by the statistic, not by a setting. confidence and deviation compute a mean as their center, and smooth_band and straight_band compute the fitted value. range and bounds compute none. So confidence, deviation, smooth_band and straight_band draw a pointrange, and range and bounds draw a bare error bar. A second layer can add a center where the statistic has none. point * mean over interval * range draws a pointrange from two layers, as Three layers instead of one mark shows with the median.
A setting can only hide a center that exists. A pointrange’s dot is the center the statistic computed. Sometimes you want the whisker without it. Leave the setting out and the dot stays. style(center = FALSE) drops the dot and leaves a bare error bar:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  color(species) + style(center = FALSE) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, without its center dots")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) + style(center = False) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, without its center dots"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + style(center = false) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, without its center dots")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  style({ center: false }), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("The same CI, without its center dots"))






                                     setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5  The same CI, without its center dots Petal length (cm) Species  Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length, color by species, with center off.”
center and caps each show or hide one part of what an interval draws: center its middle dot, caps its ends. Each takes two values, so a whisker can be drawn in four ways. A capped pointrange is the default. A capped bare error bar is center = FALSE. A linerange with a dot is caps = FALSE. Setting both to FALSE gives a bare linerange. The four plots below draw each of them with deviation, whose whiskers are long enough that the dot does not hide the caps. Each title names its settings:

style(center = ) belongs to interval alone, because a box has no center dot: its middle is the median line. On any other mark it is refused, and the message says what to use instead.
Writing center = TRUE is refused when the statistic computes no center. Left out, the setting draws the dot only where the statistic computes a center, so a plain interval * range still draws. range computes only the two ends of each span, so there is no dot to show:

The message names the two statistics that compute a mean as the center, confidence and deviation. It also names point * mean, a second layer that draws the mean as a dot on each whisker once the setting is removed.
The same second layer also sets the size of the dot. The interval’s own dot has one fixed size, and style(size = ) on an interval sets only the width of the whisker. So hide the interval’s dot with style(center = FALSE), and draw the mean with point * mean, whose size is the dot’s radius in pixels. This works for confidence and deviation, whose center is the mean. A point is drawn a little translucent, so opacity = 1 makes it as solid as the whisker. title: 13  Interval
text:
13.12 A dashed whisker
A dash separates one layer from another without a second color, and it still separates them when the plot is printed in black and white. A whisker is a stroke, so it takes style(pattern = ) the same way a line does. This is the settable rule: every mark drawn as a stroke (line, step, interval, path, rule, edge) takes the same pattern values, such as "dashed" and "dotted". The pattern is drawn on the whisker span only. The caps and the center dot stay solid, since a dashed cap would not look like a cap and a dot has no line to dash:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  color(species) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A dashed 95% CI")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A dashed 95% CI"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A dashed 95% CI")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  style({ pattern: "dashed" }), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("A dashed 95% CI"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length, color by species, with pattern dashed.”
pattern can also be mapped to a column. Like color, it splits an interval into one whisker per group, and each group’s whisker gets its own stroke pattern. Mapped to a second category, pattern puts several whiskers on one category of x, where they overlap. dodge sets them side by side, as it does for a split by color:

  y_label("Life expectancy range") +

title: 13  Interval
section: 13.13 A bar with its error bar
text:
13.13 A bar with its error bar
Two marks can answer two questions about the same groups. A bar shows where each group’s mean is. An interval shows how well that mean is known. Layer them and you have a plot that appears throughout the social sciences, usually with a bare error bar rather than a pointrange:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") +
  interval * confidence(0.95) + style(center = FALSE, color = "black") +
  x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Mean petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval")


(data(iris_flowers) + bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") +
  interval * confidence(0.95) + style(center = False, color = "black") +
  x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Mean petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval"))


data(iris_flowers) + bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") +
  interval * confidence(0.95) + style(center = false, color = "black") +
  x(:species) + y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Mean petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, mean), style({ color: "lightgray" }),
  layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  style({ center: false, color: "black" }), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Mean petal length (cm)"),
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval"))

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by mean, colored lightgray, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95%, with center off, colored black, x is species, y is petal length.”
Each layer names its own statistic. bar * mean reduces each group to one number, and interval * confidence(0.95) computes the interval around that number. Both read the same column and report different things, and the sentence says which is which. The dot is turned off because it would be exactly on the top of the bar, which already marks the mean.
The groups of a second category go side by side, with the same dodge that separates grouped bars. dodge needs the whiskers split into groups. color(era) would split them, but it would also draw each whisker in its bar’s color, and the part inside the bar would disappear. group(era) splits the whiskers into the same slots without coloring them, so style(color = "black") can draw them all in black. A layer cannot map color and set it at once, so color(era) with style(color = "black") is refused. The left plot puts color(era) on the whiskers, and the right plot puts group(era) on them. A channel written after a mark applies to that mark alone, so the left plot writes color(era, legend = FALSE) after each of its two marks. A channel written before the first mark would apply to every layer (Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped). legend = FALSE on the left keeps one legend for the two, and theme(width = 360) makes the two panels the same width, as One axis, but not one legend explains:

   y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +

     bar * mean * dodge + color(era) +
     interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + group(era) +
     style(center = FALSE, color = "black") +
     x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("group(era) on the whiskers"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, colored by era, without a legend, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95% and dodge, colored by era, without a legend, with center off, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived by mean and dodge, colored by era, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95% and dodge, grouped by era, with center off, colored black, x is continent, y is life.”
On the left, the lower half of each whisker is hard to see against its bar, most of all in Oceania in 2007. On the right, every whisker shows in full.
Oceania has both the shortest whisker and the longest, from the same two countries. A confidence interval from two values is wide compared with the distance between them, because two values say little about the spread. In 2007 Australia and New Zealand were a year apart, and the confidence interval is thirteen years wide. In 1957 the two countries were 0.07 years apart, and the confidence interval is still nine tenths of a year wide. That is more than twelve times the 1957 range, which showed as a single cap in Splitting by color.
What this plot does not show is the data. Two groups can have the same mean and the same confidence interval and still hold very different values, and a bar reports only the one number. Three layers instead of one mark draws the spread itself, and box draws five numbers at once.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.14 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms an interval takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
—
bin, count, density, proportion


Summaries
—
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile


Fitted lines
—
smooth, straight


Running total
—
cumulative


Pairs: a low and a high
range ●, confidence ●, deviation ●, smooth_band ●, straight_band ●, bounds ●
—


Collision modifiers
dodge
stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
—
partition, flow, layout, cluster



The plots below show every transform an interval takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change. The six pair transforms are marked ●: an interval cannot draw without one of them, as Why interval needs a transform explains. Apart from dodge, which only sets whiskers side by side, the pair transforms are the only transforms an interval takes. No other mark is limited to them: a ribbon also needs a low and a high at each place, but it takes density and flow as well.
Pairs. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, and the interval spans them. range, confidence and deviation reduce the rows at each value of x, so they need a number on y. range gives the smallest and the largest value. confidence gives the 95% confidence interval of the mean, and deviation reaches one standard deviation from the mean on each side. Both also compute the mean, which the interval marks with a dot. smooth_band and straight_band need a number on each axis. They fit a line to the rows, each placed at its x and its y, and give a low and a high around it at evenly spaced places along x, 100 unless you set places. The interval draws a whisker at each place. bounds computes nothing: it reads the low and the high from two columns you name, and it needs no y. An interval refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The counts, the summaries, the fitted lines and the running total give one number at each value of x, and a whisker needs two. A point, a bar or a line draws one value. To draw a summary together with its whisker, layer the two marks, as A bar with its error bar does. stack piles up bars, areas and the dots of a dot plot, and places a label in each segment of a stacked bar. jitter moves each point a short way along the categorical axis, and repel moves text labels. partition, flow and cluster lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which zone, ribbon and path draw. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

13.15 What you can set
A setting changes how every whisker looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are an interval’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value

style(opacity = )

style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )

true or false

  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A thick, dotted 99% linerange"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.99) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) +
  style(caps = false, size = 3, color = "darkslateblue", pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A thick, dotted 99% linerange")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.99)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length),
  style({ caps: false, size: 3, color: "darkslateblue",
  pattern: "dotted" }), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("A thick, dotted 99% linerange"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 99%, x is species, y is petal length, colored darkslateblue, with caps off, size 3 and pattern dotted.”
The confidence level is not in the settings table, because it is not a setting. It is written into the transform instead. confidence(0.99) changes what is computed, not how it is drawn. To decide whether something is a setting, ask whether it changes the computed numbers. The level does, so it belongs to the transform.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.17 In short
An interval computes nothing. Its transform decides which two numbers it spans, and whether there is a center to draw. caps and center are settings, so neither reads a column. A pattern can be set for the whole layer, or mapped to a column, which splits the whiskers the way color does. size and opacity map a column only with bounds, which draws one whisker from each row of your table.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.18 What comes next
An interval never decides which two numbers it spans; its transform does. Box decides them inside the mark: it computes the quartiles and the median itself, and draws them as a box and two whiskers.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.1 A summary per group
How is each group spread out? box draws a box plot for each group, a summary of the measured column. A box spans the lower quartile to the upper, with a line at the median. Whiskers reach to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) of the box. Any values beyond that limit are outliers, drawn individually as dots. bar * mean gives only one number per group, while box shows how the whole group is spread. An interval needs a transform to supply its low and high values, while a box computes its whole summary itself. Boxes are vertical when the categories are on x and horizontal when they are on y; see Horizontal boxes.
The construction is John Tukey’s, from Exploratory Data Analysis (Tukey, 1977). His book gives two versions. The box-and-whisker plot runs its whiskers to the smallest and largest values, as Mary Eleanor Spear’s range bar (Spear, 1952) had done a quarter century earlier, in 1952. The schematic plot sets a fence 1.5 times the length of the box beyond each end of the box, and stops each whisker at the last value inside it. Each value beyond a fence is drawn on its own, as an outlier. Readers kept the first name, now usually shortened to box plot. Most software, gog included, gives that name to the schematic plot and draws it by default.
There is one difference from his book. Tukey’s box spans hinges: the median of the lower half of the values and the median of the upper half. To find them, sort the values and cut the sorted list in half; when the count is odd, the middle value belongs to both halves. Then take the median of each half. gog spans the lower and upper quartiles instead, as most software does. The two agree when a group has an odd number of values, and can differ slightly when the number is even. For the four values 1, 2, 3 and 4, the hinges are 1.5 and 3.5, while gog’s box runs from 1.75 to 3.25.
How do the three species differ in petal length, not only on average but in how widely each varies? The iris_flowers table holds 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species, measured in centimeters. Put the categorical column, species, on x, and put the measured column, petal_length, on y. title: 14  Box
text:
14.3 How much to summarize
The box above draws five values for each continent, but the same table can also be drawn with every country, or with one value for each continent. In gog you make that choice by changing the mark or its transform; the table, x and y stay the same. point * jitter draws every row and reduces nothing: jitter only moves each point a little sideways, so that countries with close values do not hide one another. A box reduces each group to five values and still draws each outlier. interval * range keeps two values, the lowest row and the highest. point * mean draws one value, the mean. Here are the four plots, from every row to one value for each continent:

Each plot to the right reduces the data more, and drawing more values or fewer each has a cost. Drawing many values risks information overload: there are so many marks that the shape of the data is hard to see. Drawing few values causes information loss: whatever the rows held beyond those few values is no longer drawn. The left plot draws all 52 African countries, spread over 36.8 years, and it is hard to see where most of them lie. The box shows Africa in five values: the middle half runs from about 48 to 59 years, and the whiskers reach the lowest and highest countries. Asia’s Afghanistan is still a dot of its own. interval * range keeps only the two ends. Asia’s whisker reaches down to Afghanistan’s 43.8 years, and the plot does not show that only one country is that low. point * mean draws one value for each continent. It is the easiest to compare across continents, and it does not show how far apart Africa’s countries are.
So every amount of summary has one of the two costs, and no single amount is right for every plot. You can start from every row and summarize step by step, losing a little information at each step. Or you can start from a summary and add detail step by step, with a little more to read at each step. The question decides where to stop. To compare the continents’ averages, one value is enough. To find the countries far below the rest, draw the box or every row. A plot can also draw two amounts at once, a summary and the rows it summarizes. title: 14  Box
text:
14.4 Horizontal boxes
When the category names are long, or there are many of them, the boxes should be horizontal. Swap the two positions, and the plot is drawn with its axes exchanged. gog has no word like ggplot2’s coord_flip(), because it would be a second way to say the same thing. gog reads the two bindings and decides from them which axis carries the numbers, exactly as bar does.

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Continent") +
  title("The same five distributions, horizontal")

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Continent") +
  title("The same five distributions, horizontal"))

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Continent") +
  title("The same five distributions, horizontal")

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Continent"),
  title("The same five distributions, horizontal"))

“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is life, y is continent.”
Compare it with the vertical version in Distribution across many groups. Every box, whisker and outlier dot keeps its place relative to its neighbors. Only the two axes have changed places. Afghanistan and Haiti are still the two dots beyond their continents’ whiskers. Everything later in this chapter works the same on either axis: the whisker rule, the color split, dodge and style().
The swap matters most when the names are long. The tenure table is invented: five teams, thirty people in each, and the years each person has been at the company. Each category takes a slot, the stretch of the axis that belongs to one category. 14.5 Whiskers to the extremes
Sometimes you do not want outliers drawn separately. You want the whiskers to run to the true minimum and maximum. The box then shows the five-number summary: the minimum, the lower quartile, the median, the upper quartile and the maximum. The mark takes one parameter for this, a named option inside its parentheses: box(whiskers = "range"):

  x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range")

  x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range"))

  y(:life) + x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range")

  y(col.life), x_label("Continent"), y_label("Life expectancy (years)"),

Now Afghanistan and Haiti are the ends of their whiskers rather than dots, and no value is drawn as an outlier. The default is "tukey": fences and outliers, the standard box plot. "range" draws the whole five-number summary. whiskers is not a setting, because it changes the summary itself: which values the whiskers reach. A setting changes only how the summary looks, such as its color or line width; Changing how a box looks shows them.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.6 Why box needs no transform
An interval cannot draw without a transform to give it a low and a high. A box never needs one. An interval is only a shape, a span from a low value to a high one. Which low and high it spans is a real choice: a min–max range, a confidence interval, or a pre-computed pair. A box always draws the same kind of summary: quartiles, a median and whiskers. Only the whisker rule can change, through the mark’s own whiskers. A statistic that is always drawn by the same mark belongs inside that mark, not in a separate transform. So the shortest sentence that draws a box is box + x + y, with no transform. Adding any transform other than dodge is refused, and the message says what to write instead, as What it refuses shows.
The same principle keeps the channel vocabulary small: a value that only one mark can use is computed by that mark, not added to the channels every mark shares. In ggplot2 you can give a box its five values yourself, as five aesthetics: ymin, lower, middle, upper and ymax. If gog did the same, it would need five more channels. ymin and ymax could also give an interval or a ribbon its two ends, but lower, middle and upper would mean something only on a box. Instead the box computes its summary itself, and the channel vocabulary does not grow.
The table below sets the four marks side by side. Three of them read a low and a high value from a transform, and box computes its own summary:



Mark
The spread it draws




interval * range
a whisker from the low value to the high


ribbon * range
the band between the two values, filled


line * range
the two values as two separate strokes


box
quartiles, median and whiskers, with no transform to write



box is also one of several marks that draw a distribution, and each answers a different question. bar * bin draws one variable’s histogram: how many values fall in each bin? interval draws a range or an error bar: between which two values do a group’s values fall? box gives the summary per group: where are its middle half, its median and its unusual values? The violin (ribbon * density) draws an estimate of the whole distribution that summary is computed from: where are the values dense, and where are they sparse? An interval can also span the box’s two quartiles: interval * range(0.25, 0.75) draws the same middle half, as A band between two quantiles shows.
The Interval chapter builds the same parts from three layers: the full range, the middle half and the median. Drawn beside a box on the same table, the box and the middle half match, and so does the median. The whiskers match only when the box runs them to the range. So the figure draws three plots: the default box, a box(whiskers = "range"), and the three layers:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(iris_flowers) + box + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
    x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("box")) |

      x_label("Species") + title("box, whiskers to the range")) |
   (data(iris_flowers) +
      interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
      interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
      point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
      x(species) + y(petal_length) +
      x_label("Species") + title("three layers"))) +
  theme(width = 960, height = 420)

      x_label("Species") + title("box, whiskers to the range")) |

      interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +
      interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + style(color = "steelblue", size = 8) +
      point * median + style(color = "gold", size = 5, opacity = 1) +
      x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
      x_label("Species") + title("three layers"))) +
  theme(width = 960, height = 420))

  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("box")) |

  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") +
  title("box, whiskers to the range")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + interval * range + style(color = "darkgray") +

“Given the iris flowers: boxes, x is species, y is petal length, beside boxes with whiskers to the range, x is species, y is petal length, beside intervals derived by range, and also intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, and also points derived by median, x is species, y is petal length.”
The box sets a fence 1.5 times the length of the box beyond each end, ends each whisker at the last flower inside it, and draws the five flowers past it as dots. Setosa has four of them but shows three dots, because two of its flowers are both 1.9 cm long and share one dot. Versicolor has one, at 3.0 cm. So on the left, setosa’s whiskers are shorter than the gray range at both ends, and versicolor’s at the bottom, by a few tenths of a centimeter. title: 14  Box
text:
14.8 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a box takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
—
bin, count, density, proportion


Summaries
—
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile


Fitted lines
—
smooth, straight


Running total
—
cumulative


Pairs: a low and a high
—
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds


Collision modifiers
dodge
stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
—
partition, flow, layout, cluster



A box takes only one transform, dodge, so one figure shows it. It is the only mark that computes a summary with no transform written: it works out its own quartiles, median and whiskers from the rows, as Why box needs no transform explains. Every summary and every pair transform is refused, since the box has already done that work. The figure shows the same boxes twice, first without dodge and then with it.
Collision modifiers. Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another. When a split draws several boxes at one place, dodge sets them side by side, and it changes nothing in their summaries. Here the split is color(era), which gives two boxes for each continent, one for 1957 and one for 2007. Without dodge, as in the upper plot, the two boxes share one place, so they overlap and their fills turn translucent. With dodge, each box takes its own half of the slot:

      title("box * dodge"))) +
  theme(height = 800)

   (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
      title("box * dodge"))) +
  theme(height = 800))


((data(gm_eras) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) + color(:era) +
  title("box")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + color(:era) +
  title("box * dodge"))) + theme(height = 800)


below(plot(data(gm_eras), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), title("box")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(box, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), title("box * dodge")), theme({ height: 800 }))

“Given the gapminder eras: boxes, x is continent, y is life, color by era, above boxes derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”
Each box marks the same quartiles, median and whiskers in both plots. Only its place and its width change: the two boxes share the slot, so each is half as wide.
A box refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. It computes its own summary, as Why box needs no transform explains, so it refuses the counts, the summaries and the pairs. For the same reason it refuses the fitted lines and the running total. A point, a bar or a line draws the counts, the summaries, the fitted lines and the running total. interval, ribbon, line and step draw the pairs. Of the collision modifiers, a box takes only dodge. A box’s position on the axis that carries the numbers is set by its values. Piling one box on another would move its quartiles away from the values they mark. stack piles up bars, areas and the dots of a dot plot, and places a label in each segment of a stacked bar. jitter moves each point a short way along the categorical axis, and repel moves text labels. partition, flow and cluster lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which zone, ribbon and path draw. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

14.9 What you can set
A setting changes how every box looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a box’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels


style(caps = )
true or false


style(gap = )
a share of the mark’s place, from 0 to just under 1




14.9.1 Changing how a box looks
To see what each setting in the table changes, think of a box as a fill, lines and dots. The fill is the inside of the box, the lines are the outline, the whiskers, the caps (the short lines across the whisker ends) and the median, and the dots are the outliers. 14.10 What it refuses
Five refusals follow. The first three concern how a box is drawn, and the last two concern what it summarizes. A dashed pattern is the first. On a box, pattern sets the fill’s texture and the lines stay solid, so it takes a fill texture, not a stroke pattern. "solid" (the default), "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid" and "dots" are accepted, and "dashed" is refused.

  style(pattern = "dashed")

  style({ pattern: "dashed" }))

title: 14  Box
text:
14.11 In short
For each group, a box draws quartiles, a median, whiskers to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the IQR, and a dot for each outlier. The summary is inside the mark, so a box refuses every statistic and takes only dodge. whiskers is its one parameter. Its line width and opacity are set once for the layer. gog’s box spans the quartiles, so when a group has an even number of values it can differ slightly from Tukey’s hinges.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.12 What comes next
A box occupies one slot on its axis, and its width carries no value from the table. Ribbon fills the band between a low value and a high one at every position along the axis.




Spear, M. E. (1952). Charting statistics. McGraw-Hill.


Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory data analysis. Addison-Wesley.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.1 A band from a range
How far apart were the lowest and highest values at each date? ribbon draws a filled band from a low boundary to a high one across x: a confidence band, a spread band, the shaded region around a trend. It fills one region, the way an area does. It reads a low value and a high value at each position, the way an interval does. An area fills from the data down to a baseline at zero. A ribbon has no baseline, and both of its edges come from the data, always through a transform. With a category on one axis and density, the same mark draws a violin plot.
The gapminder_asia table holds five Asian countries: China, India, Indonesia, Japan and South Korea (Korea, Rep. in the table). Each is measured every five years from 1952 to 2007. Did the life expectancies of those five move closer together over the years, or further apart? The gap between the lowest and the highest in each year answers that. A band drawn between those two values shows every year at once, as one shape. The two boundaries come from a transform, exactly as an interval’s two extents do. range reduces y to its minimum and maximum within each x, and the ribbon fills between them. title: 15  Ribbon
section: 15.4 Why a ribbon needs a transform
text:
15.4 Why a ribbon needs a transform
A low and a high are two numbers, and a plain y() supplies one. An area closes on zero: its region’s other edge is zero, which the grammar supplies. A ribbon has no such second number. Law 7, the minimum syllable, says a mark draws only with every position it needs. For a ribbon those are an x, a low and a high. Like an interval, it needs a transform that supplies the low and the high. Write a ribbon without one and the engine refuses it, rather than drawing an empty panel. What it refuses shows the message.
Computing the boundaries in a transform also keeps the channel vocabulary small. The alternative, used by ggplot2, would add ymin and ymax as two more channels that only a few marks use. A box plot would then need five such channels, one for each number it summarizes. With a transform instead, the same low and high values can be drawn as a whisker, as two lines, or as a filled band.
A ribbon can take eight transforms that supply the low and the high. Six are the pair transforms: range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band and bounds. Transforms explains each one. The other two are density, over a category, and flow. density gives one curve per category, and the ribbon draws that curve and its mirror image as the two boundaries. That is the violin, later in this chapter. flow is shown in Transforms it takes.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.5 A confidence band
How well is the mean life expectancy known in each year? That is a different question from how far the five countries spread. range shows the full spread. For the uncertainty of the mean, use confidence. It computes a t-interval for the mean at each x, and the ribbon fills between its two boundaries. Here is the 95% band for the same five countries, on the right, beside the min–max band from the start of this chapter:

     y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * confidence(0.95)"))

The confidence band is wide because each mean comes from only five countries. Those five differ by more than fifteen years, so the interval around their mean is wide. A confidence level above 0.95 draws a wider band still.
The two bands are almost the same width. That comes from having only five values, not from the two transforms agreeing. Over the 142 countries of gm_all, the 95% band in 2007 is about 4 years wide, while their range is 43 years. The plots in Transforms it takes show both. What the band means is decided by the transform you name: range draws the observed spread, and confidence draws the uncertainty of the mean. The mark stays the same in both plots, exactly as it does for interval.

15.6 A pre-computed band
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band and straight_band compute the band from the raw values in the table, at the moment gog draws the plot. Many bands are computed earlier, by the analysis itself. A model’s standard error, a standard error of measurement, a bootstrap interval: each of these is computed before the plot. Each gives a low value and a high one, and those two become two columns in the table. gog draws what you computed, and it does not re-fit the model. The score_band table holds one row per raw score on a test scored from 0 to 20. Each row also holds the expected true score for that raw score, the score a model predicts, and the two ends of a 95% band around it. In this table the expected true score equals the raw score, so a line through it is a diagonal:

The band takes the same setting, with different values. On a stroke, pattern takes "dashed", "dotted", "dotdash" or "longdash". 15.7 Filled, or two dashed edges
Some plots need the band without a fill. A band starts as a low and high pair, and the mark decides how that pair is drawn. That is the No Exceptions law: a transform computes the same values whichever mark reads it. The same bin gives a bar chart, a frequency polygon and a step histogram. In the same way, the first figure in A band from a range drew the same pairs with three marks: interval as a whisker at each x, line as two lines, and ribbon filled between them. The unfilled band many journals prefer is the line version, which traces the pair’s two boundaries. With style(pattern = ) it becomes the dashed pair of curves those journals often print. “Given the score band: x is score, y is expected, a ribbon from lower to upper, and also a line and points, beside x is score, y is expected, lines from lower to upper, and also a line and points.”
line * bounds is one layer that draws both edges, splitting the pair into a low curve and a high one. So you do not write one y() for the low edge and another for the high edge. Two plain line layers can draw two columns you already have. They cannot split a pair that range computes, because that pair never becomes a column you can name. A line draws every pair transform the same way. line * range traces the lowest and the highest values, and line * confidence traces the two ends of a confidence interval. step * bounds draws the same two edges as staircases. All four marks take the same six pair transforms: range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band and bounds. Filled or unfilled, solid or dashed, the pair stays the same and only the mark changes, so ribbon needs no option for any of them.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.8 A fan chart
A forecast for next year is more certain than one for three years ahead, so a forecast is usually published with bands that widen with each year. A fan chart draws several such bands, such as an 80% and a 50% band, one inside the other. They start as one point at the last observed value and spread out like a folding fan when it opens, which gives the chart its name.
A fan chart has two parts that meet at the last observed year. Up to that year, the observed values are a line with no band. From that year on, the forecast is a line inside its bands. No single mark draws both parts: a line does not fill a band, and a ribbon fills a band but draws no line through it. So the chart is built in layers: a line for the observed values, and for the forecast a ribbon for each band with a line on top. Each part also comes from its own table, because the observed sales are recorded and the forecast is computed by a model. actuals holds the sales observed from 2019 to 2023:

15.9 One band per group
How does the spread of one continent compare with another’s, year by year? The gm_continents table holds every country of three continents (Asia, Europe and the Americas), measured every five years from 1952 to 2007. One band per continent puts all three spreads in one panel. A categorical column splits a ribbon into one band per group. color splits the rows into one series per continent, the rows that one band is drawn through, and group and pattern split them the same way. It is the same split that gives area one region per group and line one stroke per group. Here each continent gets its own band, the range of its countries’ life expectancy over time:
