Europe’s band narrows from about 29 years wide in 1952 to about 10 in 2007, and the Americas’ from 31 to 20. Asia’s stays about 37 to 40 years wide, except for a dip in its lower edge in 1977.
The bands overlap where two continents cover the same range of life expectancy. A split area draws each region nearly opaque, as it draws a single one, so little of the region behind shows through. For an area, stack solves this: it starts each region at the top of the ones below, so no two regions overlap. A ribbon split into groups draws each band translucent by default instead, so a band behind another stays readable. The difference follows from what each mark measures. An area measures a height from the baseline, so its groups can be piled into a total. A ribbon already spans a low to a high and measures no such height, so there is nothing to stack. Overlapping bands are read through transparency and never stacked, which is why ribbon * stack is refused and the refusal names style(opacity = ).

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.10 One region, one fill
The bands above are equally translucent, and each has its own color. Can you map a column to a band’s opacity instead? No, whether the column is a category or a number. On a ribbon, opacity belongs to the layer, not to each band: every band in the layer has the same opacity, exactly as on area. So opacity is a setting here and not a channel. One band cannot be lighter in one year and darker in another, and one continent’s band cannot be lighter than another’s.
color is different, because it belongs to each band. A categorical column gives each band its own color, as in the plot above. One band still has one color, so a continuous column, which would change the color within a band, is refused. What it refuses shows both refusals.
size is refused both ways: a ribbon neither maps it nor sets it. A band’s extent comes entirely from its x values and its two boundaries, so there is no size to choose. To outline the band, layer a line along its boundaries rather than setting an outline on the mark. The plot in What you can set does this with line * bounds.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.11 A category on the domain
What happens when x holds categories instead of years? The spread of each continent and its center can be drawn as one band across the categories. You then see one shape across the panel, as with an area’s filled profile. A band’s two axes do different jobs, as an area’s do. The domain is the axis the band runs along, and the measure is the axis its low and high are read on. In every band so far the domain was x, holding years; here it holds continents. A ribbon takes a category on x, the same way an area does, and fills the spread across the categories in the order they first appear in the table: Asia, Europe, Africa, the Americas, Oceania. section: 15.12 The violin: a distribution per category
text:
15.12 The violin: a distribution per category
A range on a category gives two numbers per group, the lowest and the highest. density gives a whole shape per group, and a ribbon can draw that shape. With density, the category is no longer the domain. Each continent is given a slot, the part of the x axis that belongs to one category. density estimates one curve per continent, and the curve runs along the other axis, y. At each life expectancy, the curve’s value is larger when more of the continent’s countries lie near it. The ribbon draws that value as a width across the slot, from left to right, half on each side of the slot’s center line, so the two halves mirror each other. In the bands drawn so far, the width was the distance between the lower and the upper edge, in years of life expectancy. A violin’s width runs across the slot instead. That is the violin plot (Hintze & Nelson, 1998). By default, each continent’s curve is first multiplied by its number of countries, for the reason given in What the width means. The sentence below is the one that drew the band across the continents in A category on the domain, with density in place of range and without the line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent"))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  ribbon * density: one distribution per continent Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
density is not the ribbon’s own transform. Over one continuous column, such as x(life), five other marks draw the same estimated curve, and only the shape changes. That is the No Exceptions law: a mark draws whatever rows a transform returns, in the mark’s own way.



Mark derived by density
Shape




line * density
the curve as a stroke


step * density
the curve as a staircase


area * density
the curve filled to the baseline


point * density
one dot at each point the curve was estimated


bar * density
one thin bar at each of those points


ribbon * density
the curve mirrored, the violin above



With a category on one axis, three more marks draw across each category’s slot, as the ribbon does: line, step and area. Each draws one connected curve: area fills half the violin, and line and step draw that half unfilled. The area version is drawn in Sideways, and halved. point and bar instead draw a separate mark at each place the curve was estimated. gog draws an estimate across a slot only as one connected curve, so with density it refuses both when one axis holds a category.
Nothing new was added to the grammar to draw the violin. A ribbon closes on a second boundary the data supplies, and a violin closes on the mirror image of its own curve. density estimates a distribution, and this plot computes one estimate for each group. There is no violin word to learn. Such a word would have to say four things at once: the mark, the transform, the mirror and the slot. The sentence already says all four: ribbon is the mark and supplies the mirror, density is the transform, and the category on x gives the slot.
Compare it with the box drawn from the same two columns:

  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized"))


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized"))






                                                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life.”
A box gives you five numbers you can name. The violin gives you the shape those five numbers summarize. Africa’s violin is widest near 52 years, and it has a second, smaller bulge near 73. Africa’s median is 53, and none of the box’s five numbers shows that second cluster.

15.12.1 What the width means
A violin’s width at one life expectancy is measured across its slot, from its left edge to its right edge. By default, it is proportional to the estimated number of countries per year of life expectancy around that value. gog draws the widest point in the panel 0.8 of a slot wide, 0.4 on each side of its center line. Every other width is drawn in proportion to it, so widths can be compared between violins. density(reach = ) sets that 0.4, as Letting the ridges overlap shows.
A density curve is an estimated probability density, so the area under the whole curve is 1: the whole group. Its value at one life expectancy is the share of the group’s countries per year of life expectancy there. By default, gog multiplies each continent’s curve by its number of rows, here its number of countries, which turns each share into a number of countries. Africa’s violin, with 52 countries, then covers 26 times the area of Oceania’s, with 2. Without that step, the two would cover the same area.
The number of countries sets a violin’s area. How wide the violin is also depends on its length, from its bottom tip to its top tip, because its area is its average width times its length. The length comes from how far apart the group’s values lie, plus about six years at each end. Compared with ggplot2’s violin explains the six years. Europe’s thirty countries lie within ten years of each other, so its violin is short and wide. Africa’s fifty-two countries span thirty-seven years, so its violin is long, and its widest point is narrower than Europe’s. Oceania’s violin is the shortest, but its area is so small that its widest point is still the narrowest.
density(compare = "shape") leaves out the multiplication, so every violin covers the same area. The first violin plot used the default, compare = "count". With "shape", each width is proportional to the share of the continent’s countries per year of life expectancy, and only a violin’s length decides its average width:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area')


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area'))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") +
  x(:continent) + y(:life) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("density(compare = \"shape\"): every violin the same area")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density({ compare: "shape" })),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("density(compare = \"shape\"): every violin the same area"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density compared by shape, x is continent, y is life.”
Oceania’s violin, the shortest, is now the widest: a continent of two countries is drawn wider than Africa, with fifty-two. With equal areas, you might expect the longest violin to have the narrowest widest point. Asia’s violin is the longest, because its values span thirty-nine years, two more than Africa’s. Yet Africa’s widest point is the smallest of the five. Equal areas fix each violin’s average width, not its widest point. Nineteen of Asia’s thirty-three countries lie between 70 and 80 years, so a large part of Asia’s area lies there, and its widest point is wider than Africa’s. Africa’s countries are spread more evenly along its violin, so no part of the violin is wide.
The two plots answer different questions. The default shows how many countries lie near each life expectancy, per year. compare = "shape" shows how each continent’s values are spread, whatever its number of countries.


15.12.2 Compared with ggplot2’s violin
If you have used ggplot2, you will notice that gog’s violins differ from those geom_violin() draws on the same data. Three choices cause the difference, and gog makes each one on purpose.
First, the ends narrow to a point. A violin is the density curve mirrored, and gog draws the whole curve. The curve runs three bandwidths past each group’s smallest and largest value. The bandwidth is the width of the bell-shaped kernel that density places on each value. No row in the table lies in these tails. Oceania’s two countries lie at 80.2 and 81.2 years, but with the bandwidth of 2.04 years that all five violins share, its violin runs from 74.1 to 87.4. line * density, split by color(continent), draws the same estimate as the violins, so its curves have the same tails. In One transform, four readings, Oceania’s curve also runs from 74.1 to 87.4. geom_violin() stops each violin at its group’s smallest and largest value, so its ends are flat. With trim = FALSE, it draws tails the same way, three bandwidths long.
Second, by default each gog violin’s area is proportional to its row count, as What the width means explains. geom_violin() scales every violin to the same area, as compare = "shape" does in gog.
Third, every violin in a plot is smoothed by one bandwidth, so a difference in shape comes from the data and not from the smoothing (One transform, four readings). geom_violin() gives each violin its own bandwidth.
In gog, only the second choice can be changed to match geom_violin(). The ends always narrow to a point, and every violin shares one bandwidth, whether gog chooses it or you set it with density(bandwidth = ) (Choosing the bandwidth).


15.12.3 Sideways, and halved
A violin turns as the band did in A category on the domain. Here density makes the category a slot, and gog reads the orientation from the bindings, as it does for a bar or a box. A category on y is the form with room for long category names:

15.12.4 Letting the ridges overlap
The ridgeline above keeps every ridge inside its own slot. That comes from how far a shape reaches by default. The widest shape in a panel reaches 0.4 of a slot from the slot’s center line, and every other shape is drawn in proportion to it. A slot ends 0.5 from that line, so each shape stays inside its own slot, with empty space before the next category. Bars follow the same rule, for the same reason: the gap shows that the categories are separate groups, not pieces of one continuous scale.
A ridgeline, as it is usually drawn, breaks that rule on purpose: its ridges are tall enough to reach into the slot above, and the overlap is intended. density(reach = ) says how far, in slots:

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: the tallest ridge two and a half slots tall")

  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: the tallest ridge two and a half slots tall"))

  y(:continent) + x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("reach = 2.5: the tallest ridge two and a half slots tall")

  x(col.life), y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("reach = 2.5: the tallest ridge two and a half slots tall"))

“Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density reaching 2.5 slots, x is life, y is continent.”
The number is measured from the slot’s center line to the shape’s furthest point. That is why the number means the same thing to both marks. A ribbon reaches that far on each side, an area on one side only. The half violin therefore stays exactly half of the violin, at any reach. Past 0.5 the shapes leave their own slots. gog does not refuse this: a reach above 0.5 is unusual but legal, so gog draws what your sentence asks for. Where two ridges overlap, the lower one is drawn later and covers the one above it.
The categorical axis grows to hold the ridges. Normally the axis leaves half a slot of space beyond the first and last categories, which is enough for a bar or a box, since each stays inside its slot. A ridge 2.5 slots tall does not stay in its slot, so the axis adds the room it needs. Without that room, the panel edge would hide the top of the highest ridge.
The edge is a layer here, as it was wherever this chapter drew a band’s edge. Neither area nor ribbon takes a border setting. A line given the same transform traces the outline of the fill. That is the Filled, or two dashed edges rule again, this time inside a category’s slot:

                                          40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  One hue per ridge Continent Life expectancy  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is life, y is continent, areas derived by density reaching 2.2 slots, colored by continent, and also lines derived by density reaching 2.2 slots, colored black, with size 0.9.”
The color(continent) is written after the area, so it belongs to that layer alone. Written before both marks, it would also reach the line, whose style(color = "black") sets the color. One layer cannot both map a channel and set it, so gog would refuse the sentence, as What it refuses shows. The place where a channel is written in the sentence decides its scope, and Encoding scope explains that in full.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.13 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a ribbon takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
density ●
bin, count, proportion


Summaries
—
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile


Fitted lines
—
smooth, straight


Running total
—
cumulative


Pairs: a low and a high
range ●, confidence ●, deviation ●, smooth_band ●, straight_band ●, bounds ●
—


Collision modifiers
—
dodge, stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
flow ●
partition, layout, cluster



The plots below show every transform a ribbon takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change. The six pair transforms, density and flow are marked ●: a ribbon cannot draw without one of them. Why a ribbon needs a transform explains this for the pairs and density. For flow, the flow section of Transforms shows the bands it gives a ribbon. Every transform a ribbon takes gives it a low and a high at each place: the six pair transforms it shares with interval, and density and flow, whose results it draws as the two edges of a band. Unlike an interval, it takes no collision modifier. dodge refuses a ribbon, because a filled band has no width to divide. style(opacity = ) makes overlapping bands translucent instead, so each one shows.
Counting. density is the one counting transform a ribbon takes. For each category, it estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along the number axis. So it needs a category on one axis and a number on the other. The ribbon draws each curve and its mirror image across the category’s slot, and the shape is the violin. Without a category, density gives one curve, which is only one edge, so the ribbon refuses it. The category can be on either axis:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
   title("ribbon * density")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
     title("ribbon * density"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
   title("ribbon * density")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
     title("ribbon * density")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  title("ribbon * density")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  title("ribbon * density"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), title("ribbon * density")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent), title("ribbon * density")))






                                     Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  ribbon * density Life Continent


                                   40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  ribbon * density Continent Life






“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life, beside ribbons derived by density, x is life, y is continent.”
Pairs. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, and the ribbon fills the band between them. range, confidence and deviation reduce the rows at each value of x, so they need a number on y. range gives the smallest and the largest value. confidence gives the 95% confidence interval of the mean, and deviation reaches one standard deviation from the mean on each side. smooth_band and straight_band need a number on each axis. They fit a line to the rows, each placed at its x and its y. They then give a low and a high around that line at 100 evenly spaced places along x, or as many as places sets. bounds computes nothing: it reads the low and the high from two columns you name, and it needs no y. Five plots read the gm_all table, shown in Nested percentile bands. The sixth reads the score_band table, shown in A pre-computed band, with score on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gm_all) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) +
    title("ribbon * range")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * confidence + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("ribbon * confidence")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * deviation + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("ribbon * deviation"))) /
  ((data(gm_all) + ribbon * smooth_band + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("ribbon * smooth_band")) |
     (data(gm_all) + ribbon * straight_band + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("ribbon * straight_band")) |
     (data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
        title("ribbon * bounds")))


(((data(gm_all) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
    title("ribbon * range")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * confidence + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
     title("ribbon * confidence")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * deviation + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
     title("ribbon * deviation"))) /
  ((data(gm_all) + ribbon * smooth_band + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
      title("ribbon * smooth_band")) |
     (data(gm_all) + ribbon * straight_band + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
        title("ribbon * straight_band")) |
     (data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + x(col.score) +
        title("ribbon * bounds"))))


((data(gm_all) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  title("ribbon * range")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * confidence + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  title("ribbon * confidence")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * deviation + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  title("ribbon * deviation"))) /
  ((data(gm_all) + ribbon * smooth_band + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  title("ribbon * smooth_band")) |
  (data(gm_all) + ribbon * straight_band + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  title("ribbon * straight_band")) |
  (data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) + x(:score) +
  title("ribbon * bounds")))


below(beside(beside(plot(data(gm_all), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year),
  y(col.life), title("ribbon * range")),
  plot(data(gm_all), layer(ribbon, confidence), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  title("ribbon * confidence"))),
  plot(data(gm_all), layer(ribbon, deviation), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  title("ribbon * deviation"))),
  beside(beside(plot(data(gm_all), layer(ribbon, smooth_band),
  x(col.year), y(col.life), title("ribbon * smooth_band")),
  plot(data(gm_all), layer(ribbon, straight_band), x(col.year),
  y(col.life), title("ribbon * straight_band"))),
  plot(data(score_band), layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  x(col.score), title("ribbon * bounds"))))






                             1960 1980 2000   40 60 80  ribbon * range Life Year


                           1960 1980 2000   40 60 80  ribbon * confidence Life Year


                           1960 1980 2000   40 60 80  ribbon * deviation Life Year


                           1960 1980 2000   40 60 80  ribbon * smooth_band Life Year


                           1960 1980 2000   40 60 80  ribbon * straight_band Life Year


                                   0 5 10 15 20   0 5 10 15 20  ribbon * bounds Score






“Given all the gapminder years: a ribbon derived by range, x is year, y is life, beside a ribbon derived by confidence, x is year, y is life, beside a ribbon derived by deviation, x is year, y is life; above a ribbon derived by smooth_band, x is year, y is life, beside a ribbon derived by straight_band, x is year, y is life, beside a ribbon from the score band, from lower to upper, x is score.”
The five plots that read life share one scale, so the widths of their bands can be compared. The range is the widest band. Its lower edge is the single lowest country in each year, so it drops in 1977 and in 1992. The confidence band is about 4 years wide in every year, because a mean computed from 142 values has little uncertainty. The smooth_band and straight_band plots look like thick lines, but they are bands as well. Each is the confidence band of one line fitted through all 1,704 rows, so it is only 1 to 3 years wide, narrower than the confidence band of a single year’s mean.
Layouts. flow follows an amount from one stage to the next. Each stage is a categorical column, named inside flow(). The ribbon draws one band for each combination of categories across the stages, as thick as the amount in that combination. The amount is the column on y, and without one every row counts as 1. A zone and a text layer given the same flow draw the slots at each stage and their names, as the Flow chapter shows. The titanic table counts the people on board by class, sex, age and whether they survived, so y(n) sums those counts:

data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, survived) + color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) +
  text * flow(class, survived) +
  title("ribbon * flow, with zones and names")

  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + color(col["class"]) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  title("ribbon * flow, with zones and names"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + color(:class) +
  zone * flow(:class, :survived) + text * flow(:class, :survived) +

plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),

“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, colored by class, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived, and also text derived by flow through class and survived.”
The widest band goes from Crew to No: 673 of the 885 crew did not survive.
The count axis helps while you build the diagram: it shows that the bands at each stage add up to the same total. A diagram you publish usually leaves it out, with the gridlines and the frame (Leaving out the count axis and the grid). Below, y(n, axis = FALSE) drops the count axis, and theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") drops the gridlines and the frame and makes the panel white:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  ribbon * flow(class, survived) + color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) +
  text * flow(class, survived) +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") +
  title("The same flow, with no count axis")

  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + color(col["class"]) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") +
  title("The same flow, with no count axis"))


data(titanic) + y(:n, axis = false) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) +
  color(:class) + zone * flow(:class, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :survived) +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") +
  title("The same flow, with no count axis")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n, { axis: false }),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), color(col.class),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  theme({ grid: "none", frame: "none", background: "white" }),
  title("The same flow, with no count axis"))






                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Yes No       class survived    The same flow, with no count axis  Class    1st  2nd  3rd  Crew 





“Given titanic: y is n without an axis, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, colored by class, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived, and also text derived by flow through class and survived.”
A ribbon refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. bin, count, proportion, the summaries, the fitted lines and the running total give one number at each value of x, and a band needs two edges. An area fills one value down to the baseline, and a line draws it as a stroke. A ribbon takes no collision modifier: gog never moves a band aside or piles one band on another. Bands that share a place overlap instead, even two violins split by color in one slot, and a ribbon draws each band translucent, so a band behind another still shows, as One band per group explains. jitter moves each point a short way along the categorical axis, and repel moves text labels. partition and cluster lay out rectangles and branches, which zone and path draw. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.14 What you can set
A setting changes how the band looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a ribbon’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(pattern = )
solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots



A ribbon takes area’s list, and for area’s reasons. There is no size, because the band’s shape comes from the two boundaries its transform supplies. There is no border, because the edge is a line traced along the same pair.
One setting this chapter has not shown on a band is a fill pattern. Here is a band with pattern = "grid", and a dashed line along both of its boundaries. The plot uses the score_band table, shown in A pre-computed band:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + x(score) +
  ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges")


(data(score_band) + x(col.score) +
  ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges"))


data(score_band) + x(:score) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") +
  title("A textured band, and its two edges")


plot(data(score_band), x(col.score),
  layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "slateblue", pattern: "grid", opacity: 0.45 }),
  layer(line, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "slateblue", pattern: "dashed" }),
  y_label("Expected true score"),
  title("A textured band, and its two edges"))






                                        0 5 10 15 20   0 5 10 15 20  A textured band, and its two edges Expected true score Score





“Given the score band: x is score, a ribbon from lower to upper, with pattern grid, and also lines from lower to upper, with pattern dashed.”
Both marks read the same bounds(lower, upper) there, exactly as the two ridge layers did, so the edges stay on the band. The two pattern values follow the rule from A pre-computed band: "grid" is a fill texture, and "dashed" a stroke pattern.
The ribbon is written before the line, and the order matters, because a later layer is drawn over an earlier one. Written after its edges, a band covers the inner half of each dashed stroke, and with a ribbon’s default, nearly solid fill, a line inside the band would almost disappear under it.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.15 What it refuses
gog refuses six kinds of ribbon sentence: a category on both axes, a ribbon with nothing to supply its two boundaries, a mapped opacity or a continuous color, any size, a split that leaves one position in every series, and a collision modifier. The first refusal comes from the measure. A band from range spans a low value to a high one, and both are quantities, so one axis must hold a continuous column. With categories on both axes there is nothing to span:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(continent) + y(country)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(col.continent) + y(col.country)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(:continent) + y(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.continent),
  y(col.country))




Error:
! gog: `ribbon` has categorical columns on both axes — `x(continent)` and `y(country)` — so there is nothing for it to span. One axis must hold a continuous column: that is the column the band's low and high come from.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A category on one axis alone is accepted, on either axis. On y, beside a number on x, the band turns down the page and spans each category’s low and high along x, as the profile does in Line. With density, the violins above use a category on y as a slot instead.
A bare ribbon is the second refusal. A plain y() supplies one number, and a band needs two boundaries, as Why a ribbon needs a transform explained. The engine says so rather than drawing an empty panel:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(year) + y(life)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(col.year) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(:year) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), ribbon, x(col.year), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `ribbon` draws a span from a low value to a high one, but nothing here produces those extents. Add a pair transform — `ribbon * range + x(t) + y(value)` draws a band between the min and max at each x, or `ribbon * bounds(lo, hi) + x(t)` a pre-computed one.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two of the six pair transforms, range and bounds, and shows how to write each.
density with no category is refused for the same reason. Over one continuous column it estimates one curve, and one curve is one boundary, not two. The message points to the violin, which needs a category, and to area and line, which draw the curve on its own:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `ribbon * density` estimates one curve, and a ribbon needs two boundaries to span between. Bind a category and the estimate is drawn across its slot — `ribbon * density + x(<category>) + y(<measure>)` is the violin, one distribution per group. For the curve itself, `area * density + x(<measure>)` fills it to the baseline and `line * density + x(<measure>)` traces it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A mapped opacity or a continuous color is the third. A ribbon’s opacity belongs to the layer, and its color to each band, as One region, one fill explains. The message for opacity names style(opacity = ):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + opacity(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  opacity(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `ribbon` — a ribbon takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `gdp` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A categorical column gives each band its own color. A continuous column on color is refused, because one band has one color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + color(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + color(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  color(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `color(gdp)` maps a continuous (numeric) column, but `color` on `ribbon` needs a categorical (text) column.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A size is the fourth, and it is refused both ways. A band’s extent comes from its x values and its two boundaries, so there is no size to map and none to set:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + style(size = 3)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + style(size = 3)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  style(size = 3)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  style({ size: 3 }))




Error:
! gog: `style(size = 3)` — a ribbon has no size to set. Remove it, or use a mark that has one: `point`, `line`, `step`, `interval`, `box`, `text`, `path` or `rule`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Mapping size to a column is refused as well, and the message says to remove the mapping:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + size(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + size(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) + size(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  size(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `size` cannot be bound to `ribbon` — a ribbon has no size feature. Remove the `gdp` mapping from `size`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The fifth refusal comes from a split. Without one, ribbon * range + x(continent) + y(life) draws a single band that runs across all five continents, as in A category on the domain. color(continent) splits that band into five, one per continent. Each of the five then has only one position on x, its own continent, and a band needs at least two positions to run between. So none of the five can be drawn, and gog refuses the sentence. The message suggests interval * range, which draws one whisker at each position:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(continent) + y(life) +
  color(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `ribbon` draws each series through at least two positions, and split by `color(continent)`, every series has one, so nothing would be drawn. Use `interval * range`, which draws each position on its own, or remove a split so each series has more rows.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A collision modifier is the sixth. stack piles the marks that land on one position on top of one another, and dodge sets them side by side. A band measures no height from a baseline, so there is nothing to pile, and it has no width to divide, as One band per group explains. Both messages name style(opacity = ), which lets overlapping bands show through:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range * stack + x(year) + y(life) +
  color(continent)


(data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range * stack + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent))


data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range * stack + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent)


plot(data(gm_continents), layer(ribbon, range, stack), x(col.year),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `stack` piles on top of one another the bars or areas that a `color` split draws at one position — but `ribbon` is not one of those. A ribbon already spans a low to a high, so it measures no height from a baseline to pile — overlapping bands are told apart by transparency (`style(opacity = )`).
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.




RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range * dodge + x(year) + y(life) +
  color(continent)


(data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range * dodge + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent))


data(gm_continents) + ribbon * range * dodge + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent)


plot(data(gm_continents), layer(ribbon, range, dodge), x(col.year),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `dodge` sets side by side the bars, boxes, whiskers or points that would land on one position — but `ribbon` is not one of those. A filled band has no width to subdivide — overlapping bands are told apart by transparency (`style(opacity = )`).
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


One more refusal is not about the ribbon itself. It comes from the colored ridges in Letting the ridges overlap. Written before both marks, color(continent) reaches the line layer too, and that layer already sets its color with style(color = "black"). One layer cannot both map a channel and set it, so gog refuses the sentence rather than choose one of the two. The message names both fixes:

  area * density(reach = 2.2) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9)

  area * density(reach = 2.2) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9))

  area * density(reach = 2.2) + line * density(reach = 2.2) +
  style(color = "black", size = 0.9)

Written after area * density(reach = 2.2), as in that section, color(continent) belongs to the area layer alone, and the sentence draws.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.16 In short
A ribbon fills the space between two boundaries, and refuses to draw until a transform supplies them. The transform decides what the band means: the extremes from range, the middle from two quantiles, the mean’s uncertainty from confidence, and a band computed elsewhere from bounds. Over a category, density makes the ribbon a violin. Both edges come from the data, so the band’s shape is never a setting. opacity belongs to the layer, and color to each band.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.17 What comes next
A ribbon shows a region and names nothing inside it. Text draws a string at each position, read from a column.




Hintze, J. L., & Nelson, R. D. (1998). Violin plots: A box plot–density trace synergism. The American Statistician, 52(2), 181–184. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1998.10480559

title: 16  Text
text:
16.1 The mark and its content
Which point is which? text draws a string, a piece of text such as a name or a number, at each (x, y) position. It is point’s sibling: both place one glyph per row. A point’s glyph is a dot by default. A text mark’s glyph is a string, and that string comes from a column, through the label channel. This chapter uses it four ways: to name the points of a scatter, to print a value on a bar, to write a note on a plot, and to name the parts that a transform places, such as the nodes of a network.
Every plot in this chapter is drawn on a white panel, with theme(background = "white"), instead of gog’s light gray. Dark letters and gray dots are easier to read on white. The panel’s background shows the setting.
A point tells you where a row is; it cannot tell you which row. The medals table holds five countries, one row each, with the number of gold, silver and bronze medals each country won. Drawn as dots, the five countries are five points with nothing to say which country is which:

title: 16  Text
section: 16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter
text:
16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter
A dot marks one position on the panel. A word is much wider than a dot, so a name on its own only shows roughly where its row is. The two marks can be drawn together: layer a point mark and a text mark on the same x and y, with the + operator. The dot gives the exact position and the string gives the name. That is a labeled scatter, built from two marks rather than a third mark of its own.
Each style() applies to the mark written before it. So style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") sets the dots’ size and colors them a medium gray. The words keep their own size and color. Without a nudge, each label is drawn centered on its dot, and the word hides the dot, as on the left. style(nudge = "up") moves every label above its dot, as on the right:

    title("No nudge: each name sits on its dot") +
    theme(background = "white")) |

  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)

You do not give a distance. The engine sets it from each label’s own font size, far enough that the word does not touch a dot of the default size. That is why nudge asks only for a direction, and every label moves in that one direction. jitter and dodge work differently: they compute each mark’s offset from the data, so marks can move by different amounts. Only text accepts a nudge. A point or a bar has no label to move, so the engine refuses the setting there and names the mark that does.

Every name is centered on its own dot, and where the countries crowd together the words overlap. Germany, Belgium, Finland and the United Kingdom have almost the same gdp and life, so their four names are drawn on top of one another.
repel solves that. It is one of the four collision modifiers, with jitter, dodge and stack, so it is written after the mark with *, not inside style(). It measures where the labels and the dots actually are, then moves each label off the words around it:

  theme(background = "white")

  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same thirty, moved apart"), theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”
Notice three things in this plot. Every label is drawn just outside its dot, so no word covers the dot it names. A label with other words near it moves to whichever side has room. A label with space around it stays directly above its dot. The first two follow from one rule: repel pulls each label toward its own dot, and pushes it away from every other word and every dot, its own included. The third follows from where repel starts. A plain label is centered on its dot, but repel starts every label just above its dot, so a label with nothing near it stays there.
In a more crowded plot, repel can move a label much further from its dot. Once the gap is larger than the height of one line of text, gog draws a thin line from the dot to the word, so you can still see which dot the name belongs to. No label in this plot moved that far, so none has a line.
The placement is deterministic. It uses no random-number generator and does not read the computer’s clock, so the same sentence draws the same picture every time. It does depend on the order of the rows, though. repel settles the overlaps pair by pair, in the order of the rows, so the same rows in a different order can end with some labels in different places.
Sometimes no placement keeps every label apart. repel then still draws every label, and gog prints a message saying how many still overlap. Which names to leave out is your decision, so repel never removes one. In this plot all thirty fit, so gog prints no message.

Three things give crowded labels more room, and the message names all three: fewer rows, a smaller style(size = ), and a larger plot. theme(width =, height =) sets the plot’s size in pixels, and the Composition chapter explains it.
Fewer rows is often the right choice. On a large table you usually name only the few rows that matter: give the text layer its own table that holds just those rows, as A note is a layer does with one row. In the web edition, clicking a dot on a plot with brush() shows its values beside it, which Selection calls a stamp. Stamps help you choose those rows. title: 16  Text
section: 16.3 Number labels: the value on each mark
text:
16.3 Number labels: the value on each mark
A label does not have to be a name, and it does not have to be drawn on a scatter. A bar shows which country won more gold medals. To read how many more, a reader has to measure each bar against the axis, and that measurement is only an estimate. Sometimes the number itself is the answer. Bind a column that holds numbers and each row’s value is drawn. By default, a whole number is printed without a decimal point, and any other number is rounded to at most three decimal places. Layer text over bar to print each bar’s height. Without a nudge, each number is centered on its bar’s top edge, and the edge crosses the digits. style(nudge = "up") moves each number just above its bar:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(country) + y(gold) + label(gold) + style(nudge = "up") +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + label(col.gold) + style(nudge = "up") +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") + text + x(:country) +
  y(:gold) + label(:gold) + style(nudge = "up") + y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") + theme(background = "white")


plot(data(medals), bar, style({ color: "steelblue" }), text,
  x(col.country), y(col.gold), label(col.gold), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  y_label("Gold medals"), title("Each bar labeled with its height"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: bars and also text, x is country, y is gold, label by gold, with nudge up.”
Each bar now carries its number, so the difference between the USA’s 46 and China’s 38 can be read without the axis.
The medals table already holds the numbers. A bar chart that counts rows computes its numbers itself. In bar * count, the count transform writes the number of rows in each bar into a column called count. text * count uses the same transform, so label(count) can print that column on each bar. The count column is not in gapminder_2007. The transform writes it, so only a layer that runs the transform can name it. The column each transform writes lists the column each transform writes. As in the medals plot, the numbers are nudged up:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  text * count + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  text * count + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + text * count +
  label(:count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") + theme(background = "white")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  layer(text, count), label(col.count), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Each bar labeled with its count"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, and also text derived by count, label by count, with nudge up.”
Africa’s bar is labeled 52, and Oceania’s bar is labeled 2.
To draw the bars horizontally, put the category on y instead of x. Each bar is then drawn from left to right, and the counts are on the x axis. The text layer reads the same positions, so each number is centered on the right end of its bar. The nudge points in the direction the bars grow, so it is now style(nudge = "right"), which moves each number just past that end:

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, y is continent, and also text derived by count, label by count, with nudge right.”
Africa’s 52 is past the end of the longest bar, and Oceania’s 2 is past the shortest. The axis already reaches a little past the longest bar, and Africa’s 52 fits in that room. A label that would not fit inside the panel widens its axis instead (Scales).
A histogram is labeled the same way. The bin transform also writes a column called count, the number of rows in each bin. So text * bin with label(count) prints how many countries fall in each bin of life expectancy:

data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  text * bin + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")

  text * bin + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))

  style(nudge = "up") + theme(background = "white")

  label(col.count), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, and also text derived by bin, label by count, with nudge up.”
The last bin, from about 78 to 83 years, holds the most countries: 32.
Add proportion to both layers, and each bar is a share of all the countries instead of a count. bin writes a count column, and proportion then turns each count into a share, so the rows hold a column called proportion and no count. The text layer therefore names label(proportion):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")

  style(nudge = "up") + theme(background = "white")

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and proportion, x is life, and also text derived by bin and proportion, label by proportion with 2 decimal places, with nudge up.”
The last bin is now labeled 0.23. Its 32 countries make a share of 0.2254 of the 142, and decimals = 2 rounds the share to two decimal places. decimals is explained a few plots below, where each continent’s mean life expectancy is printed. These rows hold no count, so label(count) is refused, and the message names the transform that replaced it:

After a summary such as mean, there is also one row for each bar. In bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life), each of those rows holds its continent’s mean, written into life itself. A summary is given a column to reduce, here the life named on y, so its answer replaces that column. count, bin and proportion are given no column, so they write a new column with a name of their own. So text * mean with label(life) prints each continent’s mean life expectancy:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  text * mean + label(life) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +

  theme(background = "white")

  y(col.life), layer(text, mean), label(col.life), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also text derived by mean, label by life, with nudge up.”
Asia’s mean, 70.72848, is printed as 70.728. For sum, median, max, min and quantile, write label() with the column the summary reads.
Asia’s label, 70.728, has more decimal places than this plot needs. You cannot round a mean before gog computes it, so label() takes the number of decimal places to print. label(life, decimals = 1) prints Asia’s mean as 70.7:

data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +

  theme(background = "white")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  text * mean + label(col.life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))

  text * mean + label(:life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),

  style({ nudge: "up" }), theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also text derived by mean, label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge up.”
Each label now has one decimal place, from Africa’s 54.8 to Oceania’s 80.7. Every label gets exactly one decimal place, so a mean of exactly 77 would print as 77.0, and all five labels show the same precision. decimals = 0 rounds each mean to a whole number, so Asia’s prints as 71. gog reads a categorical column as names, not numbers, so there is no number to round, and label(country, decimals = 1) is refused:

data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country, decimals = 1)

A sum can be a very large number. bar * sum with y(population) adds up the people of each continent, and label(population) prints Asia’s sum in full, as 3811953827. A number that long is hard to read. label(population, short = TRUE) prints it short, with K for thousands, M for millions, B for billions (a thousand millions) and T for trillions (a million millions):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
  text * sum + label(population, short = TRUE) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")

  text * sum + label(col.population, short = True) + style(nudge = "up") +

Asia’s label is now 3.81B, and Oceania’s is 24.5M. A short number keeps three significant digits. decimals sets the number of decimal places instead, so label(population, short = TRUE, decimals = 1) prints 3.8B for Asia. An axis takes short too: y(population, short = TRUE) takes each tick’s letter from the tick’s own size, as Scales shows. Without short, an axis chooses one letter for all its ticks from the distance between them. Here the ticks are a billion apart, so the axis already writes 1B, 2B, 3B and 4B, and short would change nothing.

The axis takes the same argument on y(proportion), so the axis and the labels are written the same way. Without decimals, a percent keeps one decimal place and leaves it off when it is 0, so a share of 0.190 prints as 19%, not 19.0%. percent and short cannot be used together, because they are two ways to write one number. After bin * cumulative, each bin holds two numbers: its own count, and the total so far. cumulative writes the total to a column named cumulative, and the count column that bin wrote stays beside it. So label(cumulative) prints the height of each bar, and label(count) prints each bin’s own count on the same bar:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)

    text * bin * cumulative + label(col.cumulative) + style(nudge = "up") +

    theme(background = "white")) |

  text * bin * cumulative + label(:count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("label(count): each bin on its own") +

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life, and also text derived by bin and cumulative, label by cumulative, with nudge up, beside bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life, and also text derived by bin and cumulative, label by count, with nudge up.”
The bars, and the places of the labels, are the same in both plots, because x and y place a label and label chooses only the number it shows. On the left, each number is the bar’s height, so it matches the y axis: the last bar reaches 142. On the right, the numbers do not match the y axis, and that is not a mistake. Each is the count of one bin: 32, the last, is 142 minus the 110 before it.

16.3.2 Labels on stacked bars
With stack, the groups are piled up in one bar instead of being set side by side, so each group is one segment of the bar. Only the lowest segment can be read from the y axis, because each other segment starts where the one below it ends. A label layer with the same stack and a split of its own prints each segment’s value in the middle of that segment. A third layer, text * sum with no split, adds up all of a class’s rows, so it prints the class’s total. style(nudge = "up", size = 18) moves that total above the bar and draws it larger than the labels inside the segments:

  text * sum * stack + group(:survived) + label(:n) + text * sum +
  label(:n) + style(nudge = "up", size = 18) + y_label("People") +
  theme(background = "white")


plot(data(titanic), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.class), y(col.n),
  color(col.survived), layer(text, sum, stack), group(col.survived),
  label(col.n), layer(text, sum), label(col.n),

It ends at 885 on the y axis, but its label prints 673, the people in that segment alone. stack moves each segment up to where the one below it ends, and the label still prints the segment’s own count. No segment’s label shows the class’s total, so the third layer prints it above the bar.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.4 Color
You see a hue faster than you can read a word, so a color split shows you the groups before you read a single name. Every label so far has been printed in one color, which is the default. Map a categorical column to color and the labels split by that column. A continuous column on color is refused on a text mark, and the message suggests size or opacity instead, as What it refuses shows. The mapping gets a legend to name the groups, and the colors come from the same palette that points and bars use. In the plot below, which draws the medals table shown in The mark and its content, each country is its own group, so the hue repeats the name. style(size = 15) draws the letters a little larger than the default 13 pixels, as Styling: one color, one size explains:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + color(country) +
  style(size = 15) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + color(col.country) +
  style(size = 15) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  color(:country) + style(size = 15) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  color(col.country), style({ size: 15 }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("One hue per country"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, color by country, with size 15.”
The legend names the five hues. A column whose value several rows share, such as continent, is more useful: one hue marks every name in a group before you read any of them. The gm_populous table, shown in repel: moving labels off each other, has such a column. Its ten countries come from three continents:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  label(country) + color(continent) +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  label(col.country) + color(col.continent) +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  label(:country) + color(:continent) + theme(background = "white")


plot(data(gm_populous), layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), label(col.country), color(col.continent),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

The six Asian names share one hue, the three from the Americas share another, and Nigeria is the only name in a third hue.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.5 Styling: one color, one size
The color channel takes its hues from a column. When the words are the whole plot, with no dots or bars beside them, you may want one color of your own and a larger font. The default size, 13 pixels, is often too small to read comfortably. Neither comes from a column, so both are settings rather than mappings. style(color = ) sets the color of the words, and style(size = ) sets the font size in pixels. Each applies to every label in the layer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ color: "seagreen", size: 17 }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("Bigger, greener labels"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))






             USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Bigger, greener labels Silver Gold





“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, colored seagreen, with size 17.”
A setting gives every label in the layer the same font size. To size each label by a value of its own, map a column instead, as the next section shows.

title: 16  Text
section: 16.6 Sizing and fading labels by a column
text:
16.6 Sizing and fading labels by a column
size and opacity are channels on text, as they are on point. A mapped size draws each label at a font size from 8 to 24 pixels. The smallest value gets 8, the largest gets 24, and the others fall in proportion between them. Here, the more bronze medals a country won, the larger its name:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + size(bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + size(col.bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  size(:bronze) + x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  size(col.bronze), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))






             USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Each name sized by its bronze medals Silver Gold  Bronze   a 9 a 23.5 a 38 





“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, size by bronze.”
The legend shows the letter a at three sizes between 8 and 24 pixels, because a label is read by the size of its letters. A mapped opacity works the same way. The smallest value is drawn at opacity 0.15, faint but visible, and the largest at 0.95:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + opacity(bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + opacity(col.bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  opacity(:bronze) + x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") + theme(background = "white")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  opacity(col.bronze), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))






             USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Fewer bronze medals, fainter name Silver Gold  Bronze   a 9 a 23.5 a 38 





“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, opacity by bronze.”
These two plots show that size and opacity work on text as they do on point, not that they suit this table. Size is hard to read on words, because a long name looks larger than a short one at the same font size, and a faint name is hard to read at all. To compare bronze medals, a position such as x(bronze), or the number itself, as in Number labels, shows them more clearly.
gog sets each channel’s scale from every row of the layer, so one value draws at the same size and opacity in every panel.
A word cloud also sizes each word by a value, but its positions carry no data: each word is placed wherever there is room. In gog a label is drawn at its row’s x and y, and repel only moves it off its neighbors, so gog draws no word cloud.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.7 Labels in the cube
A 3-D scatter has the same problem as a flat one: a dot does not say which row it is. A label can be drawn in the cube, as a point can. Bind z, and each label is drawn at the place its row’s three positions give it. Nearer labels are drawn over farther ones:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(gold) + y(silver) + z(bronze) +
  label(country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + z(col.bronze) +
  label(col.country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white"))


data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + z(:bronze) +
  label(:country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white")


plot(data(medals), point, layer(text, repel), x(col.gold), y(col.silver),
  z(col.bronze), label(col.country),
  title("Each country at its three medal counts"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))






                              Germany Russia Great Britain China USA   40 30 20 30 20 10 30 20 10 Gold Silver Bronze  Each country at its three medal counts





“Given the medals: points and also text derived by repel, x is gold, y is silver, z is bronze, label by country.”
repel moves labels off each other and off the dots, as on a flat plot. A nudge moves a label on the picture, not in the cube: "up" is toward the top of the image at every angle.
In the web edition, turn the cube with the pointer, as Three measurements on three axes shows: drag left and right to turn it, and up and down to tip it. At every angle repel places the labels again, so you can watch each name move away from the other names and from the dots.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.8 A halo around each label
A label drawn over a dot or a line can be hard to read, because the mark shows around its letters. style(border_size = ) draws a halo: a band of the panel’s background color around each letter, drawn under the text. It hides the mark next to each letter and does not change the letters. The ten most populous countries, from the gm_populous table shown in repel: moving labels off each other, have names that cross other countries’ dots. Here they are without a halo and with one. Neither plot draws the life axis, so the two are the same size and repel puts every name in the same place in both:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
    x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life, axis = FALSE) +
    data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(country) +
    x_label("GDP per person") + title("No halo") +
    theme(background = "white", grid = "none")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
      x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life, axis = FALSE) +
      data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(country) +
      style(border_size = 2) +
      x_label("GDP per person") + title("Names with a halo") +
      theme(background = "white", grid = "none"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460)


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
    x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life, axis = False) +
    data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(col.country) +
    x_label("GDP per person") + title("No halo") +
    theme(background = "white", grid = "none")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
      x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life, axis = False) +
      data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(col.country) +
      style(border_size = 2) +
      x_label("GDP per person") + title("Names with a halo") +
      theme(background = "white", grid = "none"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life, axis = false) + data(gm_populous) +
  text * repel + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("No halo") + theme(background = "white", grid = "none")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life, axis = false) + data(gm_populous) +
  text * repel + label(:country) + style(border_size = 2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Names with a halo") +

beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life, { axis: false }),
  data(gm_populous), layer(text, repel), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("No halo"),
  theme({ background: "white", grid: "none" })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life, { axis: false }),
  data(gm_populous), layer(text, repel), label(col.country),
  style({ border_size: 2 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Names with a halo"),
  theme({ background: "white", grid: "none" })),
  theme({ width: 1100, height: 460 }))






                                                                                                                                                              China India United States Indonesia Brazil Pakistan Bangladesh Nigeria Japan Mexico           1K 10K    No halo GDP per person


                                                                                                                                                            China India United States Indonesia Brazil Pakistan Bangladesh Nigeria Japan Mexico   China India United States Indonesia Brazil Pakistan Bangladesh Nigeria Japan Mexico           1K 10K    Names with a halo GDP per person






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life without an axis, and also text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, label by country, beside points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life without an axis, and also text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, label by country, with border size 2.”
On the left, the dots behind United States, Mexico and Brazil show through their letters. On the right, a thin band of the panel’s color separates every letter from the dots behind it. border_size sets the width, in pixels, of the line drawn around each letter to make the halo. Half of that line lies under the letters, so a width of 2 shows as a band 1 pixel wide. border_color sets its color, if you want one other than the background. Either setting alone draws a halo: an unset width is 3 pixels, and an unset color is the panel’s background color. With neither, a label has no halo.
repel moves a name off dots that have no name only a little, and a nudge would move every name the same way, often onto other dots. A halo makes each name readable where it is. It also suits a label that has to stay where it is: a note written along the line it describes, as in Turning a label, or the name of a network node with edges passing behind it, as in Transforms it takes.
A halo hides the marks it covers, so use it where the words matter more than those marks. Within one layer it never hides another label’s letters, because every halo in a layer is drawn before any of that layer’s letters. A text layer written later is drawn on top, so its halos can cover the letters of an earlier text layer. A halo does not move overlapping labels apart. That is the job of repel.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.9 Turning a label
A note beside a vertical line is easiest to read when it is written along the line, not across it. style(angle = ) turns every label in its layer by the number of degrees you give, counterclockwise from horizontal, so 90 reads upward and -90 downward. Each label turns around its own position, the point its x and y give. The milestones table holds two notes. Each is drawn at the income in at and the height in value:



milestones: all 2 rows


at
value
note




10000
72
less steep from here


40000
80
almost flat here





In this plot a vertical rule marks each income, and each note is drawn along its rule:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  data(milestones) + rule + x(at) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  data(milestones) + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note) +
  style(angle = 90, border_size = 2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Notes turned 90 degrees") +
  theme(background = "white")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  data(milestones) + rule + x(col.at) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  data(milestones) + text + x(col.at) + y(col.value) + label(col.note) +
  style(angle = 90, border_size = 2) +

title: 16  Text
text:
16.10 Why label is a channel
A setting is a value you type into the sentence. You might expect to type a label into the sentence in the same way, like a title. A label is not a title: it is one value per row, and that makes it data. One rule of the grammar decides whether a label is a setting or a channel: data reaches a mark only through a channel. That makes label a channel, so no mark takes the words themselves as an argument. A fixed note is therefore a table with one row, given to data(), and never a value given to style().
Only text accepts label; every other mark refuses it, which is why a labeled scatter is point + text and never a label on point. text requires a label: the label is part of the mark’s minimum syllable, as x and y are. Ask for a text mark with no label and the engine refuses, and says what to write instead, as What it refuses shows. text is the mark, and label is the channel that carries the column it draws.

title: 16  Text

If you have used ggplot2, a note there is a separate function, annotate(). In gog it is a table with one row, and the plot below draws it. A second data() gives the mark written right after it its own table (Data), and a table with one row in it puts one string on the plot:
