The note is in an empty corner of the scatter: no country in 2007 has an income that high with lives that short.
That plot needed nothing new in the grammar. A mark written directly after a data() already reads that table, and text already draws one string per row. The note is data like any other, so it is scaled like any other. Give the note an x far from the points, and the axes stretch to cover it, so check the axes each time you place a note.
That is more to write than ggplot2’s annotate(): a table, even for one note. In return, a note follows every rule a row follows. It is placed on the axes’ scale, it can take channels such as color, several notes are rows of one table, and one table can feed several layers, as milestones feeds a rule and a text in Turning a label.
One rule applies while writing a note. The text layer names no position of its own, so it reads the columns the axes use, gdp and life, from its own table. That is why income_note has a column with each of those names. When a note table’s columns have other names, write its positions after text, as Turning a label does for the milestones table: + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note). Any other mark at a place you choose is written the same way: a small table, and a layer over it. A dot on the plot is a point over the same one-row table, and several notes are several rows.

title: 16  Text

16.12 Text that a transform places
You choose where a note goes. A transform can choose the place instead, and then the text names whatever that transform built. The table’s first three transforms, layout, flow and partition, are explained in later chapters, so you do not need to know them yet: the table only shows where a label can go. In the first seven rows, a second layer with the same transform draws the shape that the text names:



Text derived by
What it labels




text * layout
the nodes of a network, beside point * layout and edge * layout (Network)


text * flow
each stage’s slots in a flow, beside ribbon * flow and zone * flow (Flow)


text * partition
the regions of a hierarchy, beside zone * partition (Polar)


text * count, text * bin
the count of each bar, beside bar * count or bar * bin (Number labels)


text * mean, text * sum and the other summaries
the summary of each bar, beside bar * mean or bar * sum (Number labels)


text * dodge
each group’s bar in a slot, beside bar * dodge (Labels on dodged bars)


text * stack
each group’s segment of a pile, beside bar * stack (Labels on stacked bars)


text * repel
the scatter labels of repel, moved off each other



The plots in Transforms it takes, below, draw the first three, one at a time. In each, the text is a layer over the mark that drew the shape, and both layers read the same transform.

A text mark refuses every transform in the Refuses column of the table at the start of this section. smooth and straight compute a line at evenly spaced places along x, not at the values in your rows. A label there would print no value from your table. A line draws the fitted values instead. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, two numbers where a label prints one. interval and ribbon draw the pair, and text * max or text * min prints one end of a range. jitter moves each point a short way along the categorical axis, and it does not measure the space a label’s letters take, so jittered labels can still cover each other. repel does measure it, so it is the collision modifier that moves labels apart. cluster joins the closest categories into a tree, which path draws.

title: 16  Text

16.14 What you can set
The Styling section set a color and a size. Those are two entries in a longer list, and the whole of it is here: which color, how transparent, which size, which way to shift the label, by how many degrees to turn it, and the color and width of its halo. A setting gives one value to every label in the layer. Three of them, color, size and opacity, can instead be mapped from a column, as the sections above show. Each mark takes its own settings. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a text mark’s settings, with the values each accepts:



Setting

pixels


style(border_color = )

style(border_size = )
pixels


style(nudge = )
up, down, left, right


style(angle = )
degrees, counterclockwise from horizontal

title: 16  Text
text:
16.16 In short
A text mark will not draw without a label, and no other mark accepts one. Its words come from a column, so a fixed note is a table with one row. repel draws every label and reports how many still overlap, because which names to leave out is your decision.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.17 What comes next
Without repel, row order never moves a word: each one is drawn at the position its own row gives it. For a path, row order decides which rows are joined: the mark joins each row to the next, in the order the table holds them.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.1 The connected scatterplot
How did income and life expectancy change together in each country, year by year? path draws one stroke through the rows’ points, in the order the table gives them. That is the whole definition of the mark, and it is the one thing line does not do. A line sorts its vertices along its domain first, because a line is read as a function: one value for each place on the domain. If two rows have the same x, such as two readings in one year, and no color or group splits them into separate lines, the line still joins both: it runs straight up or down at that x, and gog prints a warning, as the plots below show. With two numbers the domain is x, so the line is read from left to right. A path draws a route. It visits row 1, then row 2, and it may turn back, cross itself, or return to where it started.
The gapminder_asia table holds five Asian countries, each measured every five years from 1952 to 2007, twelve times in all. So every year has five rows, one for each country, and the table lists China’s twelve rows first, then India’s. The top plots draw a line and the bottom plots a path, without and with group(country):
“Given gapminder Asia: a line, x is year, y is life, beside the same grouped by country; above a path, x is year, y is life, beside the same grouped by country.”
On the top left, nothing splits the rows, so the line sorts them by year and joins the five values of each year. It runs straight up and down at every year, and gog prints the warning above the plot. On the bottom left, the path keeps the table’s order: it draws China from 1952 to 2007, then jumps back to India in 1952, and so on, so four long lines run back to the left. gog prints no warning, because following the rows’ order is what a path is for. On the right, group(country) gives each country its own stroke. Each country’s rows are already in year order, so the line and the path draw the same picture.
The two marks draw the same kind of stroke. They take the same splits by color, group and a mapped pattern, and the same style(size = ) and style(pattern = ) settings. One question separates them: does the order of the rows mean something? A path keeps that order, and three things follow from it. It can carry an arrowhead, because its last vertex is the table’s last row. In polar it can go around the circle more than once, because two rows with the same angle stay apart, each on its own turn. And it can run through the cube, because the row order does not depend on any axis. None of the three needs a rule of its own, and each has a section with a plot later in this chapter.
The plots above put the year on x and show one measure, life expectancy. To see how income and life expectancy changed together, put income on x and life expectancy on y. No axis is left for the year, but each country’s rows are already in year order. Check the order before you draw any path. A path joins the rows exactly as the table lists them and never sorts them, so rows in the wrong order draw a route that never happened. If they are not in order, sort the table first, in your own language, by the column the route should follow, here year. A path joins these rows in year order, so it still shows time:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Fifty-five years, five countries, one plane")


(data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Fifty-five years, five countries, one plane"))


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Fifty-five years, five countries, one plane")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), path, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.country), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Fifty-five years, five countries, one plane"))






                                     0 10K 20K 30K   40 50 60 70 80  Fifty-five years, five countries, one plane Life expectancy GDP per person  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep.
“Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country.”
Each route is one country’s history. The plot has no time axis, but it still shows time: time is the order in which the points are joined. China’s route goes almost straight up at very low income. That shape belongs to a country whose life expectancy rose long before its income did, and India’s and Indonesia’s routes rise the same way. Korea’s route starts upward and then turns a sharp corner to the right. Past that corner its income climbs fast and its life expectancy rises more slowly. Japan’s route is the flattest of the five. It begins where Korea’s route turns: Japan had that income and life expectancy in 1952, twenty years before Korea. This is a connected scatterplot, and path is the only mark that draws it.
A connected scatterplot usually also draws a dot at each measurement, as a scatterplot does. The plot above leaves the dots out, so the routes are easier to follow. text:
17.2 What line draws instead
line is the mark you would probably write first, because it is the familiar way to join rows with a stroke. So compare what line draws from the same table. One word changes in the sentence, and two of the five routes visibly change shape:

  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("the same data, sorted by x")

  color(col.country), x_label("GDP per person"),

                                     0 10K 20K 30K   40 50 60 70 80  the same data, sorted by x Life expectancy GDP per person  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is gdp, y is life, color by country.”
Look at Indonesia’s route. Its income did not rise steadily: it fell three times, in 1962, in 1967 and in 2002. So the year order and the income order differ, and line joins the points in income order. Near the bottom of the plot, Indonesia’s line now goes up to its 1967 point, back down to its 1957 point, and up again. Near the top of its route, the fall in 2002 makes a second zigzag. Every point is still in the right place, but the stroke between them no longer follows the years. Japan’s income fell once, in 2002, and its route changes the same way near its right end. China’s income also fell once, in 1962, by less than 100 dollars. On an axis that runs past 30,000 dollars, China’s points from 1952 to 1967 lie almost in one vertical line, so its route looks the same in both plots. India’s and Korea’s income rose at every measurement, so for them both marks draw the same picture. This is not a defect in line. A line is read as a function, with one value for each x, and these rows have one value for each x. Sorting the rows by x cannot change which value belongs to which x. For a time series read along a date axis, the sort simply puts the rows in date order.
The two marks answer different questions. Both sentences are legal, so gog draws either plot and prints no message. Choosing the mark is your decision (Law 8), and one rule helps you make it. If the reader should follow the points in any order other than left to right, that order has to come from the table, and only path takes its order from the table.
The bump chart, which follows each country’s rank from year to year, needs a path for another reason. Its y is the rank, stored as text (1st, 2nd and so on), so y is a categorical axis. A line with a categorical y runs down that axis: it joins each country’s points from the top rank to the bottom, not from the first year to the last. A path joins them in the table’s order, which is year order. The gm_twelve table holds the ranks in life expectancy of twelve Asian countries in each of twelve years. It lists all twelve countries for 1952, then all twelve for 1957, and so on. That order matters for the path: color(country) splits the rows into one path per country, and within each country the rows come in year order, so each path runs from 1952 to 2007:

17.3 Which end is the last row?
A route has a direction, and a plain stroke does not show it. Japan’s route could be read from either end. So path takes a setting that a line cannot:

Now each route points at its last row. arrow takes "end", "start", or "both": an arrowhead (a head, for short) at the last row, at the first row, or at both ends.
Two marks take it: path, and edge, the line between two nodes of a network. Every other mark refuses it. A line’s last vertex is the row with the largest x, so a head there would point at the end of the sort, not at the last row. A path’s end comes from the data. So a line with style(arrow = "end") is refused:

  style(arrow = "end")

  style(arrow = "end"))

  style(arrow = "end")

  color(col.country), style({ arrow: "end" }))




Error:

Use `path`, which strokes the rows in the data's own order and so has an end the data chose.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Here x is the year, and each country’s rows are already in year order. So for each country’s line the sort and the table order agree, and each head would land on 2007. gog refuses it anyway, because on a line the end of the stroke always comes from the sort.

"end" puts the head on the last row of the arrow’s table. In botswana_arrow that is row 2, beside Botswana’s dot, so the arrow points from the note to the dot. With the two rows in the other order, the head would point at the note.
This grammar has no separate function for notes, such as ggplot2’s annotate(). An annotation, a note with its arrow, is made of layers, each over a small table. Its marks are the marks everything else uses: text for the words, path for the arrow, and point for a dot at a place you choose. The arrow’s table holds data, so gog scales it like any other table. That is why the arrow’s ends are written in the data’s own units rather than in pixels.
On a scatterplot drawn with point, there is another way to label a point, though you cannot set how the label looks. Add brush() to the sentence, and on a web page a click on a point stamps it: a card with the point’s values stays beside it, joined to it by a short line. Drag the card away from the crowded points, and the line ends in an arrowhead at the point, much like the arrow above. Stamping a point shows how. A stamp is gone when the page reloads, but the camera button saves the plot with its stamps as a picture file. A note drawn with text and path is part of the sentence, so it is drawn again every time, for anyone who has the data.

title: 17  Path
section: 17.5 Two transforms, and the rest refused
text:
17.5 Two transforms, and the rest refused
Every path so far has been drawn directly from the rows. The next question is what happens when a transform changes the rows before the path draws them. line, step, area and ribbon compose with many transforms. path composes with two, density and cluster, and refuses every other transform. The summaries show the reason most clearly. What it refuses shows path * mean being refused.
A summary replaces the rows. mean reduces each country to one number, so what is left to connect is one point per country. Those points are in the order of the keys (here, the countries), not in the order of the table’s rows. One point per country, joined left to right, is what line already draws. A path’s meaning is the row order, and a summary discards that order. That is why this mark refuses almost every transform, and why its row on the Combinations grid is nearly empty.
This chapter shows density in detail. It draws cluster once, in Transforms it takes, and Cluster explains it in full. Like a summary, density replaces the rows. Unlike a summary, its new rows have an order that means something: they are the points around each ring, in the order the ring is traced.

“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length, beside a surface derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length, in the cube.”
The zones color each small cell by the density there, and the surface lifts the same values into two peaks, the two places the contour’s rings surround. The surface needs space(), because a sheet lives in the cube. density supplies its height, the density at each place, so the sentence binds only x and y. Without space(), gog refuses the surface. On the web page you can turn the cube with the pointer. Surface draws each one larger and explains them.
That contour needed nothing new in the grammar. One rule produced it, and the same rule makes zone * bin draw a heatmap. The rule is that the mark decides how many positions a transform reads. For density, that is the number of positions it is estimated over, and you never state it yourself. A bar shows the density as its length, and that length takes one axis. So bar * density estimates the density along the other axis, and draws one thin bar at each point where it was estimated. A path traces the density’s contours, and a contour needs both axes, so path * density estimates the density over both. So there is no contour atom: a contour is written as path * density.
Each ring is traced at one value of the density, called its level. Read the outermost ring, then the ones inside it. The outermost is a single ring around both groups, and the next level inward splits into two separate rings. One level can therefore be several separate rings. So a level is not one stroke, the way one color value is one line. Each ring is drawn as its own stroke, and the level decides only its color. The two rings of one level are never joined across the gap between them.

17.6.1 The parameters
The rings are colored by their level, and you did not bind color to get that. Just as bin writes a column named count, density writes a new column, level, into the rows it returns. Each ring’s level is the estimated density, which is the same at every place on that ring, and those are the numbers on the legend. In the plot above they run from about 0.02, for the palest and outermost ring, to about 0.14 for the darkest. gog bound color to level, the same way bar * bin binds y for you. Bind it yourself if you prefer, and change how many rings are traced:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 10) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + color(level) +
  title("ten levels, named out loud")


(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 10) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + color(col.level) +
  title("ten levels, named out loud"))

The rings now come in ten levels instead of the default six, so they are closer together.
density is one transform, and the mark decides what it computes. With line it computes a curve over one column. With zone or path it computes a field over two columns: a zone fills the field, and a path draws its rings. The parameters follow from this. A width suits the curve, and a number of levels suits the field.
levels sets how many levels the contour is traced at, as levels = 10 did above. Of the three marks that read the field, zone and path accept it, and surface refuses it, for a reason Surface gives. line * density refuses it too. Over one column, the density is drawn as a single curve. A curve has no contour, so there are no levels to count:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(levels = 4) + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(levels = 4) + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(levels = 4) + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ levels: 4 })),
  x(col.life))

To estimate a density, density places a small bell-shaped curve on each row and adds the curves up. bandwidth is the width of each of those curves, written in the column’s own units: bandwidth = 1 on life makes each one a year wide (Choosing the bandwidth). A contour is estimated over two columns, and two columns usually have different units, such as dollars and years, so one number cannot be a width in both. gog therefore refuses bandwidth on a contour. It refuses it here too, although sepal length and petal length are both in centimeters, because the rule counts the columns, not their units. What it refuses shows that refusal.
adjust multiplies the bandwidth gog chooses by itself. It is a plain number rather than a length, so it means the same thing on either axis. line, zone, surface and path all accept it. The four plots below draw the same flowers at four values of adjust:

Each species has its own set of rings. Both sets take their colors from the levels, so the colors do not say which set is which species. Versicolor has the shorter petals, so its set is the lower one. The two fields are smoothed alike. On each axis, the two species share the same bandwidth: the average of the bandwidths each species would get alone. A difference between the two sets of rings therefore comes from the flowers and not from the smoothing.


17.6.2 One field, two marks
A zone given both positions also estimates density over both, so it reads the same field as a path. The difference is in the geometry. A path draws the rings as strokes. A zone given levels fills the bands between them, and without levels it fills small cells. Give both marks the same levels and you get the same curves twice, once as strokes and once as the edges of filled bands:

     x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + title("zone: the bands between them"))

     x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + title("zone: the bands between them")))

  y(:petal_length) + title("zone: the bands between them"))

  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), title("path: the rings")),

The left plot draws the four levels as rings. The right plot fills the bands between the same rings, so the edges of its bands are the rings on the left. A band is darker where the density is higher. The two legends give the same levels, from about 0.03 to about 0.13. The filled version is the filled contour, and zone * density draws it; the zone chapter covers the color ramp it uses. One field, two marks. It is the same division of work as in bar * bin and line * bin: the mark chooses the geometry, and the transform stays the same.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.7 A path in polar
The arrowhead was the first of the three things the row order gives a path. The second appears in polar, when the same angle appears in more than one row. Some routes go around: a compass bearing that turns through all 360 degrees, or a time of day that starts again at midnight while another value keeps growing. The spiral table holds two days of readings, one every 15 minutes. a is the hour of the day, which goes back to 0 at midnight, and r grows the whole time:

r

On flat axes the route has to jump back at midnight:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(spiral) + path + x(a) + y(r) +
  title("a path on flat axes")


(data(spiral) + path + x(col.a) + y(col.r) +
  title("a path on flat axes"))


data(spiral) + path + x(:a) + y(:r) + title("a path on flat axes")


plot(data(spiral), path, x(col.a), y(col.r), title("a path on flat axes"))






                               0 10 20   0 1 2 3 4  a path on flat axes R A





“Given the spiral: a path, x is a, y is r.”
The long stroke across the middle joins 23:45 on the first day to midnight on the second, and no reading lies along it. On a straight axis the end of one day is drawn far from the start of the next. On a circle the two are at the same angle, so the route continues instead of jumping.
polar() bends the flat plot into a circle. The x value becomes the angle around the center, and the y value becomes the distance from the center. Here a runs from 0 to 23.75, so one day is one full turn, with midnight at the top. r grows from 0.1 to 4, so each reading is a little farther out than the one before. The same hour on the two days has the same angle, but the second day’s reading is farther from the center, on the second turn. Polar teaches the space in full. path works in polar like every other mark:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(spiral) + path + x(a) + y(r) + polar() +
  title("a path in polar")


(data(spiral) + path + x(col.a) + y(col.r) + polar() +
  title("a path in polar"))


data(spiral) + path + x(:a) + y(:r) + polar() + title("a path in polar")


plot(data(spiral), path, x(col.a), y(col.r), polar(),
  title("a path in polar"))






                  0 10 20   0 1 2 3 4  a path in polar R A





“Given the spiral: a path, x is a, y is r, in polar.”
The route goes around twice, one day after the other, and turns outward in a spiral. A line cannot draw this. It sorts the rows by a, so each moment of the first day is joined to the same moment of the second, and the stroke zigzags between them inside one turn:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(spiral) + line + x(a) + y(r) + polar() +
  title("a line in polar")


(data(spiral) + line + x(col.a) + y(col.r) + polar() +
  title("a line in polar"))


data(spiral) + line + x(:a) + y(:r) + polar() + title("a line in polar")


plot(data(spiral), line, x(col.a), y(col.r), polar(),
  title("a line in polar"))

“Given the spiral: a line, x is a, y is r, in polar.”
A segment is one straight piece of a stroke, between two of its points. One segment is drawn by line but not by path: the one that closes a radar chart, a profile drawn around a circle as in Line. The continents fill the whole turn, and without that segment one sector of the circle would be left open. The path leaves that segment out. Its last vertex is where the data stopped, so closing the route would add a segment that is not in the table. If a route does return to its start, repeat the first row at the end of the table.

title: 17  Path

17.8 A path in the cube
In polar the path still joined the same rows in the same order. A third axis does not change that either, because the row order does not depend on any axis. A glider’s route has three positions: east, north and altitude. A flat page holds only two of them. Drawn flat, two circling gliders are two rings, one inside the other, and nothing on the page shows that they are rising. The thermals table holds one row for each recorded position of two gliders. Both circle the same thermal, a rising column of warm air, as they climb. The table is made up for this example: east and north are meters from the thermal’s center, and altitude is the height in meters. A real flight recorder stores latitude and longitude, which you would convert to meters first:

Bind z and the route runs through the cube instead of across the page. Of the marks that join their rows into one stroke, path is the only one that takes z, the third position. The reason is the row order this whole chapter is about:

data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + color(col.glider) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal"))

  color(:glider) + style(arrow = "end") +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")

  color(col.glider), style({ arrow: "end" }),
  title("Two gliders, one thermal"))

“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider, with arrow end.”
At every viewing angle, each route joins its rows in the table’s order. Its head marks the glider’s last recorded position, at the top of its climb. A line sorts by x, and the cube has no left to right. In the cube x is one of three equal positions. At some viewing angles x points straight into the page, so a line would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see. So a line’s sort by x has no meaning in the cube, and line, step, area and ribbon refuse z rather than draw a stroke the reader cannot read:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + line + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude)


data(thermals) + line + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude)

Error:
! gog: `line` reads a *domain* left to right — it sorts by `x` and draws one value for each — and a cube has no left to right: `x` is one of three equal positions, and at some viewing angles it runs into the page and becomes depth. A `line` in space would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see, so this is refused rather than drawn. For a route through three dimensions use `path`, which is `line` with that sort removed: `path + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(altitude)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Where the two routes cross, the one nearer to you covers the other: at some crossings Alpha’s route is in front, and at others Bravo’s. gog draws the short segments of both routes from the farthest to the nearest, so this stays right at every angle. That drawing order is the depth sort.
As on a flat line, color can vary along the route, because a color belongs to one place on the stroke rather than to the whole stroke. Bind altitude to color as well as to z. The climb is then said twice: once by where the route is, once by what color it is:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(altitude) + group(glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Altitude, said twice")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) +
  color(col.altitude) + group(col.glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Altitude, said twice"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:altitude) + group(:glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) + title("Altitude, said twice")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.altitude), group(col.glider), palette("viridis"),
  space({ turn: -25, tilt: 20 }), title("Altitude, said twice"))

palette("viridis") chooses the color ramp that shows the altitudes. space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) sets the viewing angle, which Space explains; a z binding alone would draw the cube from its default angle. group(glider) tells gog that the rows belong to two routes rather than one. A category on color splits the mark into one stroke per group, but altitude is a measure and has no categories to split on. Remove group(glider), and gog draws a single route with no message, joining the last row of one glider to the first row of the other with one straight segment:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  color(altitude) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Without group(glider): one route, joined")

  color(col.altitude) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Without group(glider): one route, joined"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:altitude) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Without group(glider): one route, joined")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.altitude), palette("viridis"), space({ turn: -25, tilt: 20 }),
  title("Without group(glider): one route, joined"))

“Given the thermals: a path, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by altitude, with the viridis palette.”
That segment cuts down through the cube, from the top of Alpha’s climb to where Bravo’s climb starts. color shows a value along the route; group says which route each row belongs to. They are two different questions, so they need two atoms.
A route in the cube can be dashed, as on the flat page:

  style(pattern = "dashed") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20)

title: 17  Path
text:
17.9 What a path is for
In the three spaces this chapter used (the flat plane, polar and the cube), the path did one thing: it joined the rows in the table’s order. The connected scatterplot is the best known use, but the mark is more general than that. A path is the right mark whenever the reader should follow the rows in the order the table gives them. A route through space is one, as the gliders showed, and so is an arrow, as the note on Botswana showed. The test is always the same question. Does the order of the rows mean something? If it does, the mark is path; if the reader should read left to right, it is line.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.10 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a path takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
density
bin, count, proportion


Summaries
—
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile


Fitted lines
—
smooth, straight


Running total
—
cumulative


Pairs: a low and a high
—
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds


Collision modifiers
—
dodge, stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
cluster
partition, flow, layout



The plots below show the two transforms a path takes. Each one returns its new rows in an order that means something. The path joins them in that order, as Two transforms, and the rest refused explains.
Counting. Of the four counting transforms, a path takes only density, and only with a number on both x and y. density then estimates how closely the rows lie at each place on the plane, one value at each place. The path draws the rings on which that value is the same. Here the two numbers are the length and the width of each flower’s sepal, from the iris_flowers table shown in The contour:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + path * density + x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) +
  title("path * density")


(data(iris_flowers) + path * density + x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.sepal_width) +
  title("path * density"))


data(iris_flowers) + path * density + x(:sepal_length) + y(:sepal_width) +
  title("path * density")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(path, density), x(col.sepal_length),
  y(col.sepal_width), title("path * density"))

“Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density, x is sepal length, y is sepal width.”
The rings mark two crowded places. Setosa’s short, wide sepals make the small group at the left, and the other two species share the larger one.
Layouts. cluster joins the closest categories into a tree, and the path draws that tree. It needs a column of values, a second column after over = that names what each value measures, and the categories on one axis, which become the leaves of the tree. cluster returns the rows in the order the tree is traced. The nutrients table holds one row for each pair of food and nutrient:

“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food.”
Each food is described by its amount of the five nutrients, and the foods with the closest amounts join first. cluster writes a column, distance, and the y axis shows it under the name Distance. The height at which two branches join is how far apart their amounts are. Beans and lentils join lowest, so they are the two most alike, and almonds join the rest at the top. Cluster explains how the tree is built.
A path refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. Two transforms, and the rest refused gives the reason, using the summaries: the new rows have no order of their own for a path to follow. line draws the counts, the summaries, the fitted lines and the running total, joined from left to right. interval and ribbon draw the pairs. The collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as point, bar and text. partition is drawn by zone and flow by ribbon. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.11 What you can set
A plain stroke does not show which way the route runs. arrow adds a head that shows it. The head belongs to the whole route, not to any one row, so arrow is set in style() rather than mapped from a column. A path’s size, its width, and its opacity are set too, because a path takes one of each for the whole layer. Each mark takes its own settings. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a path’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash, longdash


style(arrow = )
end, start, both



arrow belongs to path and edge only, for the reason Which end is the last row? gave.
A route can take the heads, a width and a stroke pattern together. The plot uses the gapminder_asia table, shown at the start of this chapter:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route")


(data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route"))


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), path, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.country),
  style({ arrow: "both", size: 2.5, pattern: "dotted" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route"))

“Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow both, size 2.5 and pattern dotted.”
arrow takes a value rather than a true-or-false flag. "both" is an ordinary thing to ask for, and a flag would have needed a second setting to say it. The heads are drawn solid on a dotted path. The dots are the route’s texture, and a head cut into dots no longer reads as an arrow.
This chapter covers the parameters of one transform, density: levels, bandwidth and adjust, in The parameters. Its fourth, places, sets the number of places along each axis where the field is computed: 64 by default, which makes a grid of 64 × 64 places. How many places covers it. Cluster covers those of cluster. Every other property of a path is either mapped to a column or set with style().
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.12 What it refuses
You might want the route to thicken as income rises, so that the stroke itself shows a third measure. A mapped color can change along a path, one color for each segment, and a width could change along it in the same way. gog does not do that: a path takes one size and one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. That is the first refusal: mapping gdp to size is refused:

data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:gdp)

  opacity(col.gdp))

! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `path` — a path takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `gdp` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`, or use a mark that maps `opacity`: `point` or `bar`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Set either one instead and every segment takes the same width or opacity, which is the Setting vs mapping distinction again.
A summary is the second refusal. A path draws the rows in their order, and a summary replaces those rows, as Two transforms, and the rest refused explained:

  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length))

title: 17  Path
text:
17.13 In short
A path joins the rows in the order the table holds them, so sorting the table changes the picture. That order is the mark’s meaning. The arrowhead belongs to path and edge only, and the two transforms a path takes are density and cluster.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.14 What comes next
A path takes both positions from every row. Rule draws a different kind of stroke: it reads one position from each row and draws a stroke across the whole panel at that value.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.1 A line at a threshold
Where is the line you want to compare every value against? Most marks read two positions. rule reads one and draws a line there, across the whole panel along the other axis. That line is a reference line at a threshold. A short line drawn in from the edge of the panel is a tick. One tick for each row makes a rug, which shows where the observations are.
Most plotting libraries draw a reference line and a rug with three marks: a vertical reference line, a horizontal one, and a rug. gog has one. A vertical and a horizontal reference line differ only in which axis holds the position. gog finds that axis from the columns, as it does for a bar.
Is a country’s life expectancy above 70 or below it? On a scatter the reader has to find 70 on the axis and judge each point against it. With a line at 70, each point is compared with the line instead of with the axis. gapminder_2007 holds 142 countries in 2007, one row for each. life_bands holds three thresholds, one row each: 60, 70 and 80 years. Here they are as a scatter of life expectancy against income, with a line at each threshold. The plots in this chapter turn the gridlines off with theme(grid = "none"), so the reference lines are the only lines across the panel, and style(color = "firebrick") draws them in a color apart from the blue points.

“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is petal length; then given two rows with sepal length 4 and 8 and petal length 4 and 8: a line colored firebrick, with pattern dashed.”
Every flower lies below the line, so every petal is shorter than its sepal. The line runs only between its two end points, so choose them near the ends of the axes. An end point outside the data stretches the axis, which is why the petal axis here reaches 8. For a slope b through the point (x0, y0), the height at an end x1 is y0 + b * (x1 - x0).

title: 18  Rule
text:
Mark
The reference it draws




rule
a line at each value in a column you supply (A line at a threshold)


line * mean
the mean of each group, joined into a profile; drawn here as a radar in In polar


ribbon * bounds
a band between a low column and a high one (A pre-computed band)


zone * bounds
a block across the panel, between the same two (Thickness as data)


line * straight
the least-squares line through the points, a sloped reference line (straight: the least-squares line)

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.2 Horizontal or vertical
Nothing in the read-aloud sentences under the two plots above said “horizontal”. The mark took the direction from the columns instead. life_bands has a life column and no gdp column, and the plot’s y is life. So only the y axis has its column in the rule’s table. The rule marks each value on that axis and spans the other one.
A threshold on income needs a vertical line, and there is no second mark for it. Give the rule a table that holds gdp instead, and the same word draws the line vertically. Here the table is one row holding one income, $10,000, written inside the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(data.frame(gdp = 10000.0), name = "gdp_threshold") + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis") +
  theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data({"gdp": [10000.0]}, name = "gdp_threshold") + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  data((gdp = [10000],), name = "gdp_threshold") + rule +
  style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis") + theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data({ gdp: [10000] }, { name: "gdp_threshold" }), rule,
  style({ color: "firebrick", pattern: "dashed" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same mark, the other axis"), theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                           0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  The same mark, the other axis Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with gdp 10000: a rule colored firebrick, with pattern dashed.”
The table holds gdp, the plot’s x, so the line is vertical.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.3 A rug of ticks
A scatter shows where each country is on two axes at once. Another question asks only how the countries spread along the income axis. A rug tick reads one position too. It marks one value and extends a short distance into the panel from its edge. That is a threshold line, only shorter, and the setting that makes it short is style(reach = "edge"):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries are on the income axis") +
  theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(col.gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries are on the income axis") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + rule + x(:gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries are on the income axis") +
  theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), rule, x(col.gdp), style({ reach: "edge" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Where the countries are on the income axis"),
  theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Where the countries are on the income axis Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp, with reach edge.”
The rule names x(gdp) even though the points already named it. This layer has no table of its own, so it reads the scatter’s, which holds both gdp and life. The rule could be placed on either axis, so it has to say which one it is on.
style(reach = ) takes one of two words: panel, the default, and edge. A tick’s length comes from the panel: 3.5 percent of the panel’s height, or of its width for a rug up the side. It is never less than 4 pixels and never more than 14. The minimum keeps a tick visible in a small facet, and the maximum keeps it short in a large plot. Every setting except reach works as on any rule.
Look along the bottom. Each tick is one country, drawn at its own income. Below $5,000 the ticks merge into one solid block: 66 of the 142 countries are in the first tenth of the income axis. The scatter holds the same countries but spreads them up the other axis, so the crowding is harder to see.
In general a rug puts the one-dimensional distribution of one column in the margin of a plot that already shows something else. You read the spread of gdp and still see the scatter, in the same panel.
A second plot can show the same spread. Here a histogram of gdp, cut into 30 bins by bin(30), is drawn under the scatter, and the two plots share one gdp axis. Composition shows how plots are put together this way.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("The same incomes, counted below the scatter") +
   theme(grid = "none")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(gdp) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + theme(height = 150, grid = "none"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
   y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("The same incomes, counted below the scatter") +
   theme(grid = "none")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(col.gdp) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + theme(height = 150, grid = "none")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same incomes, counted below the scatter") +
  theme(grid = "none")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(:gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + theme(height = 150, grid = "none"))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same incomes, counted below the scatter"),
  theme({ grid: "none" })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(30)), x(col.gdp),
  x_label("GDP per person"), theme({ height: 150, grid: "none" })))






                                                                                                                                                                      40 50 60 70 80  The same incomes, counted below the scatter Life expectancy


                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   0 10 20 30 40  Count GDP per person






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, above bars derived by bin into 30, x is gdp.”
The first bar is the tallest: 40 countries below about $1,900. Together with the next two bars, up to about $5,200, it holds 66 countries, the same 66 the rug draws as a solid block of ticks.

18.3.1 The other axis
The rug so far has been along the bottom, on income. Life expectancy has a distribution of its own, and overlapping points hide it on the y axis too. A rug is not only for the horizontal axis. The position you name on the layer decides which axis it is on. Write y(life) instead of x(gdp) and the ticks run up the left edge. Write both, as two layers, and the scatter has a rug along the bottom and another up the left at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp)  + style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") +
  rule + y(life) + style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both margins, from two layers") +
  theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(col.gdp)  + style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") +
  rule + y(col.life) + style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both margins, from two layers") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + rule + x(:gdp) +
  style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") + rule + y(:life) +
  style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Both margins, from two layers") +
  theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), rule, x(col.gdp),
  style({ color: "firebrick", reach: "edge" }), rule, y(col.life),
  style({ color: "firebrick", reach: "edge" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Both margins, from two layers"),
  theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Both margins, from two layers Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp, colored firebrick, with reach edge, and also rules, y is life, colored firebrick, with reach edge.”
Each rug names one axis, and both read the scatter’s table. A single rule layer that names both is refused, because a rule draws one line per row, placed by one column. The message suggests two layers, one per axis, as What it refuses shows.
The left edge shows a different distribution from the bottom edge. The ticks are dense above 70, thinnest between 60 and 70, and a little denser again from 60 down to 40. Of the 142 countries, 83 are above 70 and 43 below 60, with only 16 between. This is a distribution with two groups and a thin stretch between them, not a single group. The bottom rug cannot show this, because its ticks are placed by income. In the scatter it is harder to see, because the same countries are spread over two axes.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.4 Coloring the lines
The three threshold lines in the plot under A line at a threshold are all drawn alike, and nothing says what each one stands for. Give each line its own color instead, and the legend prints the band’s name beside that color. A rule draws one line per row of its table, so color gives each row its own color. life_bands has a band column naming each threshold, and that is the column to use. The points are light gray and the lines are 3 pixels wide, set by style(size = 3), twice the default of 1.5, so the three colors are easy to see against the points:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(band) + style(size = 3) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend") +
  theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(col.band) + style(size = 3) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + data(life_bands) + rule + color(:band) +
  style(size = 3) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend") + theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "lightgray" }), data(life_bands), rule, color(col.band),
  style({ size: 3 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One line per band, named in the legend"),
  theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                             0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  One line per band, named in the legend Life expectancy GDP per person  Band    Low  Middle  High 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands, colored by band, with size 3.”
The legend now says what each line is: Low at 60 years, Middle at 70 and High at 80.
On a rule, color takes only a categorical column, such as band. That is gog’s choice for this mark; point and line take a continuous column too. A continuous column on a rule, as in color(life), is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(life)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(col.life))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + data(life_bands) + rule + color(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "lightgray" }), data(life_bands), rule, color(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `color(life)` maps a continuous (numeric) column, but `color` on `rule` needs a categorical (text) column. Use `size` or `opacity` to show a continuous column.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 18  Rule
section: 18.5 Width and opacity from a column
text:
18.5 Width and opacity from a column
A rule at a mean of 52 countries looks the same as a rule at a mean of two. A rule draws one line per row, so its width and its opacity can come from a column and show the difference. Unlike color, both need a continuous column, such as a count. The continents_2007 table has one row for each continent, with its number of countries and the mean of their GDP per person:



continents_2007: all 5 rows


continent
countries
mean_gdp




Asia
33

Europe

Africa

Americas

Oceania

29810





Each continent’s mean becomes a rule at x(mean_gdp), colored by its continent. On the left, size(countries) draws a rule wider when its mean comes from more countries. On the right, opacity(countries) draws it darker. Layers are drawn in the order they are written. The rules come first, so no wide rule hides a point:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(continents_2007) + rule + x(mean_gdp) + color(continent) +
   size(countries) +
   data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Wider for more countries") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data(continents_2007) + rule + x(mean_gdp) + color(continent) +
     opacity(countries) +
     data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("Darker for more countries") + theme(grid = "none"))


((data(continents_2007) + rule + x(col.mean_gdp) + color(col.continent) +
   size(col.countries) +
   data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Wider for more countries") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data(continents_2007) + rule + x(col.mean_gdp) + color(col.continent) +
     opacity(col.countries) +
     data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("Darker for more countries") + theme(grid = "none")))


(data(continents_2007) + rule + x(:mean_gdp) + color(:continent) +
  size(:countries) + data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Wider for more countries") +
  theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data(continents_2007) + rule + x(:mean_gdp) + color(:continent) +
  opacity(:countries) + data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) +
  y(:life) + style(opacity = 0.45) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Darker for more countries") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


beside(plot(data(continents_2007), rule, x(col.mean_gdp),
  color(col.continent), size(col.countries), data(gapminder_2007), point,
  x(col.gdp), y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.45 }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Wider for more countries"), theme({ grid: "none" })),
  plot(data(continents_2007), rule, x(col.mean_gdp), color(col.continent),
  opacity(col.countries), data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.45 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Darker for more countries"),
  theme({ grid: "none" })))






                                                                                                                                                                                 0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Wider for more countries Life expectancy GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Countries    2  27  52 


                                                                                                                                                                          0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K    Darker for more countries GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Countries    2  27  52 






“Given continents 2007: rules, x is mean gdp, colored by continent, sized by countries; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; beside, given continents 2007: rules, x is mean gdp, colored by continent, opacity by countries; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
Africa’s mean, near $3,000, comes from 52 countries, so its rule is the widest on the left and the darkest on the right. Oceania’s, near $30,000, comes from two, and its rule is the thinnest and the faintest. The widths run from 1 pixel for the smallest count to 6 for the largest, and the opacities from 0.15 to 0.95.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.6 Thickening a rule
A thin line marks a threshold, but it is not the first thing a reader sees. Sometimes the thresholds are the reason the plot exists. Then the reader should find those lines first, before reading the data around them. style(size = ) sets a rule’s width, and a wide, faint rule reads as a highlighted band:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.55) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.20) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels") +
  theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.55) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.20) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.55) + data(life_bands) + rule +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels") +
  theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.55 }), data(life_bands), rule,
  style({ color: "seagreen", size: 26, opacity: 0.2 }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels"),
  theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                             0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands, colored seagreen, with size 26 and opacity 0.20.”
A wide, faint rule is a good way to emphasize a value. Its width is measured in pixels, not in data. Each wide rule in that plot covers a little over two years of life expectancy, only because this axis runs from 40 to 80. That does not matter while the width is only for emphasis. It matters once the width is meant to show a range of values.

18.6.1 Thickness as data
Sometimes the thickness is itself a measurement, not “look here”: an area between two exact values, from one edge of the panel to the other. This is what a highlight usually needs. The two edges are then data, and the mark whose edges are positions is zone. A zone takes a pair of values on one axis and spans the other, as a rule takes one value and spans the other. Zone has its own chapter, the next one, which covers it in full. It is introduced here because it does for a range what a rule does for one value, and a highlight like this is one of the most common reasons to draw a rule. On the left, a zone shades life expectancy from 60 to 70, with the rules from life_bands on top. On the right, a zone shades incomes below $5,000 and runs up the panel, with a rule at $5,000. Each one-row table is written inside the sentence. Up the panel, the two columns are start and end, written by name, as A band up the panel explains:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(data.frame(lower = 60, upper = 70), name = "sixties") +
   zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
   data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Across: life from 60 to 70") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data(data.frame(start = 0, end = 5000), name = "under_5k") +
     zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
     style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
     data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     data(data.frame(gdp = 5000), name = "at_5k") + rule +
     style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("Up: income below $5,000") + theme(grid = "none"))


((data({"lower": [60], "upper": [70]}, name = "sixties") +
   zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
   data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
   data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Across: life from 60 to 70") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data({"start": [0], "end": [5000]}, name = "under_5k") +
     zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) +
     style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
     data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
     data({"gdp": [5000]}, name = "at_5k") + rule +
     style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("Up: income below $5,000") + theme(grid = "none")))


(data((lower = [60], upper = [70],), name = "sixties") +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) + data(gapminder_2007) +
  point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(life_bands) + rule +
  style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Across: life from 60 to 70") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data((start = [0], var"end" = [5000],), name = "under_5k") +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) + data(gapminder_2007) +
  point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data((gdp = [5000],), name = "at_5k") +
  rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Up: income below \$5,000") + theme(grid = "none"))


beside(plot(data({ lower: [60], upper: [70] }, { name: "sixties" }),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "seagreen", opacity: 0.18 }), data(gapminder_2007),
  point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), data(life_bands), rule,
  style({ color: "seagreen", pattern: "dashed" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Across: life from 60 to 70"), theme({ grid: "none" })),

  style({ color: "seagreen", opacity: 0.18 }), data(gapminder_2007),

  style({ color: "seagreen", pattern: "dashed" }),

“Given one row with lower 60 and upper 70: a zone from lower to upper, colored seagreen, with opacity 0.18; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands, colored seagreen, with pattern dashed; beside, given one row with start 0 and end 5000: a zone from start to end, colored seagreen, with opacity 0.18; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with gdp 5000: a rule colored seagreen, with pattern dashed.”
The dashed rules lie exactly on the zones’ edges, because both marks read their positions from data. The edges rescale with the axis and keep the same values in every facet. Each zone is written first, and layers are drawn in the order they are written, so the points are drawn over it. The left zone holds the 16 countries between 60 and 70, the thin stretch between the two groups in The other axis. The right zone holds the 66 countries below $5,000, the solid block of ticks in A rug of ticks.

title: 18  Rule
section: 18.7 In polar: the ring and the spoke
text:
18.7 In polar: the ring and the spoke
Wind comes from a compass direction, so its speed can be drawn on a circle, as a radar chart. A target speed on that chart is a threshold like any other. In polar one of the two axes is bent into a circle. The question is what shape the line takes then. The mark does one thing: it draws a line at one position and spans the whole of the other axis. In polar that is unchanged. A polar plot has two axes, the angle and the radius. A rule that spans the angle is a ring, and one that spans the radius is a spoke: a straight line from the center to the rim, the outer edge of the circle. The Polar chapter explains how the circle itself is built.
winds is a table made for this book, introduced in The book’s data. Each row is one observation of the wind, with its compass direction and its speed in kilometers per hour. speed_target holds one target speed, 15 km/h:



winds: first 5 of 264 rows


direction

speed

The angular axis runs all the way around the circle, and one full circle of it is called the turn. A rule that spans the whole turn closes into a ring. Here it marks a target speed on the radar chart of mean wind speed by direction, and speed is on the radial axis, the one that runs from the center outward. limits = c(0, NA) starts that axis at the center, so a ring’s distance from the center is its speed:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed, limits = c(0, NA)) + polar() +
  data(speed_target) + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring") +
  theme(grid = "none")


(data(winds) + line * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.speed, limits = [0, None]) + polar() +
  data(speed_target) + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring") +
  theme(grid = "none"))


data(winds) + line * mean + x(:direction) +
  y(:speed, limits = [0, missing]) + polar() + data(speed_target) + rule +
  style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring") + theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(winds), layer(line, mean), x(col.direction),
  y(col.speed, { limits: [0, null] }), polar(), data(speed_target), rule,
  style({ color: "firebrick", pattern: "dashed" }),
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring"), theme({ grid: "none" }))






             N NE E SE S SW W NW   10 20  A target speed, drawn as a ring Speed Direction





“Given the winds: a line derived by mean, x is direction, y is speed from 0, in polar, and also rules from the speed target.”
The dashed ring is drawn at 15. The mean speed is above it at two compass points only, W at about 21 and SW at about 17. At E it comes close, at about 14.
Without limits = c(0, NA), the radial axis starts at the smallest value the plot draws. Here is the same plot both ways:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed, limits = c(0, NA)) + polar() +
   data(speed_target) + rule +
     style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
   title("Radius from 0") + theme(grid = "none")) |

     data(speed_target) + rule +
       style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
     title("Radius from the smallest mean") + theme(grid = "none"))


((data(winds) + line * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.speed, limits = [0, None]) + polar() +
   data(speed_target) + rule +
     style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
   title("Radius from 0") + theme(grid = "none")) |
