“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 12 and mean, x is gdp on a log scale, y is continent, color by life.”
One axis was cut and the other was already in slots. A mesh made of one of each is called a mixed mesh.


19.11.4 One of each: the mixed mesh
How does the spread of life expectancy differ by continent? Five histograms can answer it, one panel per continent:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) + x(life) / facet(continent) +
  title("Life expectancy, five histograms")


(data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) + x(col.life) / facet(col.continent) +
  title("Life expectancy, five histograms"))

  title("Life expectancy, five histograms")

  title("Life expectancy, five histograms"))

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20, x is life, split into panel rows by continent.”
Each histogram has its own panel and its own count axis. A zone can put all five distributions in one panel. Apply the tile plot’s rule (a category owns a slot, a number is a point) to one axis at a time. The rule already covers a plot with one continuous axis and one categorical axis. Nothing new has to be decided for it. bin cuts the axis that has a width to cut, and not the one that is already cut, so the result is a row of cells per category:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  palette("viridis") + title("Life expectancy, a distribution per continent")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  palette("viridis") + title("Life expectancy, a distribution per continent"))

  palette("viridis") +
  title("Life expectancy, a distribution per continent")

  palette("viridis"),

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, x is life, y is continent, with the viridis palette.”
This plot shows each distribution in shades rather than bar heights, so all five share one panel and one legend. Each row of cells is one of the five histograms above, and the rows are in the same order as the panels. Read each row and you see where a continent’s values are and how widely they spread. Africa’s largest counts are left of the center, and Europe’s are near the right end. Apart from Oceania, Asia’s row is the widest and Europe’s the narrowest, with Africa and the Americas in between. Oceania’s row is the narrowest of all. Its two countries, Australia and New Zealand, have similar life expectancies.
Two things keep the rows comparable. Every row is cut on the same edges, as in the five histograms above. The edges are computed once from the whole life column, never per category. So each column of cells covers the same range of life expectancy for every continent, and the boundaries line up all the way down. And an empty cell stays empty. Oceania’s row starts at 69 years, its lowest life expectancy, and the cells to its left are not painted with the color for the lowest count. The uneven left edge shows where each continent’s values begin.
Swap the axes and each distribution becomes a column instead of a row:

  palette("viridis")

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, y is life, x is continent, with the viridis palette.”
Neither orientation needed anything new. Three cases, one rule read one axis at a time: bin cuts both axes in the heatmap and one in this plot, and the tile plot needs no bin at all.


19.11.5 One slot: a column highlight
The plot below uses the winds table, shown in bin cuts, count tallies. The wind blows most often from two of the eight directions, W and SW. A strip plot draws each speed as a point above its direction. Shading those two directions behind the points makes them easy to find. Reading the tile plot’s rule one axis at a time leaves one more case: a category on one axis and nothing on the other. A zone bounded on one categorical axis takes that slot and spans the panel on the other, which is what this mark does whenever no column is written for an axis. One row is still one rectangle, so the table you give it is the list of slots to shade. Here that list is a table of two rows, one for each direction, written inside the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(data.frame(direction = c("SW", "W")), name = "prevailing") + zone +
  x(direction) + style(color = "goldenrod") +
  data(winds) + point * jitter + x(direction) + y(speed) +
  y_label("Speed") + title("The two directions the wind actually comes from")


(data({"direction": ["SW", "W"]}, name = "prevailing") + zone +
  x(col.direction) + style(color = "goldenrod") +
  data(winds) + point * jitter + x(col.direction) + y(col.speed) +
  y_label("Speed") + title("The two directions the wind actually comes from"))


data((direction = ["SW", "W"],), name = "prevailing") + zone +
  x(:direction) + style(color = "goldenrod") + data(winds) +
  point * jitter + x(:direction) + y(:speed) + y_label("Speed") +
  title("The two directions the wind actually comes from")


plot(data({ direction: ["SW", "W"] }, { name: "prevailing" }), zone,
  x(col.direction), style({ color: "goldenrod" }), data(winds),
  layer(point, jitter), x(col.direction), y(col.speed), y_label("Speed"),
  title("The two directions the wind actually comes from"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     N NE E SE S SW W NW   5 10 15 20 25  The two directions the wind actually comes from Speed Direction





“Given two rows with direction SW and W: zones, x is direction; then given the winds: points derived by jitter, x is direction, y is speed.”
Nothing was built for that. The zone layer, zone + x(direction), is the tile plot’s zone + x(week) + y(weekday) with y left out. In the tile plot, a week’s slot gives each cell its left and right sides. Here a direction’s slot gives the highlight its sides in the same way. A slot gives a zone its sides in any plot, not only in the tile plot.
The two-row table does what rule’s table does, and for the same reason: a zone’s position is a column, so one table shades as many slots as it has rows.
In the plot above, winds cannot replace the two-row table. A position is not like color: written after one mark, it still reaches the other layers (Encoding scope). y(speed) would reach the zone, and a continuous y gives a zone no sides, so gog refuses the sentence. The two-row table has no speed column, so the zone spans the panel from bottom to top.
One difference is easy to see. The column highlight is translucent and the calendar heatmap is not. A zone that spans the panel on one axis is a highlight, and gog draws it at 20%. A zone whose cells come from the data on both axes is the data itself, and gog draws it opaque. style(opacity = ) overrides either.

19.12 Sides the data drew: the choropleth
In every section above except the filled contour, each rectangle takes its sides from one row: a row of your table, or a row a transform made. bounds names the sides, bin cuts them, density estimates them, and a category owns a slot. There is a fifth way, where one shape takes its outline from many rows of your own table.
A map with every country shaded is a plot most readers have seen, and a country’s shape is not a rectangle. A boundary is a list of points around the edge of a region: a coastline, a border, the outline of a sales territory. It is stored as one row per point, so a single shape needs many rows, and the sentence needs a word for which rows belong together. That word is group. The world_borders table holds one row per point. Its piece column numbers a country’s separate outlines, such as its islands. The zone does not need it. In the table, the last row of each outline repeats the lon and lat of its first row. When gog reaches that repeated point, it closes the outline, and the next row starts a new one. group(country) then gathers all of a country’s outlines into one region (Rings). The zone fills each region, and color(continent) gives the fill its color:

text:
19.13 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a zone takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
bin ●, count ●, density ●, proportion ●
—


Summaries
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile
—


Fitted lines
—
smooth, straight


Running total
—
cumulative


Pairs: a low and a high
bounds ●
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band


Collision modifiers
—
dodge, stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
partition ●, flow ●, cluster
layout



A transform marked ● gives a zone its sides. These are the seven that the refusal above names. A zone draws only with one of them, or with positions that give it its sides. Two categorical positions give those sides, and so does one categorical position with nothing on the other axis, so the tile plot and the column highlight draw with no transform at all. So does the choropleth, whose sides are the points of a boundary.
The plots below show every transform a zone takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change. Most of the transforms already have a section above, and the paragraph before each figure links to it.
Counting. count and proportion tally the rows in each cell, so on their own they need a category on both positions. bin and density work on numbers. bin cuts each continuous axis into cells and counts the rows in each. density needs two numbers, and estimates how closely the rows lie in each cell. A zone measures nothing by length, so all four transforms write their result to color. bin cuts, count tallies shows the tally on its own. The top two plots read the winds table, shown in that section, with direction on x and season on y. The bottom two read the iris_flowers table, shown in Cells the data estimated, with sepal_length on x and petal_length on y:

      title("zone * bin")) |

        title("zone * density")))

Summaries. The six summaries reduce the rows of each cell to one value. They need a category on both positions, and color() naming the number to reduce, because a zone shows its measurement in color. Its sum reads n, the number of people in each row, because only an amount has a total that means something:

partition divides a whole among nested categories. Name one column for each level inside partition(), from the largest parts to the smallest. x(amount) sets each part’s width; without it, every row counts as 1. The zone draws one rectangle for each part: each group, each item and each detail. partition also writes a column called name, which holds each part’s name. A text * partition layer with label(name) puts that name in each rectangle, and style(angle = 90) turns the text so that it fits:

  style(angle = 90) + title("zone * partition")


plot(data(spending), x(col.amount),
  layer(zone, partition(col.group, col.item, col.detail)),
  color(col.group), style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  layer(text, partition(col.group, col.item, col.detail)),
  label(col.name), style({ angle: 90 }), title("zone * partition"))

“Given the spending table: x is amount, zones derived by partition through group, item and detail, colored by group, with border color white and border size 2, and also text derived by partition through group, item and detail, label by name.”
Read the plot from the bottom up. The groups make the bottom row, the items the middle row, and the details the top row. Each rectangle is as wide as its share of amount, and it is drawn directly above the part it belongs to. Only Utilities and Car are split into details, so the top row holds just their four details. Above every other item, such as Rent, detail is missing, so the top row is empty there. This plot is the icicle. With cross = TRUE, zone * partition draws the mosaic instead, where the second level divides the height of each column of the first.

The count, here y(n), sets each slot’s height; without it, every row counts as 1. The zone draws the slots. A zone refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. smooth and straight fit a line, and cumulative adds a running total, which line, point and bar draw. The other pair transforms compute a low and a high from the rows, which interval, ribbon, line and step draw. The collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as bar, point and text. layout places names as a network, which edge, point and text draw.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.14 What you can set
A highlight has to stay in the background, and a heatmap cell has to be solid. gog gives each kind its own default, and a setting in style() overrides it for the whole layer. Each mark takes its own settings. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a zone’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(pattern = )
solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels


style(gap = )
a share of the mark’s place, from 0 to just under 1



Five of the table’s six settings are what a filled shape with an outline takes: a color, an opacity and a pattern for the fill, and a color and a width for the border. The sixth, gap, is the share of a slot left empty. A zone takes it only where one of its sides comes from a category’s slot, as in the schedule. opacity has two defaults, one for each kind of zone. It is 0.2 for a placed zone: one whose sides you named with bounds, or one that spans the panel on an axis. It is 1 when the data gives every side: cells bin cut, cells density estimated, the slots two categories own, the regions a boundary gives, and the rectangles partition and flow compute. A placed zone is usually a highlight. It stays pale so the gridlines, and any layer written before it, show through. A zone of the second kind is the data, with nothing behind it to reveal. Where a placed zone is the data, as in the schedule and the candlestick, style(opacity = 1) draws it solid.
The next plot draws three bands behind the sales of the quarterly table, shown in A band across the panel. Each band reads a table of one row, written inside the sentence, and adds one setting: a color, then an opacity, then a hatch:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(data.frame(start = 2006, end = 2009), name = "early") +
    zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(data.frame(start = 2011, end = 2014), name = "middle") +
    zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "indianred", opacity = 0.55) +
  data(data.frame(start = 2017, end = 2020), name = "late") +
    zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "hatch", opacity = 0.7) +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Color, then opacity, then a hatch")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data({"start": [2006], "end": [2009]}, name = "early") +
    zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data({"start": [2011], "end": [2014]}, name = "middle") +
    zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(color = "indianred", opacity = 0.55) +
  data({"start": [2017], "end": [2020]}, name = "late") +
    zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "hatch", opacity = 0.7) +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Color, then opacity, then a hatch"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  data((start = [2006], var"end" = [2009],), name = "early") +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "seagreen") +
  data((start = [2011], var"end" = [2014],), name = "middle") +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "indianred", opacity = 0.55) +
  data((start = [2017], var"end" = [2020],), name = "late") +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "hatch", opacity = 0.7) + line +
  point + y_label("Sales") + title("Color, then opacity, then a hatch")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  data({ start: [2006], end: [2009] }, { name: "early" }),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "seagreen" }),
  data({ start: [2011], end: [2014] }, { name: "middle" }),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "indianred", opacity: 0.55 }),
  data({ start: [2017], end: [2020] }, { name: "late" }),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "steelblue", pattern: "hatch", opacity: 0.7 }), line,
  point, y_label("Sales"), title("Color, then opacity, then a hatch"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales; then given one row with start 2006 and end 2009: a zone from start to end, colored seagreen; then given one row with start 2011 and end 2014: a zone from start to end, colored indianred, with opacity 0.55; then given one row with start 2017 and end 2020: a zone from start to end, colored steelblue, with pattern hatch and opacity 0.7; then given quarterly again: a line and points.”
The default opacity keeps the first band pale with nothing set, so the line and points stay the strongest marks on the page. Raise it when the zone is the subject of the plot rather than its background, as the red band does here.
Use the hatch when a plot will be printed in gray, or when two overlapping zones need more than color to separate them. Give it more opacity than a flat fill needs, as the blue band does: a hatch is a set of lines with gaps between them, so fading it to 0.2 leaves very little to see. A zone takes the fill textures, not the stroke patterns. style(pattern = "dashed") on a zone is refused, and the message lists the six fill textures instead:

  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(pattern = "dashed")

  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) + style(pattern = "dashed")

  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)), style({ pattern: "dashed" }))

A zone can be drawn with or without a border, and both are good choices. A highlight behind a line reads better with no border. If you want its edges drawn, two rules do it better than a border: they can be dashed, and each is at a real value on the axis. The target band comes from the target_band table, shown in A band across the panel. The rules read a table of two rows, one for each edge, written inside the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(data.frame(sales = c(150, 175)), name = "edges") + rule +
    style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone for the region, rules for its edges")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data({"sales": [150, 175]}, name = "edges") + rule +
    style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone for the region, rules for its edges"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data((sales = [150, 175],), name = "edges") + rule +
  style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone for the region, rules for its edges")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)), style({ color: "seagreen" }),
  data({ sales: [150, 175] }, { name: "edges" }), rule,
  style({ color: "seagreen", pattern: "dashed" }), line, point,
  y_label("Sales"), title("A zone for the region, rules for its edges"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper; then given two rows with sales 150 and 175: rules colored seagreen, with pattern dashed; then given quarterly again: a line and points.”
The two marks read their positions differently, which is why the edges need a table of their own. A zone is told which columns hold its sides, with bounds(lower, upper). A rule takes its direction from its table instead (Horizontal or vertical). The plot’s y is sales, and the edges table has a sales column and no year column. So each rule marks a value of sales and spans the panel. The rule chapter draws the same two marks over a scatter of life expectancy, in Thickness as data.
But the mark is not only a highlight. It draws the candlestick, the heatmap’s cells, the icicle and the mosaic, and in every one of those the zone is the data rather than a background behind it. There the composition above cannot help. A rule spans the whole panel, or makes a short tick at its edge, so it cannot outline one cell of a mosaic. So a zone takes style(border_color = , border_size = ), like bar, box, point and surface. The plot outlines the two slumps of the recessions table, shown in A band up the panel:

data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(border_color = "black") +
  line +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone with a border of its own")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(border_color = "black") +
  line +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone with a border of its own"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(recessions) +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(border_color = "black") + line + y_label("Sales") +
  title("A zone with a border of its own")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(recessions),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ border_color: "black" }), line, y_label("Sales"),
  title("A zone with a border of its own"))






                                     2005 2010 2015 2020   100 120 140 160 180  A zone with a border of its own Sales Year





“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end, with border color black, and also a line.”
Both choices stay available, and which one is right depends on whether the zone is the background or the subject. By default a zone has no border: with no border_color and no border_size, it draws no outline.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.15 What it refuses
A point or a line needs only the plot’s x and y, so the first thing to try is a zone with no transform on the same table. It is refused. A continuous value marks a single point, so two continuous positions give a rectangle no width and no height:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) + zone + line


data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + zone + line


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + zone + line


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), zone, line)




Error:
! gog: `zone` shades a rectangle, but nothing here says where its sides are. Five things can: a categorical position, whose category owns a slot, or a date, whose slot is the smallest distance between two dates — `zone + x(method) + y(dataset) + color(score)` fills every cell where two categories cross; `bounds`, which names the sides from columns you hold — `zone * bounds(lo, hi)` on the measure axis, `zone * bounds(start = a, end = b)` on the domain axis, all four for a box, and the axis you leave out spans the panel; `bin`, which cuts them out of two continuous axes and counts the rows in each cell; `density`, which cuts the same cells and estimates a value at each; and a boundary, many rows around one region, named by `group` in `map()` or `globe()` — `zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(<region>) + map()`. A continuous position on its own is none of them — a number is a point, and a point has no width.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A categorical column on one axis and a continuous one on the other do not make a cell either. The category gives the zone its sides on its own axis, but a continuous column gives it none on the other. Here that column is year, and gog refuses the sentence rather than drop a column you wrote. The message names three ways to fix it. First, cut year into ranges with zone * bin * mean, as in the summary heatmap. Second, store year as a categorical column before plotting. If a cell then holds more than one row, write zone * mean. Without it, gog refuses the sentence rather than show only the last row in each cell. Third, leave out x(year) and color(life), so that the zone has only y(continent). Each zone then fills its slot across the whole panel, as in the column highlight:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone + x(year) + y(continent) + color(life)


data(gm_all) + zone + x(col.year) + y(col.continent) + color(col.life)


data(gm_all) + zone + x(:year) + y(:continent) + color(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), zone, x(col.year), y(col.continent), color(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(year)` is continuous, and on a `zone` a continuous column is a point with no width, so it gives the zone no sides on `x`: each zone would span the panel and `year` would be dropped. To cut `year` into ranges, write `zone * bin * mean + x(year) + color(<column>)`, which colors each cell by a mean. For one cell per value, store `year` as a categorical column before plotting, and write `zone * mean` if a cell would hold more than one row. To shade each `continent` slot across the whole panel, leave `x` out of the zone: a position written before the marks reaches every layer, so if another layer needs `x(year)`, write it after that layer's mark.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


bounds() takes its columns in pairs, so one column is not enough. The refusal names the half you gave, here lower, and lists the pairs that complete it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower = lower) +
  line


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower=col.lower) +
  line)


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(lower = :lower) + line


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds({ lower: col.lower })), line)




Error:
! gog: `zone` was given `lower` but not the other half of any pair. A rectangle needs both ends of a side: `bounds(lower, upper)`, `bounds(start, end)`, or all four.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A zone with bounds() reads a position in only two cases: when a categorical column or a column of dates gives it slots, and when the position names one of its own sides, such as y(lower). gog refuses a position that no layer reads. So the score_band table from A band up the panel, written as a zone with x(score), is refused. The zone takes its sides from lower and upper, and score places nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score)


data(score_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + x(col.score)


data(score_band) + zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) + x(:score)


plot(data(score_band), layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  x(col.score))




Error:
! gog: no layer reads `x(score)`: a `zone` given its sides by `bounds()` reads `x` only as the slots of a categorical column or a column of dates, or as one of its own sides, and `score` is none of these. Leave `x(score)` out, or write a mark that draws along `score`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The start/end pair bounds the axis that does not carry the measure. In the candlestick that is x, which holds the 14 sessions as categories. Write open and close in that pair, and gog reads each price as a place among the sessions. There are only 14 sessions, so a price near 100 points far beyond the last one, off the panel, and gog refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(candles) + zone * bounds(start = open, end = close) + x(session)


data(candles) + zone * bounds(start=col.open, end=col.close) + x(col.session)


data(candles) + zone * bounds(start = :open, var"end" = :close) +
  x(:session)


plot(data(candles),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.open, end: col.close })),
  x(col.session))




Error:
! gog: `bounds(start = open, end = close)` places the zone on `x`, and `x` holds the 14 categories of `session`, so the pair's numbers are slot positions: 0 is the first category's slot and 13 the last's. All 14 of its rows lie outside every slot (the first of them runs from 100.39 to 100.45), so the zone would be drawn off the panel. If `open` and `close` are values on `y`, they bound the measure axis: write `bounds(open, close)`. If they are slot positions, keep them between -0.5 and 13.5, the outer edges of the first and the last slot.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests the other pair, bounds(open, close), which bounds the measure axis, as the candlestick does.
A zone needs two things from its transforms: where its cells are, and what each cell shows. bounds gives only where. count and proportion give only what, inside the cells your categories already make. density gives both. bin gives both, or only where when mean follows it, as in bin * mean. Two transforms that give the same thing contradict each other, and gog refuses the pair. mean gives only what, yet bounds * mean is refused too. bounds makes one rectangle per row, and mean makes one per cell your positions make, so the sentence says what the rectangle is twice:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * mean +
  line


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) * mean +
  line)


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) * mean + line


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper), mean), line)




Error:
! gog: `zone * bounds * mean` says what this rectangle is twice — `bounds` names its sides from columns you hold, one rectangle per row, and `mean` summarizes a column within the cells your *positions* make. Keep whichever you meant: `zone * bounds(...)` to shade a region you chose, or `zone * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + color(<column>)` to summarize one within every cell two categories cross. To shade a band the data computed, `ribbon * range` is the mark that spans a statistic.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


To shade a region the data computed rather than one you chose, use ribbon. For example, ribbon * range fills between the minimum and the maximum at each x. A zone with bounds shades where you say, and a ribbon shades between values a transform computed from the rows.
Asking for two measurements is also a contradiction. count writes one measurement and mean writes another, but a cell holds a single number. count makes no cells of its own, so once mean measures the cells, count has nothing left to do:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone * count * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)


data(winds) + zone * count * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) + color(col.speed)


data(winds) + zone * count * mean + x(:direction) + y(:season) +
  color(:speed)


plot(data(winds), layer(zone, count, mean), x(col.direction),
  y(col.season), color(col.speed))




Error:
! gog: `zone * count * mean` measures each cell twice — `count` supplies only a measurement: its cells are the slots the positions already own, so with `mean` measuring them too the cell is measured twice and `count` has nothing left to contribute. Keep whichever you meant: `zone * count` to measure what `count` computes, or `zone * mean + color(<column>)` to reduce the column you name. To cut a continuous axis into cells and reduce a column inside each, `bin` is the transform that cuts without keeping the measurement: `zone * bin * mean + x(<measure>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


bin * mean, in the summary heatmap, has the same shape as count * mean but is not a contradiction: bin makes the cells, and mean measures inside them.
Write mean with no column to reduce, and gog asks for the column rather than guessing. A zone measures by color, so the refusal asks you to name the column in color():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season)


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.season)


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(:direction) + y(:season)


plot(data(winds), layer(zone, mean), x(col.direction), y(col.season))




Error:
! gog: `zone * mean` reduces a column within each cell, but nothing says which column — `zone` measures by `color`, and no `color()` is bound. Name it: `zone * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + color(<column>)`. To count the rows in each cell instead of reducing a column, `count` needs no such binding: `zone * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


bounds names the sides from columns you hold, and bin cuts sides from the data, so bounds * bin says where the sides are twice. gog does not pick one of the two, and refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * bin +
  line


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) * bin +
  line)


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) * bin + line


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper), bin), line)




Error:
! gog: `zone * bounds * bin` says where the sides are twice — `bounds` names them from columns you have, `bin` cuts them from the data. Keep whichever you meant: `zone * bounds(...)` to shade a rectangle you chose, `zone * bin` to tile the panel with measured cells.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A bin needs something to cut, and two categorical axes leave it nothing. Each category is one slot, and a slot cannot be cut smaller. A cell for each pair of categories is the tile plot, which needs no binning. So the refusal names count, which tallies the rows into the cells the categories already make:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + zone * bin + x(weekday) + y(week)


data(six_weeks) + zone * bin + x(col.weekday) + y(col.week)


data(six_weeks) + zone * bin + x(:weekday) + y(:week)


plot(data(six_weeks), layer(zone, bin), x(col.weekday), y(col.week))




Error:
! gog: `zone * bin` cuts an axis into cells, and there is no axis here it can cut — `x(weekday)` and `y(week)` are both categorical. A category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows into the cells two categorical axes already make, `count` is the transform that does it: `zone * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>)` draws a cell per pair, colored by how many rows fell there. (With *one* categorical axis `zone * bin` draws the mixed mesh — the continuous axis cut into cells, one row of them per category.)
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


zone * bin does draw with one categorical axis and one continuous axis: that is the mixed mesh. zone * density does not. A density is estimated between the data points, so each axis must give it an interval to spread along, and a category gives none. A density for each category is a different plot, so the refusal names what to use instead: line * density + color(continent), a density curve for each category:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * density + x(life) + y(continent)


data(gm_all) + zone * density + x(col.life) + y(col.continent)


data(gm_all) + zone * density + x(:life) + y(:continent)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, density), x(col.life), y(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `zone * density` estimates a density over the *plane*, and `y(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no interval for the estimate to spread along. Both axes must be continuous. To compare one continuous distribution across categories, `line * density + color(continent)` draws a curve per group.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


bin(tiling = "hex") is refused on the mixed mesh. A hexagonal mesh shifts every second row by half a cell, and its rows fit into each other. So each hexagon reaches partly into the space between its neighbors. On a categorical axis there is no such space: nothing lies between Asia and Europe. A category’s slots have an order but no distance, so the mixed mesh always has rectangular cells:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(life) + y(continent)


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(col.life) + y(col.continent)


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(:life) + y(:continent)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin({ tiling: "hex" })), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bin(tiling = "hex")` partitions a *plane*, and `y` here is categorical — its slots are an order, not a distance, so there is nothing for a hexagon to be regular against. This plot is the mixed mesh: one axis cut into cells, one row of them per category, and its cells are rectangles by construction. Drop the tiling, or bind continuous columns to both axes for `bin(tiling = "hex")` to have a plane to cut.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


count over two continuous axes is the opposite of bin over two categorical axes. count tallies rows into cells that already exist, and a continuous value marks a point, which owns no cell. So the refusal names bin, which cuts the cells first:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * count + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gm_all) + zone * count + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gm_all) + zone * count + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, count), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `zone * count` tallies rows into the cells that two *categorical* axes already make, and `x(gdp)` and `y(life)` are both continuous — a number is a point, and a point owns no cell. To cut a continuous axis into cells first, `bin` is the transform that does it: `zone * bin` counts the rows in each, which is the heatmap.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The six summaries, such as mean, follow the same rule. mean reduces a column inside a cell, and a continuous position gives it no cell. The refusal names two fixes: a category on each position, or bin on the continuous axis first:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(bearing) + y(season) + color(speed)


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(col.bearing) + y(col.season) + color(col.speed)


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(:bearing) + y(:season) + color(:speed)


plot(data(winds), layer(zone, mean), x(col.bearing), y(col.season),
  color(col.speed))




Error:
! gog: `zone * mean` summarizes `speed` inside the cell each pair of categories owns, and `x(bearing)` carries numbers — a number is a point, so it owns no cell to summarize into. Either put a category on both positions, or cut the continuous axis into cells first: `zone * bin * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + color(speed)` bins where your data lives and means `speed` inside each cell.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


zone * bin already measures each cell by its count, and the count goes to color. Binning replaces each cell’s rows with one count, so color(continent) has no rows left to read:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)


data(gm_all) + zone * bin + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)


data(gm_all) + zone * bin + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin), x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `zone * bin` already measures each cell by how many rows fell in it, and color is where that measurement goes — so `color(continent)` has nothing to read: the transform replaced those rows with its own. Drop the binding and the measurement colors the cells, or say `color(count)` to name it out loud. To compare across a category, facet on it: `| continent`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A tiling that gog does not offer is refused, and the message lists the two that it does offer, rect and hex. gog does not quietly draw rectangles instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "octagon") + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "octagon") + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "octagon") + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin({ tiling: "octagon" })), x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `octagon` is not a tiling. `bin(tiling = )` takes `"rect"` or `"hex"`. `"rect"` cuts equal-interval cells on each axis; `"hex"` staggers alternate rows, which stops the eye reading the mesh's own alignment as structure in the data.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


On a zone, density(bandwidth = ) is refused for a reason of its own. A bandwidth is a width in one column’s units, and a zone’s density spreads over two columns, which measure different things. One number cannot be a width in both, so gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length)


(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length))


data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(bandwidth = 0.5) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density({ bandwidth: 0.5 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length))




Error:
! gog: `density(bandwidth = )` is a width in one column's own units, and `zone * density` spreads over *two* columns measuring different quantities — one number cannot be a width in both. Use `density(adjust = )`, which scales the automatic bandwidth on each axis by the same dimensionless factor.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


That is why the density section uses adjust: it multiplies the width that gog picks for each axis, so it means the same on both.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.16 In short
A zone’s sides come from five places: bounds, bin, density, a category’s slot, or a boundary named by group. partition and flow compute whole rectangles themselves. Where nothing gives sides, the zone reaches the panel edge, which a ribbon cannot do. The pair you name decides which axis it bounds; the column types decide which one measures.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.17 What comes next
A zone shows a measure as a color, and you read its value from the legend. Surface gives that measure a height instead, and the same field is raised into the cube as a sheet.




Carr, D. B., Littlefield, R. J., Nicholson, W. L., & Littlefield, J. S. (1987). Scatterplot matrix techniques for large N. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(398), 424–436. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478445


Wilkinson, L. (2005). The grammar of graphics (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.1 A sheet through the samples
What shape does a landscape have, sampled on a grid? surface draws a sheet through your samples. It is a sheet through three positions: x, y and a height. The height comes from a column bound to z or from a transform, and without it there is no sheet at all. That makes it the only mark that must be drawn in the cube, where a third axis carries the height. Every other mark draws in the plane. Six of them can also draw in the cube: point, bar, interval, box, text and path.
It is not area with a z. An area fills the space between a curve and a baseline. A surface has no baseline. Both are fills, and that is all they share.
A grid of elevations is a table of numbers. Nobody can see a hill in a column of numbers. Draw the same numbers as a sheet and the hill appears. Here is Maunga Whau, a volcano in Auckland. The original grid has a sample every 10 m. The book’s copy keeps every second sample in each direction, so its 1364 samples are 20 m apart. Ross Ihaka digitized the elevations from a topographic map, and R’s datasets package is where the book reads them (R Core Team, 2026):

  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +

“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation.”
Three positions and a mark. There is no space() in that sentence and none is needed: binding z is what puts a plot in the cube, exactly as it is for a 3-D scatter. A bare space() draws the same plot. Write space(turn =, tilt =) when you want a different angle. z_label() names the third axis, the way x_label() names the first, and Space explains it.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.2 One row per crossing
What shape must a table have before a surface can draw it? A scatter’s table does not have that shape, and knowing why tells you which of your tables can become a sheet. Given two position columns and no transform, a surface reads each row as a crossing: the point where one x value meets one y value. Between four neighboring crossings, gog draws one face, a small four-sided piece of the sheet. A zone also fills a rectangle, but a flat one, and shows its value by color. Each corner of a face is at its crossing’s height, so a face can slope. The grid those faces make is the sheet’s mesh. You never declare which crossings are neighbors. gog finds them from your two position columns: the distinct x values and the distinct y values (here east and north) become the mesh lines, one set in each direction. A cell is the rectangle between two neighboring mesh lines in each direction, and a face is drawn wherever all four corners of a cell are present.
So this reading needs a table with one row per (x, y) crossing: every x value paired with every y value.
Maunga Whau has that shape. It holds 1364 rows, 31 distinct east values and 44 distinct north values: 31 × 44 = 1364, so the grid is full, and 30 × 43 = 1290 faces get drawn.
The same count shows why a scatter cannot be a surface. The gapminder 2007 table below holds 142 countries, and no two of them share a gdp value or a life value. That makes a grid 142 wide and 142 deep holding only 142 crossings, so no cell has all four corners. The sheet would be empty:

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.3 A continuous floor
Some tables hold a category in one column, such as a continent, and a number in another, such as a year. Every continent is paired with every year, so the rows form a grid, and a sheet over them seems reasonable. The two position columns make the sheet’s floor, the plane under it, and both have to be continuous. A face stretches from one sample to the next and so claims every height between them, and between one category and the next there is nothing to claim. So a category on either position is refused.
Numbers cut into cells are different, and a surface takes those, as When each cell holds one value shows. Cut cells meet edge to edge, and the edge between two cells is itself a number on the axis. A category instead owns a slot, a share of the axis that is its own, and the line between two slots stands for no value at all. So gog draws a surface over cells cut from numbers, and refuses it over the slots of categories. The flat marks show the same difference: bars over categories have gaps between them, and the bars of a histogram touch.
The refusal, shown in What it refuses, names the mark that does take a category on both positions: the 3-D bar. A 3-D bar is in its slot and claims nothing about the space between slots. The gm_eras table has two rows for each of 142 countries, one for 1957 and one for 2007. The year is in two columns: year holds it as a number, and era holds it as a category. With continent on x and era on y, both floor positions hold a category. The refusal’s message writes bar * count, which counts rows. This table has a measurement, so bar * mean averages life, bound to z, for each continent in each era. style(gap = 0.5) leaves half of each slot empty, so the space between the bars is easy to see:

“Given the iris flowers: a surface derived by density, x is petal length, y is sepal length, in the cube, turned 120.”
The sheet is turned to 120 degrees because of where the two peaks are. They are on a diagonal of the floor. At the default angle the near peak is directly in front of the far one and hides it, so the sheet shows one peak where the data has two. One sheet, four angles returns to that, because every 3-D view has this problem, not only this one.
All three plots say the same thing about these two clusters: they are nearly equally dense at their centers. The cluster with long petals is the denser one, by about four percent. What each plot asks of the reader is different. In the cells you compare two shades against a legend. In the contours you count rings. On the sheet you compare two heights, and that needs no legend at all. Which of the three you want depends on what you are asking, not on which mark is better.
One transform, three marks, and the estimate itself is the same in all three. What differs is where each mark puts the measurement. A zone puts it in color. A path puts it in the level each contour was cut at. A surface puts it in height. That is why the third sentence never binds z() and still gets a third axis, labeled Density. The transform supplies the measurement, and the mark puts it on the height. A flat bar * bin does the same for y.







Mark derived by density, over two positions
Where the measurement goes




zone * density
into the color of each cell


path * density
into the level each contour was cut at


surface * density
into the height of the sheet, the third plot above



Here the transform stays the same, and each mark supplies its own geometry. So gog has no separate atom for a contour plot or a density heatmap: each is density drawn by a different mark.
The sheet is computed on the same grid as the heatmap’s cells: 64 places along each axis, so 63 × 63 cells. Each cell is drawn as a flat top, and each step between two cells as a vertical face. The steps are too small to see separately, so the sheet looks smooth. When each cell holds one value shows such steps on larger cells, where they are easy to see. density(places = ) changes the number of places, and the plot’s file grows with the square of places. This sheet’s file is about 1.6 MB at the default, three times the heatmap’s, because gog draws nearly three faces for each cell. At 128 places it is about 6.5 MB, and at 256, the most places a field allows, about 26 MB. Fewer places draw a coarser sheet in a smaller file. How many places lists the default of every reading of density.
The surface * density sentence above writes space(), and the chapter’s first sentence, for the volcano, did not. A bound z can mean only one thing: the table has three columns to place on positions. When a transform computes the measure, gog knows only that the layer has one, not which axis it goes on. density computes that measure in the plane too, where it becomes a color, so space() is what tells gog to put it on a third axis. Leave space() out, and gog refuses the sentence, as What it refuses shows.

title: 20  Surface
section: 20.5 When each cell holds one value
text:
20.5 When each cell holds one value
The volcano’s sheet joins its samples with sloping faces. Does the ground rise smoothly between your samples, or does each cell hold one value that says nothing about its neighbors? bin is the other transform that tiles a floor. It cuts the floor into cells, and mean gives each cell the average elevation of the rows inside it. The surface is then flat across each cell, with a step at each boundary. The density sheet above is drawn the same way, from much smaller cells. Here is the same volcano, read as a coarse grid rather than a fine one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean + x(:east) + y(:north) +
  z(:elevation) + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell")


plot(data(maunga_whau), layer(surface, bin(12), mean), x(col.east),
  y(col.north), z(col.elevation), z_label("Elevation (m)"),
  title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                600 400 200 800 600 400 200 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell





“Given Maunga Whau: a surface derived by bin into 12 and mean, x is east, y is north, z is elevation.”
Nothing about the volcano changed. What changed is the claim. The sheet at the top of this chapter says the ground rises smoothly between its samples. This one gives each cell one elevation, the mean of its samples, and says nothing about how the ground varies inside the cell. Each claim is right for a different kind of data, and which one you want is a question about how yours was measured.
That question has a clear answer in an experiment or a simulation, where the conditions form a grid with exactly one number in each cell. Read as crossings, such a table gives fewer faces than it has values. Nine values make a 3 × 3 grid of crossings. A face needs four crossings at its corners, so the sheet has 2 × 2 = 4 faces, and no face stands for any one value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


cells <- data.frame(
  a = c(-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2),
  b = c(-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2),
  v = c(0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039)
)

data(cells) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) + title("Nine values, four faces")


cells = {
  "a": [-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2],

}

  a = [-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2],
  b = [-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2],
  v = [0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039],
)
data(cells) + surface + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  title("Nine values, four faces")


const cells = {
  a: [-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2],

Nine numbers became four faces, and each face slopes between the four values at its corners. Cut the floor into cells instead, and each cell gets a flat top of its own, a plateau:

  color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus")

  color(col.v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus"))

  color(:v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus")

  z(col.v), color(col.v), palette("plasma"),
  title("Nine values, nine plateaus"))






                                              1 0 -1 1 0 -1 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Nine values, nine plateaus  V            0.039 0.029 0.019 





“Given the cells: a surface derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v, color by v, with the plasma palette.”
Nine plateaus, and three colors. The nine values make a symmetric bowl: the four corner cells share the highest value, the four edge cells share the middle one, and the center cell holds the lowest. The ramp makes that symmetry visible. In the plain sheet above, you had to read the symmetry from the axis.
A 3-D bar uses the same sentence: bin cuts the x and y axes into cells, and mean averages the column named on z inside each one. The transforms mean the same thing on both marks, and only the geometry laid on the cell differs. Here mean does no averaging, because this table holds one row per cell. It is still needed: without it, bin counts the rows in each cell, so z(v) would name a column the plot never reads, and gog refuses the sentence.
The step between two plateaus is drawn as a vertical face along the line the two cells share. That line has no width, so the vertical face claims nothing about any area: it is simply what a jump looks like. Vertical faces keep the plateaus joined at every step, so a gap in the sheet always means a missing cell.
A vertical face spans the difference between two neighbors, and a 3-D bar on every cell does not. A bar always reaches down to the floor of the cube, so a grid of bars hides its own back rows as soon as you turn it. A vertical face is only as tall as its own step. The next plot turns both to 60 degrees, so you can see which one is still legible. Both are set to one color, so the only thing that differs between them is the shape:

    space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
   (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
      space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Plateaus, turned"))) +
  theme(height = 430)

    space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
   (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(col.a) + y(col.b) + z(col.v) +
      space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Plateaus, turned"))) +
  theme(height = 430))


((data(cells) + bar * bin(3) * mean + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
  (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") +
  title("Plateaus, turned"))) + theme(height = 430)


beside(plot(data(cells), layer(bar, bin(3), mean), x(col.a), y(col.b),
  z(col.v), space({ turn: 60 }), style({ color: "#76b7b2" }),
  title("Bars, turned")),
  plot(data(cells), layer(surface, bin(3), mean), x(col.a), y(col.b),
  z(col.v), space({ turn: 60 }), style({ color: "#76b7b2" }),
  title("Plateaus, turned")), theme({ height: 430 }))

                                              1 0 -1 1 0 -1 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Plateaus, turned






“Given the cells: bars derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v, turned 60, beside a surface derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v, turned 60.”
| composes them (Composition), so the two are one figure and turn together. That is what makes this a fair comparison, rather than two pictures the reader has to match angle by angle.
theme(height = ) sets the whole arrangement’s height in pixels. It is set here because two cubes side by side each get half its width but the full height, so each panel is tall and narrow. A cube keeps its proportions, so it never stretches to fill a tall panel. Without the setting, blank space would be left above and below each cube.
gog has no special rule for empty cells. bin leaves them out, because a cell with no rows is not a measurement of zero. A plateau claims only its own cell, so a cell with nothing in it is simply a cell with no top. It is the same opening a missing crossing makes in the mesh, for a different reason.
What a surface refuses is a grid of slots, the cells two categories make. What it refuses shows that refusal.

title: 20  Surface
section: 20.6 The mesh, and what the shading means
text:
20.6 The mesh, and what the shading means
A smooth sheet hides where its samples were. A line hides its measurements the same way, and a dot at each row shows them again. On a surface, the mesh lines show the grid again, so a reader can see how fine the sampling was. border_color and border_size draw them. A face is a closed-shape fill, like a bar or a box, so the settable rule gives it a border. On a surface, those borders are the mesh lines:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 0.4 }),
  z_label("Elevation (m)"), title("The mesh, drawn"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  The mesh, drawn





“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, with border color white and border size 0.4.”
The mesh lines add no shapes to the picture, because every face is already stroked in its own shade. That thin stroke covers the pale seam that would otherwise show between neighboring faces. border_color replaces the stroke’s color, and border_size its width. Leave both out for a seamless sheet. A border_size of 0 removes the stroke, and the pale seams appear.
Look at the shading on the sheet above, and on the turned one below it. The faces are shaded by their slope: a steep one is darker, a flat one keeps its full color. That is a fact about the terrain, not about where a light is, so turning the scene rearranges the faces on the page and repaints none of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.7 Color by height, per face
Slope shading says how steep a face is, not how high it is. How high is the summit, and how deep is the crater? color maps on a surface, and a continuous column colors it face by face along a ramp. palette() chooses which ramp. "viridis" suits a topographic sheet, because it gets steadily lighter from its lowest color to its highest:

data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + color(elevation) +
  palette("viridis") +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) + color(col.elevation) +
  palette("viridis") +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  color(:elevation) + palette("viridis") + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp")

  z(col.elevation), color(col.elevation), palette("viridis"),
  z_label("Elevation (m)"),
  title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp"))

Compare that with the chapter’s first plot, in A sheet through the samples. The summit and the crater rim are in that plot too. With slope shading alone you have to infer them from which faces are dark. The ramp states the heights, and the legend decodes them.
Mapping the height to color when z already shows it is redundant on purpose. It is what a reader of a topographic map expects. It also shows why a surface can take a continuous color when an area cannot. An area is one region with one color. A continuous column would change the color inside that region, so color on an area refuses one. A surface has faces, and a face is small enough to hold one value.
A face has four corners and one color. Its color is the mean of its four corner values, which stands for the field at its center. So the ramp describes the mesh you have, not only the field you sampled from. Here is one bowl-shaped field, sampled coarsely and then finely. This figure draws from two tables, coarse and fine. gog finds each plot’s table by the name data() records, so two different tables in one figure need two different names (Two tables with one name).
The left sheet is one uniform color, and that is correct rather than broken. Every face has one high corner, one low corner and two middle ones, so all four faces get the same average. The mesh is too coarse to hold the shape, and the ramp says so instead of inventing a gradient across it. The right sheet has the same field under it and enough faces to resolve it, so the bowl appears.
This is the reading that makes the legend trustworthy. A color is the height at one stated place, the center of a face, so two faces of one color really are at one height there, and a sheet of one color has all its face centers at one height.
The ramp does not replace the slope shading. A face takes its color from the ramp and is then darkened by how steep it is, so a steep face with a dark color gets darker still. Viridis gives its dark colors only to the low ground, and low ground is usually flat, so few faces are both dark and steep.
An estimated height takes a ramp the same way, and you name it the same way. density writes its estimate into a column called density, so density is the name you give color, exactly as on a zone. On a path, density writes the estimate into a column called level instead, one value for each ring. Here the sheet shows the estimate as a height and as a ramp. Nothing there is a special case. The transform writes a column, the column has a name, and a name can be bound. Whether the height came from your table or from an estimate is only a difference in source. It does not change what you may say about it.
You do not always need the color as well as the height. The plain sheet in A sheet through the samples already shows the height by position alone. Use the ramp when the low ground matters. Slope shading darkens a steep face but not a flat one, so a broad, low mound and the flat ground around it are drawn almost the same color. The ramp is what separates them.
Sometimes faces belong to named parts of the ground rather than to heights. A categorical color gives each face the color of its category. Unlike on a line, it does not split the rows: the sheet stays one sheet, and only group makes separate sheets. title: 20  Surface
section: 20.9 Opacity by a measure, per face
text:
20.9 Opacity by a measure, per face
A color decides what a face says. An opacity decides whether you can see through it. Part of a sheet is often not the subject. The flat ground around a hill only hides what is behind it, and fading those faces makes the hill the solid part of the picture. opacity maps on a surface, and it maps for the reason color does. A face is small enough to hold one value, so it can hold an opacity too. Every face takes its own opacity, and a face fades where its measure is small:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + opacity(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Faint where the ground is low")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) + opacity(col.elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Faint where the ground is low"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  opacity(:elevation) + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Faint where the ground is low")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), opacity(col.elevation), z_label("Elevation (m)"),
  title("Faint where the ground is low"))

“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, opacity by elevation.”
Over the low ground the fill fades to almost nothing and each face keeps its outline, so that part of the sheet shows as mesh lines alone. A ramp cannot do that; an opacity can. The legend beside the plot reads the same way color’s does, with the smallest, middle and largest values of the column.
No face disappears completely. A mapped opacity runs from 0.15 to 0.95, so the faintest face here is still drawn, which is the rule every mapped opacity follows (Channels).
A face reads its opacity the way it reads its color, from the mean of its four corners. A plateau reads its own cell’s row. A vertical face is between two cells and reads the taller one’s row, the way a bar’s side takes the bar’s color. Either way one face has one reading, whichever channel asks for it.
The sentence behind the first plot in this section binds elevation twice: once to z and once to opacity. A different column on opacity shows more: the shape stays in z, and another measure decides which faces fade. One value for the whole sheet is still style(opacity = ). Set it when you want to see one sheet through another, and map it when you want each face to fade by its own value.

Read them as a set and you can see what each angle hides. The crater is the most interesting thing about this hill, and only the lower-left plot, tilted up, shows it. The rim nearest you is in front of the crater, so turning alone does not show it while the tilt is low. Tilt up and you can see into the crater, because you are now looking down from above. The same tilt flattens the heights, until the sheet looks like a flat colored map. Tilt down instead and you get the opposite: the heights read clearly, the view from above is gone, and the sheet shows as an outline. One or the other, never both.
These four plots show why you would want to turn a plot. Here you need both the view from above and the view from the side, and no single still view shows this hill whole. So, in the web edition, turn the four with the pointer. Raise the tilt until the crater appears, and watch the heights flatten as the tilt rises.
Drag any one of the four, and all four turn and tilt the same way at once, because | and / composed them into one figure. Each panel keeps the angle its own sentence asked for, and the drag adds the same change to every one. So the four views stay the same angles apart, and you can compare them at every angle. The reset button returns each to the angle it opened at. To turn one alone, write it alone.
That is composition rather than faceting, and the two share the same pair of operators. A facet names a column (Faceting), and a viewing angle is not a column: it is a property of the coordinate space, the way a polar() start angle is. gog does build small multiples of cubes, one cube for each value of a column, but these four panels are not small multiples. Space has that example.
One limit shows in these four plots, and it belongs to the cube rather than to the mark. Notice the Elevation axis in the tilted-up panel. You are looking down along it, so it is drawn at about a third of its full length. gog labels three heights on that axis, while the default view, top left, labels five. gog leaves numbers out rather than let them overlap. Space says which numbers a crowded axis drops, and why the scale itself never changes.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.11 What a surface is for
A surface is for anything that is a height over a plane. Terrain, and the sea floor. A response surface from a designed experiment. A model’s fit measured over two of its parameters. A model’s predictions over a grid of two predictors. And, through density, the shape of a two-dimensional distribution.
A surface is not for data that only has three numbers per row. That is a 3-D scatter, and the refusal in One row per crossing names it for you. Here is the gapminder 2007 table from that section, drawn the way the refusal’s message says, with point and z(population):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + z(col.population)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + z(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  z(col.population))






                                                                                                                                                                       50K 40K 30K 20K 10K 0 80 70 60 50 40 1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, z is population.”
Each point is a country, and the empty space between two points stands for no country. So before you draw a surface, ask whether your table has a value between two samples. A grid of elevations does: the ground between two measured points has a height too, even though nobody measured it there. Between two countries there is no country, so there is no value.

20.12 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a surface takes and the ones it refuses:

The plots below show every transform a surface takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change. In each one, the sheet is drawn over a floor of cells. bin and density cut that floor themselves, and a summary needs bin to cut it first.
Counting. bin and density read two continuous positions. bin cuts the floor into cells, and each cell’s height is the number of rows inside it. density estimates how closely the rows lie at each place on the floor, and the sheet’s height is that estimate. Neither one takes z(), because the transform writes the height itself. So the sentence needs space() to put that height on a third axis, as The third geometry of one field explains. The left plot draws surface * bin on the iris flowers, with x(petal_length), y(sepal_length) and the cube turned 120 degrees. By default, each cube fits its height axis to its own values. The five volcano plots all write limits = c(90, 200) on z, so they share one range, and the same height means the same elevation in each of them. So the max sheet is drawn taller than the min sheet because its elevations are higher, not because its axis differs. When each cell holds one value explains the plateaus and the vertical faces between them.
A surface refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. count and proportion tally rows into the slots of two categories, and the 3-D bar draws one bar in each slot, as What it refuses shows. smooth and straight fit a line, and cumulative adds a running total, which line, point and bar draw. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, which interval, ribbon, line and step take. The collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as bar, point and text. partition is drawn by zone and text, and flow by ribbon, zone and text. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw. cluster joins the closest categories into a tree, which path and zone draw.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.13 What you can set
No column says whether the mesh lines show, or how transparent the whole sheet is. A setting decides both for the layer without reading any column, and each mark takes its own settings. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a surface’s settings, with the values each accepts:



Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels



A surface is a closed-shape fill, so it takes what a bar and a box take: a color, an opacity, and a border. pattern is the one fill setting it refuses, and like a bar it has no size. The next section says why for both.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.14 What it refuses
Every flat mark is written with only x and y as positions, so it is easy to write a surface that way by mistake. A surface is a sheet through three positions, so it needs a height, and the height is what puts the plot in the cube. So gog refuses a surface with no height:

data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(col.east) + y(col.north)

! gog: a `surface` is a sheet through three positions, so it needs the cube. Bind the height — `surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(h)` — or let a transform invent it: `surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space()`. For the same field drawn in the plane, `zone` paints it as cells and `path` traces its contours.

Its message names both ways to draw in the cube: bind the height to z, or let a transform compute it and add space(). It also names the two marks that draw the field in the plane instead, zone as cells and path as contours.
A category on either position is the second refusal, for the reason A continuous floor gave. A face stretches from one sample to the next, and between two categories there is nothing for it to span. The sentence below puts continent on x and era on y, from the gm_eras table, shown in the same section. x and y both hold a category, and gog refuses both, with one message for each:
