A face spans the gap between two samples, and between two categories there is nothing to span. Over two categories, draw a bar in each cell instead: `bar * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + space()` — a bar is drawn in its own cell and claims nothing in between.
gog: `y(era)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `y` on `surface` needs a continuous (numeric) column. A face spans the gap between two samples, and between two categories there is nothing to span. Over two categories, draw a bar in each cell instead: `bar * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + space()` — a bar is drawn in its own cell and claims nothing in between.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


That refusal lists the two transforms that do tile a floor, bin and density.
density(levels = ) cuts the field into a few steps. Like the band between two contour lines on a map, each step holds the places where the density falls between two values. A step is a flat region of the floor, and a surface draws the estimate as a height instead, so gog refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space()


(data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) +
  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + space())


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) + x(:petal_length) +
  y(:sepal_length) + space()


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(surface, density({ levels: 5 })),
  x(col.petal_length), y(col.sepal_length), space())




Error:
! gog: `density(levels = )` cuts a field into level sets, which are regions in the plane — a `surface` draws the field itself, with the estimate as its height, so it has no axis left to put a band on. Drop `levels` for the sheet, or `zone * density(levels = )` to fill the bands and `path * density(levels = )` to trace their boundaries. For a sheet in steps, cut the floor rather than the height: `surface * bin * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(<column>)` lays a flat plateau on every cell.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the two marks that draw those bands in the plane: zone, which fills them, and path, which traces their boundaries.
A sheet can be cut into steps in two ways, and only one of them draws. Cutting the floor into cells is surface * bin, which When each cell holds one value draws. Each square cell gets a flat top at its own height, so the steps run along the straight lines of the grid. Cutting the height into bands is what levels asks for, and gog refuses that one. Its bands follow the contour lines, the curved lines that join places of equal density, not the cells of the floor. So for a sheet in steps, cut the floor with bin. For bands of equal density, fill them flat with zone, as the message above says.
bandwidth is a length in one column’s own units, and a field spreads over two columns that measure different quantities. One number cannot be a width in both, so gog refuses bandwidth on every mark that draws a field, a surface included:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space()


(data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + space())


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(:petal_length) + y(:sepal_length) + space()


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(surface, density({ bandwidth: 0.5 })),
  x(col.petal_length), y(col.sepal_length), space())




Error:
! gog: `density(bandwidth = )` is a width in one column's own units, and `surface * density` spreads over *two* columns measuring different quantities — one number cannot be a width in both. Use `density(adjust = )`, which scales the automatic bandwidth on each axis by the same dimensionless factor.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests density(adjust = ) instead. adjust is a multiplier with no unit, so it scales the automatic bandwidth on both axes by the same factor.
There is no size on a surface. Its extent is set by the grid it is drawn on, so a size has nothing left to set, and gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(size = 2)


(data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  style(size = 2))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  style(size = 2)


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), style({ size: 2 }))




Error:
! gog: `style(size = 2)` — a surface has no size to set. Remove it, or use a mark that has one: `point`, `line`, `step`, `interval`, `box`, `text`, `path` or `rule`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message says to remove it, or to use a mark that has a size, such as point or line.
area refuses a size for the same reason. A surface also refuses pattern, and it is the only fill mark that does:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), style({ pattern: "hatch" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = )` sets a fill texture, and a `surface` is a mesh of fills — but a fill texture is drawn in *screen* space, and a projected mesh foreshortens every face differently, so one texture would read as a different line spacing on every face. That is a texture that changes with the viewing angle instead of with the data. A surface says its shape with slope shading; `style(border_color = )` draws its mesh lines, and `color` ramps it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A fill texture is drawn as lines or dots at one spacing on the screen, but each face of the mesh is seen at its own angle, so the same spacing looks different on every face. The texture then changes with the viewing angle rather than with the data, which is the one thing this mark’s shading is built to avoid. The message names what a surface uses instead: slope shading for its shape, border_color for its mesh lines, and color for a ramp.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.15 In short
A surface stretches between neighboring samples, so it needs a floor whose cells tile. A scatter’s table does not give it one. A face needs all four of its corners, so a missing crossing leaves an opening rather than a guessed height.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.16 What comes next
A surface needs two continuous positions under it. Edge is the mark for tables with no column to place on a position: rows naming two things and saying they are connected.




R Core Team. (2026). R: A language and environment for statistical computing. R Foundation for Statistical Computing. https://www.R-project.org/

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.1 The network diagram
Which things in your table are connected to which? edge draws one stroke per row of the table, between the two things named in that row. Every other mark that draws a stroke is placed by its values on the axes. A line and a path join points at their x and y values, and an interval spans two values on one axis. An edge is different: each row gives it only two names, and no column says where a name is placed on the page. A plot of edges is a network diagram.
So an edge takes no x, y or z. It is the only mark that takes none of the three. An edge’s endpoints come from a layout, a transform that reads the two columns of names and places each distinct name once. Write the from column first and the to column second, so the sentence states the direction of each relation. If you swap the two columns, the picture does not change. It changes only when you add arrowheads: style(arrow = "end") points each edge from the first column to the second (What you can set).
A network diagram needs a table with one row per relation. In trade_partners, each row names an exporter and an importer, gives the value of the goods in rounded billions of dollars, and names the exporter’s continent:
trade_partners: first 5 of 22 rows


exporter
importer
billions
continent




China
United States
500
Asia


Mexico
United States
455
Americas


Canada
United States
420
Americas


United States
Mexico
320
Americas


United States
Canada
355
Americas
Name the table, then write three things: the mark, the layout that derives it, and the space network():
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network())
“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The 15 countries get 15 positions on the panel, and gog draws one stroke for each of the 22 rows. Five pairs of countries trade in both directions, and each pair’s two strokes lie on one line. So you can count only 17 lines, and those five look slightly darker than the rest. No country is labeled: the layout placed the countries, but no layer draws their names.
An edge draws in two spaces only, network() and space(). A layout computes its positions from the graph. Here a graph is not a chart: it is a set of things and the relations between them. Each thing is a node, and each row is one relation between two nodes. A node is one name, however many rows it appears in: Germany is one node in seven rows. A layout counts each row as one step between its two nodes. Two countries that trade are one step apart, so they are placed close together, and nodes with more steps between them are placed farther apart. No column holds a node’s position, and turning or flipping the picture changes no distance, so a position on its own means nothing. In every other space, a position means something: a value on an axis, a place on the earth, or a share of a whole, so gog refuses an edge there. In the cube that space() draws, the box around the network carries no numbers, so a position is not read as a value there either.
A layout is not for edges alone. It gives every node one position. It also writes two columns. name holds each node’s name, and degree holds the number of rows the node appears in. Two other marks read a layout and draw at those same positions:
The first plot names no country. The plot below draws all three marks, and it uses both columns the layout writes. size(degree) draws a node’s dot larger when the node appears in more rows. label(name) draws each node’s name, and repel moves each name off the dots and off the other names:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Each node, sized by its degree")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("Each node, sized by its degree"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + size(:degree) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel + label(:name) + network() +
  title("Each node, sized by its degree")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("Each node, sized by its degree"))






                                             China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  Each node, sized by its degree  Degree    1  5  9
“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
China appears in nine rows, the United States in eight and Germany in seven. No other country appears in more than three, so these three have the largest dots. A pair that trades both ways is two rows but one line, so only seven lines end at China’s dot.
Each layer computes the layout for itself. A layout uses no random numbers, so the same two columns always give the same positions in the plane. That is why every dot is exactly where its strokes end. The Network chapter draws this plot again, in The nodes and their names.
The next section draws each stroke with an opacity, a width, a color or a stroke pattern from its own row.

title: 21  Edge
section: 21.2 Opacity, width, color and pattern, one per row
text:
21.2 Opacity, width, color and pattern, one per row
In the plots above, every stroke is drawn the same way, so a relation worth 500 billion dollars looks like one worth 50 billion. Each edge is drawn from one row, so it can take its opacity, its width, its color and its stroke pattern from that row’s values. On an edge, size is the width of the stroke. opacity and size show a continuous column such as billions, the value of each relation, and the first plot maps it to opacity. A faint stroke’s ends are hard to find, so the plot keeps the point * layout(exporter, importer) layer, which draws a dot at each node:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("More trade, darker stroke"))






                                            More trade, darker stroke  Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The three darkest strokes meet at one node. This plot draws no names, but every node is at the same position as in the plot with names, in The network diagram. So the node where they meet is the United States. China, Mexico and Canada each export more than 400 billion dollars of goods to it.
The width of a stroke can come from its row in the same way. size(billions) draws a stroke wider where the relation is worth more:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + size(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, wider stroke")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, wider stroke"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  size(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network() +
  title("More trade, wider stroke")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("More trade, wider stroke"))






                                            More trade, wider stroke  Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The three widest strokes are the three darkest in the plot above, and they meet at the United States. The legend draws a line at three values: 50, 275 and 500 billion dollars. Width also keeps the smallest relations in view: France to Spain, worth 50 billion, is a thin stroke here, and nearly disappears in the opacity plot.
On line, size and opacity are only settings: gog keeps one width and one opacity for a whole line (Stroke width and opacity). An edge draws one stroke per row, so each row gives its stroke a width and an opacity of its own.
Which exports come from each continent? On an edge, color needs a categorical column. The continent column holds the continent of each row’s exporter, and it has four values. A continuous column such as billions is refused there; map it to opacity or size, as above. The names are written in this plot, so you can see which two countries each stroke joins:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(continent) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter's continent")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + color(col.continent) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter's continent"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  color(:continent) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel + label(:name) + network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter's continent")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), color(col.continent),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter's continent"))






                                             China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  Each stroke, colored by its exporter's continent  Continent    Asia  Americas  Europe  Oceania 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, colored by continent, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
Europe’s strokes all touch Germany, except France’s stroke to Spain. The Americas’ strokes all touch the United States, except Brazil’s stroke to China. Oceania has one stroke, from Australia to China.
color(exporter) draws as well, with one color for each of the twelve exporters. Twelve colors are hard to distinguish on a stroke a pixel or two wide. Mexico, Canada and the Netherlands also get a color in the legend and on no stroke, because each trades with one partner only, and the partner’s row is drawn over theirs. With continent, four colors are easy to distinguish, and every color in the legend is on a stroke.
Strokes are drawn in row order, so where two countries trade both ways, the later row’s stroke covers the other. Between China and Germany, Germany’s row comes later, and the stroke shows mostly Europe’s color.
The stroke pattern can come from a column too. pattern(continent) gives each continent a stroke pattern, the way color(continent) gave each a color above:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + pattern(continent) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, patterned by its exporter's continent")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + pattern(col.continent) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, patterned by its exporter's continent"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  pattern(:continent) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel + label(:name) + network() +
  title("Each stroke, patterned by its exporter's continent")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), pattern(col.continent),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("Each stroke, patterned by its exporter's continent"))






                                             China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  Each stroke, patterned by its exporter's continent  Continent    Asia  Americas  Europe  Oceania 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, patterned by continent, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
The stroke patterns follow the order in which the continents first appear in the continent column: Asia’s strokes are solid, the Americas’ are dashed, Europe’s are dotted and Oceania’s are dotdash. Between China and Germany, Germany’s dotted stroke is drawn over China’s solid one, and the solid stroke shows through the gaps, so the line looks solid.
There are five stroke patterns: solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash and longdash. A column with more than five categories repeats them from the start.

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.3 Transforms it takes
A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms an edge takes and the ones it refuses:



Kind
Takes
Refuses




Counting
—
bin, count, density, proportion


Summaries
—
sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile


Fitted lines
—
smooth, straight


Running total
—
cumulative


Pairs: a low and a high
—
range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds


Collision modifiers
—
dodge, stack, jitter, repel


Layouts of a whole picture
layout ●
partition, flow, cluster



An edge takes one transform, layout. It is marked ●: gog cannot draw an edge without it, because without a layout an edge has no ends. The plots below show it twice: in the plane, and in a cube.
Layouts. layout places each node once, and an edge draws one stroke between the two nodes of each row. It needs network() or space(), where no axis carries numbers, because a node’s position is not a value on any axis. network() places the nodes in the plane, as every plot above does. Write space() in its place, here with a viewing angle, space(turn = 35, tilt = 20), and the layout places them in a cube instead. Both numbers are degrees, and The viewing angle explains them. A point layer draws a dot at each node, so the ends of each stroke are easy to find:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
    point * layout(exporter, importer) + network() + title("edge * layout")) |
   (data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
      point * layout(exporter, importer) + space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
      title("edge * layout, in a cube"))) +
  theme(height = 420)


(((data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
    point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network() + title("edge * layout")) |
   (data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
      point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
      title("edge * layout, in a cube"))) +
  theme(height = 420))


((data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network() +
  title("edge * layout")) |
  (data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("edge * layout, in a cube"))) + theme(height = 420)


beside(plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("edge * layout")),
  plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  space({ turn: 35, tilt: 20 }), title("edge * layout, in a cube")),
  theme({ height: 420 }))






                                              edge * layout


                                                               edge * layout, in a cube






“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network, beside the same in the cube, turned 35, tilted 20.”
The cube holds the same 22 strokes. Every node takes a new position in the cube, because the layout places the nodes in three directions instead of two. The Network chapter names each node in the cube, in The network in the cube, and shows how to turn it with a drag in the web edition.
An edge refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. Most of them compute a value to place on an axis, or move a mark along one, and an edge has no axis. The other three, in the same row of the table as layout, compute shapes for different marks: partition gives rectangles to a zone, flow gives bands to a ribbon, and cluster gives branches to a path.

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.4 What you can set
Some choices come from no column: how thick every stroke is, or one stroke pattern for all of them. You set those in the sentence, with style(), and each mark takes its own settings. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are an edge’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash, longdash


style(arrow = )
end, start, both



style(size = ), style(color = ), style(opacity = ) and style(pattern = ) give every stroke the same value. A mapping such as size(billions) gives each stroke its own. The settings table above lists every stroke pattern that style(pattern = ) accepts.
One layer cannot both map a channel and set it. gog refuses this sentence, which maps continent to color and also sets the color to red:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(continent) +
  style(color = "red") + network()


(data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + color(col.continent) +
  style(color = "red") + network())


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  color(:continent) + style(color = "red") + network()


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), color(col.continent),
  style({ color: "red" }), network())




Error:
! gog: `color(continent)` maps color and `style(color = "red")` sets it — one layer cannot do both. Keep `color(continent)` to show the data, or `style(color = "red")` to fix every edge at one value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two fixes: keep color(continent) to show the data, or style(color = "red") to give every edge one color.
style(arrow = ) draws an arrowhead on each stroke. With "end", it is at the node in the second column of layout(), the to column. With "start", it is at the node in the first column, and with "both", at both nodes. Each arrowhead ends outside the dot that a point * layout layer draws at the node, so the dot does not cover it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + style(arrow = "end") +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke points at its importer")


(data(trade_partners) +

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.5 What it refuses
The other marks take their positions from x and y, so you may try binding x and y to an edge. Only a layout places an edge’s two ends. With x and y and no layout, the edge has nothing to draw, so gog refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge + x(billions) + y(exporter)


data(trade_partners) + edge + x(col.billions) + y(col.exporter)


data(trade_partners) + edge + x(:billions) + y(:exporter)


plot(data(trade_partners), edge, x(col.billions), y(col.exporter))




Error:
! gog: an `edge` connects two nodes, and only `layout` places them, so an `edge` with no `layout` has nothing to draw. Name the two endpoint columns and draw it in the network: `edge * layout(<from>, <to>) + network()`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message shows what to write instead: name the two endpoint columns in layout() and draw it in network().
A layout computes its positions from the graph, and no column holds them, so an axis has no value to show for them. Without network(), a sentence is in the plane, and the plane has axes. So gog refuses this sentence, which leaves network() out:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer)


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)))




Error:
! gog: a `layout`'s positions are the graph's, not the data's — an axis under them would number something no reader can mean. Draw it flat with `+ network()`, or in the cube with `+ space(turn = 30, tilt = 25)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message gives two ways to draw it: flat with + network(), or in the cube with + space(turn = 30, tilt = 25).
The Network chapter shows four more refusals: a mark other than edge, point or text with * layout, an x() in a sentence with a layout, network() with no layout, and a row from a node to itself. It explains why a brush is refused there too.

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.6 What comes next
An edge never has an axis, because a layout places both of its endpoints. Most other marks are placed by their values on the axes. Scales shows how a value becomes a position on an axis.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.1 A scale is not a transform
What do you do when most of your values are close together at one end of an axis, and a few are far away? You change the scale, which decides how a number becomes a position. It is written inside the channel’s parentheses, beside the column, and not as an atom of its own:
A scale belongs to one channel, so it is written where that channel is bound. gog has no scale() atom. You name the channel once, when you bind it, and write its scale in the same place, so a scale cannot end up on the wrong channel, such as a log scale written for y when gdp is bound to x.
Writing the scale on the binding also makes a sentence easier to read. To see how gdp is placed, you look at x(gdp, scale = "log") and nowhere else. Nothing else in the sentence can change it, and there is no second atom to look up.
A log scale is not the only way to spread out incomes that run from hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars. You could take the logarithm of the column yourself and plot the result. That is a different operation, and it changes which numbers the ticks show.
bin and mean are transforms: they read your table and compute new values from it. A scale produces no new values at all. It changes how far along the axis a number lands and what the ticks say, and nothing else.
The difference is visible in the finished plot. The gapminder_2007 table holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007, with its income per person (gdp) and its life expectancy (life). Here is gdp plotted with a log scale:

That is about 3,162 dollars, a number most people need a calculator to find. On a log scale you need no calculation, because the ticks are already in dollars.
So the choice depends on what the numbers stand for. Take the logarithm of the column when that logarithm is itself the quantity of interest: a log-odds, a decibel, a pH. Use a log scale when the numbers still count dollars or people, and you only want to spread out values that run from hundreds to tens of thousands.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.2 The order of a scale and a transform
text:
22.2 The order of a scale and a transform
Once a transform is in the plot, a scale is no longer only about display, because gog must decide whether the transform computes on your numbers or on their logarithms. gog follows one rule for every transform except the fits:

A transform groups the rows by their values on one axis, the grouping axis, and computes values for the other, the measured axis. On the grouping axis the scale comes first, so a log scale there makes the transform group the logarithms. On the measured axis the scale comes last: the transform computes in your data’s units, and the scale only places the result.

The fits are smooth, straight and their bands. A fit is fitted to the points where they are drawn, so for a fit the scale comes first on both axes. A straight line therefore stays straight on a log y axis, as straight: a line on a log axis shows. This is gog’s choice, and ggplot2 makes the same one.
Which axis is the grouping axis depends on the sentence, not on whether it is x or y. In bar * bin + x(gdp), the rows are put into bins by their x values, so x is the grouping axis. y is the measured axis, where the counts go. So a log x is applied before the bins are cut, and a log y after the counts are made. bar * bin + y(gdp) draws the histogram on its side: there y is the grouping axis, and the counts go on x.
The two plots below are two histograms of the same incomes, one with a log x and one with a log y. On the right, y(count, scale = "log") names the column bin writes its counts into, count (The name on a measure axis):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp, scale = "log") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log x: bins cut on the logarithms")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp) + y(count, scale = "log") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log y: counts placed on a log axis"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log x: bins cut on the logarithms")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp) + y(col.count, scale = "log") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log y: counts placed on a log axis")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Log x: bins cut on the logarithms")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp) + y(:count, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log y: counts placed on a log axis"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Log x: bins cut on the logarithms")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp),
  y(col.count, { scale: "log" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Log y: counts placed on a log axis")))

22.2.1 Scaling the grouping axis
The left plot above cut its bins on the logarithms of income. The upper end of each bin is about 1.8 times its lower end, and the bars fill the axis from end to end. Here it is again on the right, beside the same sentence on the default linear scale, where the bins are cut in dollars:

  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp, scale = "log") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log scale: bins cut on the logarithms"))

   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear scale: bins cut in dollars")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log scale: bins cut on the logarithms")))

  title("Linear scale: bins cut in dollars")) |

  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Log scale: bins cut on the logarithms"))

  x_label("GDP per person"), title("Linear scale: bins cut in dollars")),

gog never draws the dollar bins on the left on a log axis. On the log axis at the right, the first of those bins’ ranges, 278 to about 5,700 dollars, covers more than half the width. That bin holds 69 of the 142 countries, and the ranges of the other eight fill only the narrow strip to its right. That is why the grouping axis is scaled first.


22.2.2 The measured value keeps its own units
Put the log on the measured axis instead and a different question follows. Does a bar on a log scale stand for a sum of dollars, or for a sum of logarithms?
sum writes to y, so a log y is applied after the sum. The receipts table holds four receipts from two stores: North’s are 10 and 90, and South’s are 1 and 9. So the two bars in this plot stand for 100 and 10:

  title("A sum is still a sum")

  title("A sum is still a sum"))

  title("A sum is still a sum")

“Given the receipts: bars derived by sum, x is store, y is sales on a log scale.”
If the scale had been applied first, gog would have added the logarithms, and a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product. North’s bar would then show 900, ten times ninety, which is not North’s total of 100. gog adds the dollars first and scales the total afterwards, so sum reports a sum of dollars.
If you have used ggplot2, note the order, because ggplot2 does the opposite. Under scale_y_log10(), a stat_summary(fun = mean) averages the logarithms of the values. The result is a geometric mean, the average computed on the logarithms. gog computes the summary in your data’s units and scales the result, so the number the bar stands for is the number you would get by taking the sum or the mean yourself. For a fitted line, gog and ggplot2 do the same thing: both fit it to the logarithms, as straight: a line on a log axis shows.


22.2.3 smooth: a curve on a log axis
The grouping axis raises the same question for smooth: is the curve fitted to dollars, or to their logarithms? On incomes that run from a few hundred dollars to nearly fifty thousand, the answer changes the shape of the curve.
smooth is a fit, so it takes a log scale first, on y as on x. With a log x, the curve is fitted against log income. Life expectancy rises by about the same amount for each tenfold rise in income, so the curve on the right is close to a straight line.      line * smooth + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A trend fitted against log income"))

   line * smooth + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +

  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
     style(color = "lightgray") +
     line * smooth + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +

22.3 What a log scale refuses
Some columns cannot take a log scale, and they are not rare: a depth that goes below zero, a balance that went negative, a count of zero.
A logarithm is undefined at zero and below, so rows with such values have no position on the axis. gog refuses the sentence rather than dropping them quietly. The depth_readings table holds four readings of depth and temperature, and two of them have a depth of 0 or less: 0 and -4.

The message names how many rows are affected and the smallest value in the column, because “some of your data cannot be drawn” is not enough to act on. It then offers two fixes: filter those rows before plotting, or use a linear scale.
A categorical column has no logarithm either. It already gets a categorical axis with no scale written, so the message asks you to remove scale = "log":

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.4 Choosing the base
Not every quantity is best read in powers of ten. Ten is the usual base for money and for population. But a sound’s frequency doubles with every octave, so it is read in powers of 2. A quantity that grows or shrinks continuously at a constant rate is read in powers of e, about 2.718.
scale = "log" means base 10 unless you also write a base. Base 2 and base e are written this way:
x(freq, scale = "log", base = 2)
x(amount, scale = "log", base = exp(1))
R has no constant named e, so the second line writes it as exp(1). The other three bindings have one: Python’s math.e, Julia’s ℯ, and JavaScript’s Math.E. Natural log draws this scale below.
The base is a number, not a name. There is no "log2" or "ln" scale. One base argument takes any base, so gog has no separate name for each. For the same reason, gog has no function like ggplot2’s scale_x_log10.

22.4.1 What the base changes
You might expect a change of base to move the points. It does not: each point keeps its place along the axis. The base-2 logarithm of any value is always about 3.32 times its base-10 logarithm. gog places every value by where it falls between the axis’s two ends, so that fixed multiplier cancels. The transforms are unaffected too: bins of equal width in base 2 are equal width in base 10, so bar * bin cuts at the same values whichever base you name.
What the base actually chooses is where the gridlines fall and how they read. Here are six frequencies, each one an octave above the one before it, with base 10 above and base 2 below:



octaves: first 5 of 6 rows


freq
level




55
3


110
6


220
9


440
7


880
4







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(octaves) + point + x(freq, scale = "log") + y(level) +
    x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 10: gridlines at 100, 1K")) /
   (data(octaves) + point + x(freq, scale = "log", base = 2) + y(level) +
      x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 2: gridlines on every octave"))) +
  theme(height = 800)


(((data(octaves) + point + x(col.freq, scale = "log") + y(col.level) +
    x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 10: gridlines at 100, 1K")) /
   (data(octaves) + point + x(col.freq, scale = "log", base = 2) + y(col.level) +
      x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 2: gridlines on every octave"))) +
  theme(height = 800))


((data(octaves) + point + x(:freq, scale = "log") + y(:level) +
  x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 10: gridlines at 100, 1K")) /
  (data(octaves) + point + x(:freq, scale = "log", base = 2) + y(:level) +
  x_label("Frequency (Hz)") +
  title("Base 2: gridlines on every octave"))) + theme(height = 800)


below(plot(data(octaves), point, x(col.freq, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.level), x_label("Frequency (Hz)"),
  title("Base 10: gridlines at 100, 1K")),
  plot(data(octaves), point, x(col.freq, { scale: "log", base: 2 }),
  y(col.level), x_label("Frequency (Hz)"),
  title("Base 2: gridlines on every octave")), theme({ height: 800 }))






                                   100 1K   2 4 6 8  Base 10: gridlines at 100, 1K Level Frequency (Hz)


                                         64 128 256 512 1024 2048   2 4 6 8  Base 2: gridlines on every octave Level Frequency (Hz)






“Given the octaves: points, x is freq on a log scale, y is level, above points, x is freq on a log scale in base 2, y is level.”
Each point is directly above its partner, at the same place along its axis. The lower plot puts a gridline on each doubling, which is what “an octave” means. So for pitch, bits, or doubling times, base 2 puts a tick at every doubling, the unit you are counting.


22.4.2 Natural log
The amounts in the decay table shrink at a constant rate, by a factor of e every hour, so there is one gridline between each reading and the next. A change by a factor of e is called an e-folding.

hours
amount

  x_label("Amount remaining") +
  title("Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e")


(data(decay) + point + x(col.amount, scale = "log", base = math.e) + y(col.hours) +
  x_label("Amount remaining") +
  title("Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e"))


data(decay) + point + x(:amount, scale = "log", base = ℯ) + y(:hours) +
  x_label("Amount remaining") +
  title("Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e")


plot(data(decay), point, x(col.amount, { scale: "log", base: Math.E }),
  y(col.hours), x_label("Amount remaining"),
  title("Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e"))






                                           1 e e² e³ e⁴   0 1 2 3 4 5  Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e Hours Amount remaining





“Given the decay table: points, x is amount on a log scale in base e, y is hours.”
Notice the labels: 1, then e, e2, e3, e4, not 2.718, 7.389, 20.086, 54.598. That follows from one rule gog applies to every base:

Write the value itself when it is a whole number with few digits; otherwise write the power.

Base 10 gives 1, 10, 100, 1K, 10K and so on, up to 100T. K means a thousand, M a million, B a billion (109) and T a trillion (1012). A number before a letter has at most three digits, and no letter comes after T. So from 1015 upward, a tick is labeled as a power instead, such as 1015. Base 2 gives 1, 2, 4 and so on, up to 8388608. A number with more than seven digits is labeled as a power instead, such as 224. No power of e above 1 is a whole number, so every tick past the first reads as a power, which is what a reader counting e-foldings wants. If instead you want the axis to read 0, 1, 2, 3, the natural logarithms themselves, you do not want a log scale at all. You want log() applied to the column, and an axis labeled in log units, like the log_gdp plot in A scale is not a transform. A scale keeps your units; a column of logarithms changes them.
A base only means something as the base of a logarithm, so gog refuses one that has no log scale to belong to:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(octaves) + point + x(freq, base = 2) + y(level)


data(octaves) + point + x(col.freq, base = 2) + y(col.level)


data(octaves) + point + x(:freq, base = 2) + y(:level)


plot(data(octaves), point, x(col.freq, { base: 2 }), y(col.level))




Error:
! gog: `x(freq, base = …)` has no scale to be the base of. A base belongs to a logarithm — add `scale = "log"`, or remove the base.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message asks you to add scale = "log" or remove the base.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.5 Time: a date column gets a calendar axis
text:
22.5 Time: a date column gets a calendar axis
A column of dates raises a question the other columns do not. Where do the ticks go, and what do they say, when the units are years and months rather than tens and hundreds?
The time scale is one you never have to write. A column of dates or date-times is temporal, because its type already says so: a Date or a POSIXct in R, a date, datetime or datetime64 in Python, a Date or a DateTime in Julia, and a Date in JavaScript. gog reads the calendar from the type, the same way a column of text already gets a categorical axis. The revenue table holds one year’s sales for each of 26 years, 1994 to 2019, each dated June 30:



revenue: first 5 of 26 rows


day
sales




1994-06-30
52


1995-06-30
57


1996-06-30
55


1997-06-30
61


1998-06-30
64







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + line + x(day) + y(sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years")


(data(revenue) + line + x(col.day) + y(col.sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years"))


data(revenue) + line + x(:day) + y(:sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years")


plot(data(revenue), line, x(col.day), y(col.sales),
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years"))






                                 1995 2000 2005 2010 2015 2020   60 80 100  Twenty-six years, ticked in years Sales Day





“Given the revenue table: a line, x is day, y is sales.”
The sentence names no scale at all. Writing scale = "time" is allowed and adds nothing, exactly like writing scale = "linear" on a number.
The ticks land on calendar boundaries, because the calendar does not count in tens: a year has twelve months, and a week has seven days. An axis of years steps 1, 2 or 5 like any number line. For units smaller than a year those steps mean nothing: nobody reads an axis cut into fifths of a year. Months step by 1, 2, 3 or 6, and each of those divides twelve. A gridline therefore always falls on January, and a 3-month step marks each quarter. Days step by 1 or 2. Weeks step by 1 or 2, and a week tick is always on a Monday. Hours step by 1, 3, 6 or 12, and each of those divides twenty-four, so a gridline always falls on midnight. Minutes and seconds step by 1, 5, 15 or 30. The six_weeks table holds 42 days of orders, starting on Friday, March 1, 2024:

“Given the six weeks table: a line, x is day, y is orders.”
A tick is written in the unit of its step: 2010 for a year step, Jan 2024 for a month step, Mar 4 for a day step. A column of dates never gets clock ticks, however narrow its range. A column of date-times can, because it stores a time of day. That is a POSIXct in R, a datetime in Python, a DateTime in Julia, and in JavaScript a Date column whose values are not all midnight. “Given the monitoring table: a line, x is at, y is load.”
00:00 happens every day, so that label names no particular day. The midnight tick shows the date instead. Every other label on a time axis follows one rule: a tick is written in the unit of its step, and it leaves out what it shares with its neighbors.

22.5.1 Bars on a date axis
Daily orders make a natural bar chart, one bar per day, and forty-two bars raise the question of where the ticks go.
Bars positioned at dates are an ordinary time series. The ticks still come from the calendar, and there is not a tick for every bar. Wilkinson’s stock-price example puts its ticks on Sundays rather than on every trading day (Wilkinson, 2005), and gog ticks these six weeks at the start of each week:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(day) + y(orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks")


(data(six_weeks) + bar + x(col.day) + y(col.orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks"))


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(:day) + y(:orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks")


plot(data(six_weeks), bar, x(col.day), y(col.orders),
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks"))






                                                                       Mar 4 Mar 11 Mar 18 Mar 25 Apr 1 Apr 8   0 10 20 30  Daily bars, weekly ticks Orders Day





“Given the six weeks table: bars, x is day, y is orders.”
A date sets where a bar stands, never how long it is. A bar’s length is an amount, and a moment in time is not an amount. A bar “reaching” 2007 would be measured from 1970, the year a stored date counts from, which nobody chose as a baseline. So the bars are always placed along the dates, on whichever axis you write them. Write the dates on y and the orders on x, and the same bars are horizontal:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + bar + y(day) + x(orders) +
  title("Daily bars, drawn horizontally")


(data(six_weeks) + bar + y(col.day) + x(col.orders) +
  title("Daily bars, drawn horizontally"))


data(six_weeks) + bar + y(:day) + x(:orders) +
  title("Daily bars, drawn horizontally")


plot(data(six_weeks), bar, y(col.day), x(col.orders),
  title("Daily bars, drawn horizontally"))






                                                                       0 10 20 30   Mar 4 Mar 11 Mar 18 Mar 25 Apr 1 Apr 8  Daily bars, drawn horizontally Day Orders





“Given the six weeks table: bars, y is day, x is orders.”
With dates on one axis and a category on the other, a bar has nothing to measure. Neither column is an amount. gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(day) + y(weekday)


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(col.day) + y(col.weekday)


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(:day) + y(:weekday)


plot(data(six_weeks), bar, x(col.day), y(col.weekday))




Error:
! gog: `bar` would measure its length along `day`, and that is a date column — a bar's length is an amount, and a moment in time is not an amount. The other axis holds no continuous column to measure. Write a continuous column on `y` instead, `bar + x(day) + y(<measure>)`, or use `point`/`line` for values that are dates.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message asks for a continuous column in place of the category, or for point or line instead of bar.


22.5.2 Marks on a date axis
A date is a moment, and most marks have no width along a date axis. A point, a line, a step, an area, a text label and a rule are drawn at their dates. An interval or a ribbon runs between two values on the other axis, at each date.
Three marks have a width: bar, box and zone. On a date axis, each one takes a slot as wide as the smallest distance between two dates in its table. In a table with one row a day, the slot is one day. style(gap = ) leaves a share of the slot empty, as it does on a categorical axis. A date with no row stays empty, because a calendar axis has a place for every date, weekends included.
To give every date an equal slot, with no empty days, convert the dates to text before the plot. A column of text gets a categorical axis, with one slot for each value, in the order the values first appear in the table.
The sessions table holds 14 trading sessions, the days a market was open. They are the weekdays from Monday, March 2, to Thursday, March 19, 2026, so unlike six_weeks, the table has no rows for weekends.
