22.5.3 What a time axis refuses
A date is stored as a number underneath. You might therefore expect a date to take a log scale, and a number to take a time scale. Neither is allowed.
A moment has no logarithm. The zero a stored date counts from is a convention: dates could be counted from 1900 as easily as from 1970, and the same day would then have a different logarithm. A number that changes with that choice measures nothing about the day:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + line + x(day, scale = "log") + y(sales)


data(revenue) + line + x(col.day, scale = "log") + y(col.sales)


data(revenue) + line + x(:day, scale = "log") + y(:sales)


plot(data(revenue), line, x(col.day, { scale: "log" }), y(col.sales))




Error:
! gog: `x(day, scale = "log")` — `day` is a date column, and a moment in time has no logarithm: the calendar's zero is an arbitrary origin. Log the measured axis instead, or remove the scale.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests a log scale on the measured axis instead, or no scale.
gog can read the calendar off a date column, but scale = "time" cannot turn a column that is not a date column into one. The engine cannot know whether a number like the 52 in sales counts days, seconds or years since some starting date:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + point + x(sales, scale = "time") + y(sales)


data(revenue) + point + x(col.sales, scale = "time") + y(col.sales)


data(revenue) + point + x(:sales, scale = "time") + y(:sales)


plot(data(revenue), point, x(col.sales, { scale: "time" }), y(col.sales))




Error:
! gog: `x(sales, scale = "time")` — `sales` is not a date column, and a number alone does not say what moment it is. Store it as dates, or as date-times, before plotting; gog reads the calendar from the column's type.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Only the data says what the number counts, so the fix belongs in the data. Store the column as dates or date-times, in your language’s date or timestamp type. In R that is as.Date() or as.POSIXct(). The chapters for Python, Julia and JavaScript name the types in each.
For the same reason, a plain number cannot set the width of a bin on a time axis. bin(width = 7) does not say whether 7 counts days or seconds. The engine measures time in seconds, so these bins would be seven seconds wide, far too thin to see:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(day)


data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(col.day)


data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(:day)


plot(data(six_weeks), layer(bar, bin({ width: 7 })), x(col.day))




Error:
! gog: `bin(width = 7)` does not say what unit 7 is in, and `x(day)` holds dates. gog measures time in seconds, so these bins would be 7 seconds wide. Give the number of bins instead, such as `bin(30)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


To cut a time axis into bins, give the number of bins instead: bin(6) cuts these six weeks into six bins.
Time zones are never converted. gog draws the clock time you gave it. In R, a POSIXct is formatted in its own time zone when it is drawn, so the axis shows the times your session showed you. In Python, a datetime is drawn at the clock time it holds, and one with a time zone is drawn in its own zone. In Julia, a DateTime holds no time zone, so it is drawn as written. In JavaScript, a Date is drawn as your computer’s clock shows it, in local time. Two tables may record their times in different time zones, such as one logged in Seoul and one in London. To draw them on one axis, convert both to one time zone before plotting. Which zone to use is your decision, not gog’s.


22.5.4 Time on the other channels
A scale answers how far along? on every channel that measures, and a date column is no exception. Coloring rows by how recent they are is common. An axis tick can read Mar 4, because the ticks beside it place it in a sequence. A legend row is read on its own, so each row carries the full date:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + point + x(day) + y(orders) + color(day) +
  title("Recent days, darker")


(data(six_weeks) + point + x(col.day) + y(col.orders) + color(col.day) +
  title("Recent days, darker"))


data(six_weeks) + point + x(:day) + y(:orders) + color(:day) +
  title("Recent days, darker")


plot(data(six_weeks), point, x(col.day), y(col.orders), color(col.day),
  title("Recent days, darker"))






                                                                               Mar 4 Mar 11 Mar 18 Mar 25 Apr 1 Apr 8   15 20 25 30 35  Recent days, darker Orders Day  Day         2024-04-11 2024-03-21 2024-03-01 





“Given the six weeks table: points, x is day, y is orders, color by day.”

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.6 The scales
The chapter has used linear, log and time so far, and category comes later, in The column’s type picks the axis. The table names all four and what each one does.







Scale
What it does




linear
Equal steps for equal differences. The default


log
Equal steps for equal ratios, on x, y, z, color, size and opacity, with any base above 1


time
Positions dates and times, chosen from the column type: columns of dates and date-times, on every channel that measures


category
One slot per distinct value, chosen from the column type: columns of text, and columns with a declared order

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.7 The axis fits your data
Where should an axis end, on the data or on the next round number past it? Padding to a round number leaves part of the panel blank, and implies that the data reaches further than it does.
An axis shows round numbers on its ticks, but the range follows your data, not the round numbers. Each tick is a round number that falls inside the data, or at most a little past it into the margin. The axis does not extend to the next multiple of ten only to end on a round number. A span of 1952–2007 is drawn as 1952–2007, with ticks at 1960, 1980 and 2000, not padded to 1940–2020 with a third of the panel left blank. The gapminder_asia table, shown in straight: a line on a log axis, holds five Asian countries, each from 1952 to 2007. The plot draws the five as overlapping areas of one color, because only the year axis matters here. Area tells the countries apart with color.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(year) + y(life) +
  group(country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it")


(data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  group(col.country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it"))


data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), area, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ opacity: 0.4 }),
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it"))






                                   1960 1980 2000   0 20 40 60 80  The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: areas, x is year, y is life, grouped by country.”
Two more rules refine that fit. An end you do not state is set by the data’s smallest or largest value, and that end is a free end. A free end leaves a small margin, so a glyph never touches the panel edge. A point at the exact maximum would otherwise be cut in half by that edge. The plot uses the gapminder_2007 table, shown in A scale is not a transform:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("No point touches the panel edge"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  No point touches the panel edge Life GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
A baseline gets no margin. The area plot titled The year axis fits 1952–2007 shows it: the shape starts on the panel’s bottom edge, not a little way above it. When a bar or an area measures from zero, the zero is part of what it measures. A gap beneath it would show a stretch of axis below zero that no bar can reach, so the baseline is on the panel edge.
An area also runs from the left edge of the panel to the right. The margin exists so that a point at the end of an axis is not cut by the panel edge. An area has no point to cut, and a margin beside it would show as an empty band, so the area is drawn up to the edges. That is why the area plot spans the full width while the scatterplot of incomes keeps its margins. A line keeps the margin too, like a point. So does an area with a point layer in the same plot: the two layers share one axis, and the points need the margin.
A label reaches past its value too, by the width of its letters. When a label near a free end would not fit inside the panel, the axis is widened just enough to hold its letters. Oceania has the longest bar below, and its label is printed past the end of that bar. The labels are a text layer (Number labels):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + y(continent) + x(life) +
  text * mean + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "right") +
  title("The life axis is widened to fit Oceania's label")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + y(col.continent) + x(col.life) +
  text * mean + label(col.life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "right") +
  title("The life axis is widened to fit Oceania's label"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + y(:continent) + x(:life) +
  text * mean + label(:life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "right") +
  title("The life axis is widened to fit Oceania's label")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), y(col.continent),
  x(col.life), layer(text, mean), label(col.life, { decimals: 1 }),
  style({ nudge: "right" }),
  title("The life axis is widened to fit Oceania's label"))






                  70.7 77.6 54.8 73.6 80.7                   0 20 40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  The life axis is widened to fit Oceania's label Continent Life





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, y is continent, x is life, and also text derived by mean, label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge right.”
Oceania’s 80.7 ends just inside the panel’s right edge. Only a free end is widened. A baseline stays where it is. An end you state with limits also stays, and a label past it is cut at the panel edge.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.8 A scale is not only for axes
text:
22.8 A scale is not only for axes
Most of this chapter has put a scale on an axis. But on a linear color ramp most values can get nearly the same color, just as on a linear axis most points can fall at one end. x, y and, in a 3-D plot, z turn a number into a position, but so do color, size and opacity: a place on the ramp, a radius, an opacity. All six answer how far along?, so all six take a scale. A log scale on z, in the Space chapter, draws one on z.
This matters most for a column spread across orders of magnitude. population runs from about 200 thousand to 1.3 billion. On a linear ramp the median country is in the bottom one percent of that range, so nearly every point gets the same color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear color: nearly one flat color")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear color: nearly one flat color"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Linear color: nearly one flat color")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Linear color: nearly one flat color"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Linear color: nearly one flat color Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 659.4M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log color: the whole ramp is used")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log color: the whole ramp is used"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Log color: the whole ramp is used")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("Log color: the whole ramp is used"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Log color: the whole ramp is used Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 16.2M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population on a log scale.”
Look again at the middle number in the color legends of the two plots titled Linear color and Log color. On a linear ramp it is halfway between the two ends. On a log ramp it is the geometric midpoint, √(min · max), the square root of the smallest value times the largest: about 16M rather than 660M. The label has to be the geometric midpoint, because it names the color drawn at the middle of the ramp.
Whether a log scale suits a column is your decision, on color as on an axis. gog takes the logarithm of any column of numbers that are all above zero, and it does not check whether the plot becomes easier to read. A log ramp on life is drawn, for example, although life runs only from about 40 to 83, less than one power of ten. gog refuses a sentence only when it cannot draw it as written, as with a column that reaches zero (What a log scale refuses). A valid sentence is drawn even when the plot it makes is not a useful one (Law 8).
The same is true of size. With a linear scale, almost every point is drawn at the smallest radius, and only China and India are large:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   size(population) + style(color = "steelblue") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear size")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     size(population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
   size(col.population) + style(color = "steelblue") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear size")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
     size(col.population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  size(:population) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear size")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  size(:population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), size(col.population), style({ color: "steelblue" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("Linear size")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), size(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  style({ color: "steelblue" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Log size")))






                                                                                                                                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Linear size Life GDP per person  Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 


                                                                                                                                                                      1K 10K    Log size GDP per person  Population    199.6K  16.2M  1.3B 






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, size by population, beside the same with population on a log scale.”
shape, pattern and group answer which one?, not how far along?: there is no distance between a circle and a square. So gog refuses scale on all three, as shown here for shape:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  shape(continent, scale = "log")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  shape(col.continent, scale = "log"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  shape(:continent, scale = "log")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  shape(col.continent, { scale: "log" }))




Error:
! gog: `scale` on `shape(continent)`: `shape` distinguishes categories rather than measuring them, so there is no scale for it to run along. Drop `scale`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message asks you to drop it.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.9 limits: stating the range yourself
Every rule so far takes the range from the data. That is the right default, but sometimes an axis should cover values that no row reaches. The tide table holds a gauge’s readings, one height every three hours from hour 1 to hour 22, so none falls at midnight. polar() draws an axis as a circle, and Polar teaches that space in full. Nothing in a column of hours tells that circle that hour 24 is the same place as hour 0. limits states the range the axis covers. The left plot below has no limits, and the right plot states them:



tide: first 5 of 8 rows


hour
height




1
2.1


4
4.4


7
3.6


10
1.2


13
0.9







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(tide) + line + x(hour) + y(height) + polar() +
    title("Without limits: hours 1 to 22")) |
   (data(tide) + line + x(hour, limits = c(0, 24)) + y(height) + polar() +
      title("With limits: the whole day"))) +
  theme(width = 800, height = 420)


(((data(tide) + line + x(col.hour) + y(col.height) + polar() +
    title("Without limits: hours 1 to 22")) |
   (data(tide) + line + x(col.hour, limits = [0, 24]) + y(col.height) + polar() +
      title("With limits: the whole day"))) +
  theme(width = 800, height = 420))


((data(tide) + line + x(:hour) + y(:height) + polar() +
  title("Without limits: hours 1 to 22")) |
  (data(tide) + line + x(:hour, limits = [0, 24]) + y(:height) + polar() +
  title("With limits: the whole day"))) + theme(width = 800, height = 420)


beside(plot(data(tide), line, x(col.hour), y(col.height), polar(),
  title("Without limits: hours 1 to 22")),
  plot(data(tide), line, x(col.hour, { limits: [0, 24] }), y(col.height),
  polar(), title("With limits: the whole day")),
  theme({ width: 800, height: 420 }))






                    5 10 15 20   1 2 3 4  Without limits: hours 1 to 22 Height Hour


                 0 10 20   1 2 3 4  With limits: the whole day Height Hour






“Given the tide: a line, x is hour, y is height, in polar, beside a line, x is hour from 0 to 24, y is height, in polar.”
Without limits, one turn covers only 1 to 22, so the first and last readings are drawn on the same spoke, at the top of the left circle. With limits, each hour is drawn at its own fraction of the turn: hour 0 at the top, hour 6 a quarter of the way around, hour 12 halfway. The curve still does not close, and should not. The gauge took no reading at midnight, and limits says what range the axis covers rather than inventing an observation. The gap is in the readings, and the plot shows it at its true size, the three hours from 22 to 1. Polar describes three cases: two in which the curve closes, and this one, in which it does not.
limits is written on the binding, beside scale and base, for the same reason they are: the range belongs to one channel, and an atom of its own would name that channel twice. A stated end is drawn exactly where you state it. The margin exists to keep a glyph off the panel edge, and an end you chose is not a data extreme that needs the room.
limits can widen the axis as easily as it narrows it. Nothing was dropped in the plot titled “With limits: the whole day”: the readings run 1 through 22 and all of them lie inside 0 through 24. Narrowing is the direction that removes rows, and gog reports how many rows it removes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, limits = c(0, 30000)) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Limits of 0 to $30,000")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, limits = [0, 30000]) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Limits of 0 to $30,000"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, limits = [0, 30000]) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Limits of 0 to \$30,000")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { limits: [0, 30000] }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Limits of 0 to $30,000"))




gog: `x(gdp, limits = …)` excludes 20 of 142 rows, which fall outside [0, 30000]. Stating limits is what removes them — widen the limits if they should be drawn.




                                                                                                                                                           0 10K 20K 30K   40 50 60 70 80  Limits of 0 to $30,000 Life GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp from 0 to 30000, y is life, color by continent.”
The message above the plot is that report: it names how many rows fell outside and what the limits were. The plot still draws, because removing those rows is what you asked for, but gog does not remove data without saying so. Ask for limits no row can satisfy and gog refuses instead, because the alternative is an empty panel with axes drawn over nothing. No country has an income between one and two million dollars. The message gives the range gdp does cover, about 278 to 49,357 dollars, and asks you to widen the limits or remove them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, limits = c(1e6, 2e6)) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, limits = [1e6, 2e6]) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, limits = [1e+06, 2e+06]) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { limits: [1e+06, 2e+06] }),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(gdp, limits = …)` leaves no rows at all — `gdp` runs 277.5518587 to 49357.19017, which does not meet [1000000, 2000000], so the panel would be empty with axes drawn over nothing. Widen the limits, or remove them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Keeping every country in the plot and marking one group of them is a different operation, and it has a different word. limits removes rows before the plot is drawn. brush removes nothing: it dims the rows outside its range. Selection shows the two side by side.
When a transform computes the values on an axis, as count does, limits leaves out each bar or point whose value falls outside the limits. count writes its tally into a column named count, and you write y(count) to give that axis its limits (The name on a measure axis). Here the count axis stops at 40, below Africa’s count of 52:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y(count, limits = c(0, 40))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + y(col.count, limits = [0, 40])


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  y(:count, limits = [0, 40])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  y(col.count, { limits: [0, 40] }))




gog: `y(count, limits = …)` leaves out 1 of 5 computed values, which fall outside [0, 40]. Stating limits is what removes them — widen the limits if they should be drawn.




                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 10 20 30 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, y is count from 0 to 40.”
Africa keeps its label and has no bar. A bar stopped at the top edge would show 40, not 52. The message above the plot says how many values were left out, so the empty space above Africa does not mean zero.
You can state one end alone. Write NA for the end you leave out. NA is R’s word for a missing value; Python writes None, Julia missing and JavaScript null, as the chapters for Python, Julia and JavaScript show. The end you leave out stays a free end. That is how you start an axis at zero and let the top follow the data, or end it at 100 and let the bottom follow:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life, limits = c(0, NA)) +
   title("y from 0, the top fitted to the data")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(continent) +
     y(life, limits = c(NA, 100)) +
     title("y up to 100, the bottom fitted to the data"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life, limits = [0, None]) +
   title("y from 0, the top fitted to the data")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(col.continent) +
     y(col.life, limits = [None, 100]) +
     title("y up to 100, the bottom fitted to the data")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(:continent) +
  y(:life, limits = [0, missing]) +
  title("y from 0, the top fitted to the data")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(:continent) +
  y(:life, limits = [missing, 100]) +
  title("y up to 100, the bottom fitted to the data"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life, { limits: [0, null] }),
  title("y from 0, the top fitted to the data")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life, { limits: [null, 100] }),
  title("y up to 100, the bottom fitted to the data")))






                                         Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  y from 0, the top fitted to the data Life Continent


                                       Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80 90 100  y up to 100, the bottom fitted to the data Life Continent






“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by mean, x is continent, y is life from 0, beside the same with life up to 100.”
In the right plot, the axis ends at exactly 100. The bottom is a free end, so it keeps a margin below Africa.
limits reaches more than the axes. The range is a property of the scale, so limits reaches every channel that measures. That is how you keep one color ramp the same across plots built from different data. Here the legend runs from 100K to 2B, wider than the data, which runs from about 200 thousand to 1.3 billion:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log", limits = c(1e5, 2e9)) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log", limits = [1e5, 2e9]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log", limits = [1e+05, 2e+09]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life),
  color(col.population, { scale: "log", limits: [1e+05, 2e+09] }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B Life GDP per person  Population         2B 14.1M 100K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population on a log scale from 1e5 to 2e9.”
On a categorical axis limits is refused, and the refusal names the two ways to get what you meant. A category has no range to lie inside. Choosing which categories appear is filtering your table, and choosing what order they appear in is order().


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, limits = c(0, 3)) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent, limits = [0, 3]) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent, limits = [0, 3]) +
  y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean),
  x(col.continent, { limits: [0, 3] }), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent, limits = …)` — `continent` is text, and a category has no range to lie inside. To choose which categories appear, filter the table before plotting; to change the order they appear in, use `order(continent)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.10 The column’s type picks the axis
text:
22.10 The column’s type picks the axis
The time section showed that a column of dates gets a calendar axis without being asked. A column of text gets its own axis in the same way, and this section states the rule behind both. Other tools, ggplot2 among them, make you name a scale whenever you want to change one, so you may expect to write scale = "category".
The four scales are not all chosen the same way. You ask for log. A continuous column gets linear when you ask for nothing. You do not ask for time or category: gog reads those off the column. A column of dates gets a calendar axis, and a column of text gets one slot per distinct value.
You may still write them. As with scale = "time" on a date column, writing scale = "category" on a categorical column is allowed and changes nothing. The plot below is identical to the same sentence with the scale left off:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, scale = "category") + y(life) +
  title("Writing it changes nothing")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent, scale = "category") + y(col.life) +
  title("Writing it changes nothing"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent, scale = "category") +
  y(:life) + title("Writing it changes nothing")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean),
  x(col.continent, { scale: "category" }), y(col.life),
  title("Writing it changes nothing"))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Writing it changes nothing Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent as a category, y is life.”
What you cannot do is use a scale to contradict the column. Ask for a categorical axis on a continuous column and gog refuses:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "category") + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "category") + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "category") + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "category" }),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(gdp, scale = "category")` — a scale says how a measured column is placed; whether an axis measures at all is the column's type. Removing the scale alone would leave the continuous axis you were trying to escape. Store `gdp` as a categorical column before plotting, and drop the scale. To cut the numbers into ranges instead, use `bin`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The reason behind that refusal also explains the others in this chapter. A scale says how a measured column is placed. The column’s type decides whether the axis measures at all. So log on a categorical column is refused, and time on a column that is not a date column is refused. A date column cannot be turned back into raw numbers by asking for linear either:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + line + x(day, scale = "linear") + y(sales)


data(revenue) + line + x(col.day, scale = "linear") + y(col.sales)


data(revenue) + line + x(:day, scale = "linear") + y(:sales)


plot(data(revenue), line, x(col.day, { scale: "linear" }), y(col.sales))




Error:
! gog: `x(day, scale = "linear")` — `day` is a date column, and a date always reads as a calendar. If you truly want raw epoch numbers, store the column as numbers before plotting.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


None of those refusals offers another scale. Each tells you to change the column or remove the scale, because the column’s type is what the axis reads.
There are two things you might mean by “draw this number as categories”, and there is a different answer for each. For one slot per distinct value, declare the column’s categories: a factor in R, a pandas Categorical in Python, a CategoricalArray in Julia, and ordered() in JavaScript, all shown in Data. For intervals of numbers, use bin, which cuts the column into intervals and is covered in Transforms.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.11 tick_count: how many ticks the axis aims for
text:
22.11 tick_count: how many ticks the axis aims for
An axis picks about five ticks by default, and most of the time that is the best choice. You can still choose how many ticks it gets. A crowded axis is easier to read with fewer; an axis someone will take numbers from is easier with more. How many ticks an axis gets is a property of the scale. So tick_count is written on the binding, beside scale, base and limits, and not in theme(), which sets how the whole plot looks.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A high count: for reading values off"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(col.life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A high count: for reading values off")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A high count: for reading values off"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 12 }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("A high count: for reading values off")))






                                                                                                                                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80  A low count: the shape, not the numbers Life GDP per person


                                                                                                                                                                                        0 5K 10K 15K 20K 25K 30K 35K 40K 45K 50K    A high count: for reading values off GDP per person






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, beside the same with 12 ticks.”
The count is a target, not an exact number. gog keeps every tick on a round number, so the axis may draw a few more or a few fewer ticks than you asked for. To find the look you want, try a few counts and keep the one you like.
Both plots above cover the same range. That is the rule the count obeys: it changes how densely an axis is labeled, never where the axis stops. Ask for two ticks and the axis does not shrink to the two values it draws. The plot below reads the gapminder_asia table, shown in straight: a line on a log axis:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year, tick_count = 2) + y(life) +
  group(country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year, tick_count = 2) + y(col.life) +
  group(col.country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year, tick_count = 2) + y(:life) +
  group(:country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year, { tick_count: 2 }),
  y(col.life), group(col.country), style({ opacity: 0.4 }),
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007"))






                                 1950 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007 Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year with 2 ticks, y is life, grouped by country.”
A log axis and a date axis take a count too. Their ticks keep to values that suit the axis, such as powers of ten or whole weeks, so the number drawn can be further from the number you asked for:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log", tick_count = 12) + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Twelve asked for, seven drawn")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log", tick_count = 12) + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Twelve asked for, seven drawn"))

  y(:life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Twelve asked for, seven drawn")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point,
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log", tick_count: 12 }), y(col.life),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("Twelve asked for, seven drawn"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale with 12 ticks, y is life.”
The sentence asks for twelve ticks, and the axis draws seven. Without a count, this axis reads only 1K and 10K, as at the start of the chapter.
A date axis takes a count too. The plot uses the six_weeks table, shown in the time section:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + line + x(day, tick_count = 3) + y(orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks")


(data(six_weeks) + line + x(col.day, tick_count = 3) + y(col.orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks"))


data(six_weeks) + line + x(:day, tick_count = 3) + y(:orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks")

  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks"))

“Given the six weeks table: a line, x is day with 3 ticks, y is orders.”
By default these six weeks get a tick every Monday, six in all. Asked for three, the axis steps two weeks at a time, still on Mondays.
A categorical axis has one tick per category, so the data sets the count and you do not. gog refuses a tick count there:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, tick_count = 3) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent, tick_count = 3) +
  y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean),
  x(col.continent, { tick_count: 3 }), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent, tick_count = 3)` — `continent` is text, and a categorical axis has one tick per category, so the count is the data's rather than yours. To change which categories appear, filter the table before plotting; to change their order, use `order(continent)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two fixes: filter the table before plotting to change which categories appear, or use order(continent) to change their order.
A legend is not an axis, and it takes no tick count. limits reaches every channel that measures, because every one of them has a range of values; tick_count reaches only the three position channels that draw an axis: x, y and z. A color legend writes three numbers, both ends and the middle, and the scale, linear or log, sets their values, not a count you choose. The middle number is the midpoint explained in A scale is not only for axes: the label for the color drawn halfway along the ramp. So gog refuses a tick count on color(), size() or opacity(): they draw no axis, so there are no ticks to count.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, tick_count = 3)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, tick_count = 3))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, tick_count = 3)

  y(col.life), color(col.population, { tick_count: 3 }))




Error:
! gog: `tick_count` on `color(population)`: `color` has no axis, so there are no ticks to count. Put `tick_count` on a position, `x`, `y` or `z`, or drop it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.



22.11.1 Crowding in the plane and in the cube
A flat panel and a cube follow one rule for crowded numbers: no number may be printed over another. A flat continuous axis draws every tick it chose, as long as no two numbers overlap. Where panels are side by side, a number at the end of an axis that would reach past its panel is moved toward the middle of its own panel. In narrow panels, such as the five panels of a plot faceted by continent (Faceting), the numbers can still overlap.
The axis then draws fewer numbers, and the ticks and gridlines of the others are left out too. For example, of 0, 10K, 20K, 30K and 40K, it keeps 0, 20K and 40K. A number left out can be read from the numbers on either side, so no message is printed. If you stated a tick_count, a message says how many ticks were drawn. A map’s axes follow the same rule. A polar plot, and an axis freed with free = TRUE, still draw every number they chose.
The sentence below asks for twelve ticks, but each panel has room for three, and a message says so:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(life) |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(:life) |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 12 }),
  y(col.life), across(col.continent))




gog: `x(gdp, tick_count = 12)` asks for about 12 ticks, and the 11 ticks it chose do not fit side by side at this size, so 3 of them are drawn. A smaller `tick_count`, or a wider plot (`theme(width = )`), draws them all.




                                                                0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                         0 20K 40K                                                                                 0 20K 40K                                                      0 20K 40K                               0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 12 ticks, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
A cube can also have too little room for its numbers. In a 3-D plot (Space), each axis is longer or shorter depending on the viewing angle. Turning the cube lengthens one axis and shortens another. The cube then draws as many numbers as fit and leaves the rest out. When a count you stated cannot fit, the engine says so rather than quietly drawing fewer.
Names on a categorical axis follow the same rule: no name may be printed over another. The axis tries to name every category, and a name is usually much wider than a number. When names do not fit side by side, a flat axis first turns them 90 degrees, to read upward. A turned name needs room along the axis only for its height, not its width. When even turned names are too close, the flat axis leaves some out, as the cube does. It draws one name in every two or three, each with its tick, and prints a message. The 142 countries of 2007 do not fit, even turned:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(country) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(:country) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), bar, x(col.country), y(col.life))




gog: the 142 names of `country` on the x axis do not fit side by side, even turned to read upward: they are 5.1px apart, and a name needs 8.9px. One in every 2 is drawn (71 of 142), with its tick; the rest keep their places, unnamed. To name every one, swap the two axes so `country` runs down the y axis, in a taller plot (`theme(height = 1330)`), or draw fewer rows.

Cote d'Ivoire Cuba Denmark Dominican Republic Egypt Equatorial Guinea Ethiopia France Gambia Ghana Guatemala Guinea-Bissau Honduras Hungary India Iran Ireland Italy Japan Kenya Korea, Rep. Lebanon Liberia Madagascar Malaysia Mauritania Mexico Montenegro Mozambique Namibia Netherlands Nicaragua Nigeria Oman Panama Peru Poland Puerto Rico Romania Sao Tome and Principe Senegal Sierra Leone Slovak Republic Somalia Spain Sudan Sweden Syria Tanzania Togo Tunisia Uganda United States Venezuela West Bank and Gaza Zambia   0 20 40 60 80  Life Country





“Given gapminder 2007: bars, x is country, y is life.”
Every bar is still drawn, and a bar without a name keeps its place between two named ones. The message gives two ways to name every country: put country on the y axis in a taller plot, or draw fewer rows.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.12 percent, short and decimals: writing the numbers
text:
22.12 percent, short and decimals: writing the numbers
An axis chooses how to write its own numbers, and so does a legend. Most of the time their choice is easy to read. When it is not, three arguments on the binding choose how the numbers are written, beside scale, limits and tick_count. percent = TRUE writes a number as a percent. short = TRUE writes a large number with K for thousands, M for millions, B for billions and T for trillions. decimals sets how many decimal places each number has. A binding without any of the three keeps the axis’s own choice.
A share is the clearest case. proportion gives each bar its share of all the rows, a number between 0 and 1, and the axis writes 0.0 to 0.3. As a percent, the same axis writes 0% to 30%. The transform writes the y column and names it proportion, so the argument goes on y(proportion):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  y(proportion, percent = TRUE) + title("Each continent's share of the countries")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  y(col.proportion, percent = True) + title("Each continent's share of the countries"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:proportion, percent = true) +
  title("Each continent's share of the countries")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.proportion, { percent: true }),
  title("Each continent's share of the countries"))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0% 10% 20% 30%  Each continent's share of the countries Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent, y is proportion written as a percent.”
Only the numbers on the axis change. Each bar is as tall as it would be without percent, and limits stays in the column’s own units: limits = c(0, 0.5) means 0 to 0.5, which the axis writes as 0% to 50%.
short matters on an axis whose numbers are large and close together. The two_readings table holds France’s rows for 2002 and 2007:

With short = TRUE, each tick’s letter comes from the tick’s own size, so the same ticks are 60M, 60.5M and 61M:

All three arguments work on a legend as well as on an axis. The color legend of gdp writes 49.4K, 24.8K and 277.6 by default. With decimals = 0 it writes 49K, 25K and 278:

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +

  color(col.gdp, { decimals: 0 }))

On an axis, decimals keeps the letter the axis chose and changes only the number of decimal places. A population axis that writes 500M and 1000M writes 500.0M and 1000.0M with decimals = 1. If the places you ask for cannot tell two ticks apart, the axis draws fewer ticks. With decimals = 0, ticks at 0, 0.5 and 1 would write 0, 0 and 1, so the axis keeps only the whole numbers. When that would leave fewer than two ticks, gog refuses the plot, because one tick shows a place but no direction. No continent holds more than about 0.37 of the countries, so on their share axis 0 is the only whole number:

  y(proportion, decimals = 0)


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  y(col.proportion, decimals = 0))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:proportion, decimals = 0)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.proportion, { decimals: 0 }))

! gog: `y(proportion, decimals = 0)`: the axis runs from 0 to 0.385, and at 0 decimal places every tick on it but one would print the same number. An axis needs at least two ticks. Ask for more decimal places, or leave `decimals` out.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the axis’s range and asks for more decimal places, or for decimals to be left out.
percent and short are two ways to write one number, so gog refuses the pair:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  y(proportion, percent = TRUE, short = TRUE)


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  y(col.proportion, percent = True, short = True))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:proportion, percent = true, short = true)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.proportion, { percent: true, short: true }))




Error:
! gog: `y(proportion)` asks for both `short` and `percent`, two ways to write one number. Keep one of them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The three arguments work only where an axis or a legend writes plain numbers. A date axis writes dates, so there is no number to write another way, and gog refuses the three arguments there. A log axis writes the powers of its base or the values they name, and a map writes degrees. gog does not yet write those in another way, so it refuses the three arguments there too, and the message says so. label(), which sets the text a text mark prints, takes the same three arguments, as the text chapter shows.
On a web page, the three arguments also set how a number is written on the card that shows a point’s values, as Pointing at a mark explains. With x(gdp, short = TRUE), the card writes Germany’s gdp as 32.2K rather than 32170.37442. Without any of the three, the card writes the number as it is in your table.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.14 In short
A scale changes where a number is drawn, never the number itself; a fit or a grouping works on the axis as drawn. limits states the range a channel covers, and narrowing it removes rows and reports how many. tick_count is a target. A crowded axis draws fewer numbers, and a crowded categorical axis turns its names first. axis = FALSE leaves an axis out and keeps its scale. percent, short and decimals change only how the numbers are written.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.15 What comes next
A scale decides how far along a channel a number lands. It does not decide which visual property shows the column. Channels covers that: which property carries a column, and what guide it gets.




Wilkinson, L. (2005). The grammar of graphics (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.1 color
Which visual property should carry which column? A channel binds a data column to a visual property of a mark, and the channels do not all do the same work. x, y and z are the vowels: a mark does not render without a position, which you write or a transform computes. Some sentences write no position at all, because transforms compute every one: a network (layout), a pie chart (bar * count * stack in polar()), a sunburst (partition). Five other channels get a legend: color, size, shape, pattern and opacity. Those five are the final consonants, the optional ㅁ (m) that turns 가 (ga) into 감 (gam): never required, and each one shows one more column. Every channel atom has the same form:
No exceptions: x and y are channels too, and take a column the same way.
Different disciplines use different words for this, so you may know it by another name. Bertin wrote the vocabulary down first, in Sémiologie graphique (Bertin, 1967). He separated the two dimensions of the page from six retinal variables: size, value (his word for lightness), texture, color, orientation, and shape. A reader compares two amounts more precisely as positions than as sizes or colors (Munzner, 2014), so the two dimensions of the page are read more precisely than the retinal variables. Wilkinson and ggplot2 both say aesthetic, which is why ggplot2 code has aes(). gog has nothing like it: each channel is a word of its own. The visualization literature says channel instead, and describes each channel together with the mark whose look it changes (Munzner, 2014). That is the word gog uses. In everyday English, a channel carries a signal. Here the column is the signal, and color or size is the channel that carries it to the reader. Choosing an everyday word follows gog’s Plain Names law. Encoding is the same idea named as an act rather than a thing, and this book keeps both words. A channel is what you write; an encoding is what it does. Encoding scope is about what an encoding reaches: which layers of a plot a channel applies to.
The five channels from the start of this chapter are the refining channels: color, size, shape, pattern and opacity. Bind one to a column and a legend appears, with nothing to configure. x, y and z get an axis instead, and group gets neither: it splits a mark without encoding anything, so there is nothing for a legend to decode. label belongs to the text mark, and play has a chapter of its own.
Which points belong together? A scatterplot of positions alone cannot say, so the grouping has to come from a column.
color(field) maps a column to color, and a legend appears automatically. On point, line, step, path, zone and surface it takes either kind of column, and the kind decides what color means. On the other marks it takes only a categorical column.
It is spelled color, and only color. gog writes American English throughout and accepts no second spelling, so colour, which ggplot2 accepts, does not exist here. Writing it is refused, and the refusal names the fix (see Law 3).
A categorical column answers “which one?” Each category gets its own color from the palette:

  To fix one value for the whole layer instead — no legend, nothing to decode — that is a setting: `style(color = "red")`.
The message says that color("red") gives a value where a column belongs, and offers style(color = "red"), which sets one color for the whole layer.
A continuous column answers “how much?” Its values run along a ramp. A ramp is a range of colors that a number is placed along, the way an axis is a range of positions. This one runs light to dark, and the legend is the ramp itself, labeled at its minimum, midpoint, and maximum:

  color(life) + style(size = 6)

  color(col.life) + style(size = 6))

  style(size = 6)

  color(col.life), style({ size: 6 }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by life.”
Notice the legend: color gets one continuous strip. The size and opacity legends later in this chapter show three sampled examples instead. A legend should let the reader find any value the channel can draw. A strip of color does this directly. Circles cannot form a strip, so the legend draws three circles of different sizes, and a reader can picture the sizes between them. Colors cannot be sampled that way, and the difference matters most for a multi-hue ramp. Three sampled colors from viridis, one of the ramps below, say nothing about the colors between them.
The default ramp is one hue, not a rainbow, and that is deliberate. A sequential ramp, one that runs from low values to high, encodes magnitude. A reader reads a darker color as more, so lightness is what such a ramp varies. One hue running light to dark is read quickly, stays readable in grayscale and under color blindness, and matches the categorical palette when both appear in one figure. A rainbow encodes magnitude as hue, which has no intrinsic order, so the reader has to consult the legend for every point. gog’s default is a single blue built on the same hue as the first categorical color, so the ramp and the categorical palette look like one set of colors. Ramps has the multi-hue alternatives, and the sections after it have the diverging ramps and the ramps you build from colors you choose.

Where a channel is written decides which marks it reaches. Written before any mark, it reaches every layer. Written after a mark, it belongs to that mark alone, never to an earlier one: here color(country) colors only the lines, and size(population) sizes only the points. The positions are the exception: every mark shares the axes, so a mark with no x or y of its own reads the first column written for each axis. Which marks a channel reaches draws the difference, and Encoding scope gives the whole rule.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.2 size
The color section used size without saying what it does. Here is the problem it solves. In the 2007 scatter, x carries GDP per person and y carries life expectancy. Population is a third number with no position left for it.
size(field) scales point radius linearly from 3px (min) to 12px (max). A size legend shows the minimum, the midpoint and the maximum of the column. On edge and rule, and on an interval drawn with bounds, each row draws one stroke. There size sets the stroke’s width, from 1px to 6px, and the legend draws a line at each width. Rule shows an example.

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:population)

  size(col.population))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, size by population.”

title: 23  Channels and legends

23.3 shape
A journal prints your figure in black and white, and the colors you chose print as grays that look almost the same. The grouping has to come from the glyph instead.
shape(field) maps a categorical column to one of seven glyphs: circle, square, triangle, diamond, cross, star, wye (a Y shape). Seven is the whole set. It is also about as many shapes as a reader can recognize quickly. Map shape to a column with more than seven categories and the eighth category starts again at the circle. Two categories then share a glyph, and gog prints a message to say so. The Shape section of the point chapter shows what to do when a column has more than seven categories.

  shape(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  shape(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + shape(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  shape(col.continent))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, shape by continent.”
color and shape can be bound to the same column. Binding one column to two channels is redundant encoding, and it makes the plot easier to read:

  color(continent) + shape(continent)

  color(col.continent) + shape(col.continent))

  shape(:continent)

  color(col.continent), shape(col.continent))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, shape by continent.”
Either channel alone would separate the continents. Using both separates them in two ways, so a reader who cannot see the colors still has the shapes. gog draws one legend for the two, with each glyph in its continent’s color.

title: 23  Channels and legends

23.4 pattern
shape answers the black-and-white problem for points. A bar or a line has no glyph to change, so it needs a different answer, and that answer is texture.
pattern(field) maps a categorical column to a texture, the way shape maps one to a glyph. The mark’s geometry decides what the texture looks like. On the filled regions (bar, box, area, ribbon, zone) it is a fill texture: solid, or lines or dots repeated across the region. On the strokes (line, step, interval, path, rule, edge) it is a stroke pattern: solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash or longdash. Textures do not depend on color, so they work in grayscale and for a colorblind reader. The first category always gets solid, and the rest get the others in order:

The set of textures is deliberately small: six on a fill and five on a stroke, and the first of each is solid. A fill covers a large area, so a reader can distinguish more textures on it. A stroke pattern needs a long enough line to be seen, so a reader can distinguish fewer on a stroke. Because both sets are small, pattern suits a few categories rather than dozens. A seventh category on a fill, or a sixth on a stroke, repeats a texture. gog says so, and suggests color() or facet() instead. To set one texture for a whole layer instead of mapping a column, use style(pattern = ).

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.5 opacity
Sometimes a number should decide how faint a mark is drawn, so that small values fade and large ones stay opaque.
opacity(field) maps a continuous column to opacity: a larger value gives a more opaque mark.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + opacity(population) +
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more opaque")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + opacity(col.population) +
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more opaque"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + opacity(:population) +
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more opaque")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.population),
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more opaque"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Opacity: larger populations drawn more opaque Life Gdp  Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, opacity by population.”
Only China and India are drawn nearly opaque, because their populations are several times larger than any other country’s. A ramp on a skewed column shows the fix, a log scale, and it works on opacity too.
Like size, opacity produces a legend showing the minimum, midpoint, and maximum of the column. Here it is three gray squares, labeled 199.6K, 659.4M and 1.3B.
The smallest value is drawn faint but never fully transparent, so every mark stays visible.
With no opacity binding, the default depends on the mark, so you may notice that some marks are paler than others. The defaults follow one rule: a mark is as translucent as it needs to be so that it does not hide other marks, and no more.



Mark
Default
Why

0.82
marks may overlap a little, and the overlap shows

the ones underneath stay visible


the bands of a flow
0.45
bands cross one another


a highlight zone
0.2
the plot behind it stays readable


a line, most strokes, and text
opaque

a zone of cells such as a heatmap, a surface, and a bar or box in the cube
opaque
they do not overlap on the flat page, and in the cube the nearer one hides the farther



style(opacity = ) sets your own value on any of them.
On line, opacity cannot be mapped: a line joins many rows into one stroke, a stroke has one opacity, and one value cannot carry a column. This is the same rule that refuses a per-row size on a line, not a special case for opacity:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(population)


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + opacity(col.population)


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + opacity(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.population))




Error:
! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `line` — a line takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `population` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`, or use a mark that maps `opacity`: `point` or `bar`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two fixes: set one opacity for the layer with style(opacity = ), or use a mark that maps opacity: point or bar. An edge, a rule and an interval drawn with bounds draw one stroke for each row, so on those marks opacity and size can both be mapped.
A stroke still has an opacity, so you can set one for every line in the layer. Here group(country) splits the rows into one line per country, and style(opacity = 0.4) draws all five at 0.4:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  style(opacity = 0.4)

  style(opacity = 0.4))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(opacity = 0.4)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ opacity: 0.4 }))

“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, with opacity 0.4.”
group has a section of its own below. To give each line its own color as well, use color.
That refusal looks like an inconsistency: color maps onto a line and opacity does not. It is not one. A width and an opacity are one value for the whole stroke: the width is the same at every point along it. A stroke pattern is also one value for the whole stroke, so pattern on a line draws one stroke per category. A color is not like that. You can point at one place on a line and ask what color it is, so the values of a continuous column can vary along it, and color on line, step and path accepts either kind of column:

  color(gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person")

  color(col.gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  color(:gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), color(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  palette("viridis"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person"))

“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, color by gdp on a log scale, with the viridis palette.”
A categorical column on color splits the mark into one stroke per group. A continuous column varies the color along each stroke and gets a ramp legend, not one swatch (a small sample of the color) per series. One channel and one mark give two behaviors, and the column’s type decides which behavior you get.
A continuous column on color does not split the rows. Without group(country), the five countries are joined into one zigzag stroke, and gog says so:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  color(gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Without group: one stroke for all five countries")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Without group: one stroke for all five countries"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  color(:gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Without group: one stroke for all five countries")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  color(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), palette("viridis"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Without group: one stroke for all five countries"))




gog: up to 5 rows of `line` share one value of `x(year)`, and nothing splits them, so they are joined in x order and the stroke zigzags inside that value. `color(gdp)` is continuous, so it colors along the stroke rather than splitting it. If you have several series, add `group(<field>)`; for one value per `x`, summarize them with `line * mean`.




                                                                                         1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Without group: one stroke for all five countries Life expectancy Year  Gdp            31.7K 3560.4 400.4 





“Given gapminder Asia: a line, x is year, y is life, color by gdp on a log scale, with the viridis palette.”
With group(country), as in the plot titled “One line per country, colored by GDP per person”, there is one line per country, and the ramp runs along each. Japan’s line, at the top, runs from teal in 1952 (GDP per person about $3,200) to yellow in 2007 (about $31,700).

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.6 group
The section above used group twice. It is the one channel that splits a mark and encodes nothing.
group(field) splits the mark into one series per value in the column. On a line, that is one stroke per value, and every stroke gets the same color. Use it when the lines must be kept apart but one color is what you want.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) +
  group(country)


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  group(col.country))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country.”
When you want color and grouping, use a categorical color(field) alone: it implies grouping automatically. A surface is different: there a color gives each face its color, and only group makes separate sheets (Two sheets over one floor).
A bar, a point or a text draws one shape or one label per row, so splitting their rows into groups changes nothing by itself. gog draws group on them only together with a transform that does something with the groups: a statistic such as mean, which computes a value for each group, dodge, which sets the groups side by side, and on a bar or a text also stack, which piles them up. The gm_eras table holds two rows for each country, one for 1957 and one for 2007, and its era column says which year a row is. On it, bar * mean * dodge + group(era) draws one bar for each era, side by side and in one color, as Splitting without color shows. Beside bar * mean * dodge, text * mean * dodge + group(era) prints each era’s mean on its own bar, as Labels on dodged bars shows.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.7 Multiple channels
Two positions and one refining channel carry three columns. A table usually has a fourth you want on the page.
You have already seen two refining channels on one mark several times. Any channels a mark accepts can be bound together, so you can bind more of them at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Two positions and three refining channels
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) + shape(continent) +
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + size(col.population) + shape(col.continent) +
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  size(:population) + shape(:continent) +
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), size(col.population), shape(col.continent),
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, size by population, shape by continent.”
Five channels (x, y, color, size and shape) carry four columns here (gdp, life, continent and population). The three refining channels draw only two legends, because shape repeats color and the two share one. Each column on a refining channel adds a legend for the reader to check. So add a channel only when the plot needs its column, or when it makes a column easier to read, as shape does here.
A continuous column on both size and opacity gets one legend, as continent on color and shape does. With population on both, a country with more people gets a larger and more opaque point:

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  size(population) + opacity(population) + title("Population, shown twice")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  size(col.population) + opacity(col.population) + title("Population, shown twice"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:population) +
  opacity(:population) + title("Population, shown twice")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  size(col.population), opacity(col.population),
  title("Population, shown twice"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, size by population, opacity by population.”
The legend has three circles, each drawn at the size and the opacity of the value beside it. A continuous column on color and size gets two legends, because three circles would show only three colors of its ramp (see color). Here is the same plot with color in place of opacity:

  size(population) + color(population) + title("Population on size and color")

  size(col.population) + color(col.population) + title("Population on size and color"))

  color(:population) + title("Population on size and color")

  size(col.population), color(col.population),
  title("Population on size and color"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, size by population, color by population.”
The color legend is the ramp in one strip, and the size legend below it is three gray circles. The strip has the largest value at the top, while the size legend lists the smallest first, so read each legend by its own labels.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.8 Palettes
Most plots so far used the colors gog chose by default. To choose your own, use palette().
palette() chooses the colors the color channel assigns. There is no separate atom for ramps, which ggplot2 calls gradients. One atom serves both, because the column’s type decides which meaning the colors get. For a categorical column, gog reads a set of colors as one color per category. For a continuous column, it reads the same set as stops, the fixed colors a ramp passes through.
There are three kinds of named palette, and they say three different things: a categorical palette gives each category its own color, a sequential ramp runs from low values to high, and a diverging ramp measures distance from a center in either direction. The type of the column decides which kinds you may name: a categorical column takes a categorical palette, and a continuous column takes a sequential or a diverging ramp. The sections below follow that order.
gog’s default palette holds 20 colors, which is more than most tables need. When a column has more categories than that, gog makes more colors, so no two categories share one. With many more than twenty, though, neighboring colors are hard to distinguish.

23.8.1 Categorical palettes
Most of the time the default is what you want. You change it when a reader may be colorblind, when a journal requires particular colors, or when the marks are large enough that the default is too strong.
A categorical palette gives one color to each category, so a reader matches a swatch in the legend to a name. gog provides three, and the last column says which one to pick:



Name
Colors
Best for




"gog"
20 (default)
General use


"okabe"
8 base + 8 light variants
Colorblind accessibility


"soft"
8, lighter
Filled marks: bars, areas, zones



"okabe" is Okabe and Ito’s set (Okabe & Ito, 2008), chosen so that its eight colors stay distinct for readers with the common forms of color blindness. gog adds eight lighter versions of these colors, used when a column has more than eight categories:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("okabe")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("okabe"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("okabe")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("okabe"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with the okabe palette.”
The default is designed for points and lines, where a color occupies a few pixels and must stay visible at reading distance. A fill is large, so it is already easy to see, and a color strong enough to make a small point easy to find is more than a bar needs. In a row of such bars, the strong color takes attention away from the heights, which are what the bars show. soft is a different set of eight colors, lighter than the default. Compare these two. Apart from the title, the palette is the only difference:

data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + color(continent) +
  title("The default, over filled bars")

  title("The default, over filled bars"))

  title("The default, over filled bars")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  color(col.continent), title("The default, over filled bars"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, color by continent.”

  palette("soft") + title("palette(\"soft\")")
