“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, color by continent, with the soft palette.”
The default still works on bars, and on points it is the better choice. A point is small, so its color must be strong enough to find; a bar is already visible, and its color only has to differ from its neighbors.


23.8.2 Sequential ramps
A continuous column has no categories to give a color to, so a palette has to mean something else. For a continuous color column, palette() names a ramp instead. The ramps below run one way, from low values to high. Lightness changes steadily along the ramp, and that is what shows the order.








Name
What it is
Use it when




"blue"
the default: one hue, light→dark
almost always


"viridis"
many hues, with equal color steps for equal value steps
dense data where small differences must stay visible


"magma"
viridis’s family: black through purple to cream
a plot on a dark panel (theme(background = )), where the pale top end shows; values drawn in the darkest colors are then hard to see


"inferno"
the same family: black through red and orange to pale yellow
as for magma, with more red and orange


"plasma"
the same family, blue through magenta to yellow
as for magma, starting at dark blue rather than black


"cividis"
the family’s colorblind-optimized member
the ramp itself has to stay readable under two-color vision (dichromacy)


"gray"
no hue at all: light gray to near-black
figures that will be printed in black and white



Those seven names do not tell you what the ramps look like. Here are six of the seven, every one except the default blue, on Maunga Whau, a volcano in Auckland. The volcano is cut into cells, each colored by its mean elevation. A dense grid of continuous values like this is what a ramp is for. palette() is a property of the plot, so six ramps means six plots, and | and / put them in one arrangement:

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            200 400 600   200 400 600 800  plasma North East  Elevation            191.5 142.8 94 


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            200 400 600   200 400 600 800  cividis North East  Elevation            191.5 142.8 94 


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            200 400 600   200 400 600 800  gray North East  Elevation         191.5 142.8 94 






“Given Maunga Whau: zones derived by bin into 16 and mean, x is east, y is north, color by elevation, with the viridis palette, beside the same with magma; above the same pair with inferno and plasma; above the same pair with cividis and gray.”
That is the same sentence six times, with only the ramp’s name changed, in palette() and in title(). It is written out in full because a loop or a variable is written differently in each of the book’s four languages.
Those six plots show four things, one in each paragraph.
gray runs from light to dark, and the other five run from dark to light. In the gray plot the summit is dark, while in the other five it is bright. Both directions are correct. gog’s own ramps (gray and the default blue) run light to dark, because with one hue a darker color reads as a larger value, and a photocopier keeps those lightness differences. The viridis-family ramps run dark to light because their designers made them that way, and gog keeps their direction, so magma still looks like magma. In any plot, look at the top of the legend: the color there is the color of the highest value (191.5 here).
Of the five viridis-family ramps, magma and inferno end on a near-white. magma’s last stop is nearly the same color as the panel behind it, so the colors of the highest values almost disappear. You can see this in the pale, flat summits in the magma and inferno plots. The viridis family ends on very light colors by design. blue and gray never reach white, so their pale end stays visible against the panel, and that is why blue is the default rather than one of these.
cividis uses the fewest hues of the five, and that is deliberate: it uses only blue and yellow, the two hues that stay distinct under the common forms of color blindness. The other four run through many more, so they separate neighboring values by hue as well as by lightness. cividis separates them mostly by lightness. Choose it when the ramp has to stay readable for a colorblind reader.
gray is for the figure that will be photocopied. It is a ramp only, and there is no categorical gray palette. Grays differ only in lightness, so readers can distinguish only a few of them. For categories in a print figure, use shape on points and pattern on bars and lines, which separate them and leave the color channel free. gog refuses palette("gray") on a categorical column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("gray")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("gray"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("gray")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("gray"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("gray")` is a sequential ramp for a continuous column, but `color` is bound to a categorical column. Use a categorical palette — `gog`, `okabe`, or `soft` — or list one color per category. For categories in a figure that has to print in black and white, reach for `shape(<column>)` instead — it tells them apart without spending color.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message says why. It offers three fixes: a categorical palette, a list with one color for each category, or shape() for a figure printed in black and white.


23.8.3 Diverging ramps
A sequential ramp means more. A diverging ramp means away from a center, in two directions. A change, a residual, a correlation and an anomaly (a difference from the usual value) can each fall on either side of zero. gog provides two:



Name
What it is
Use it when




"blue_red"
blue → gray → red
the usual choice


"brown_teal"
brown → gray → teal
readers may be colorblind



The name reads low to high, so blue_red paints the smallest values blue and the largest red. Both pass through the same gray at the center of the scale.
The palette does not decide which value gets the neutral color. That value is the middle of the scale’s range, which limits sets. Without limits, the middle falls on the data’s own midpoint. Here delta runs from -32 to 120, so the midpoint is 44. That value is painted gray, and zero is painted blue.



cashflow: first 5 of 6 rows


step
delta

RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  color(delta) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0")


(data(cashflow) + point + x(col.step) + y(col.delta) +
  color(col.delta) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0"))


data(cashflow) + point + x(:step) + y(:delta) + color(:delta) +
  palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0")


plot(data(cashflow), point, x(col.step), y(col.delta), color(col.delta),
  palette("blue_red"), style({ size: 9 }),
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0"))






                                       Opening Sales Refunds Costs Tax Closing   0 50 100  44 is painted gray, not 0 Delta Step  Delta           120 44 -32 





“Given the cashflow table: points, x is step, y is delta, color by delta, with the blue red palette.”
No row is 44, but Sales, at 45, is drawn almost gray, and Closing, at 0, is blue.
State symmetric limits and zero becomes the center of the scale, so zero is the value painted gray. Read the “Closing” point, which is exactly zero:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(cashflow) + point + x(step) + y(delta) +
  color(delta, limits = c(-120, 120)) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray")


(data(cashflow) + point + x(col.step) + y(col.delta) +
  color(col.delta, limits = [-120, 120]) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray"))


data(cashflow) + point + x(:step) + y(:delta) +
  color(:delta, limits = [-120, 120]) + palette("blue_red") +
  style(size = 9) + title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray")


plot(data(cashflow), point, x(col.step), y(col.delta),
  color(col.delta, { limits: [-120, 120] }), palette("blue_red"),
  style({ size: 9 }), title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray"))






                                       Opening Sales Refunds Costs Tax Closing   0 50 100  Symmetric limits paint zero gray Delta Step  Delta           120 0 -120 





“Given the cashflow table: points, x is step, y is delta, color by delta from -120 to 120, with the blue red palette.”
Two things follow from centering the ramp with limits. The ramp stays linear: equal distance in color is equal distance in the data on both sides of the center. Some plotting tools set a midpoint and then stretch each side to the data’s own ends; a scale built that way is no longer linear. And limits removes rows outside it, so the range has to be wide enough to hold the data. Here c(-50, 50) leaves out the Opening row, whose delta is 120, and a message says that 1 of 6 rows falls outside the limits.
Symmetric limits have one drawback, and the plot above shows it. The lowest delta is -32, so the blue half of the ramp from -32 down to -120 is unused, and the three negative points (Refunds, Costs and Tax) are a pale gray-blue. Accept that when the sign is what matters, since zero has to be painted gray. When the sign does not matter, a sequential ramp such as blue uses all of its colors.


23.8.4 Stops of your own
Sometimes you need a ramp between two particular colors, and no named ramp runs between them. Pass those colors to palette(): they become the stops, and gog fills in the colors between them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(life) + palette(c("white", "navy")) + style(size = 6) +
  title("Custom stops")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.life) + palette(["white", "navy"]) + style(size = 6) +
  title("Custom stops"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:life) +
  palette(["white", "navy"]) + style(size = 6) + title("Custom stops")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.life), palette(["white", "navy"]), style({ size: 6 }),
  title("Custom stops"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Custom stops Life Gdp  Life        82.6 61.11 39.61 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by life, with a palette of white and navy.”
gog refuses a palette that does not match the column, rather than guessing what you meant. A categorical palette cannot color a continuous column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(life) + palette("okabe")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.life) + palette("okabe"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:life) +
  palette("okabe")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.life), palette("okabe"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("okabe")` hands out one color per category, but `color` is bound to a continuous column. Use a ramp — `blue`, `viridis`, `magma`, `inferno`, `plasma`, `cividis`, or `gray` run one way, `blue_red` or `brown_teal` diverge from a center — or give `palette()` your own stops, the colors themselves, such as "white" and "navy".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message lists the ramps such a column can take, or asks for your own stops.


23.8.5 A ramp on a skewed column
No ramp reads well on a skewed column, and changing the palette does not fix it. A linear ramp spreads its colors evenly across the scale’s range, so when most rows fall in a narrow part of it they all receive almost the same color. When you color by population, nearly every country falls at the light end:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(population) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.population) +
  x_label("GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:population) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.population), x_label("GDP per person"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 659.4M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by population.”
The two dark points are China and India, whose populations are several times larger than any other country’s. The cause is the data, not the palette, so the fix is a log scale on the channel, and on x as well, since GDP per person is skewed the same way:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log") + x_label("GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 16.2M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population on a log scale.”
On the log scale the colors spread along the whole ramp, so countries of different sizes get different colors.
Of the refining channels, three take scale =: size, opacity, and color on a continuous column. All three measure how large a value is. shape and pattern only separate categories, and group shows nothing at all, so gog refuses scale on them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  shape(continent, scale = "log")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  shape(col.continent, scale = "log"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  shape(:continent, scale = "log")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  shape(col.continent, { scale: "log" }))




Error:
! gog: `scale` on `shape(continent)`: `shape` distinguishes categories rather than measuring them, so there is no scale for it to run along. Drop `scale`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message says to drop it.


23.8.6 Custom colors
Often the colors are decided before you begin: a journal asks for them, or an earlier figure already used them.
Pass the colors yourself: hex values, CSS color names such as firebrick, or a mix of the two:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  palette(c("#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) +
  palette(["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette(["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"]))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with a palette of #e41a1c, #377eb8, #4daf4a, #984ea3 and #ff7f00.”
The same call takes CSS color names, which are easier to recognize when you read the code later:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  palette(c("firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple", "darkorange"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) +
  palette(["firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple", "darkorange"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple", "darkorange"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette(["firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple",
  "darkorange"]))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with a palette of firebrick, steelblue, seagreen, rebeccapurple and darkorange.”
gog refuses a color name it does not know. Otherwise the misspelled name would go into the plot, and a browser draws an unknown color as black:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette(c("firebrick", "stelblue"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette(["firebrick", "stelblue"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["firebrick", "stelblue"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette(["firebrick", "stelblue"]))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` entry "stelblue" is not a color. Did you mean "steelblue"? Use a CSS color name, or a hex value like "#4e79a7".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests the nearest color name, steelblue.
Colors are assigned in first-appearance order: the first unique value gets the first palette color, the second gets the second, and so on. If the column declares its order, that order is used instead. Either way, the same rows in the same order always get the same colors.
One mistake to know about: a single color is not a palette. palette() reads a single word as a palette name, and "red" is not one, so gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("red"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("red")` is not a known palette. Named palettes are gog, okabe, soft for categories; blue, viridis, magma, inferno, plasma, cividis, gray for continuous columns; blue_red, brown_teal for continuous columns that diverge from a center. `"red"` is a color, not a palette. To paint every mark one color use `style(color = "red")`; to give each category its own color, give `palette()` several colors, "red" among them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message offers two fixes. To paint every mark one color, use style(color = "red"). To give each category its own color, give palette() several colors.


23.8.7 Colors by name
Colors passed without names are assigned in first-appearance order, so a category’s color depends on where it falls in that order. Sorting the rows can change a category’s color, and so can another table that lists the categories in a different order. Two plots placed side by side in a report then disagree about which color a continent is. To assign a color to a category, write the category’s name beside the color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c(Africa = "seagreen", Americas = "goldenrod", Asia = "tomato",
            Europe = "steelblue", Oceania = "orchid"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette({"Africa": "seagreen", "Americas": "goldenrod", "Asia": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue", "Oceania": "orchid"}))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["Africa" => "seagreen", "Americas" => "goldenrod", "Asia" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue", "Oceania" => "orchid"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette({ Africa: "seagreen", Americas: "goldenrod", Asia: "tomato",
  Europe: "steelblue", Oceania: "orchid" }))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with a palette naming Africa seagreen, Americas goldenrod, Asia tomato, Europe steelblue and Oceania orchid.”
Each continent now takes the color written beside its name, however the rows are ordered. The legend still lists the continents in first-appearance order, with Asia first. Once colors are named, the names and the categories must match. A name that is not a category would color nothing. A category without a name would get a color nobody chose. gog refuses both. Here the palette names only four continents:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c(Africa = "seagreen", Americas = "goldenrod", Asia = "tomato",
            Europe = "steelblue"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette({"Africa": "seagreen", "Americas": "goldenrod", "Asia": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue"}))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["Africa" => "seagreen", "Americas" => "goldenrod", "Asia" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette({ Africa: "seagreen", Americas: "goldenrod", Asia: "tomato",
  Europe: "steelblue" }))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` names colors for levels of `continent` and leaves out "Oceania". Once colors are named, every level drawn needs one, or it would be drawn in a color nobody chose. Give it a color too, or pass the colors without names to hand them out in the column's order.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the category it leaves out, Oceania, and offers two fixes: give Oceania a color too, or pass the colors without names.
A palette that names all five continents is also refused on a table that holds only three, unless the column’s declared order includes all five. A misspelled name is refused the same way:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c(Africa = "seagreen", Americas = "goldenrod", Asai = "tomato",
            Europe = "steelblue", Oceania = "orchid"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette({"Africa": "seagreen", "Americas": "goldenrod", "Asai": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue", "Oceania": "orchid"}))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["Africa" => "seagreen", "Americas" => "goldenrod", "Asai" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue", "Oceania" => "orchid"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette({ Africa: "seagreen", Americas: "goldenrod", Asai: "tomato",
  Europe: "steelblue", Oceania: "orchid" }))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` names "Asai", and `continent` has no category called that, so its color would go to nothing. Did you mean "Asia"? The categories of `continent` are "Asia", "Europe", "Africa", "Americas", and "Oceania".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests the category you probably meant.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.9 Legend placement
Every plot above that maps a refining channel drew a legend automatically, to the right of the panel. gog shrinks the panel to make room, so there is no margin to set. To move all of a plot’s legends to another side, write theme(legend = ) with "bottom", "top" or "left". Here the continent legend is below the panel:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(legend = "bottom") + title("Legend below the panel")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(legend = "bottom") + title("Legend below the panel"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  theme(legend = "bottom") + title("Legend below the panel")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), theme({ legend: "bottom" }),
  title("Legend below the panel"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Legend below the panel Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with the legend at the bottom.”
Above or below the panel, a legend’s entries are placed side by side, as the five continents are here. They continue on a new line when the plot is too narrow, and the panel then gets shorter instead of narrower. The legend of a continuous color is drawn horizontally there, with the smallest value on the left. A legend too big for the plot is left out rather than drawn outside the image. gog says so, and names the theme() width or height that would give it room.

23.9.1 Leaving a legend out
A legend decodes a channel, and sometimes an axis already shows the same column. Here color and x map the same column, so the axis already names the continent under every bar. A legend would repeat those names. Write legend = FALSE on the channel and the legend is left out:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  color(continent, legend = FALSE)


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  color(col.continent, legend = False))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  color(:continent, legend = false)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  color(col.continent, { legend: false }))






                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, color by continent, without a legend.”
The bars keep their colors, because the channel still maps the column. Only the legend is gone, and the panel takes the legend’s space. legend belongs to the five refining channels, the ones that draw a legend. x, y and z are read from their axes, and group, label and play draw no legend. gog refuses legend on all six:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent, legend = FALSE)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent, legend = False)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent, legend = false)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count),
  x(col.continent, { legend: false }))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent)` is given `legend` — `x` is read off its axis, so there is no legend to show or leave out. `legend` belongs on the five channels that draw one: `color`, `size`, `shape`, `pattern` and `opacity`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the five channels that draw a legend.
A legend is one kind of guide, the part of a plot that decodes a channel (Grammar). A position’s guide is its axis, and axis = FALSE on the position leaves it out, as Scales shows.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.10 In short
A channel takes a column, never a value: gog refuses color("red") and points to style(). The five refining channels get a legend, and x, y and z get an axis; legend = FALSE and axis = FALSE leave them out. group and label get neither, and play gets a strip that names the frame. A mark’s geometry decides which channels it accepts. palette() chooses the colors: a categorical palette for a categorical column, a ramp for a continuous one.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.11 What comes next
Every channel here reads a column, so every plot answers a question about the data. Setting vs mapping covers the opposite case: a value you choose yourself, which reads no column and gets no legend.

Munzner, T. (2014). Visualization analysis and design. CRC Press.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.1 Why a constant is not a channel
Should a mark’s color come from your data, or from you? There are two ways to make something red, and gog keeps them apart on purpose.
Mapping lets the data decide a visual property. color(continent) says let the continent decide the color, so gog builds a scale, assigns a color per continent, and draws a legend to decode it.
Setting means you give the property a value yourself. style(color = "tomato") says make them all tomato. No column is read, no scale is built, and no legend appears, because there is nothing to decode.
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored tomato.”
Every channel in gog maps a data column to a visual property. A constant maps nothing, so it does not meet the definition. The same definition settles a question that comes up with 3-D plots: is the viewing angle a channel? It is not, because no column sets the angle. The angle is a property of the coordinate space, as The viewing angle shows.
A practical test gives the same answer: a mapping to color, size, shape, pattern or opacity draws a legend, and a setting draws none. If the plot needs a legend to be read, it was a mapping. A mapping written with legend = FALSE leaves its legend out, so a plot with no legend can still use a mapping. Here color(continent) is a mapping, and the x axis already names each continent, so the legend is left out:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) +
  color(continent, legend = FALSE) + title("Mapped, with no legend")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent, legend = False) + title("Mapped, with no legend"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent, legend = false) + title("Mapped, with no legend")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent, { legend: false }),
  title("Mapped, with no legend"))






                                                                                                                                                                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Mapped, with no legend Life Continent
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life, color by continent, without a legend.”

Those rows are every setting there is. x, y, z, group, label and play are absent because they are channels and nothing else, which Two questions, not one explains.
color (a CSS name or a hex value) and opacity (0–1) can be set on every mark. The other rows follow from each mark’s geometry rather than from a list someone chose. A setting is available on every mark whose geometry can carry it, and it behaves the same way on all of them. That is the settable rule: a setting covers its whole geometry class, the group of marks drawn with the same kind of shape.
size is a measurement in pixels: a radius, a stroke width, or a font size. It belongs to point, text, every stroke mark, and the lines of a box. The grid marks it — for bar, area, ribbon, zone and surface. Their positions already decide their size, so there is nothing to set. shape chooses one of seven glyphs. Only point takes it.
pattern is the texture of a mark’s paint. It is one property drawn differently by each geometry, the way color is a fill on a bar and a stroke on a line. On the six stroke marks (line, step, path, interval, rule, edge) it is a stroke pattern: "solid"/"dashed"/"dotted"/"dotdash"/"longdash", so an error bar can be dashed too. On the five filled regions (bar, box, area, ribbon, zone) it is a fill texture: "solid"/"hatch"/"crosshatch"/"stripes"/ "grid"/"dots". A surface takes no fill texture: the texture is drawn flat on the screen, so on a tilted sheet it would look denser on some faces than on others. Both kinds keep a plot readable in grayscale or in black-and-white print. pattern changes the paint, never the shape: a dashed line and a solid one pass through the same points. A staircase changes the shape, not the paint, so it is a mark of its own: step holds each value until it changes.
A trend drawn through the data is often dashed, so that it reads as a summary rather than as a measurement:

  style(pattern = "dashed", size = 1.5) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("A dashed trend line")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(line, mean), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  style({ pattern: "dashed", size: 1.5 }),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy"), title("A dashed trend line"))

“Given gapminder Asia: a line derived by mean, x is year, y is life, with pattern dashed and size 1.5.”
On a fill the same setting gives the region a fill texture, which stays visible on a black-and-white photocopy:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  style(pattern = "crosshatch") +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("A crosshatched bar")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  style(pattern = "crosshatch") +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("A crosshatched bar"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(pattern = "crosshatch") + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("A crosshatched bar")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ pattern: "crosshatch" }),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy"), title("A crosshatched bar"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  A crosshatched bar Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, with pattern crosshatch.”
The texture is one per layer: style() gives every bar in the layer the same texture. It cannot give each category its own texture. That is a mapping (a category to a texture), and the pattern() channel does it for fills and strokes the way shape() does it for points.
border_color and border_size draw an outline separate from the fill. A border_size of 0 means no border. Both belong to the five closed-shape fills (bar, box, point, zone and surface). On those marks you cannot draw the outline as a second layer. A setting is the only way to get it. color fills the shape; border_color outlines it; the two are independent, so a box can be pale inside and dark-edged:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) +
  style(color = "lightsteelblue", border_color = "#26456e", border_size = 1.6) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("A box: light fill, dark outline")


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "lightsteelblue", border_color = "#26456e", border_size = 1.6) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("A box: light fill, dark outline"))


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "lightsteelblue", border_color = "#26456e", border_size = 1.6) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("A box: light fill, dark outline")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "lightsteelblue", border_color: "#26456e",
  border_size: 1.6 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("A box: light fill, dark outline"))






                                                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  A box: light fill, dark outline Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life, colored lightsteelblue, with border color #26456e and border size 1.6.”
The same two settings outline a point, exactly as on bar and box, so each point stays visible where points overlap:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.7, size = 5, border_color = "white", border_size = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A point with a white border")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.7, size = 5, border_color = "white", border_size = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A point with a white border"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.7, size = 5, border_color = "white", border_size = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A point with a white border")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.7, size: 5,
  border_color: "white", border_size: 1 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("A point with a white border"))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  A point with a white border Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored steelblue, with opacity 0.7, size 5, border color white and border size 1.”
opacity fades what color paints, which here is the fill. The white outline stays fully opaque. To make an outline partly transparent, put the transparency in border_color: in "#4682b44d", the last two hex digits make steelblue 30% opaque. Transparency in a hex value shows how to find those two digits for any opacity.
On text, the same two settings draw a halo, a band of color under the letters. The Text chapter shows one.
A curve fill (area, ribbon) takes no border. Its edge is a data curve, so you draw it as a line layer (area + line, line * bounds), and a line can be dashed, which a border cannot. And a cross point has no fill to outline, so a border on a cross-shaped glyph has nothing to draw on, and gog refuses it. The message offers fixes: color the cross with style(color = ) and draw it larger and thicker with style(size = ), or choose a glyph with a fill, such as style(shape = "circle"). When shape is mapped to a column, the categories drawn as crosses go without a border, and gog prints a message that names them.
If you set border_size without border_color, gog chooses the outline’s color in one of three ways. A bar, a box or a surface draws the outline in the color of its fill. In a histogram the outline is drawn in the panel’s background color instead. It separates one bar from the next, as The panel’s background shows. A zone’s outline and a halo on text are drawn in that background color too. A point draws no line around itself, so its outline is a fixed dark gray.
The last seven rows of the grid above each control one part of a mark’s drawing. caps shows or hides the caps at the ends of a whisker, on an interval and a box. center shows or hides an interval’s center dot. nudge moves a text label off its position. arrow draws an arrowhead at one end, or both ends, of a path or an edge. reach says how far a rule reaches across the panel. And angle turns the labels of a text layer by a number of degrees (Turning a label). gap sets how much of the slot of a bar, a box or a zone is left empty (The gap beside each bar). A row has a ✓︎ under every mark that has the part its setting controls. For caps that part is a whisker; for arrow, a start and an end that come from the data.
A line shows why arrow does not belong to it. An arrowhead marks the direction the data runs in. A line over two continuous columns sorts its vertices by x, so its last point is simply the largest x in the table, not the last row, and an arrowhead there would mark the largest x rather than the end of the data. A path joins the rows in the order the table holds them, so each country’s path ends at its last row, 2007, and the arrowhead marks where the data ends:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each path ends at 2007")


(data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each path ends at 2007"))


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:country) +
  style(arrow = "end") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Each path ends at 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), path, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.country), style({ arrow: "end" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Each path ends at 2007"))






                                          0 10K 20K 30K   40 50 60 70 80  Each path ends at 2007 Life expectancy GDP per person  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow end.”
It takes "end", "start" or "both", not true or false. Arrowheads at both ends are often wanted, and a true-or-false value would need a second setting for them.

24.2.1 One color, any mark
Having set a point’s color once, you should not need a second spelling for a line or a bar.
style(color = ) is the same instruction whichever mark it attaches to. It fills points and bars, and it colors the stroke of a line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "red") +
  title("point")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "red") +
  title("point"))

  title("point")

  style({ color: "red" }), title("point"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored red.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(color = "red") +
  title("line")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  style(color = "red") +
  title("line"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(color = "red") + title("line")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ color: "red" }), title("line"))

  To fix one value for the whole layer instead — no legend, nothing to decode — that is a setting: `style(color = "red")`.


color() takes a column. "red" in quotes is a value, so gog refuses it; color(red) without quotes would map a column called red. The message offers the setting instead: style(color = "red") gives every point one color, with no legend. Setting a value and mapping a column are different requests, and gog makes you say which one you mean.


24.2.2 Several at once
A figure for publication rarely needs only one setting. Color, opacity, size and shape are decided together, so they are written together:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  style(color = "#2a6f97", opacity = 0.45, size = 7, shape = "diamond")

  style(color = "#2a6f97", opacity = 0.45, size = 7, shape = "diamond")

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored #2a6f97, with opacity 0.45, size 7 and shape diamond.”
One style() call carries as many settings as the mark can take, and every row in the layer is drawn with all of them. The four here are independent: remove any one and the other three are unchanged. Each mark’s chapter lists its settings in a section called What you can set, starting with Point.


24.2.3 CSS colors
A color usually comes as a hex value copied from a design document, or as a name remembered from another tool. Not every name you remember is one gog knows.
A name from CSS, the language web pages are styled with, and a hex value both work anywhere a color is accepted, in style() and in palette():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  style(color = "darkslateblue") +
  title("A CSS color name")

  style(color = "darkslateblue") +
  title("A CSS color name"))


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  style(color = "darkslateblue") + title("A CSS color name")

  style({ color: "darkslateblue" }), title("A CSS color name"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, colored darkslateblue.”
gog refuses a name it does not recognize and offers the closest valid one, instead of passing it on to be painted black:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + style(color = "stelblue")


data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + style(color = "stelblue")


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + style(color = "stelblue")


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  style({ color: "stelblue" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(color = "stelblue")` is not a color. Did you mean "steelblue"? Use a CSS color name, or a hex value like "#4e79a7".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


R users often assume R color names are CSS color names. They are not. R’s colors() includes numbered shades (gray80, gray50, steelblue3) that CSS does not have. gog uses CSS colors because that is what SVG accepts and what the other three bindings use too, so the vocabulary is the same in every language:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + style(color = "gray80")


data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + style(color = "gray80")


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + style(color = "gray80")


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  style({ color: "gray80" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(color = "gray80")` is not a color. `gray80` is an R color name. gog uses CSS colors, which have no numbered shades — use "lightgray", "darkgray", or "gray", or a hex value like "#cccccc" for an exact shade.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names three CSS grays to use instead, "lightgray", "darkgray" and "gray". For an exact shade it suggests a hex value, such as "#cccccc".


24.2.4 Transparency in a hex value
A color can be partly transparent, and for a border that is the only way to fade it, because opacity fades only the fill. The transparency is two more digits at the end of a hex value, so this section first shows how to read the six digits before them.
A hex value is # followed by six digits in base 16. Hex is short for hexadecimal, which means base 16. Its sixteen digits are 0 to 9, then a to f for 10 to 15. The six digits are three pairs, one each for red, green and blue. In a pair, the first digit counts sixteens and the second counts ones, so b4 is 11 × 16 + 4, or 180. Each pair runs from 00, none of that color, to ff, which is 255, the full amount. Steelblue is #4682b4: red 46, green 82 and blue b4.
Two more digits, written after the six, set how opaque the color is. They run from 00, fully transparent, to ff, fully opaque. To turn an opacity into two digits, multiply it by 255 and round the result. For 30%, 0.3 × 255 is 76.5, which rounds up to 77. That is 4 × 16 + 13, so in base 16 it is 4d, and #4682b44d is steelblue at 30% opacity. These are the two digits for some common opacities:



Opacity

100%

A hollow point shows it most clearly. With color = "none" it has no fill, so only its border is drawn, and the border’s color is the only place for the transparency:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

   style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b4", size = 4) +
   title("border_color = \"#4682b4\"")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 4) +
     title("border_color = \"#4682b44d\""))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
   style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b4", size = 4) +
   title("border_color = \"#4682b4\"")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
     style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 4) +
     title("border_color = \"#4682b44d\"")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b4", size = 4) +
  title("border_color = \"#4682b4\"")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 4) +
  title("border_color = \"#4682b44d\""))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "none", border_color: "#4682b4", size: 4 }),
  title("border_color = \"#4682b4\"")),

On the right, every outline is drawn at 30% opacity, so each point is lighter but still visible. The Point chapter draws the same border on all 1,704 rows of gm_all, where many faint outlines add up to a darker area.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.4 Two questions, not one
A mapped opacity works on a point. Try the same binding on a line and gog refuses it.
A line takes one width and one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row, so on a line you cannot map a column to size or opacity (Line says why):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + group(country) + opacity(life)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + line + group(col.country) + opacity(col.life)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  opacity(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), opacity(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `line` — a line takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `life` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names one fix: set one value for every line with style(opacity = ).
But the line still has a width and an opacity. Those are settings, one value for the whole layer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.5) +
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.5) +
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.5) +
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ size: 4, opacity: 0.5 }),
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity"))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Set on a line: one width, one opacity Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, with size 4 and opacity 0.5.”
This is where the distinction matters most. “Can a column be mapped here?” and “Does this mark have this property?” are different questions, and line is where the answers differ.
Each mark has an answer to both questions. Five properties are a channel and a setting under the same name, and the table shows, for each mark, whether it can map them, set them, or both:











Mark
color

A cell that reads “set only” means the mark has the property, but one value for the whole layer, not one per row: a line has one width, and a rule layer one opacity. Bind a column there and the refusal explains that, and names the setting to write instead. Where a mark maps a property from one kind of column only, the cell says which. area and bar map color from a category, one color for each region or bar, while line and point map it from a category or a number. Every mark that maps opacity or size maps it from a number.
The table above has a column for five of the kernel’s eleven channels. The other six, x, y, z, group, label and play, are only ever mapped, and they have no row on the settings grid either. Positions, groups, labels and the steps of an animation come from data, or they do not exist at all. There is nothing to set. Nine settings are only ever set, and never appear on the channel grid. border_color, border_size, caps, center, nudge, angle, arrow, reach and gap read no column.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.5 Mapping and setting the same property
text:
24.5 Mapping and setting the same property
It is easy to write both by accident: a color(continent) left from an earlier draft, and a style(color = ) added to try one shade.
gog never discards one of the two instructions in silence, so it refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + style(color = "tomato")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + style(color = "tomato"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  style(color = "tomato")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), style({ color: "tomato" }))




Error:
! gog: `color(continent)` maps color and `style(color = "tomato")` sets it — one layer cannot do both. Keep `color(continent)` to show the data, or `style(color = "tomato")` to fix every point at one value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names both fixes: keep color(continent) to show the continents, or style(color = "tomato") to give every point one color.
A mapping can also be one you did not write. A heatmap drawn with zone * bin colors each cell by the number of rows in it. Its sentence has no color(). That color is still a mapping, so the sentence cannot also set a color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + zone * bin + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "black")


data(gapminder_2007) + zone * bin + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color = "black")


data(gapminder_2007) + zone * bin + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "black")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(zone, bin), x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "black" }))




Error:
! gog: `zone * bin` maps color to its `count` by itself, and `style(color = "black")` sets it — one layer cannot do both. Drop `style(color = "black")` to keep the `count` colors, and give `palette()` the colors you want them drawn in.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


To draw the counts in other colors, keep the mapping and choose its colors with palette().

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.6 style and the layer it follows
text:
24.6 style and the layer it follows
A trend line is easiest to see when the points under it are faint and the line is not, so the two layers need different settings.
color() written before any mark applies to every layer that can take it. style() attaches to the nearest mark before it, and to no other mark, because a setting written for one layer should not change another:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  line * smooth +
  point + style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Only the points are tomato")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  line * smooth +
  point + style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Only the points are tomato"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + line * smooth + point +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Only the points are tomato")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), layer(line, smooth),
  point, style({ color: "tomato", opacity: 0.4 }),
  title("Only the points are tomato"))






                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Only the points are tomato Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, a line derived by smooth, and also points, colored tomato, with opacity 0.4.”
To style both layers, write a style() after each mark.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.7 palette: choosing the colors a mapping uses
text:
24.7 palette: choosing the colors a mapping uses
Setting a color and mapping a column are the two choices this chapter has kept apart. Sometimes you want part of each: the continents separated by color, and those five colors chosen by you rather than by gog.
style(color = ) is written instead of a mapping. palette() keeps the mapping and chooses which colors the categories receive:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c("tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette(["tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette(["tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"]))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with a palette of tomato, steelblue, seagreen, goldenrod and orchid.”
A palette needs a mapping to give its colors to. With no column bound to color it has nothing to color, so it is refused rather than accepted and then ignored:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + palette("okabe")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + palette("okabe")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + palette("okabe")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  palette("okabe"))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` chooses the colors a `color` mapping hands out, and nothing here maps `color`, so it would have no effect. Bind a column with `color(<column>)` to use it — or, to paint every mark one color, that is a setting rather than a palette: `style(color = "…")`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two fixes, because there are two things you may have meant. To give each category its own color, bind a column, here color(continent). To paint every mark one color, write a setting, such as style(color = "steelblue"), rather than a palette.
The heatmap in Mapping and setting the same property has a color mapping you did not write, and so does a zone * density (Zone). palette() works on both.
One color, though, is not a palette. palette() takes either a palette name ("gog", "okabe") or the colors themselves, and it reads a single word as a palette name. "red" is not a palette name, so gog refuses it rather than quietly using the default palette:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette("red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette("red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("red"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("red")` is not a known palette. Named palettes are gog, okabe, soft for categories; blue, viridis, magma, inferno, plasma, cividis, gray for continuous columns; blue_red, brown_teal for continuous columns that diverge from a center. `"red"` is a color, not a palette. To paint every mark one color use `style(color = "red")`; to give each category its own color, give `palette()` several colors, "red" among them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Making everything one color is setting, not choosing a palette. The message lists the palette names and offers two fixes: style(color = "red") to paint every mark red, or several colors in palette(), "red" among them, to give each continent its own color.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.8 theme: settings that belong to no mark
text:
24.8 theme: settings that belong to no mark
The gridlines distract on a slide. You want the category names along the bottom at 45 degrees.
style() sets a mark’s own appearance. The gridlines, the shape of the panel and the angle of the tick labels belong to no mark, so they have a word of their own: theme().


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                    1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
The gridlines are gone, and nothing about the points changed, because theme() never changes a mark.
grid names each set of gridlines by the axis whose ticks they mark, not by the direction they run. So "x" keeps the lines belonging to the x axis and removes the rest. That naming is the same when the plane is bent into a circle. The next plot keeps the x axis gridlines in polar, a space later in the book. They radiate from the center instead of running from bottom to top:



winds: first 5 of 264 rows
