RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar() + theme(grid = "x")


data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction) + polar() + theme(grid = "x")


data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction) + polar() + theme(grid = "x")


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction), polar(),
  theme({ grid: "x" }))






                         N NE E SE S SW W NW   20 40 60  Count Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction, in polar.”
ratio sets the panel’s width divided by its height. The image keeps the size it was given and the panel shrinks inside it, so the plot still takes the same room on a page. The four plots below draw the same points at four ratios, from a panel twice as wide as it is tall to one twice as tall as it is wide:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
    theme(ratio = 2) + title("ratio = 2")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
      theme(ratio = 1.5) + title("ratio = 1.5"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
      theme(ratio = 1) + title("ratio = 1")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
        theme(ratio = 0.5) + title("ratio = 0.5")))


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
    theme(ratio = 2) + title("ratio = 2")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
      theme(ratio = 1.5) + title("ratio = 1.5"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
      theme(ratio = 1) + title("ratio = 1")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
        theme(ratio = 0.5) + title("ratio = 0.5"))))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(ratio = 2) + title("ratio = 2")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(ratio = 1.5) + title("ratio = 1.5"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(ratio = 1) + title("ratio = 1")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(ratio = 0.5) + title("ratio = 0.5")))


below(beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point,
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), theme({ ratio: 2 }),
  title("ratio = 2")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ ratio: 1.5 }), title("ratio = 1.5"))),
  beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ ratio: 1 }), title("ratio = 1")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ ratio: 0.5 }), title("ratio = 0.5"))))






                                                                                                                                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  ratio = 2 Life Gdp


                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  ratio = 1.5 Life Gdp


                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  ratio = 1 Life Gdp


                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  ratio = 0.5 Life Gdp






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with ratio 2, beside the same with ratio 1.5; above the same with a square panel, beside the same with ratio 0.5.”
The four plots draw the same points on the same axes, and only the panel changes. On the wide panels the rise in life expectancy with GDP per person looks gentle, and on the tall one it looks steep. When you compare slopes across plots, draw them at the same ratio.
tick_angle turns the x tick labels to the angle you give, in degrees. You do not need it to keep names apart. When category names do not fit side by side, gog turns them 90 degrees by itself, to read upward. Scales shows what gog does when even turned names do not fit. tick_angle is for choosing the angle yourself. gog keeps the angle you choose, even when fewer names fit at it, and prints a message saying how many are drawn. The bottom margin grows to hold the turned labels, and the axis name is below them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  theme(tick_angle = 45)


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  theme(tick_angle = 45))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  theme(tick_angle = 45)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), theme({ tick_angle: 45 }))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, with the tick labels at 45 degrees.”
axis_label says where an axis’s name is placed. By default each name is centered along its own axis, so the y name is turned through 90 degrees. Ask for "end" and both names move to their axis’s far end and stay horizontal, so nothing on the plot has to be read sideways. It is one property, not one per axis, so the two names never follow different rules:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme(axis_label = "end")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme(axis_label = "end"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme(axis_label = "end")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)"), theme({ axis_label: "end" }))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life expectancy (years) GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the axis names at their ends.”
A legend on the right makes the panel narrower by the legend’s own width. On a narrow figure, such as one column of a journal page, that leaves little room for the data. legend says which side of the plot the legends are on. The default is "right", and the other sides are "left", "top" and "bottom". Above or below the panel, a legend’s entries are placed side by side, so the panel gets shorter instead of narrower:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(legend = "bottom")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(legend = "bottom"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme(legend = "bottom")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), theme({ legend: "bottom" }))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, with the legend at the bottom.”
The panel now takes the width the legend used beside it, and the five continents are listed side by side under the x axis’s name. To leave one legend out instead, write legend = FALSE on its channel (Leaving a legend out).
font_size sets how big the plot’s text is. It is one number, not three. The number itself is the size of a tick label, in pixels. The axis names and the title are a fixed proportion larger. The default of 11 draws tick labels at 11, axis names at 13 and the title at 16. Ask for 16 and those three become 16, 19 and 23:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Bigger text, one number") + theme(font_size = 16)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Bigger text, one number") + theme(font_size = 16))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  title("Bigger text, one number") + theme(font_size = 16)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), title("Bigger text, one number"), theme({ font_size: 16 }))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Bigger text, one number Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with font size 16.”
Look at the margins. They grew with the text, because the room an axis needs is measured from the labels that go in it. Larger text therefore never overlaps the panel.
A smaller number leaves more room for the data in a small figure:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Smaller text, same plot") + theme(font_size = 8)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Smaller text, same plot") + theme(font_size = 8))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  title("Smaller text, same plot") + theme(font_size = 8)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), title("Smaller text, same plot"), theme({ font_size: 8 }))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Smaller text, same plot Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with font size 8.”
One number sets all the text, so one plot never carries three unrelated text sizes. You cannot ask for a bigger title on its own: the title grows only when the tick labels grow.
The number is a measurement in pixels, not a multiplier. font_size = 1.5 is refused, because a number that small is almost always meant as a multiplier:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(font_size = 1.5)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(font_size = 1.5)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + theme(font_size = 1.5)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ font_size: 1.5 }))




Error:
! gog: `theme(font_size = )` is how many pixels a tick label is, not a multiplier, so it needs one number of at least 4. The default is 11, and the axis names and the title are derived from it.


The message asks for a number of pixels of at least 4, and gives the default, 11.
font_size does not name a typeface. The engine measures text with its own table of character widths, so it can lay out a plot with no font installed. It asks for the reader’s system font, and the computer that opens the plot supplies the letters.
A preset is a named bundle of these properties, and you ask for one by its name. You can still change any property in it, so one small change never means writing every property yourself:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  theme("minimal", ratio = 1)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  theme("minimal", ratio = 1))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme("minimal", ratio = 1)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme("minimal", { ratio: 1 }))






                                                                                                                                                                    1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the minimal preset and a square panel.”
gog has three presets: "gog", the default, "minimal" and "bw". "minimal" removes the gridlines, the same as theme(grid = "none"), and ratio = 1 then makes the panel square.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.9 Axes, legends, gridlines and the frame
text:
24.9 Axes, legends, gridlines and the frame
A map, a small figure or a slide often needs less around the data than gog draws by default. The settings that leave each part out are explained in different places, so this section collects them in one table. An axis and a legend are guides: each one decodes a channel, so you leave it out inside that channel’s call, as in color(continent, legend = FALSE). The gridlines and the placement of the legends belong to the whole plot, so theme() sets them. theme() also sets the frame: by default, the two lines along the bottom and the left of the panel.



To
Write
Explained in




leave out an axis: its tick marks, its numbers and its name
x(gdp, axis = FALSE)
Scales


leave out only an axis’s name
x_label("")
this section, below


leave out a legend
color(continent, legend = FALSE)
Channels


leave out the gridlines
theme(grid = "none"), or "x" or "y" to keep one set
theme, above


leave out the frame, or draw all four sides
theme(frame = "none"), or "full" for all four sides
this section, below


put the legends on another side
theme(legend = "bottom"), "top" or "left"
theme, above, and Channels



The plot below uses four of them at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life, axis = FALSE) +
  color(continent) + theme(grid = "x", frame = "none", legend = "bottom")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life, axis = False) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(grid = "x", frame = "none", legend = "bottom"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life, axis = false) + color(:continent) +
  theme(grid = "x", frame = "none", legend = "bottom")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life, { axis: false }), color(col.continent),
  theme({ grid: "x", frame: "none", legend: "bottom" }))






                                                                                                                                                             1K 10K    Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life without an axis, color by continent, with the legend at the bottom.”
The y axis is gone, with its numbers and its name, and grid = "x" keeps only the gridlines of the x axis. The panel has no frame, and the legend lists the continents side by side under the x axis’s name. Each point keeps its place among the others, because none of these settings changes the data. With the y axis left out, though, a reader can see which points are higher, but not by how many years. So leave out an axis only when its numbers are not needed, as on a map.
To leave out only an axis’s name, give it an empty one: x_label(""). The tick marks and the numbers stay, so the reader can still read values from the axis.
frame says which sides of the panel get a line, and it takes three values. "axes", the default, draws one line along the bottom and one along the left, where the axes are. "full" draws all four sides, and "none" draws none:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  theme(frame = "full", grid = "y")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  theme(frame = "full", grid = "y"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  theme(frame = "full", grid = "y")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), theme({ frame: "full", grid: "y" }))






                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, with a full frame.”
The panel now has a line on all four sides. It is called frame and not border because style(border_color = ) already uses that word for something else. A border belongs to a mark, such as a bar or a point. A frame surrounds the panel.
A flow whose two columns name one set of places, flow(a, b, shared = TRUE), has two other defaults. It has no numbers to read values from, so its panel has no frame and is white instead of gray. frame and background change both, as on any other plot.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.10 A figure for a journal
A journal often asks for a figure on a white background inside a framed panel.
theme("bw") is the preset most often wanted for publication: a white panel inside a full rectangle.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme("bw")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme("bw"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme("bw")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), theme("bw"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, with the bw preset.”
"bw" stands for black and white, and the name misleads. What becomes black and white is everything around the data, never the data itself. The continents in that plot keep every color the palette gave them. In a “bw” plot only the data carries color, and everything around it is black, white or gray.
The whole preset is three settings, written out below. This sentence draws the same picture theme("bw") just drew:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(background = "white", frame = "full", strip = "white")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(background = "white", frame = "full", strip = "white"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) +
  theme(background = "white", frame = "full", strip = "white")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent),
  theme({ background: "white", frame: "full", strip: "white" }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, with a white background, a full frame and a white strip.”
Here background makes the panel white and frame draws a rectangle around it. frame is explained in the section above, strip in the next section, and background in The panel’s background.
Every preset in gog follows the same rule: a preset only names settings you could have written yourself. A preset that did more than that would be a second set of words to learn.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.11 The strip, and how it prints
text:
24.11 The strip, and how it prints
The third setting inside theme("bw") is strip. It colors the band above each panel, the band that names the category the panel holds. You only see it on a faceted plot, and its color matters more in print than on screen.
By default the band is a light gray. On a screen that is fine, and it shows which panel each name belongs to:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), across(col.continent))






                                                                0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                         0 20K 40K                                                                                 0 20K 40K                                                      0 20K 40K                               0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
On paper it is not fine. A light gray is printed as many tiny black dots, and those dots are directly under small text. The label gets harder to read, and a photocopy makes it worse. This is the same reason pattern exists for fills: what is easy to see on a screen can be hard to see on paper.
So theme("bw") makes the band white as well. The framed panel already separates one panel from the next, so the tint is no longer needed:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) + theme("bw") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) + theme("bw") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme("bw") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), theme("bw"), across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, with the bw preset, split into panel columns by continent.”
You can also name the color yourself, for a poster or a slide where a tint makes the name easier to read rather than harder:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
  theme(strip = "#dce8f0", frame = "full") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
  theme(strip = "#dce8f0", frame = "full") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme(strip = "#dce8f0", frame = "full") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), theme({ strip: "#dce8f0", frame: "full" }),
  across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, with a #dce8f0 strip, split into panel columns by continent.”
An animated plot has the same band (Play, later in the book). It names the moment the animation shows, such as the year, the way a panel band names its category. theme(strip = ) colors that one too. A property that colored one band and not the other would be exactly the kind of exception Law 2 forbids.

24.11.1 The label color on a dark band
Some plots use a dark band on purpose, and that creates one problem: the default label is dark too.
A dark band with light text is often wanted, and you need only one property for it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
  theme(strip = "#22223b", frame = "full") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
  theme(strip = "#22223b", frame = "full") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme(strip = "#22223b", frame = "full") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), theme({ strip: "#22223b", frame: "full" }),
  across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, with a #22223b strip, split into panel columns by continent.”
You did not name a text color, and the text is drawn white. gog reads the band color you asked for. It has two default label colors, and it picks the one that contrasts more with that band. On a pale band the label stays dark, which is why the faceted plots earlier in this chapter have dark labels.
gog chooses the label color because an unreadable name is a defect, not to save you a line of code. Without that rule, theme(strip = "black") would paint the near-black default label onto a black band. Every panel name would be unreadable while the rest of the plot looked correct. So when you do not name a label color, gog chooses a readable one.
When you want a particular label color, and not only a readable one, name it. gog then uses the color you name as written, without checking it against the band:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
  theme(strip = "navy", strip_text = "gold", frame = "full") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
  theme(strip = "navy", strip_text = "gold", frame = "full") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme(strip = "navy", strip_text = "gold", frame = "full") |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life),
  theme({ strip: "navy", strip_text: "gold", frame: "full" }),
  across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, with a navy strip and gold strip text, split into panel columns by continent.”
Every default in gog works this way: it decides what you did not say, and stops deciding as soon as you say it. The engine guarantees the plot is well-formed and leaves taste to you, which is Law 8.
A "transparent" band gives gog no color to read, because it shows whatever is behind it. So the label stays dark, which suits the white page a band is usually drawn on.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.12 The panel’s background
A slide or a journal may need a panel in a color other than gog’s light gray. background colors the panel, and it takes any color the rest of the grammar takes, a CSS name such as linen among them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  theme(background = "linen", frame = "full")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  theme(background = "linen", frame = "full"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(background = "linen", frame = "full")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ background: "linen", frame: "full" }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with a linen background.”
A histogram’s bars touch, so gog outlines each bar with a thin line in the panel’s color. The line takes the background’s color, so it separates the bars on a panel of any color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  theme(background = "white", frame = "full")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) +
  theme(background = "white", frame = "full"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) +
  theme(background = "white", frame = "full")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  theme({ background: "white", frame: "full" }))






                                      50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Count Life





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, with a white background.”
The same line separates the cells of a treemap. It also separates the parts of a stack that group splits, when they all share one color.
"transparent" is the one value that changes more than the panel. If only the panel were transparent, the margin around it would still be painted. So "transparent" also leaves the margin and the legend’s box unpainted, and the page under the figure shows through. A journal often asks for this, because it prints the figure on a page whose color gog does not know. A transparent panel has no color for the line between touching bars to take, so that line stays gog’s light gray.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.13 What theme() refuses
theme() checks every name you give it, and refuses one it does not know rather than ignoring it. For theme("dark"), the message names the presets gog has, "gog", "minimal" and "bw":


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme("dark")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme("dark")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + theme("dark")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), theme("dark"))




Error:
! gog: `theme("dark")` is not a theme. gog has `gog`, `minimal`, or `bw`. A theme is a named preset you can then adjust — `theme("minimal", ratio = 1)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The gridlines are named by their axis, "x" or "y", and not by the direction they run, so grid = "vertical" is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(grid = "vertical")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(grid = "vertical")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(grid = "vertical")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ grid: "vertical" }))




Error:
! gog: `theme(grid = )` is one of "both", "x", "y" or "none".


The message lists the four values grid takes, "both", "x", "y" and "none".

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.14 style and theme
style() and theme() differ in what they belong to. style() belongs to a mark, and a plot with three layers can carry three different ones. theme() belongs to the whole plot, and there is only one of it: no single layer has gridlines or a background of its own. The two never set the same property, and that is why they are two words rather than one.
Text size shows the split best: both atoms have a size setting, but each sets the size of different text. style(size = 17) on a text layer sets how big those labels are, and they are labels that come from a column. theme(font_size = 16) sets how big the tick labels, the axis names and the title are, and those belong to the whole plot. One is a property of a mark and the other is a property of the plot, so neither can replace the other.
gap is the one name both atoms take, and it means a different thing in each. style(gap = 0.2) leaves a fifth of a bar’s slot empty. theme(gap = 8) on an arrangement puts 8 pixels between its plots.
Grouped bars leave a fifth of each bar’s part of the slot empty unless you set gap. style(gap = 0) makes the bars of a group touch. The gm_eras table holds two years, 1957 and 2007, with one row per country in each:

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.15 In short
A mapping to color, size, shape, pattern or opacity gets a legend, and a setting gets none. That is the quickest test for which one you wrote; a mapping with legend = FALSE also has none. Five names are a channel and a setting at once: color, size, shape, pattern and opacity. Which call you write decides which you get.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.16 What comes next
A setting changes how a mark looks and computes nothing from the rows. Transforms shows how gog derives values the table does not hold: counts, means, bins, densities, and the low and high values an interval needs.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.1 One variable, or two?
How do you plot a number your table does not hold? A transform computes it for you and hands the result to a mark. It runs after the table is read and before anything is drawn, and the mark stays what it is: bar * bin still draws bars.
The family has other names. ggplot2 says stat, and the chapter Wilkinson devotes to it says statistics (Wilkinson, 2005); SQL says aggregate, dplyr says summarize, a spreadsheet says pivot. Each of those covers about half of what gog groups here. mean, count and density really are statistics, and they replace rows with a summary. But bin cuts an axis into cells. bounds reshapes two columns you already have and computes nothing at all. stack, dodge, jitter and repel are about collisions between marks rather than about the values behind them. Calling all of that a statistic would misname most of it, so the word here is the most general one that is still accurate: a transform is anything that changes what reaches the mark.
Transforms are applied with the * operator:
The result is the same mark drawing derived values, not a new atom to memorize.
The middle six (sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile) form the aggregation family. All share the same pattern: group by x, reduce y to one value. range, confidence and deviation group the same way but write a low and a high, the extents an interval spans. smooth_band and straight_band write the same pair along a fitted curve and a fitted line. These five and bounds, which comes later in this chapter, are the pair transforms.
Some transforms write their result into a new column, such as count or name, that your table never held. A sentence can name that column, and Columns a transform writes lists every one.
Grouping the transforms by what they compute is not the only useful way to sort them. Seventeen of them also fall into two families by how many columns they read, and reading one column or two is what decides whether you write y(). The other ten of the kernel’s twenty-seven transforms come later in this chapter. bounds reshapes rather than computes. partition, flow, layout and cluster each compute a whole picture, such as a mosaic or a network. dodge, stack, jitter and repel move marks that would otherwise overlap. cumulative adds up a measurement that another transform or a column supplies.
Counting transforms (bin, count, density) supply their own measurement: no column of your table holds it. Given a single variable, they show how its rows are spread. bin and count tally the rows in each bin or category. density estimates the same spread as a smooth curve, whose height is a density rather than a number of rows. proportion joins them when no other transform is written with it, because then the only measurement it has to rescale is the tally it computes itself. You name only the variable whose shape you are asking about, and the transform writes the y column and labels its axis (“Count”, “Proportion”, “Density”). bar * bin + x(life) and line * density + x(life) are the same grammatical shape: one name in, a new axis out. Leaving out y() here is not a mistake. There is exactly one sensible y, the count or the density, and the engine supplies it. If you name a column of the table on that axis, as in bar * count + x(continent) + y(life), gog refuses it, because the transform would never read that column. gog refuses any name except the transform’s own (The name on a measure axis).
Reading transforms (smooth, straight, sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band) read two columns and summarize the second as it varies with the first. They fit or aggregate an existing y, so you must bind one: without y(gold), bar * mean + x(country) has no way to guess which column to average. Leave y() off and the engine does not guess: only you know which column was meant, so it stops and names what is missing (add y(<column>)). range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band and straight_band are the five that read a y like the others but write more than one: range a low and a high, the other four a low, high and center.
Side by side, two sentences, one from each family, differ by one y(). The count sentence names only continent, and count writes its own y column. The mean sentence needs y(life) to know which column to average:

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, beside bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
The left y axis reads Count, the column count writes. The right one reads Life, the column you named.
So whether you write y() is not an arbitrary rule to memorize for each transform. The family a transform belongs to decides it. This is one instance of Explicit Over Implicit: the short form is allowed exactly when it cannot be misread, and refused when it could.
Both families replace your rows with a summary of them, and this chapter calls any transform that does so a statistic. A statistic runs within each group when a channel that splits the rows into groups is bound: color, group, pattern or shape. bar * bin + color(species) draws one histogram per species, not one combined bar that has discarded the split (see overlaid histograms). The same rule gives a density curve, a count, or a mean per group. Each output row keeps the group it came from. The mark colors it by that group, and the legend lists the same groups.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.2 bin: histogram
The first question to ask of one continuous column is how its values are spread. Where are they dense, where are they sparse, and is there one peak or two?
bin is the first counting transform. It cuts x into equal-width bins and counts the rows in each. Combine it with bar to draw a histogram:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007"))






                                       50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Histogram of life expectancy, 2007 Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life.”
bin is not the bar’s own transform. Four other marks cut the same bins, and only the shape changes:







Mark derived by bin
Shape




point * bin
one dot at the top of each bin


line * bin
the frequency polygon: straight lines through the bin centers


area * bin
the same polygon, filled to the baseline


step * bin
the staircase outline


bar * bin
filled bars, the histogram above



zone * bin cuts two axes instead of one, which is the heatmap, and surface * bin raises the same cells into the cube.
Bin count defaults to Sturges’ rule (Sturges, 1926): k = ⌈log₂(n)⌉ + 1, where n is the number of rows and k the number of bins. In words, each time the number of rows doubles, the histogram gets one more bin. Notice there is no y() in the sentence: bin writes the count column itself, and the y axis is labeled “Count” automatically.

25.2.1 Choosing the bin count
A histogram’s shape depends on how it is cut, and the default cut may hide a gap or split a peak. You will often want a finer cut, or bins whose width means something in the data’s units.
Sturges’ rule is a sensible default, not a mandate. Pass a number to set the bin count, or name a width to fix the bin width in the data’s own units:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(30)), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram"))






                                                             40 50 60 70 80   0 5 10 15  Thirty bins: a finer histogram Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin into 30, x is life.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin({ width: 5 })), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("Bins five years wide"))






                                            40 50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30 40  Bins five years wide Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life.”
The positional number is the count: bin(30) is thirty bins. A width is the less common request, so it is said out loud, bin(width = 5); the two are mutually exclusive. gog refuses bin(30, width = 5) rather than guess which one you meant, and the message shows bin(30) for a count and bin(width = 5) for a width. For the same reason a bare number always means a count: on this data, five bins and bins five years wide are very different plots.
A width also decides where the bins start: every edge is a multiple of the width. The five-year bins above therefore run from 35 to 40, from 40 to 45, and so on, not from the smallest value, 39.6. Where the bin edges fall explains why, and how ggplot2 places its edges instead.


25.2.2 Choosing a width
When you give a count of bins, you decide only how much detail to show: bin(20) draws fewer, wider bars than bin(30) on any column. When you give a width, you decide more, because a width is measured in the column’s own units. Use a width when each bin should cover a span that means something, such as five years of life expectancy or half a centimeter of petal length. Because every edge is a multiple of the width, two histograms cut at the same width share their edges, even when their data cover different ranges. You can then compare them bin by bin.
To choose a width, first decide roughly how many bars you want. Divide the column’s range, its largest value minus its smallest, by that number. Then take a nearby round number in the column’s units, such as 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 or 10. Life expectancy runs from 39.6 to 82.6 years, a range of 43. Ten bars would each be 4.3 years wide, and the nearest round number is 5.
One more rule prevents tall bars and empty bins that come from the cut rather than from the data. The width should be a whole multiple of the distance between two neighboring values the column can hold. quakes_fiji holds a thousand earthquakes near Fiji, and it records each magnitude to one decimal place, so its possible values are 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and so on, 0.1 apart:

The bar from 4.5 to 4.75 is far taller than the bars on either side. It holds 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7, while each neighbor holds two: 4.3 and 4.4 before it, 4.8 and 4.9 after it. A width of 0.2 puts two possible values in every bin, and the shape is smooth:

“Given quakes Fiji: bars derived by bin at width 0.2, x is magnitude.”
The same rule applies when you give a number of bins, because the number sets the width. Suppose a column holds whole numbers from 9 to 35, so only 27 values are possible. Thirty bins are each 0.87 wide, and at least three must stay empty. For one bar per value, use bar * count, which counts the rows at each value instead of binning them.
Two kinds of axis treat a width differently. A time axis refuses a width, as What a time axis refuses shows, so give the number of bins there. On a log axis the bins are cut on the logarithms, so a width counts powers of the base. In the default base 10, bin(width = 1) makes bins from 100 to 1,000 and from 1,000 to 10,000. In base 2, each bin ends at twice its start.


25.2.3 Why bar * bin, not a histogram() shortcut?
Because bin does the same computation regardless of the mark, and the mark decides how the bins are drawn. bar * bin fills bars. line * bin connects the bin centers into a frequency polygon, and step * bin traces the histogram as a staircase outline. Add stack and a fourth reading appears, the dot plot further down this chapter: one dot per observation rather than one mark per bin. Adding a histogram() shortcut would violate Law 2 (No Exceptions) by special-casing a particular mark+transform pair.


25.2.4 The same bin, cutting two axes
All twelve gapminder years on one scatter make 1704 points, and where they overlap you cannot see how dense the points are. The answer is to count rows in cells of the plane, not only along one axis.
The mark decides something else too: how many axes get cut. Each mark above leaves one axis free to measure the count along, so bin cuts the other one. A zone measures nothing by length, and it needs an extent on both axes to be a rectangle. So the same word cuts both, and the count goes to color, the only channel left holding a number:

25.2.5 One of each: the mixed mesh
Five continents make five histograms, and comparing five panels is harder than comparing five rows of one picture.
The rule that a zone cuts both axes needs one qualification. What bin cuts is every axis that has a width to cut, and a categorical axis has none: it is already cut, one slot for each category. Give a zone one of each and the transform does the only coherent thing, which is to cut the continuous axis and not the categorical one:

  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut")

Each continent gets a row of cells, and every row is cut on the same edges, so you can compare the continents by reading straight down. It is a distribution per category shown as shade rather than as height, which is why five of them fit where one histogram would go. The Zone chapter explains this plot, the heatmap and the tile plot below with one rule.


25.2.6 Which mesh: tiling
bin also decides the shape of the cells it cuts, because a different mesh puts different rows in different cells and so changes the counts. Rectangles are the default. Hexagons stagger alternate rows, so a reader does not mistake the straight rows of the mesh for a pattern in the data (Carr et al., 1987):

  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex")

  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex"))

  y(:life) + x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex")

  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),

The Zone chapter works through both meshes, including why an empty cell is left unpainted.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.3 count: frequency aggregation
The first question to ask of a categorical column is how many rows fall in each category. A table with one row per country does not hold that number anywhere.
count counts the number of rows for each unique value of x, and it works on both categorical and continuous columns. It is the categorical counterpart to bin: bin groups a continuous column; count groups a categorical one.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# How many countries are in each continent?
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  title("Countries per continent, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”
count is not the bar’s own transform. Five other marks tally the same rows, and only the shape changes:







Mark derived by count
Shape

one dot at each count


line * count
the counts joined into a profile


area * count
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * count
each count held flat across its slot


zone * count

bar * count

Compare these bars with the histogram at the start of the chapter. Histogram bars touch, because the bins are cut from one continuous axis and no value falls between them. Bar chart bars are drawn with a gap between them, because the categories are separate.
Like bin, count writes its own y column and labels the axis “Count”. To title that axis yourself, use y_label().

25.3.1 The same count, tallying two axes
With two categorical columns the question becomes how often each pair occurs, such as how many winds came from the west in winter.
bin cuts one axis on a bar and two on a zone, and count works the same way. A bar has a length to show the tally along, so it groups by one axis; a zone measures nothing by length, so it tallies rows into the cell where two categories cross and the count goes to color:

That is the tile plot (a confusion matrix is the same sentence with different columns), and like the heatmap, no atom was added to the kernel.
Together, bin and count state the whole rule: bin cuts, count tallies. A continuous axis has to be cut into cells before there is anything to count in; a categorical axis is already cut, one slot for each category. So on a zone each is refused where the other belongs, and each refusal names the other.
Taking the two axes one at a time gives three plots, not two. Cut both axes and it is the heatmap; cut neither and it is the tile plot; cut one of two and it is the mixed mesh above. A bin is refused only where there is nothing left for it to cut at all.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.4 proportion: relative frequency
Fifty-two of the 142 countries are in Africa, and that fact reads differently as a count than as a share of the whole.
proportion divides a measurement by its total and writes shares in [0, 1] that sum to 1. In statistics they are called relative frequencies. Used on its own it has nothing to divide yet, so it tallies the rows first exactly as count does:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# What share of countries belongs to each continent?
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("Continent share, 2007"))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  Continent share, 2007 Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent.”
The same six marks read a share as they read a count:







Mark derived by proportion
Shape

one dot at each share


line * proportion
the shares joined into a profile


area * proportion
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * proportion
each share held flat across its slot


zone * proportion
one cell per pair of categories, colored by its share


bar * proportion
one bar per category, the plot above



Use proportion when you care about relative composition rather than raw counts, for example “what fraction of respondents chose each option?” count and proportion differ only by a constant factor, which is the total. So order works the same on both: order(count) after count and order(proportion) after proportion give the same order. Here the bars are horizontal, with the largest share at the top:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  order(proportion, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Continent share, largest first")

  order(col.proportion, desc = True) +
  title("Continent share, largest first"))

  order(:proportion, desc = true) +
  title("Continent share, largest first")

  order(col.proportion, { desc: true }),

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, y is continent, ordered by proportion, largest first.”
To sort by the shares, name the column the transform writes, proportion. A column of numbers from your table, such as gdp, is refused in order() after proportion, as Your table’s columns after a transform explains.
proportion also works on two axes, as count does, so zone * proportion reads a tile plot as shares (see Zone).

25.4.1 The total is the whole plot, always
Once a second column splits the bars, each segment could be a share of its own bar or of the whole plot.
The denominator is every row the plot draws, in every context. proportion never divides by anything else. Split the bars by a second column and they still sum to 1 between them, so each bar reads as this pair’s share of everything:

Add up the sixteen segments there and you get 1, not 2. What you cannot get that way is the conditional reading: “of the summer winds, what share came from the west”. That reading is the facet. It cuts the data into panels before any of this runs, so each panel normalizes inside itself:

Compare the two plots. In the first, summer’s bars and winter’s bars share one total. In the second, each season has its own.


25.4.2 Normalizing something other than a tally
Two histograms from tables of different sizes cannot be compared by their counts, and a continent’s population means more as a share of the world’s.
Because proportion divides whatever measurement it finds, it composes with any transform that leaves one number per cell. Put it after a bin and the histogram’s own counts come back as fractions, the relative-frequency histogram, on exactly the mesh a plain bar * bin cuts:

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20 and proportion, x is life.”
Put it after a summary and each slot reads as its share of the grand total. y(population) still names the column that sum adds up. The axis shows shares, so it is titled Proportion:

  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) +
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population),
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007"))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.2 0.4 0.6  Each continent's share of world population, 2007 Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and proportion, x is continent, y is population.”
proportion writes the shares to a column called proportion, as it does after bin. A text layer with the same two transforms can print each share on its bar:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(continent) + y(population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(col.proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) + text * sum * proportion +
  label(:proportion, decimals = 2) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), layer(text, sum, proportion),
  label(col.proportion, { decimals: 2 }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar"))






                 0.61 0.09 0.15 0.14 0.00                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.2 0.4 0.6  Each continent's share, printed on its bar Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and proportion, x is continent, y is population, and also text derived by sum and proportion, label by proportion with 2 decimal places, with nudge up.”
Asia’s bar is labeled 0.61, about three fifths of the world’s population in 2007. Oceania’s share is 0.0039, so at two decimal places its label reads 0.00.
The text layer’s rows hold two columns. proportion holds each continent’s share, and population still holds the column that sum adds up. So label(population, short = TRUE) prints each continent’s population on its bar, with M for millions and B for billions (a thousand millions), as in Text:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  text * sum * proportion + label(population, short = TRUE) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(col.population, short = True) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) + text * sum * proportion +
  label(:population, short = true) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), layer(text, sum, proportion),
  label(col.population, { short: true }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population"))






                 3.81B 586M 930M 899M 24.5M                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.2 0.4 0.6  Each continent's share, labeled with its population Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and proportion, x is continent, y is population, and also text derived by sum and proportion, label by population written short, with nudge up.”
Asia’s bar reaches 0.61, and its label reads 3.81B, the population of Asia in 2007.
proportion refuses a transform that leaves it nothing to normalize, that is, no total to divide by. A density already integrates to 1, and its cells are sample points rather than parts of a whole. A smooth gives a value at each x, so the sum of those values has no meaning. A pair transform writes a low and a high, which leaves two numbers per cell, and a span is not part of any total:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(life)


data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(col.life)


data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, density, proportion), x(col.life))

For the estimated shape, `line * density + x(<measure>)`; for shares of the rows themselves, cut them into cells first: `bar * bin * proportion + x(<measure>)` is the same curve's histogram, read as fractions.

For line * density * proportion, the message offers two other sentences: line * density + x(life) for the estimated shape, or bar * bin * proportion + x(life) for the same distribution as shares.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.5 density: kernel density estimate
A histogram’s outline changes with every choice of bin, and its steps belong to the bins rather than to the data. A smooth curve describes the same distribution without the steps.
density is the third counting transform: it estimates the same distribution that bin counts, but as a smooth curve. The curve is the probability density function of x, estimated with a Gaussian kernel and computed at 256 evenly spaced places. places changes that number (How many places). By default the bandwidth (how wide each kernel is, and so how smooth the curve) is chosen automatically by Silverman’s rule (Silverman, 1986), which uses the interquartile range so that a few extreme values do not widen it.
Use it with some care. The curve is an estimate, harder to relate back to the rows than a histogram, and it assumes the values are continuous, smooth and unbounded (Wickham, 2016). A column with a floor, such as a count or a life expectancy that cannot go below zero, breaks the last assumption, so the curve can put some density where no value can be. When in doubt, draw the histogram beside it.
Combine it with line to draw a smooth density curve:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))






                               40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007 Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life.”
density is not the line’s own transform. Five other marks estimate the same curve, and only the shape changes:



Mark derived by density
Shape




area * density
the curve filled to the baseline


step * density
the curve as a staircase


point * density
one dot at each point the curve was estimated


bar * density
one thin bar at each of those points


ribbon * density
the curve mirrored, which is the violin


line * density
the curve as a stroke, the plot above



Bind two positions instead of one and density cuts both axes. zone then draws the estimate as cells, path as contour rings, and surface as a sheet.
With one position, as with the other counting transforms, you leave out y(): the transform writes the density column and labels its axis for you.

25.5.1 Choosing the bandwidth
The automatic curve can be smoother than the data supports, hiding a second peak, or rougher, showing bumps that are only noise.
The automatic bandwidth is a sensible default, not a mandate, and it is the parameter you will change most often, as the bin count is for bin. It is set the same two ways. A positional number is an adjust multiplier on the automatic bandwidth: density(2) is twice as smooth, density(0.5) half as smooth and so more jagged.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(2): twice as smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(2): twice as smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("density(2): twice as smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density(2)), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("density(2): twice as smooth"))






                                 20 40 60 80 100   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03  density(2): twice as smooth Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density adjusted by 2, x is life.”
To fix the bandwidth in the data’s own units instead, name it. Here bandwidth = 1 sets each kernel one year wide, narrower than the default, so the curve keeps more of the distribution’s fine structure:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ bandwidth: 1 })),
  x(col.life), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width"))






                                 40 50 60 70 80   0.00 0.02 0.04 0.06  bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density at bandwidth 1, x is life.”
This works exactly as bin does. The positional number is the adjust multiplier: the common request, since you rarely know the bandwidth you want in advance and only need the automatic one a little smoother or rougher. An absolute width is the less common request, so it is said out loud, density(bandwidth = 1). The two are mutually exclusive: density(2, bandwidth = 1) is refused rather than guessed at, and the message shows both forms.


25.5.2 A lowest or highest possible value
A density curve continues past the smallest and the largest value, until it is nearly zero at both ends. For most columns that is what you want. Some columns have a lowest possible value, though: no country’s income is below zero. On gdp, the curve then goes below zero, to incomes that no country has:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.gdp),
  x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero"))






                             0 20K 40K 60K   0.00000 0.00002 0.00004  No lower limit: the curve goes below zero Density GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is gdp.”
Write 0 as the axis’s lower limit and leave the upper one missing, limits = c(0, NA) (limits). The curve then starts at 0, and the estimate is corrected there. density places a bell-shaped kernel on each row. The part of a kernel that would fall below zero is mirrored back above it, so near zero the curve is higher than in the plot above:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(gdp, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.gdp, limits = [0, None]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:gdp, limits = [0, missing]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density),
  x(col.gdp, { limits: [0, null] }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there"))






                                 0 20K 40K 60K   0.00000 0.00002 0.00004 0.00006 0.00008  Lower limit 0: the curve starts there Density GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is gdp from 0.”
The curve is now highest at 0, not near 3,000 dollars. Many of the poorest countries lie within one bandwidth of zero, about 4,100 dollars, so their mirrored parts add the most height there.
An upper limit works the same way: limits = c(NA, 1) on a column of shares stops the curve at 1. Only a limit you write does this. When two composed plots share an axis, the range gog chooses for it does not (The marginal plot).


25.5.3 One transform, four readings
Once you have a curve for one column, you will want the same estimate over two columns, or one curve per category, side by side. Each of those is still density.
density estimates a distribution, and how it is drawn depends on what you bind and on the mark. There are four readings, and they are one transform rather than four transforms sharing a name.
Bind one continuous column and it is a curve over that column, with its height on the other axis, which is everything above. Bind two continuous columns to a mark with no measure axis and it is a field over the plane: zone * density paints it cell by cell, and surface * density raises it into the cube. Cut that field into steps of equal density and it becomes a set of levels: path * density traces their edges as contour lines, and zone * density(levels = 8) fills the bands between them. Bind a category and a continuous column and both axes are taken, so the estimate is drawn across the category’s slot, one distribution per group, which is the violin:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading")


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading"))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * density: the slot reading"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  ribbon * density: the slot reading Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
This plot draws five estimates, one per continent, and all five are smoothed by the same bandwidth. By default it is the average of the bandwidths Silverman’s rule gives each continent on its own. If each continent kept its own bandwidth, Oceania’s two countries would get one about a ninth of Africa’s, and the two shapes would differ partly because of that. With one bandwidth, a difference in shape comes from the data and not from the smoothing. The same sharing applies whenever one layer draws several estimates: curves split by color, the panels of a facet whose axes are shared, and the frames of an animation made with play. adjust multiplies the shared bandwidth, and a stated bandwidth replaces it.
Split the curve by color, and each continent gets its own curve, smoothed by the same shared bandwidth:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("line * density + color: one curve per continent")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("line * density + color: one curve per continent"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) + color(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("line * density + color: one curve per continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("line * density + color: one curve per continent"))






                                 40 60 80   0.00 0.05 0.10 0.15  line * density + color: one curve per continent Density Life expectancy  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: lines derived by density, x is life, color by continent.”
Each curve encloses the same area, so a continent whose countries are close together draws a tall, narrow curve. Oceania’s two countries are one year apart, so its curve is the tallest. With its own, much smaller bandwidth, it would be nearly three times as tall, and the other four curves would be pressed down against the axis.
Some of density’s parameters belong to one reading only, and gog refuses a parameter in a reading where it has no meaning, rather than ignoring it. bandwidth is a length in one column’s units, so it means nothing to a field, whose two axes measure different quantities. levels counts lines of equal density, and a curve has none to count. The slot reading has two parameters of its own. compare says what a violin’s width means from one slot to the next. reach says how far the shape extends, measured in slots, and past half a slot the shapes reach into their neighbors: the ridgeline. Neither means anything to a plot with no slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ compare: "count" })),
  x(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `density(compare = )` says what a violin's width means from one slot to the next, and `line * density` here has no slots — it estimates one curve along one axis. Bind a category to give it slots to compare: `ribbon * density(compare = "count") + x(<category>) + y(<measure>)`. Otherwise drop `compare`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message offers two fixes: bind a category to give the plot slots, as in ribbon * density(compare = "count") + x(continent) + y(life), or drop compare.


25.5.4 How many places: places
A curve on the page is drawn from a list of numbers. gog computes the estimate at evenly spaced places along the axis, and the line joins them. places sets how many. With too few, the line has visible corners. Drawn as points, the places themselves become visible:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(places = 8) + x(life) +
   x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(places = 8)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + point * density(places = 24) +
     x(life) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
     title("density, and density(places = 24) as points"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(places = 8) + x(col.life) +
   x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(places = 8)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + point * density(places = 24) +
     x(col.life) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
     title("density, and density(places = 24) as points")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(places = 8) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(places = 8)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + point * density(places = 24) +
  x(:life) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("density, and density(places = 24) as points"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ places: 8 })),
  x(col.life), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("density(places = 8)")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density),
  layer(point, density({ places: 24 })), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("density, and density(places = 24) as points")))






                                 40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  density(places = 8) Density Life expectancy (years)


                                                         40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  density, and density(places = 24) as points Density Life expectancy (years)






“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density at 8 places, x is life, beside a line derived by density, and also points derived by density at 24 places, x is life.”
The left curve has eight places, so it is seven straight pieces. The right one has the default, 256 places, and its 24 points lie on it. Fewer places give the same estimate, computed at fewer points along the axis.
Every reading takes places, as every reading takes adjust, and each one has its own default. The fitted lines of smooth and straight take it too:









What is computed
Example

At most




curve
