Six sentences, and the same histogram six times. The six are not plots that merely look alike. The engine writes six files, identical byte for byte.
So if the order does not change the picture, why does this book use one order: data, mark, positions, refinements? Because a fixed order lets the code read like an English sentence, with a natural, subject-first shape:

data(...) first. It names the table the columns come from. A bare name like petal_length means nothing until a table is bound (Bind-Once), so the table is named first. The sentence must start here.
The mark and its *-chain second. This is the subject. Nothing is drawn without a mark (Minimum Syllable): bar * mean * dodge says what you are drawing and what was done to it, as one compound word. It is the initial consonant of the block; everything after is said about it.
The positions third. x and y say where the subject is drawn, and a mark cannot be drawn without them (the vowel to the mark’s consonant), so they follow immediately.
The refinements last. color, size, order, labels, title: everything optional. Delete them, together with any modifier that needs one (such as dodge), and a legal plot remains. Delete the mark or a position and nothing is drawn. Writing the removable parts last is also how you build a plot: the minimum sentence first, then refine (First plot).

Only two parts of the order are rules: the sentence starts with a source (data() or query()), and style() follows its mark. The rest is a reading convention: inside one layer, any order draws the same plot. Where you write a channel does matter once a plot has two layers, because a channel written before a mark and one written after it bind differently. Encoding scope gives the rule. Learn one order and use it everywhere. Then your plots and the plots in this book read the same way.
Which orders matter lists what the engine enforces under + and *, and what you are free to arrange.

data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007")


plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era),
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007"))






                                       Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007 Life Continent  Era    1957  2007 





“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”
dodge and color(era) are plainly related: on a bar, dodge has nothing to set side by side until a channel such as color names the groups. So why not write them together? Because the grammar deliberately gives them different operators. dodge belongs to *, because it modifies the mark. The same modifier works on box * dodge and interval * range * dodge. color belongs to +: it binds a column to a channel. color * dodge cannot be written: * needs a mark on its left. Joining the two would make dodge depend on which channel splits the groups, and a modifier must not depend on that.
The place of color(era) in the sentence is the book’s convention, not something dodge asks for. color(era) is optional, so it goes with the refinements, at the end. dodge is optional too, but it needs a channel that splits the bars, here color(era). So you delete the two together: delete both and a legal plot remains, with one bar per continent. You do not have to remember that dodge needs a split, because the engine checks it. Without one, bar * mean * dodge is refused rather than drawn as one bar per continent:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * dodge` has no groups to set side by side — nothing splits the mark. Add `color(<field>)`, `pattern(<field>)`, or `group(<field>)` so there are groups to dodge.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the three channels that can split the bars: color, pattern and group. In a plot with one mark, a channel works wherever it is written, so color can be far from dodge and still split its bars.
Each of the three channels splits the mark into one piece per era, and dodge sets the pieces side by side. Without dodge, the pieces in one slot are drawn over one another. color gives each piece its own color, pattern gives each its own texture, and both draw a legend. group splits the mark and shows nothing more: no color, no texture, no legend. A box, an interval and a bar take all three. A bar takes group only when it is joined to a statistic (such as mean), to dodge or to stack. With no transform, each bar draws one row, so there is nothing to split.
The three sentences below differ only in that channel and in their titles: the top one splits the boxes by color(era), the middle one by pattern(era), and the bottom one by group(era). The theme(height = 900) after the outer parentheses makes the whole arrangement 900 pixels tall, so each plot has room (How big is the arrangement itself?).


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
    title("color(era)")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + pattern(era) +
      title("pattern(era)")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
      title("group(era)"))) +
  theme(height = 900)


(((data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
    title("color(era)")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + pattern(col.era) +
      title("pattern(era)")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + group(col.era) +
      title("group(era)"))) +
  theme(height = 900))


((data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + color(:era) +
  title("color(era)")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  pattern(:era) + title("pattern(era)")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + group(:era) +
  title("group(era)"))) + theme(height = 900)


below(below(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(box, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), title("color(era)")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(box, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  pattern(col.era), title("pattern(era)"))),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(box, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  group(col.era), title("group(era)")), theme({ height: 900 }))






                                                                                              40 60 80  color(era) Life  Era    1957  2007 


                                                                                             40 60 80  pattern(era) Life  Era    1957   2007 


                                                                                               Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  group(era) Life Continent






“Given the gapminder eras: boxes derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era, above the same with pattern by era, above the same grouped by era.”
The boxes are in the same places in all three plots. In the bottom one, every box has the same color, and nothing says which box is 1957 and which is 2007. Use group when another layer already shows the groups. The last plot in Interval has two layers, and both use dodge. The bars are split by color(era) and the error bars by group(era). So each error bar is drawn in black on top of its own bar, and the bars’ legend explains both.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.2 *: derive
A mark on its own draws the rows as they are. A histogram counts them first, and a trend line fits a curve to them first. That computing step needs a word of its own. * joins a transform to a mark, and the result is one compound mark.
bar * bin     # histogram
line * smooth # smoothed trend line
line * density # kernel density curve
* has one rule and one freedom. The mark goes on the left and the transforms go on the right. Among the transforms themselves, any order draws the same plot. The rest of this section explains both.

26.2.1 Why the order is fixed
Start with the rule. In Hangeul, a syllable is always initial consonant + vowel, never the reverse. gog’s * works the same way: the mark is the subject; the transform is what is done to it.
bin * bar is refused, just as ㅏ (a) + ㄱ (g) is not a valid Hangeul syllable. In the right order, ㄱ (g) + ㅏ (a) makes 가 (ga). In the same way, the mark and then the transform make bar * bin:
bar * bin   # a bar mark, derived by binning
gog refuses the other order:

bin * bar

Error in `*.gog_atom`:
! gog: `*` not defined for transform * mark.
Use `*` to combine a mark with a transform, e.g. bar * bin.


The message gives bar * bin as an example of the fix: the mark on the left.


26.2.2 One fixed place, and one free order
The mark is always on the left, and a transform there is refused. That is what makes bar * bin a compound mark rather than a function call. Why +, and not a pipe explains why it lets the atoms stay nouns.
After the mark, the transforms commute, as the mark and channels do under +: any order of them draws the same plot. Here bin and mean are written both ways:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * mean + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   title("bar * bin * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean * bin + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     title("bar * mean * bin"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * mean + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
   title("bar * bin * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean * bin + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
     title("bar * mean * bin")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * mean + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  title("bar * bin * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean * bin + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  title("bar * mean * bin"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, mean), x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life), title("bar * bin * mean")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean, bin), x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life), title("bar * mean * bin")))






                                           10K 20K 30K 40K   0 20 40 60 80  bar * bin * mean Life Gdp


                                    10K 20K 30K 40K    bar * mean * bin Gdp






“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and mean, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by mean and bin, x is gdp, y is life.”
The two plots are identical. The engine does not run the transforms in the order you type them. It finds the order the work needs, and here it runs bin first in both.
The order you write is therefore a matter of style, not a rule. This book writes the transforms in the order they run, so the sentence reads in the same order as the work: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each one.
bin must run first because of what mean needs. A statistic reduces a group to one number. In a continuous column such as gdp, values rarely repeat, so most groups hold one row. The mean of one row is that row’s own value. Ask for the mean of life at each value of gdp, and each group holds one country:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




gog: `point * mean` groups the rows by their value of `gdp`, and here every group holds a single row, so each `mean` is one row's own value. Drawn as asked. To summarize, cut `gdp` into ranges first, `point * bin * mean`, or group by a column whose values repeat.




                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by mean, x is gdp, y is life.”
The picture is the plain scatterplot, and the note printed with it says why: each mean is one row’s own value. bin is what makes the groups, by turning many distinct numbers into one band. So the cut comes first: without it, the mean has nothing to average.
So two transforms work together only when they do different jobs. There are four jobs: saying where the cells are, what is in them, what scale the answer is read on, and where the marks are drawn (Chaining transforms explains each one). A pair that does the same job twice is refused rather than run in sequence. bin and count both count the rows, so the pair below is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(12) * count + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(12) * count + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(12) * count + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(12), count), x(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * bin * count` measures each cell twice — `bin` and `count` each invent their own measurement from the rows, and neither was handed a column to give way to, so there is no reading that keeps both. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * bin` or `bar * count`. To cut an axis into cells and measure something else inside them, the second transform has to be one you hand a column: `bar * bin * mean + x(<measure>) + y(<column>)`. To read either as shares of the whole rather than as counts, `proportion` rescales whichever you keep: `bar * bin * proportion`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names three fixes: keep one of the two (bar * bin or bar * count), measure a column inside the cells (bar * bin * mean, with the column on y), or read the counts as shares (bar * bin * proportion).
The order does not decide a refusal either: bar * count * bin(12) is refused just like the pair above. What cannot be chained, and why shows why a pair is refused, one refusal at a time, and Combinations has the whole grid of pairs.


26.2.3 Live examples
The start of this section listed three compound marks: bar * bin, line * smooth and line * density. You will use them often. Here each one is drawn, so you can see what its transform made from the rows.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Histogram: life expectancy across all countries in 2007
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007"))






                                       50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Distribution of life expectancy, 2007 Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Scatterplot, with a LOESS smooth on top
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth + title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth),
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))






                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Kernel density estimate
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))






                               40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007 Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life.”
In each plot, the compound mark draws what its transform computed rather than the rows. The bars are counts of countries in bands of life expectancy. The line through the points is a fitted curve, and the last line is an estimated density. gapminder_2007 has no count or density column. bin and density compute those numbers and put them on y themselves, so neither sentence needs a y(), and the axes are labeled Count and Density. You can also write y(count) or y(density), in lowercase, to give the axis a setting such as limits. Any other name in y() is refused (Columns a transform writes).

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.3 | and /: facet, or compose
Two questions lead to the last two operators: how the same plot looks for each group, and how two different plots fit in one figure. | puts things side by side and / puts one above the other. What you write on the right decides the job: a facet() splits one plot into panels, and a second plot is placed beside or below the first.
With facet(), | produces small multiples arranged in columns, one panel per category of the column it names.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent))






                                                                0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                         0 20K 40K                                                                                 0 20K 40K                                                      0 20K 40K                               0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
/ stacks the panels in rows instead. The sentence is the same, with / in place of |:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) / facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) / facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) / facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  down(col.continent))






                                                                  40 50 60 70 80                                                                40 50 60 70 80                                                                                      40 50 60 70 80                                                           40 50 60 70 80                                        0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel rows by continent.”
Stacked, the panels line up their x axes, so a value is directly above the same value in the panel below. Side by side, they line up their y axes instead.
Write | and / in one sentence to combine them into a grid. Each operator applies to the facet written after it, read from left to right. See Faceting for when to choose rows or columns, the grid, what the panels share, and why the facet column must be categorical.
With a plot on the right, the same two operators place separate plots in one arrangement, and each plot keeps its own coordinate space:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The plot on the left shows life expectancy on y, and the plot on the right shows a count, so each draws its own vertical axis. Two plots side by side share their y axis when they name the same column on it, with the same scale and limits. The shared axis is drawn once. In the same way, two plots stacked with / that name the same column on x share that axis.
Neither reading is new. The facet reading comes from Trellis display (Becker et al., 1996), and the composition reading from patchwork (Pedersen, 2019), which writes p1 | p2 and p1 / p2 the same way (Where these operators come from).
One pair of operators, two jobs. Composition covers the second.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.4 Which orders matter
This book writes every sentence in the same order: data, mark, positions, refinements. Most of that order is the book’s habit, and the engine draws the same plot if you change it. Only a few parts are rules that the engine enforces. The table below sorts the orderings under + and under * into three kinds, and only one kind needs your attention.









Kind
What it means
Under +
Under *




Free
Either way draws exactly the same picture.
In a plot with one mark: the mark, its positions and its other channels, in any order. Labels go anywhere. Only style() must follow its mark.
The transforms after one mark, in any order. The book writes them in the order they run, as a style; the engine finds that order itself.


Refused
The engine stops and names what to write instead.
Atoms with no table named before them: point + x(gdp). A style() written before any mark.
A transform on the left: bin * bar.


Meaningful
No error, and a different picture.
A channel before the marks, or after one of them, once a plot has two. Two marks swapped: the second draws on top.
Nothing. No order under * changes the picture.



Start with the cell where * meets Meaningful. * fixes one thing only: the mark is on the left. Once the mark is there, the order of what follows changes nothing.
Free covers most orderings. The two sentences below draw the identical plot, and the book writes the first because a fixed order is easier to read:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + point + y(life))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + point + y(col.life)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + point + y(:life))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), point, y(col.life)))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                                                                                                                                                                              0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K    Gdp






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside x is gdp, points, y is life.”
Both name life on y, so the two plots share that axis and it is drawn once, on the left. Each plot still draws its own gdp axis underneath it.
Refused means an atom comes before the thing it needs. A plot needs its table first, so + must have a plot on its left. A setting needs a mark, so a style() before any mark is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + style(size = 3) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + style(size = 3) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + style(size = 3) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), style({ size: 3 }), point, x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `style()` has no mark to style. Put it after a mark, e.g. `point + style(color = "tomato")`.


The message says to put style() after a mark.
Meaningful is the only kind that needs care, because it is the only kind the engine says nothing about. With two marks in a sentence, a channel written before them belongs to the plot and reaches both marks, and a channel written after one belongs to that mark. Both are legal, neither warns, and they draw different pictures. Here only color(era) moves, from before the marks to after point:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gm_eras) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + color(era) +
   point + line * smooth + title("color(era) before the marks")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + point + color(era) +
     line * smooth + title("color(era) after point"))


((data(gm_eras) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
   point + line * smooth + title("color(era) before the marks")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + point + color(col.era) +
     line * smooth + title("color(era) after point")))


(data(gm_eras) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + color(:era) + point +
  line * smooth + title("color(era) before the marks")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + point +
  color(:era) + line * smooth + title("color(era) after point"))


beside(plot(data(gm_eras), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), point, layer(line, smooth),
  title("color(era) before the marks")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.era), layer(line, smooth), title("color(era) after point")))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  color(era) before the marks Life Gdp  Era    1957  2007 


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       1K 10K 100K    color(era) after point Gdp  Era    1957  2007 






“Given the gapminder eras: x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by era, points and also lines derived by smooth, beside x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, points colored by era, and also a line derived by smooth.”
On the left, color(era) reaches both marks, so the trend splits into one line per era. On the right, it belongs to the points alone, and one gray line is fitted to both eras together. Encoding scope gives the whole rule. It is also why this book keeps one order: when every sentence looks the same, a different order is a deliberate signal.
The order of the marks is the second case, and here too the engine gives no message. The marks are drawn in the order you wrote them, so the second mark is drawn on top of the first. Here the bars are light gray, so you can see which mark is on top:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(continent) + y(life) +
   bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") + point +
   title("bar * mean, then point")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(continent) + y(life) +
     point + bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") +
     title("point, then bar * mean"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
   bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") + point +
   title("bar * mean, then point")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
     point + bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") +
     title("point, then bar * mean")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(:continent) + y(:life) + bar * mean +
  style(color = "lightgray") + point + title("bar * mean, then point")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(:continent) + y(:life) + point + bar * mean +
  style(color = "lightgray") + title("point, then bar * mean"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  layer(bar, mean), style({ color: "lightgray" }), point,
  title("bar * mean, then point")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.continent), y(col.life), point,
  layer(bar, mean), style({ color: "lightgray" }),

“Given gapminder 2007: x is continent, y is life, bars derived by mean, colored lightgray, and also points, beside points and also bars derived by mean, colored lightgray.”
On the left, every point is drawn over the bars. On the right, the bars are drawn last, so they cover the points below each mean, which show only faintly through the gray.

26.4.1 What groups first
The three kinds above, free, refused and meaningful, are about the order in which you write the atoms. Precedence answers a different question: when a sentence holds more than one operator, which operator groups its atoms first. Arithmetic has the same idea. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14 and not 20, because * groups before +. It is read as 2 + (3 * 4), as if the parentheses were written. A sentence in gog is read the same way, so precedence decides which atoms each operator joins.
This order of grouping belongs to the language you write in, not to gog, and gog cannot change it. R and Python share one order. Julia differs in one place: it groups | together with +. When the two meet, the one written first groups first (Julia shows where this changes a sentence). The table gives the order in each of the three languages:



Groups
R
Python
Julia




First
* and /
* and /
* and /


Next
+
+
+ and |, from left to right


Last
|
|




JavaScript has no column in the table, because it spells each operator as a word, such as beside(). The things the word joins are written inside its parentheses, so you see the grouping instead of remembering it (JavaScript).
For one plot, this is the order you want in all three languages. So a plot needs no parentheses of its own, even with a facet:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  across(col.continent))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
R reads that sentence as (data(gapminder_2007) + (bar * bin) + x(life)) | facet(continent). The transform joins its mark first, the atoms join the plot next, and the facet splits the finished plot last. Python and Julia read it the same way.
A row facet needs no parentheses either, because a facet always splits the whole plot.
An atom can also be written after a facet, like the title in the sentence below:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) |
  facet(continent) + title("Each continent in its own panel")

  facet(col.continent) + title("Each continent in its own panel"))

26.4.2 Parentheses in an arrangement
That order works for one plot, with or without a facet. It can go wrong when | or / has no facet() on its right, and joins two separate plots into one arrangement instead (Composition). Then each side of the operator must be a whole plot, from its data() to its last atom. Without parentheses, precedence can join part of one plot to part of the other before either plot is complete. Here are the two plots from earlier in this chapter, set one above the other with no parentheses:


RPythonJulia


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) /
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) /
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) / data(gapminder_2007) +
  bar * count + x(:continent)




Error:
! gog: `/` places one plot below another, and it groups before `+`, so here it joined `y()` to the plot after it. Put each plot in parentheses: `(data(df) + point + ...) / (data(df) + bar + ...)`.


/ groups before +, so it takes only the atom on each side of it: y(life) on the left and the second data() on the right. R reads the sentence as … + x(gdp) + (y(life) / data(gapminder_2007)) + …. For a facet, that grouping does no harm, because a facet splits the whole plot anyway. For an arrangement it does: / must place a whole plot below another, and y(life) is only one atom of a plot. So gog refuses the sentence, and its message names y(), the atom that / took. Python and Julia give the same refusal.
With | in place of /, the result depends on the language. R and Python group | last, so both plots are complete before | joins them, and the arrangement draws. Julia groups | together with +, from left to right. So | joins the first plot to the second plot’s data() alone, and gog refuses the sentence.
So whenever this book composes plots in R, Python or Julia, it writes each plot inside its own parentheses. Then every plot is complete before | or / joins it, and the arrangement means the same thing in all three languages. In JavaScript each plot is written as plot(…), so it is complete already.
Two more places need parentheses. The first is an arrangement inside an arrangement. / groups before | in R, Python and Julia, so a | b / c is read as a | (b / c): one plot beside two plots, one above the other. The examples below use three plots from this chapter, titled a, b and c:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + title("a")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + title("b")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + title("c"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + title("a")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + title("b")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) + title("c")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + title("a")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + title("b")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) + title("c"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  title("a")),
  below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  title("b")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life), title("c"))))

The table above shows what parentheses group: whole plots and whole arrangements. You might also try them around several marks, to give a second table to all of them. title: 26  Operators
text:
26.5 Why +, and not a pipe
Readers who know R’s tidyverse packages ask why gog does not use a pipe. A pipe passes a value into a function: a |> f means f(a). Hadley Wickham, ggplot2’s author, has said publicly that the pipe would have been the better interface (Wickham, 2018). ggplot, ggplot2’s predecessor, was written as function composition, and it could have used a pipe if one had existed. ggplot2 used + instead.
He also answers the question a reader asks next: why not change ggplot2 now? It cannot change: its functions take the mapping and the data first, while a pipe needs the plot as the first argument. And he judges that a new package built only to make this change would cost more work than the change would be worth. So ggplot2’s + comes from its history, not a fresh choice, and a grammar designed today has to make that choice for itself. He gives two reasons for preferring the pipe, and neither applies to gog. A third consideration is gog’s rather than his, and it is the one that decides the question.
His first reason is about one language. A pipe is a single idea that works everywhere in R, so a grammar that spells function composition differently is one more thing to learn. Switching between the two spellings is a frequent source of errors, his own included. That is true, and it is an argument about R and its packages. gog is one syntax written in four languages, and that changes the answer. + can be given a meaning in R, Python and Julia. The pipe cannot be given a gog meaning. Julia’s |> and R’s two pipes already mean something gog must not change. Python has no pipe operator at all, and no way to add one: you can give new meanings only to the operators it already has. In R and Julia a pipe would work with the meaning it already has. Python would need another spelling, and the languages would then have two different grammars. This project exists to avoid that. JavaScript decides nothing here, because it cannot overload any operator at all, which is why it spells all four as words (JavaScript).
His second reason is about arithmetic, and it is the stronger of his two reasons. A + looks like the plus sign of arithmetic, so you expect it to behave like one, in two ways. The order should not matter: a + b should equal b + a. And the grouping should not matter: a + (b + c) should equal (a + b) + c. ggplot2’s + does not always behave either way.
The six permutations drawn earlier in this chapter answer the first half, the order. In a plot with one mark, the mark and its channels commute. Move color ahead of x, or write the positions before the mark, and the engine produces the identical file. Once a plot has two marks, two orders change the picture: where a channel is written, and the order of the marks. In both, the order says something you chose: which marks a channel reaches, and which mark is drawn on top (Which orders matter).
The second half, the grouping, never comes up in gog. To group b + c first, b + c would have to mean something without a. In gog it cannot, because a sentence must start with a table. + joins an atom to a plot, and a plot starts with data(). So two atoms joined with no table before them, such as point and x(gdp), are refused:

point + x(gdp)

Error:
! gog: these atoms have no plot to join — the sentence starts with the data: `data(df) + point + x(gdp) + ...`.


The message shows the sentence starting with data().
The third consideration is gog’s own. It is not an argument against the pipe. It is a statement of what a pipe would remove. A pipe applies functions, so every atom would have to become a function taking a plot and returning one. Make bar a function, then ask what bar * bin could mean. There is no answer: you cannot multiply two functions and get a histogram. The derive operator exists only because marks and transforms are things rather than actions. They are values, and they combine with each other before either one is joined to a plot.
This is the decision the book opens with: a plot is a specification, not drawing code. Hangeul shows the same idea. ㄱ is a letter, not an instruction: it fills one slot of a syllable block, and the block is built from its letters, not performed one step after another. gog’s atoms fill slots in the same way. The mark is the initial consonant, x, y and z are the vowel, and a channel with a legend is the final consonant (The grammar). A layer is built from them as a block is built from its letters. Hangeul’s letters are like nouns, and that is why they can be combined. gog makes its atoms nouns so that they can be combined in the same way. In a grammar built on the pipe, every atom is a verb. Such a grammar can layer, because layering really is a sequence of additions, but it cannot derive. ggplot was written as function composition, and it had no * either.
So + here is a choice rather than something inherited. Unlike the pipe, it can be given a meaning in R, Python and Julia. It commutes wherever order should not matter, and it leaves the atoms as nouns so that * can exist.

Each operator reads as a phrase when a plot is read aloud, and | and / have two readings each:

The operators say how atoms combine into a sentence. Where you write each atom decides what it binds to, and Encoding scope gives that rule in full.

title: 27  Encoding scope
text:
27.1 The rule
If you write one x() before two marks, which marks use it? Both do. Each word you write in a sentence, such as point, x() or style(), is an atom. Each atom binds to a scope: the whole plot, or one layer. Each mark you write starts a new layer. A layer holds that one mark, plus the atoms bound to the mark. For example, color() and style() are bound to a mark when you write them after it. In point + color(continent) + style(size = 3), both are bound to the point. The x() in the question is written before any mark, so it binds to the whole plot. This chapter gives the rule that decides whether an atom binds to the plot or to one layer.
The rule for every atom other than a mark or a transform fits in one table. That includes facet(), which is written after | or / instead of +. Each row names one or more atoms, the scope they bind to, and whether it matters where you write them.
In every row marked Yes, where you write the atom decides its scope. Write a channel before any mark and it binds to the plot. Write a channel or style() after a mark and it binds to that mark. data() and query() work differently. The first data() or query() opens the sentence and is the plot’s table. Each later one binds to the mark written directly after it, not to the mark before it. The atoms in the last two rows, marked No, belong to the plot wherever you write them. They are the title, the subtitle, the caption and the axis labels, palette(), theme(), order(), brush(), the spaces, and facet(), which always splits the whole plot.
The positions, x(), y() and z(), need a closer look when they are written after a mark, because this book writes them there in almost every sentence, as in data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life). These positions belong to point. They still reach every other layer that names no column of its own for that axis. So in practice every layer reads them, except a layer that names its own column for that axis. The next section shows that case with an example.
When the plot and a layer both name a column for the same axis, the layer reads its own. A data() written between two marks works the same way: it gives the next layer its own table in place of the plot’s.

27.2 One axis, and which column each layer reads
The rule above never gives a layer axes of its own. Every layer of a plot shares the same axes. That is what makes it one plot rather than two drawn on top of each other. gog allows no second axis. Each of x, y and z has one scale, one set of ticks and one label. So a second table’s values must be in the same units as the first table’s, such as dollars in both. Values in different units need a plot of their own. Composition covers the choice between layering, faceting, and an arrangement of separate plots.
Sharing an axis is not the same as sharing a column name, and the two are easy to confuse. Almost always you want to bind the positions once, before the marks, so that every layer reads them:

plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }), x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life), data(milestones), text, x(col.at), y(col.value),
  label(col.note), style({ size: 15, border_size: 8 }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given the milestones: text, x is at, y is value, label by note, with size 15 and border size 8.”
The two style() settings only make the notes easier to read: the points are gray, and each note has a halo, a band of the background color under its letters (A halo around each label).
Look at the axis labels: they are still Gdp and Life. Each axis is named after the first column written for it, unless you name the axis with x_label() or y_label(). Here those first columns are gdp and life, written after point. The axis belongs to the plot, and only the choice of column belongs to the layer. Without this rule, you would have to rename at and value in milestones to gdp and life. Renaming is easy when you build the table yourself. When the table comes from somewhere else, renaming means changing data you did not write.
A layer that names no column of its own reads the first column written for each axis, wherever the layer is written. So point + x(gdp) + y(life) + line draws a line through the points. point + line + x(gdp) + y(life) draws the same plot: the positions are written after line, and point, which names none, reads them too. color() does not work this way. Written after one mark, it never reaches another. Which orders matter shows that difference with a trend line, and Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped below gives the rule.
Naming a column per layer also lets you put two columns of one table on one axis:

The solid steelblue line is open and the dashed tomato line is close, both on one y axis. y_label("Price") names that axis. Without it, the axis would be named Open, after the first column written for it.
That plot works, but there is usually a better way to draw two series. Reshape the table to tidy data: one value column and a type column, mapped with color(type). That form draws a legend, and it works for any number of series. A y() in each layer, as above, is the better choice only in one of these situations:

A setting. The lines need a setting that no channel can map. A line’s width and its opacity can only be set, and a setting applies to a whole layer, so two widths need two layers. A color or a stroke pattern can be mapped instead, with color(type) or pattern(type).
Another table. The values are in another table, as the notes in milestones did.

A layer may name its own column, as the text layer did with milestones. It cannot name its own scale, so gog refuses the sentence below:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  data(milestones) + text + x(at, scale = "log") + y(value) + label(note)

  data(milestones) + text + x(col.at, scale = "log") + y(col.value) + label(col.note))

  text + x(:at, scale = "log") + y(:value) + label(:note)

  data(milestones), text, x(col.at, { scale: "log" }), y(col.value),
  label(col.note))




Error:
! gog: this layer's `x(at, …)` gives it its own scale, and the layers of one plot share one x axis — two scales on it would be two coordinate spaces in one panel, where every mark reads against an axis the expression never named. Set the scale once for the plot, before the marks: `x(<column>, scale = "log")`. A layer may name its own *column* for the shared axis — `x(at)` on its own is fine — but not its own scale. If the two series are genuinely in different units, facet on the measure instead.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


This sentence gives the points a linear x scale and the notes a log one. Two scales need two x axes, and a panel draws only one. The milestones plot wrote x(at). This one writes x(at, scale = "log"), and that is the only difference. A layer names its own column, never its own scale.
The message names two fixes. Set the scale once for the plot, before the marks, as in x(gdp, scale = "log"). Or, when the two series are in different units, give each its own panel. Put both in one tidy table, with a type column as described above, and add | facet(type). Then write free = TRUE in the position, and each panel’s axis is fitted to its own rows (Giving a panel its own scale).

title: 27  Encoding scope
text:
27.3 Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped
The section above was about positions alone, because every layer shares the same x, y and z axes, and that sharing gives positions their extra rules. The other channels, such as color() and size(), have no axis. They follow only the rule in the table at the start of this chapter: where you write a channel decides its scope.
A channel is often meant for one layer alone. You may want the points colored by country, and one trend line in a single color, fitted to all of them together. Written after a mark, a channel binds to that mark alone. The table gapminder_asia holds five Asian countries, one row per country and year:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  point + color(country) +   # color applies to point only
  line * smooth              # the trend line uses a single default color


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.country) +
  line * smooth)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + point + color(:country) +
  line * smooth


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.country), layer(line, smooth))






                                                                                              1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, points colored by country, and also a line derived by smooth.”
Each point is drawn in its country’s color. The line takes no color, so it is one dark gray trend line, fitted to all five countries together. Whenever a plot has a color legend, a layer that neither maps nor sets color is drawn in this gray. No country in the legend is gray, so the line cannot be mistaken for one.
Written before any mark, a channel has no mark to bind to. It binds to the plot instead, so every layer that can accept it gets it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  point +
  line * smooth


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  point +
  line * smooth)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:country) + point +
  line * smooth


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), color(col.country),
  point, layer(line, smooth))






                                                                                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, points and also lines derived by smooth.”
Now the line takes color as well. A line colored by a categorical column splits into one line per category, so the plot draws five trends, one per country.
That is the same rule that x and y follow. Written before the marks, they apply to every mark. Written after one mark, they belong to that mark. Positions add the one rule from the previous section: a layer that names no column of its own reads the first column written for that axis.

27.3.1 Why a channel binds to one mark only
Suppose you want the lines colored by country and only the points sized by population. A channel written after a mark binds to that mark alone, never to an earlier one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# `size` is written after `point`, so it belongs to the points;
# the line written above it does not change, and keeps its own color
data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line  + color(country) +
  point + size(population)


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line  + color(col.country) +
  point + size(col.population))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + color(:country) +
  point + size(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  color(col.country), point, size(col.population))






                                                                                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep.   Population    20.9M  669.8M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also points sized by population.”
This plot is possible only because a channel binds to one mark. A line takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row, so gog refuses size bound to a line. Written after point, size never reaches the line, and the plot draws.


27.3.2 One column per legend
Binding a channel to one mark has one limit. A plot draws one legend for color, and that legend names one column. So when two layers both map color, they must name the same column. The same is true of size, shape, pattern and opacity, the other channels that draw a legend.
Suppose the lines above stay colored by country, and the points are colored by population instead of sized by it. The one legend would name country, the first column written, and nothing would explain the colors of the points. So gog refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line  + color(country) +
  point + color(population)


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line  + color(col.country) +
  point + color(col.population))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + color(:country) +
  point + color(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  color(col.country), point, color(col.population))




Error:
! gog: `color` maps 2 columns in one plot: `country` (on `line`), and `population` (on `point`). A plot draws one legend for `color`, and it names `country`, so `population` would be drawn with no legend to read it by. Keep one column on `color` and show `population` another way: `size(population)` on the `point`, or `opacity(population)` on the `point`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two other ways to show population: size(population) or opacity(population) on the point. Each draws its own legend. The plot in Why a channel binds to one mark only uses size. Writing legend = FALSE on either color lets the plot draw, with no color legend at all.


27.3.3 A plot-scoped channel and the marks left unchanged
A channel bound to one mark must be one that mark can accept, or gog refuses the sentence. A channel written for the whole plot works differently. What happens when some marks can accept it and others cannot? size written for the whole plot applies to the points, and not to the line. A line takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row, so its size cannot come from a column. gog applies size to every mark that can map it, and prints a message naming the marks it left unchanged. That message is an Assumption: it says what gog decided for you instead of refusing (The kernel card names all three kinds). The plot still draws:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + size(population) +
  line + group(country) +
  point


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + size(col.population) +
  line + group(col.country) +
  point)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + size(:population) + line +
  group(:country) + point


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), size(col.population),
  line, group(col.country), point)




gog: `size(population)` is written for the whole plot, so it applies to `point` — `line` takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row, so it is left unchanged. Move `size(population)` after a mark to bind it to that mark alone.




                                                                                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Population    20.9M  669.8M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, size by population, lines grouped by country, and also points.”
If no mark in the plot can accept the channel, the binding does nothing at all, so gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + size(population) +
  line + group(country)


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + size(col.population) +
  line + group(col.country))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + size(:population) + line +
  group(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), size(col.population),
  line, group(col.country))




Error:
! gog: `size` maps `population` for the whole plot, written before the marks, and no mark here takes it: `line` takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `population` mapping and set it with `style(size = )` after `line`, or add a mark that maps `size`: `point`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the mark that could not accept the binding, and why: a line takes one size for the whole layer, its width, not one per row. It says what to do: drop the population mapping and set it with style(size = ) after line, or add a mark that maps size, such as point. gog never drops such a channel without a message.

title: 27  Encoding scope
text:
27.5 What comes next
Scope decides what an atom binds to inside one panel: the plot, or one layer. Faceting makes more panels, one per category of a column. Every panel is drawn by the same sentence, and by default every panel is read against the same scales.

title: 28  Faceting
text:
28.1 |: panels side by side
How do you compare the same plot across groups? A facet splits one plot into small multiples: one panel per category of a column. A frame is the space a plot is drawn in, with its own x and y axes. Wilkinson calls a facet a frame of frames. The facet column’s categories make the outer frame, and each of its cells is a panel. Each panel is an inner frame: the same plot, drawn from one category’s rows. The marks, channels, and transforms you have already learned draw every panel, and by default all the panels share the same scales.
The picture has been invented more than once, so you may know it under another name. Becker and Cleveland’s group at Bell Labs built it into S, the language R was modeled on, as Trellis display (Becker et al., 1996). The name comes from the garden trellis, because the panels are arranged in rows and columns like one. R still draws it this way in the lattice package (Sarkar, 2026), and the package’s own book explains the display in full (Sarkar, 2008). Base R’s coplot() is the same idea under a third name, the conditioning plot, because what a trellis conditions on is the facet column. That is also why the operator in the next section is |, the sign that statistics already uses for conditioning. Composition gives | a second meaning, and says where both meanings come from.
Tufte’s term, small multiples (Tufte, 1990), names the result rather than the operation, and this book keeps the two apart: small multiples for the picture, facet for the thing you write.
The scatter of income against life expectancy draws the countries of all five continents in one panel. You want to see each continent on its own without losing the comparison between them. The facet() atom names the column that does the splitting, and | arranges the panels in columns:

The panels share both axes, so a difference between continents is as easy to see as a pattern within one. The shared scale is what faceting is for. Five separate plots, each with its own scale, would look almost the same as these five panels. Separate scales break the comparison, and nothing on the page warns the reader.
A facet joins the plot with | or /, never with +, because the operator decides where the panels go: | puts them in columns, / in rows. Write + facet(continent) and gog refuses, and the message names | and /.

data(three_continents) + bar * bin + x(col.life) / facet(col.continent)


data(three_continents) + bar * bin + x(:life) / facet(:continent)


plot(data(three_continents), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  down(col.continent))






                              0 5 10 15                                    0 5 10 15                                   50 60 70 80   0 5 10 15    Europe  Africa  Americas  Count Life





“Given the three continents: bars derived by bin, x is life, split into panel rows by continent.”
Each panel’s bars are directly above the bars covering the same span of life expectancy in the panel below. Africa’s life expectancies spread wide toward the low end, Europe’s cluster in a narrow band at the high end, and the Americas’ fall between the two, closer to Europe’s.
That reading only works because the bars are the same width in all three panels. A histogram under a facet needs two separate decisions: which rows are counted, and where the bins are cut. Each panel counts its own rows, because a statistic is computed on the panel’s subset as if that subset were the whole table. That is true of every transform on every mark, which is the No Exceptions law applied one panel at a time.
But bin is not only a statistic. It cuts the axis into bins and counts the rows in each one. The cut is a set of positions on the x axis, so it belongs with the shared scale. One set of bins is cut from all three panels’ rows at once, and each panel then counts only its own rows into those bins.
Suppose each panel cut its own bins. Europe’s narrow spread would get narrow bins and Africa’s wide spread would get wide ones, so bars of different widths would be drawn against a single axis. An African bar about five years wide and a European bar under two years wide could each hold eight countries, and so be drawn at the same height. But the African bar holds about one and a half countries for each year of its width, and the European bar nearly five: more than three times as many. The panels are still aligned and the axis still looks correct, and yet a reader cannot compare the three distributions.
Like bin, density is not only a statistic. Its bandwidth, which sets how smooth each curve is, belongs to the whole plot, as the cut does: it is the average of the bandwidths each curve would get from its own rows. Each panel estimates its curve from its own rows with that bandwidth. A difference in shape between panels then comes from the data and not from the smoothing.

  down(col.continent))

“Given the three continents: an area derived by density, x is life, split into panel rows by continent.”
In this plot, Europe’s curve has one peak, near 80 years. Drawn alone, Europe gets a bandwidth of its own. Europe’s spread is narrow, so its own bandwidth is narrower than the one the three panels share. A narrower bandwidth smooths less. The gm_europe table holds the thirty European countries of 2007:

To see one continent’s own shape, draw it alone, as the plot of gm_europe does.

The change to compare is in life expectancy, on y. Panels side by side align their y axes, as stacked panels align their x axes. So the years go in columns with |, and the continents in rows with /. Five rows of panels share the plot’s height, which is 600 pixels unless the plot states another, so each row would get less than 120 pixels. theme(height = 1000) makes this plot 1000 pixels tall (theme(width =, height =)):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(height = 1000) |
  facet(era) / facet(continent)


(data(gm_eras) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(height = 1000) |
  facet(col.era) / facet(col.continent))


data(gm_eras) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + theme(height = 1000) |
  facet(:era) / facet(:continent)


plot(data(gm_eras), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ height: 1000 }), across(col.era), down(col.continent))






                                                           40 60 80                                                                                                                 40 60 80                                                                                                                                    40 60 80                                                                                                                               40 60 80                                                                              0 50K 100K   40 60 80                           0 50K 100K      1957  2007    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given the gapminder eras: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by era and panel rows by continent.”
Five continents and two years, fifty years apart, in one grid: every panel row is a continent, and every panel column a year. A continent’s two panels are side by side on one y axis, so the same life expectancy is at the same height in both. Read across a row to see the rise. In Europe’s row, all but one country is between 58 and 74 years in 1957, and every country between 71 and 82 in 2007.
The grid is a crossing in Wilkinson’s sense: every pair of a continent and a year gets a panel, even a pair the table holds no rows for. Every pair in this grid has rows, so no panel here is empty. When a pair has none, its panel is still drawn, and the empty panel shows that the pair is possible: it is information rather than an accident. Wilkinson’s other operation, nesting, draws only the pairs that exist. gog’s facet operators always cross. Despite its name, gog’s nest() atom is not Wilkinson’s nesting. It divides one panel into areas sized by a measure (Nest), and it makes no panels.
Facet is Wilkinson’s word too (Wilkinson, 2005), from the Latin facies (face): one side of a many-sided thing, like one face of a cut diamond. gog takes his word because it is the most general of the names for this picture. To him a trellis is one of several forms a facet can take, such as the scatterplot matrix, a grid with one scatterplot for each pair of columns. A grammar needs one term that covers them all.

                           2000   40 50 60 70 80                       2000                         2000                         2000                         2000                         2000                         2000                         2000                         2000                         2000      Bangladesh  Brazil  China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Mexico  Nigeria  Pakistan  United States  Life Year





“Given the gm top table: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, split into panel columns by country.”
The lines are still readable, but the years under them are not: the year labels overlap. The last panel’s name is also wider than its strip, the band above the panel that names it. Ten categories is a common number, and ten panels in one line are already too narrow to read.
wrap folds that line into a rectangle. The number is how many panels to draw before the line begins again:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_top) + line + group(country) + x(year) + y(life) | facet(country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(col.country) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) | facet(col.country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(:country) + x(:year) + y(:life) |
  facet(:country, wrap = 4)


plot(data(gm_top), line, group(col.country), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  across(col.country, { wrap: 4 }))






                              40 50 60 70 80                                                                                                          40 50 60 70 80                                                    1960 1980 2000                             1960 1980 2000                                  1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80                           1960 1980 2000      Bangladesh  Brazil  China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Mexico  Nigeria  Pakistan  United States  Life Year





“Given the gm top table: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, split into panel columns by country, wrapped at 4.”
The panels and the scale are unchanged, and wrap = 4 is the only addition to the sentence. The years are readable, United States fits its strip, and each country’s rise is now large enough to read.
Notice what wrap does not say: which way the panels run. The operator already decides it. | runs the line across, so four to a row; / runs it down, so four to a column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_top) + line + group(country) + x(year) + y(life) / facet(country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(col.country) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) / facet(col.country, wrap = 4)


data(gm_top) + line + group(:country) + x(:year) + y(:life) /
  facet(:country, wrap = 4)


plot(data(gm_top), line, group(col.country), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  down(col.country, { wrap: 4 }))






                              40 50 60 70 80                                                                                 40 50 60 70 80                                                    1960 1980 2000                                 40 50 60 70 80                                                         1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80                           1960 1980 2000      Bangladesh  Indonesia  Pakistan  Brazil  Japan  United States  China  Mexico  India  Nigeria  Life Year





“Given the gm top table: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, split into panel rows by country, wrapped at 4.”
This is the same number and the same ten countries, now read down the columns instead of across the rows. One number is enough because the direction is already in the sentence, which is why facet() takes no second argument for it. ggplot2 spells the same idea as nrow and ncol.
Two details in the wrapped plots come from the fold itself. The first is in the bottom right corner, where two cells stay empty. Ten panels folded four at a time fill twelve cells, so two cells are left over and nothing is drawn in them. They are not the empty panels of a crossed grid. In a crossing, an empty panel stands for a pair of categories that the table has no rows for. Here there is no pair at all, only leftover space.
The second is the extra axis beside the gap. Tick labels belong to the panels that touch the edge where the axis is drawn. In a full rectangle that edge is the bottom row. A folded line can leave the last row short, and then the panels above the gap would have no year labels. So gog uses a more general rule: a panel draws the x axis when no panel is below it. In the plot folded with |, Mexico and Nigeria are above the gap and keep their year labels. In the plot folded with /, the gap falls under United States.
Wrapping a crossed grid is refused. The crossing already makes a rectangle from two columns, so a wrap number would set the grid’s shape a second time:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) |
  facet(continent, wrap = 2) / facet(era)


(data(gm_eras) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent, wrap = 2) / facet(col.era))


data(gm_eras) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:continent, wrap = 2) /
  facet(:era)


plot(data(gm_eras), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent, { wrap: 2 }), down(col.era))




Error:
! gog: `wrap` folds one line of panels into a rectangle, but `continent` and `era` already cross into one. Drop `wrap`, or facet by one column and let `wrap` shape it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names the two columns that already make the rectangle, and asks you to drop wrap or to facet by one column.

data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(col.year) + y(col.population) | facet(col.continent, wrap = 3)


data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(:year) + y(:population) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, sum), x(col.year), y(col.population),
  across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))






                              0 1B 2B 3B 4B                                                    1960 1980 2000                                  1960 1980 2000   0 1B 2B 3B 4B                           1960 1980 2000      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Population Year





“Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by sum, x is year, y is population, split into panel columns by continent, wrapped at 3.”
Asia holds nearly four billion people and Oceania about twenty-five million. The axis is sized for Asia, so Oceania’s line lies flat along the bottom. The line is drawn correctly, but the axis is too tall for its shape to show. What the plot shows is that the five totals are of very different sizes. But the question was how each continent grew, and the plot answers a different one.
Write free = TRUE inside a position, and that position’s axis is fitted to each panel’s own rows:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(year) +
  y(population, free = TRUE) | facet(continent, wrap = 3)


(data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(col.year) +
  y(col.population, free = True) | facet(col.continent, wrap = 3))


data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(:year) + y(:population, free = true) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, sum), x(col.year),
  y(col.population, { free: true }), across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))






                              1500M 2000M 2500M 3000M 3500M                           450M 500M 550M                            1960 1980 2000   400M 600M 800M                            1960 1980 2000   400M 600M 800M                              1960 1980 2000   10M 15M 20M 25M    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Population Year





“Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by sum, x is year, y is population, freed, split into panel columns by continent, wrapped at 3.”
Now every line shows its rise, and you can see that Oceania’s population more than doubled. Notice the y axis: each panel carries its own numbers and its own gridlines, because one set of labels along the edge is enough only when the scale is shared.
Notice also what the second plot loses. Each axis is now fitted to its own line, so every line rises from the bottom of its panel to the top, and the five look much alike. Nothing in the five shapes shows that one rise is counted in billions and another in tens of millions. A reader who looks at the shapes and not at the axes will believe the five continents grew by similar amounts. The first plot cannot mislead a reader this way; the second one can. So gog frees a scale only when you ask for it.
Where you write free decides which axis is freed. You write free inside x() or inside y(), so the sentence has already named the axis and free does not name it again. There is no free_x or free_y. To free both axes, write free in both:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp, free = TRUE) + y(life, free = TRUE) |
  facet(continent, wrap = 3)


(data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp, free = True) + y(col.life, free = True) |
  facet(col.continent, wrap = 3))


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp, free = true) + y(:life, free = true) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { free: true }),
  y(col.life, { free: true }), across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))
