“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population, color by era, in the nest.”
Each continent’s region is sized by its two years added together. No continent ever had that population at one time, so the region’s size is only a frame, and its two parts are what the plot compares. The thicker light lines mark the continents, and the thinner ones divide each continent between the two eras. The legend decodes only the eras, and no continent is named in the plot. Asia fills the left side. Europe, Africa and the Americas fill the right side, from top to bottom, and Oceania is a thin strip, about seven pixels wide, at the bottom right. Africa’s region is the most uneven: more than three quarters of it is the 2007 part, because its population more than tripled in those fifty years.
The nesting needs no new word. Levels inside levels are called a dimension hierarchy, and Wilkinson shows that a dimension hierarchy is a nested facet (Wilkinson, 2005). gog’s facets always cross, so here the nesting happens inside one panel. x divides that panel as an outer facet would, but by share, not into panels of equal size.
The inner level comes from color, and the legend is what decodes it. So the inner level needs few enough values to fit in the legend beside the plot. A common treemap puts countries inside continents, and its legend would need 142 entries. The section Naming the regions, later in this chapter, shows how to write each name inside its own region instead.

title: 34  Nest
section: 34.4 What a packed panel does not have
text:
34.4 What a packed panel does not have
Look for the axes. There are none, and no setting adds them.
A flat panel’s horizontal direction means something: it stands for a variable, and a tick is a place on it. In a packing neither direction is a variable. Wilkinson states it exactly: the two dimensions of a treemap “have no intrinsic meaning related to the data because they can be reordered without changing the metric properties of the tree” (Wilkinson, 2005). That two regions touch says nothing about how close they are in the data. Moving one to the other side of the panel would not change any share the plot reports.
So there is no tick to place and no axis label to print, and gog refuses x_label():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(population) + color(continent) + nest() +
  x_label("Population")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) + nest() +
  x_label("Population"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(:population) + color(:continent) +
  nest() + x_label("Population")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum), y(col.population),
  color(col.continent), nest(), x_label("Population"))




Error:
! gog: `x_label()` names an axis, and a `nest()` plot has none — its two directions carry no variable and can be reordered without changing what the plot says. Use `title()` for the plot's own name, and the color legend to say what the regions are.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The color legend decodes a packed panel, exactly as it decodes a pie.

title: 34  Nest
text:
34.5 Naming the regions
A legend works while it has few enough entries to read. With many entries, the reader has to search the legend for each color, and 142 countries are far too many to search. So put the name where the region is. This sentence has no sum: without it, each row is its own region, so every country gets one inside its continent.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(continent) + y(population) + color(continent) +
  text + label(country) + style(color = "white") + nest() +
  title("Countries inside continents")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) +
  text + label(col.country) + style(color = "white") + nest() +
  title("Countries inside continents"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:continent) + text + label(:country) + style(color = "white") +
  nest() + title("Countries inside continents")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), bar, x(col.continent), y(col.population),
  color(col.continent), text, label(col.country),
  style({ color: "white" }), nest(), title("Countries inside continents"))

Zambia Zimbabwe  Countries inside continents  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: bars, x is continent, y is population, colored by continent, and also text, label by country, in the nest.”
The sentence has two layers, and the second is the ordinary text mark: label says which column supplies the string, exactly as it does on a scatter. label does not say where to put the name. In a nest, the packing decides. A label goes to the center of the region its own row was packed into. That is the same region the bar drew. Both marks read one packing, so no name is drawn inside another country’s region.
Notice what is missing from that sentence: the text layer carries no x and no y of its own. The sentence’s x(continent) and y(population) place the names instead. x chooses the continent’s region, and y sizes each country’s region inside it. Once a region has a size and a place, the name inside it has a place too. On a flat panel a text mark needs two positions before it can be drawn at all. Here it needs a measure and a string, and the packing places it.
All 142 countries are named. A name that does not fit its region is drawn smaller, at the size that fits. Most of the small names can be read when you zoom in on the plot, and the few smallest stay too small even then. The largest countries come first inside each continent, so their regions are close to square and their names keep their full size. A sunburst names its sectors by the same rule (Naming the nodes).
A share too small to have a region at all has nowhere to put its name. Only then is a name left out, and a message above the plot says how many names were drawn. Without that message, a treemap with a missing name would read as a complete list.
Two things make the small names larger: fewer categories, and a larger plot with theme(width =, height =). Each one gives every region more room. style(size = ) sets the size a name is drawn at when it fits, and a name never grows past its region. gog has no separate setting for fitting names into regions.

title: 34  Nest
text:
34.6 The other refusals
x_label() is one of several refusals in a nest, and the three below come from one fact: a region has an area, and nothing else. A point is placed by a position, and a packing has no position to give it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + nest()


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + nest()


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + nest()


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), nest())




Error:
! gog: `point` is placed by a position, and a packing has none to give it — its two directions are not axes, and two neighboring regions are not near each other in the data (Wilkinson §13.3.4.1). Drop `nest()` to draw `point` flat, or use `bar` or `text`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


An area cannot be negative. A measure with values below zero cannot be packed into regions. On the flat page, a bar below the baseline points down, and the reader can see the sign. A region has no direction to point in, so nothing in the picture could show the sign. The parts would also no longer fit the whole: in the cashflow table below, the positive parts add up to 165, and the whole is only 101.

! gog: `delta` has negative values, and a `nest()` plot turns a measure into an **area**, which cannot be negative. Flat, a bar below the baseline reads as a loss; a region has no direction to run in. Filter or offset the column, or draw it flat where the sign is readable.

A log scale is refused too. A region’s size is its share of the total, and that share is computed from the values as they are. A log scale places the values so that equal distances stand for equal ratios. A packing draws no distances, so a log scale has nothing to change, and gog refuses it.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(population, scale = "log") +
  color(continent) + nest()


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(col.population, scale = "log") +
  color(col.continent) + nest())


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(:population, scale = "log") +
  color(:continent) + nest()


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum),
  y(col.population, { scale: "log" }), color(col.continent), nest())




Error:
! gog: `y(scale = "log")` with `nest()` — a packed region's size is its **share of the total**, which is arithmetic on the values themselves, so a log scale would change nothing about the picture. Drop the scale, or drop `nest()` to read the values against a log axis.

title: 34  Nest
text:
34.7 Sorting the regions
Which region goes where? Two things decide: the packing method, which is fixed, and the order of the categories, which you can change. The method is the squarified one of Bruls, Huizing and van Wijk (Bruls et al., 2000): regions are placed in rows, and each row is chosen so its rectangles are as close to square as they can be. A simpler method divides one direction at a time, which makes long thin regions, and a long thin area is the hardest kind to judge. gog uses the squarified method for every packing.
Squarified packing gives the squarest regions when the rows arrive sorted by size, which is why published treemaps sort largest first. Inside a region, the rows have no position on any axis, so nothing else gives them an order, and gog packs them largest first. The regions themselves are different. They are the categories of a position, and they follow the order in which the continents first appear in the table, or a declared order if the column has one. To sort them, you add order():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
  color(continent) + order(population, desc = TRUE) + nest() +
  title("Largest continent first")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  color(col.continent) + order(col.population, desc = True) + nest() +
  title("Largest continent first"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:continent) + order(:population, desc = true) + nest() +
  title("Largest continent first")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.continent),
  order(col.population, { desc: true }), nest(),
  title("Largest continent first"))






               Largest continent first  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population, color by continent, ordered by population, largest first, in the nest.”
That is the same order() that reorders a bar chart, and it does the same work here. If the packing sorted on its own, order() would change nothing in this space. The same word would then mean one thing on a bar chart and nothing in a nest.
order() sorts the categories on a position, x or y, so a plot needs a categorical position before it can be sorted. In a nest that position draws no axis, but its categories still have an order. A one-level treemap binds no position at all, so there the atom has nothing to sort:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(population) + color(continent) +
  order(population, desc = TRUE) + nest()


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) +
  order(col.population, desc = True) + nest())


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(:population) + color(:continent) +
  order(:population, desc = true) + nest()


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum), y(col.population),
  color(col.continent), order(col.population, { desc: true }), nest())




Error:
! gog: `order(population)` sorts a **categorical position axis**, and this plot has none — so there is nothing for it to put in order. Bind a category to `x` or `y`, or, if what you meant was the order of a color split, declare the column's levels in the table: a factor in R, a pandas `Categorical` or polars `Enum` in Python, a `CategoricalArray` in Julia, `ordered()` in JavaScript.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


That refusal does not come from the packed space. It comes from order(), and it applies in every space.

title: 34  Nest
text:
34.8 What comes next
Regions in a nest are sized by the measure, and the packing decides where each one goes. Map places a mark at the point its own row names instead: longitude and latitude, projected onto the page.

Shneiderman, B. (1992). Tree visualization with tree-maps: 2-d space-filling approach. ACM Transactions on Graphics, 11(1), 92–99.


Wilkinson, L. (2005). The grammar of graphics (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0

title: 35  Map
text:
35.1 Choosing a projection
Where did it happen? Some data answers that with a place on the earth, and a place is given by two numbers. Longitude says how far east or west of Greenwich a place is, and latitude how far north or south of the equator. Both are angles in degrees, and south and west are negative.
Most plots in this book have placed their marks with two numbers, one on x and one on y. So a map is not a new kind of picture. It is the same sentence you already write, drawn in a space that treats the two numbers as angles on a sphere.
quakes_fiji records earthquakes near Fiji, one row per earthquake:
“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, in the map space.”
That is a thousand earthquakes recorded near Fiji. x is longitude and y is latitude, and map() is the only word that makes it a map. The axes are labeled in degrees, because that is what the columns hold. Every north value is negative, because Fiji lies south of the equator. east keeps counting past 180 instead of turning negative, so 185 means 175 degrees west.
In the web edition, the buttons under the plot work here too: the two magnifiers zoom in and out, and the frame button shows the whole map again. Once you have zoomed in, dragging moves the map around inside the panel, and the frame button undoes both. A map needs those controls more than most plots do, because a map is full of detail at every zoom level, from a whole ocean down to one street. Zooming changes only the view: it magnifies the picture and changes nothing the plot claims.
Zooming cannot change the projection, the method that flattens the round earth onto the page. You choose the projection, and the next section shows what each choice keeps and what it loses.
The earth is round and the page is flat. No projection can flatten a sphere without distorting it, and the choice is not between a good projection and a bad one. You choose which distortion you accept.
Two properties matter most: the area of a region, and the shape of a small region. A projection can keep one of them, never both. A projection that keeps every angle keeps every small shape, so preserve takes "area" or "angle":

   map(preserve = "area") + title("preserve = \"area\"")) /
  (data(world_borders) + path + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(piece) +
     map(preserve = "angle") + title("preserve = \"angle\""))

   map(preserve = "area") + title("preserve = \"area\"")) /
  (data(world_borders) + path + x(col.lon) + y(col.lat) + group(col.piece) +
     map(preserve = "angle") + title("preserve = \"angle\"")))


(data(world_borders) + path + x(:lon) + y(:lat) + group(:piece) +
  map(preserve = "area") + title("preserve = \"area\"")) /
  (data(world_borders) + path + x(:lon) + y(:lat) + group(:piece) +
  map(preserve = "angle") + title("preserve = \"angle\""))


below(plot(data(world_borders), path, x(col.lon), y(col.lat),
  group(col.piece), map({ preserve: "area" }),
  title("preserve = \"area\"")),
  plot(data(world_borders), path, x(col.lon), y(col.lat),
  group(col.piece), map({ preserve: "angle" }),
  title("preserve = \"angle\"")))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°  preserve = "area" Lat Lon


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°  preserve = "angle" Lat Lon
“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by piece, in the map space preserving area, above the same preserving angle.”
Look at Greenland, at the top left of each map, and compare it with Africa. Under preserve = "area", Greenland is small, which is correct: Africa is about fourteen times larger. Under preserve = "angle", the Mercator projection most web maps use, Greenland is drawn as large as Africa. The "angle" map keeps the true shape of every small region, and the areas it draws are wrong.
Both plots name lon on x, so / treats that as one axis: one scale, and one panel width. The projection sets each height, and the two heights differ. Keeping every small shape is what stretches the second one north and south.
preserve = "area" is the default, because a map is usually read by comparing how much area each region covers. A projection that draws the far north too large makes every region there look bigger than it is.
The world map above comes from a table like any other, and the next section says how that table is laid out.

title: 35  Map
text:
35.2 Drawing the outlines
To draw a boundary of your own, you need a table laid out the way the engine reads it. world_borders holds one row for every point along a coastline or a border, and it repeats the country and the continent on each of those rows.
path connects rows in the order the table gives them, which is exactly what tracing a coastline needs. A ring is one closed loop of points, ending where it returns to its starting point. group(piece) says where one ring ends and the next begins. A country is not always a single ring. An island is a ring of its own, and a country that encloses another needs a second ring for the hole. So piece has one value for each ring, not one for each country.
Without group(piece), path would join the last point of one country to the first point of the next. That would draw a line straight across the ocean between them. Grouping by country is not enough either, because a path joins every row of its group in order: South Africa’s outline would gain a line to the ring around Lesotho.

title: 35  Map
section: 35.3 The second layer is the data
text:
35.3 The second layer is the data
The chapter’s first plot drew the earthquakes with no coastline, so nothing said where on the earth they were. The outline supplies that, and here it is the background rather than the subject. Your own data goes on top of it, which is ordinary layering. The outline is one data() and one mark, and the earthquakes are another.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(world_borders) + path + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") +
  data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.35, size = 3) +
  map() + title("A thousand earthquakes near Fiji")


(data(world_borders) + path + x(col.lon) + y(col.lat) + group(col.piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") +
  data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.35, size = 3) +
  map() + title("A thousand earthquakes near Fiji"))


data(world_borders) + path + x(:lon) + y(:lat) + group(:piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") + data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) +
  y(:north) + style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.35, size = 3) + map() +
  title("A thousand earthquakes near Fiji")


plot(data(world_borders), path, x(col.lon), y(col.lat), group(col.piece),
  style({ color: "#c9ccd6" }), data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east),
  y(col.north), style({ color: "tomato", opacity: 0.35, size: 3 }), map(),
  title("A thousand earthquakes near Fiji"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°  A thousand earthquakes near Fiji Lat Lon





“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by piece; then given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, in the map space.”
The earthquakes are now drawn on a world map, north of New Zealand and east of Australia, so a reader can see where they are. Nothing in the sentence is new: two tables, two marks, and the second data() binds to the mark that follows it.

title: 35  Map
section: 35.4 A quantity goes on a channel
text:
35.4 A quantity goes on a channel
The earthquakes differ in magnitude, and the picture so far shows only where they were. In a flat plot, a cube or a polar plot, an axis can carry a quantity. A bar has its base on one axis and its length along the other. A map has no axis left for a quantity, because longitude and latitude use both.
So a quantity moves to a channel. Here size carries each earthquake’s magnitude:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(world_borders) + path + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") +
  data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + size(magnitude) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  map() + title("Sized by magnitude")


(data(world_borders) + path + x(col.lon) + y(col.lat) + group(col.piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") +
  data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + size(col.magnitude) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  map() + title("Sized by magnitude"))


data(world_borders) + path + x(:lon) + y(:lat) + group(:piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") + data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) +
  y(:north) + size(:magnitude) + style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  map() + title("Sized by magnitude")


plot(data(world_borders), path, x(col.lon), y(col.lat), group(col.piece),
  style({ color: "#c9ccd6" }), data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east),
  y(col.north), size(col.magnitude),
  style({ color: "tomato", opacity: 0.4 }), map(),
  title("Sized by magnitude"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°  Sized by magnitude Lat Lon  Magnitude    4  5.2  6.4 





“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by piece; then given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, sized by magnitude, in the map space.”
That plot has a name, the proportional-symbol map, and no single atom draws it. It is point with size bound, in this space.
Color works the same way. Here the column bound to it is a category, so each continent is given its own hue:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(world_borders) + path + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(piece) +
  color(continent) + map() +
  title("Each continent in its own color")


(data(world_borders) + path + x(col.lon) + y(col.lat) + group(col.piece) +
  color(col.continent) + map() +
  title("Each continent in its own color"))


data(world_borders) + path + x(:lon) + y(:lat) + group(:piece) +
  color(:continent) + map() + title("Each continent in its own color")


plot(data(world_borders), path, x(col.lon), y(col.lat), group(col.piece),
  color(col.continent), map(), title("Each continent in its own color"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°  Each continent in its own color Lat Lon  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  South America  Oceania  North America  Seven seas (open ocean) 





“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by piece, color by continent, in the map space.”
color reads the category exactly as it does on a flat plot. The space changed; the channel did not. The legend’s seventh entry, Seven seas (open ocean), is not a continent. The outline comes from Natural Earth, which puts the French Southern and Antarctic Lands under that name. They are islands in the southern Indian Ocean.

title: 35  Map
text:
35.5 Meridians and parallels
A map often needs a reference line, and the most common one is the equator. A rule draws a line at one position and spans the other axis. On a flat plot that is a reference line. Here, a rule at one latitude is a parallel, and a rule at one longitude is a meridian. The plot below draws one parallel, the equator:



equator: its one row


lat




0







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(world_borders) + path + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") +
  data(equator) + rule + y(lat) + style(color = "#d4674f") +
  map() + title("The equator")


(data(world_borders) + path + x(col.lon) + y(col.lat) + group(col.piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") +
  data(equator) + rule + y(col.lat) + style(color = "#d4674f") +
  map() + title("The equator"))


data(world_borders) + path + x(:lon) + y(:lat) + group(:piece) +
  style(color = "#c9ccd6") + data(equator) + rule + y(:lat) +

35.9 Filling the regions: the choropleth
Every country so far has been drawn as an outline. Filling each country by a quantity is the most familiar kind of map, and it has a name: the choropleth. The map below fills each country by its continent first; the next section fills it by a quantity.
The mark is zone, which shades a region. Everywhere else in this book a zone takes its sides from its own row: a category’s slot, a pair of bounds, a bin, a density cell, or a region that partition or flow computes. A country’s outline is different: it is the only case where many rows make one shape. So the sentence needs a word for which rows belong to which region, and group is that word already:

  color(continent) + map() + title("Every country, filled by continent")

  color(col.continent) + map() + title("Every country, filled by continent"))

  color(:continent) + map() + title("Every country, filled by continent")

  group(col.country), color(col.continent), map(),
  title("Every country, filled by continent"))

Real boundary data is not always written this carefully. GeoJSON and shapefiles, two common file formats for boundaries, repeat each ring’s first point as its last. Some plotting tools join a shape’s last point to its first by themselves. A table made for one of them might not repeat the first point. If a ring in your data does not close, gog cannot tell where one ring ends and the next begins. It draws the region and warns you that the ring ends had to be guessed. Because of the guess, an island can be joined to the mainland. To fix the table, repeat each ring’s first row as its last row.

title: 35  Map
section: 35.13 Counties: one country in finer detail
text:
35.13 Counties: one country in finer detail
Every map so far has given each country one value. One value hides how much the places inside a country differ. Each state of the United States is divided into areas called counties. A county’s poverty rate is the estimated percent of its people who live in poverty. In 2023 the median of the county rates was 13.6%. The lowest was 3.3%, and the highest was 49.6%, nearly half. A map of the counties shows where the high rates and the low rates are.
The us_counties table holds 3,109 counties: those of the 48 states between Canada and Mexico, plus the District of Columbia, which counts as one county. Alaska and Hawaii are left out. Many maps of the United States move them into small boxes beside the other states. In gog, a map draws every place at its own longitude and latitude. Alaska lies far to the northwest and Hawaii far to the southwest, so including them would make the 48 states much smaller.
The outlines and the rates both come from the US Census Bureau, for 2023. Like world_borders, the table has one row for each point of an outline, and piece names each ring. poverty holds each county’s rate, repeated on every row of its outline, so the map needs no join.
The sentence below is a choropleth, built like the map in Life expectancy on the map. group(county) says which rows make one county, and color(poverty) shades each county by its rate. Three more choices differ from that map. First, palette() names four colors, from seashell (almost white) to saddlebrown, so a county with a higher rate is drawn darker.
Second, preserve = "angle" draws the map with Mercator. The default, preserve = "area", draws only the meridian at 0 degrees as a straight vertical line, as Meridians and parallels showed. The others curve more the farther they lie from it. So the United States, at about 100 degrees west, would be drawn slanted. Mercator draws every meridian straight.
Third, theme(height = 470) sets the image’s height to 470 pixels, shorter than the default. A map keeps the proportions its projection gives it, so it never stretches to fill a tall image. Without the setting, empty space would be left above and below the map.

Mercator keeps the shape of every county, but not its size. It draws a county in South Dakota about 1.6 times as large as a county of the same area in south Texas. That is why preserve = "area" is the default, as Choosing a projection explains. So compare the counties on this map by their colors, not by how much of the map each dark region covers.
The darkest counties form three regions: along the lower Mississippi River, in the mountains of eastern Kentucky, and in South Dakota. Issaquena County, in the state of Mississippi beside the river, had the highest rate of all, 49.6%. Across the river, East Carroll Parish in Louisiana had 46.5%. Louisiana calls its counties parishes. In eastern Kentucky, Martin County had 48.1%. South Texas is lighter than these three regions. Along the border with Mexico, the six counties from Maverick County southeast to Cameron County had between 22% and 31%. That is still higher than nine counties in ten.
In South Dakota, the darkest counties lie on reservations, areas of land reserved for Native American nations. Ziebach County had 46.2%, and Oglala Lakota County had 37.1%. South Dakota also had the lowest rate of all: 3.3% in Lincoln County, which holds the southern part of the city of Sioux Falls. A map with one color for each state would give all of South Dakota one color. It would show neither Ziebach County’s rate nor Lincoln County’s.

Delaware County, the brightest county, was the highest in all three elections, with 88% in 2020. It lies in the middle of the state, just north of Columbus, the state capital. title: 35  Map
text:
35.15 What comes next
A map flattens the sphere so a page can hold it. The next chapter, Globe, draws every mark from this chapter on the sphere itself: the same marks at the same places, seen from one side.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.1 The view
What does the data look like on the earth itself? The map chapter flattened the sphere to fit a page. This chapter keeps the sphere round, and turns it toward you.
quakes_fiji holds a thousand earthquakes recorded near Fiji, one row for each. Here is the map chapter’s first sentence, which draws them, and beside it the same sentence with globe() in place of map(), turned to face Fiji:
“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, in the map space, beside the same on the globe.”
x is longitude and y is latitude, exactly as on the map. What changed is how the two numbers become a position on the page. Each point is now drawn at its place on the sphere. A sphere seen from one side is a disk, and that disk is what the plot draws.
A globe shows one half of the earth, so the choice of half matters. turn and tilt name the place the view faces, and they are the same two arguments space() takes. turn is the longitude at the center of the disk, and tilt is the latitude. The chapter’s first plot faces Fiji. Leave both out and the view faces longitude zero and latitude zero, where the equator crosses the prime meridian.
turn is a longitude, so 190 and -170 name the same view: 190 degrees east is 170 degrees west. tilt is a latitude, so it runs from -90 to 90 and no further.
In the web edition the angle you write is only the view the globe opens at. Drag it and it turns, the way the cube in Space turns, and the far half of the earth comes into view. The reset button returns to the view the sentence asked for. In the PDF a plot keeps its one view, which is why this chapter also draws some data at a second angle.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.3 The graticule
Every globe so far has drawn a grid of thin gray lines over the sphere. It is the graticule, this space’s gridlines. Its meridians run from pole to pole, one every thirty degrees of longitude, and its parallels circle the earth, one every thirty degrees of latitude. A flat panel draws its gridlines straight. A globe bends its gridlines onto the sphere, the way the polar space bends them into rings and spokes.
There are no axes beside the disk, because a sphere has no straight side to write one along. The graticule is the reference instead. theme(grid = ) works on it as on any other grid: "x" keeps only the meridians, "y" keeps only the parallels, and "none" removes it:

data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18) + theme(grid = "none") +
  title("No graticule")

  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18) + theme(grid = "none") +
  title("No graticule"))

  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18) + theme(grid = "none") +
  title("No graticule")

  globe({ turn: 178, tilt: -18 }), theme({ grid: "none" }),
  title("No graticule"))

title: 36  Globe
section: 36.8 Thousands of storm tracks on a dark globe
text:
36.8 Thousands of storm tracks on a dark globe
The routes earlier in this chapter were a few arcs between cities. A table of real records can hold thousands of lines, and then the lines are hard to tell apart. Thin lines drawn over one another on a pale sphere merge into one gray mass, and the lines inside it can no longer be followed.
cyclones is a table of that size. It holds all 2,174 storms from 1980 to 2025 that reached hurricane strength, a wind of at least 64 knots (119 kilometers per hour). The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) keeps the record. Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are one kind of storm, with a different name in each ocean. Scientists call all three tropical cyclones, which gives the table its name.
Each row is one storm’s position at one moment, and a storm’s positions joined in order are its track. The positions are twelve hours apart. They cover only the time when the storm’s wind was at least 34 knots, or 63 kilometers per hour. At that speed a storm is given a name. category is the storm’s highest category on the Saffir-Simpson scale, which ranks a storm from 1 to 5 by its strongest wind. It holds one value for each storm, in three bands: “1 or 2”, “3 or 4” and “5”. The month column is not used in this chapter. The Play chapter uses it to show the same storms one calendar month at a time.

The land is the same zone layer as in the choropleth above. style(color = ) sets every country to one dark gray, so the continents stay darker than every track. “Given the world borders: zones, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by country; then given the cyclones: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by storm, colored by category, with a palette of mediumvioletred, darkorange and gold, on the globe.”
The busiest region is the western North Pacific, on both sides of the Philippines. A third of the storms began there, 729 of the 2,174, and so did 125 of the 221 storms that reached category 5. In the north, most tracks run west, and many then bend to the north and east. In the south, many bend to the south and east. The band along the equator stays empty: no position lies closer to it than 0.7 degrees, and only 33 of the 29,669 positions lie within 5 degrees of it.
The gold tracks lie on top because of the table’s order, not because of their color. gog draws the storms in the order the table lists them, and a track drawn later covers the tracks drawn before it. The table lists the category 5 storms last. Reverse the rows, and the gold tracks go to the bottom, under all the others.

36.9 A measure along the radius
On a flat map a quantity has to go on a channel, size or color, because both positions carry the place. The sphere leaves one direction free: the radius, which runs straight out from the surface. Every place on the sphere has its own radius. Here a bar is drawn at its place as a spike, rising outward along that radius, and z names the measure. Here the measure is reach, the square root of each country’s population:

“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by piece; then given the population spikes: bars, x is lon, y is lat, z is reach, colored by continent, on the globe.”
Look at the edge of the disk. The sphere itself can hide part of a spike. A spike just behind that edge has its base hidden, so only the part that rises past the edge is drawn. A spike too short to rise past that edge is not drawn at all. At the edge you see a spike from the side, along its whole length. A spike that points straight at you is seen from its tip, so it looks shorter than it is. In the web edition, turn the globe to see such a spike from the side.
Finding each country’s center and joining its population are the host language’s job, like the join for the cities above. Choosing how to scale the measure belongs there too. The square root keeps China’s spike from making every other spike too small to see. A scale keeps an axis in the column’s own units, and a globe draws no axis, so the globe refuses scale = on z().

title: 36  Globe
section: 36.10 The depth goes to the cube
text:
36.10 The depth goes to the cube
The Fiji earthquakes from the chapter’s first plot carry a third number: elevation, their depth below the surface, written as a negative number. That number is not a height to raise above the surface. It is a third coordinate of the place itself, and on the globe z belongs to bar alone. So gog refuses the sentence below rather than guessing at it. The refusal names three things you can do instead: add a bar layer, drop z(), or draw the same table in the cube.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18)


(data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18))


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18)


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), globe({ turn: 178, tilt: -18 }))




Error:
! gog: `z(...)` on a globe is the radius, and only a `bar` reads it — a spike drawn at its place, measuring outward from the surface. Add a `bar` layer to raise spikes, drop `z(...)` to keep the marks drawn on the sphere, or drop `globe()` for the cube, where every position mark reads `z`.

A place with a depth belongs in the cube, the space with a third position. space() takes the same two arguments globe() does:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  color(slab) + space(turn = 130, tilt = 25) +
  title("The same earthquakes, read by depth")

  color(col.slab) + space(turn = 130, tilt = 25) +
  title("The same earthquakes, read by depth"))


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  color(:slab) + space(turn = 130, tilt = 25) +
  title("The same earthquakes, read by depth")


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), color(col.slab), space({ turn: 130, tilt: 25 }),
  title("The same earthquakes, read by depth"))

“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by slab.”
slab names the depth band each earthquake falls in. The globe plots looked straight down on these earthquakes, so a deep one and a shallow one were drawn at almost the same place. In the cube, depth is a third position, so they separate. Most of them lie along one sloping sheet: the ocean floor, sinking into the earth. Drag this one too. The drag that turns the earth on a globe turns the cube here.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.11 What a globe refuses
The map and the globe draw the same places as two pictures. The map flattens the sphere so a reader sees all of it at once. The globe keeps the sphere and hides the far half. To go from one picture to the other, you change one word.
The globe takes the map’s marks and one more: bar, which measures along the radius. It refuses the rest for the same reason the map does. Suppose you try a line through the earthquakes, as you would on a flat page. Both positions carry the place, exactly as on the map, and only bar reads the radius. So a line has no axis to measure along:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + line + x(east) + y(north) + globe()


data(quakes_fiji) + line + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + globe()


data(quakes_fiji) + line + x(:east) + y(:north) + globe()


plot(data(quakes_fiji), line, x(col.east), y(col.north), globe())




Error:
! gog: `line` measures along an axis, and a `globe()` plot has none to spare — longitude and latitude use both. Drop `globe()` to draw `line` flat, or use `point`, `bar`, `text`, `path`, `rule`, or `zone`. To carry a quantity on the globe, put it on a channel instead of an axis: `point + size(<column>)` sizes each place by it, and `color(<column>)` shades it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The refusal’s advice is to put a quantity on a channel instead, size or color. On a globe a quantity can also be a spike’s length along the radius, as in the population spikes earlier in this chapter.
A latitude past a pole names no place, so a view cannot face that latitude:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + globe(tilt = 100)


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + globe(tilt = 100)


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + globe(tilt = 100)


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  globe({ tilt: 100 }))




Error:
! gog: `globe(tilt = 100)` is outside -90 to 90, which is where a latitude lives. At 90 the view faces straight down on the north pole and at -90 on the south; there is no place past either. Use `globe(tilt = 90)` for the nearest view, or `globe(turn = )` to swing around the earth instead — a longitude wraps and a latitude does not.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And a globe draws no axes at all. So gog refuses an axis label rather than accepting it and drawing nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + globe() +
  x_label("Longitude")

  x_label("Longitude"))

! gog: an axis label names an axis, and a `globe()` plot draws none — a sphere has no straight side to write one along, and the graticule is the reference instead. Drop it; `title()` still names the plot.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.12 What comes next
A globe can draw a row only at the place its two numbers name. Network draws tables whose rows name no place, only a connection between two nodes, and the engine computes a position for every node.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.1 One row is one edge
What is connected to what? Some tables record relations rather than measurements: each row says that one thing is related to another. A network diagram draws those relations. Each thing becomes a node, one marked place in the picture, and each relation becomes an edge, a stroke between two nodes.
Nothing in such a table says where any node should be placed. Choosing those positions is the problem, and this chapter shows how gog solves it. The engine computes a position for every node. A space named network() draws the result, with no axes at all.
trade_partners holds one row per trade relation: who exports, who imports, the value of the goods (in billions of dollars, rounded), and the exporter’s continent:
The first question this table raises is who trades with whom. One stroke per row answers exactly that. Write the edge mark derived by layout(), give it the from column first and the to column second, and add the space:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network())
“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
Each row of the table becomes one stroke. Five pairs of countries trade in both directions, and each pair’s two strokes lie on one line. So you can see only 17 separate strokes for the 22 rows. The layout reads both columns and makes one node for each distinct name. Two countries named in one row, or in two, are one step apart. Mexico and Canada share a trade partner but no row, so they are two steps apart. The engine then places the nodes so that each distance is in proportion to the number of steps, as closely as it can. It cannot always be exact. Mexico, Canada and India each trade only with the United States. They are one step from it and two steps from each other, and on a flat page no three points can be placed at exactly those distances. This method is called stress majorization. The positions are computed by the engine that all four languages share, never by the language you write in. So this sentence draws the same picture in R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, and the four image files are identical.
The panel has no axes, no ticks and no grid, because network() draws none. A layout’s positions mean nothing as quantities. Flip the picture left to right and it means the same, so a number on an axis would state nothing about the data. gog therefore draws a layout in two spaces only: flat in network(), and in the cube, whose box carries no numbers. Every other space refuses it.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.2 The nodes and their names
The strokes alone do not say which node is which country, or which countries have the most trade relations. Two more layers finish the diagram. A point layer draws the nodes, and a text layer names them. Each one carries the same layout, and the engine computes it once per layer. The layout uses no random numbers, so all three layers get the same positions. That is why every dot is exactly where its strokes end.
The layout also computes two columns for the nodes: name, and degree, the number of rows the node appears in. A pair that trades both ways counts twice, so China, which trades with 7 countries, has a degree of 9. size(degree) then draws a node larger when it appears in more rows. The text layer also composes repel, the collision modifier that moves each label off the dots and off the other labels. So a name is just outside its dot instead of covering it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Who trades with whom")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("Who trades with whom"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + size(:degree) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel + label(:name) + network() +
  title("Who trades with whom")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("Who trades with whom"))

“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
China, the United States and Germany have the largest dots, and they are near the middle. No row of the table says that these three have the most trade relations. The layout found them by counting each country’s rows.

title: 37  Network
section: 37.3 An edge carries its own columns
text:
37.3 An edge carries its own columns
Every stroke so far is drawn alike, whether the trade is 500 billion dollars or 50 billion. Each edge is drawn from one row, so its color, its stroke pattern and its opacity can come from that row’s own columns. color and pattern need a categorical column, and opacity needs a continuous one. opacity(billions) maps each stroke’s opacity to that row’s billions, so a larger trade draws a darker stroke. A pair that trades both ways is two strokes on one line, so it looks darker than either row alone:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  size(:degree) + text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel +
  label(:name) + network() + title("More trade, darker stroke")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("More trade, darker stroke"))






                                             China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  More trade, darker stroke  Degree    1  5  9   Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
A node is different. It stands for every row it appears in, and those rows can hold different values. So the point and text layers map only name and degree, and gog refuses any other column there. Every other column belongs on the edge layer, where one row carries one value.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.4 The network in the cube
Every picture so far is flat. A plane gives the layout two directions for placing its nodes. A cube gives it three, and a cube can be turned. A crowded network has more room in three directions, and turning the cube shows which strokes pass in front of the others. With network(), the layout places the nodes in the plane. Write space() in its place, and the layout places them in the cube instead: the same cube Space draws for a plot with z. Every node takes a new position. space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) sets the angle the cube is seen from, as it does for any plot in the cube. Bare space() shows the cube at the default angle, turn 30 and tilt 25. The sentence below leaves out the names, so the shape of the network is easy to see:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, given depth")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, given depth"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  size(:degree) + space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, given depth")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  space({ turn: 35, tilt: 20 }), title("The same network, given depth"))






                                                               The same network, given depth  Degree    1  5  9   Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, in the cube, turned 35, tilted 20.”
Nothing in the table gives a node a third position, so there is nothing to bind to z. The layout places the nodes in three directions because the space is the cube. The box outlines the cube, so you can see how it is turned. It has no numbers along its edges, because a layout’s positions are not measurements. The flat form has no axes for the same reason.
In the web edition the cube turns with a drag, the way the cube in Space turns. The reset button returns it to the angle the sentence asked for. In the PDF it keeps the view it was given.
A text layer names the nodes in the cube as it does on the flat page. Each name is drawn at its node, and repel moves the names off each other and off the dots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, named in the cube")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, named in the cube"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  size(:degree) + text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel +
  label(:name) + space(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, named in the cube")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  space({ turn: 35, tilt: 20 }),
  title("The same network, named in the cube"))

“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the cube, turned 35, tilted 20.”
Each country is named beside its node, and the names do not cover the dots.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.5 What the network refuses
Each refusal in this section is a mistake in the sentence. The most likely mistake is to leave network() off, because most plots need no space at all. Without it the plot would draw axes under the layout, and the numbers along them would mean nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer)


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)))




Error:
! gog: a `layout`'s positions are the graph's, not the data's — an axis under them would number something no reader can mean. Draw it flat with `+ network()`, or in the cube with `+ space(turn = 30, tilt = 25)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Only three marks read a layout. Write any other mark and the refusal names all three:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + bar * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + bar * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + bar * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners), layer(bar, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  network())

! gog: `layout` places a graph — a position per node, computed from an edge table — and `bar` has no reading for that. Three marks do: `edge * layout(<from>, <to>)` draws the connections, `point * layout(...)` the nodes, and `text * layout(...) + label(name)` names them, all inside `network()`.

text:
37.6 Where the limits are
A sentence can be right, and the table can still hold rows a layout cannot use. A row from a node to itself is refused, because such a stroke would have no length. The first row of this small table goes from China to China:

                         billions = c(500, 455))

Error:
! gog: 1 row(s) of `self_trade` connect a node to itself, and a stroke from a point to the same point has no extent. Remove those rows in the host language: an edge joins two different nodes.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Remove the rows that connect a node to itself before you draw the plot. A row with a missing value in the from or the to column is not refused: it draws no stroke, and a message says how many rows were left out.
You may know more about each country than the edges say, such as its continent. gog does not read a second table describing the nodes, so a node shows only what the edges give it: its name and its degree. You can still show such a fact, but only on the edges. trade_partners already holds one such fact, continent, the exporter’s continent. Map it on the edge layer, as Edge does with color(continent). A fact of your own is joined onto each row in the host language first.
You may want to drag a rectangle over part of the picture and select what it covers. A brush is refused. A brush selects a range of values on the plot’s axes, and a network has no axes. The fix is again in your table: add a column that marks the rows you want, and map it with color() on the edge layer.
If your table also has a year column, you may want to show how trade changes. For most plots, play does that: it draws one frame per year and shows the frames in order. In a network, play is valid grammar that this engine does not draw.
Instead, split the plot by year with | facet(year), which draws one panel per year. All panels share one layout, so a country is in the same place in every panel where it appears. Each panel draws only the edges from its own rows. An edge missing from a later panel is a trade relation that ended.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.7 What comes next
A network draws one table at one moment. The section above suggested panels for comparing years, because this engine does not play a network. Most other plots can be played. Play adds time to a plot: it cuts the plot into frames and runs them in order, so the reader watches the picture change.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.1 The same sentence, as panels
How did the whole picture change from year to year? play cuts the plot into frames, one picture for each value of a column, and shows them in sequence. It is faceting read in time. A facet splits the rows by a column’s distinct values and lays the pieces out across the page; play splits them exactly the same way and lays them out in time, one after another.
“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, played by year.”
Twelve frames, one per year in the data, running from 1952 to 2007. The strip above the panel names the one you are looking at.
A sequence is not the only way to show the years. Panels show them too, and the choice between the two is easiest to judge over the same rows. play and facet split the rows in the same way, so here the sentence changes only at its end: | facet(period) becomes + play(period). The gm_four table holds the gapminder rows for 1952, 1972, 1992 and 2007. title: 38  Play
text:
38.2 The column’s order
play and facet split the rows the same way, so you might expect the same columns to suit both. The same columns do not suit both. The test for playing a column is not its type. It is whether the column has an order.
A facet lays its panels out across the page, and you can read a page in any order you like. Your eye goes to any panel you choose, then comes back. A sequence lays its pieces out in time, and time arrives in one order only. So a sequence claims something a grid never claims: this frame comes after that one.
Bind a column with no order, and the plot shows movement the data does not have:

A sequence claims that one frame comes after another. Declare the column's levels in the table (a factor in R, a pandas `Categorical` or polars `Enum` in Python, a `CategoricalArray` in Julia, `ordered()` in JavaScript), or use `facet(continent)`, which claims no order.




                                                                                                                                                                                                  1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80     Asia    Europe    Africa    Americas    Oceania    Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, played by continent.”
Watch the strip: Asia, Europe, Africa, Americas, Oceania. That order is not alphabetical, and it is not geographic. It is the order the continents first appear in the table, because the rows are sorted by country and Afghanistan comes before Albania. The sequence is showing you how a file was sorted. The points jump between frames, and none of the jumps mean anything.
gog draws the plot anyway, because nothing about the sentence is malformed and you may have meant that order. The message above the plot names the order it had to choose, and two answers: declare the column’s levels, or facet instead. Give the column its levels and the frames follow them. Bind facet(continent) instead and the panels claim no order at all.
Channels describes the opposite mistake. There the data had an order the hues could not carry; here the frames carry an order the data does not have, so a reader looks for a pattern that was never there.
A column does not have to hold numbers to be ordered. A year is ordered, and so is a date. So is a categorical column whose levels you declared: months in calendar order, or a rating from low to high. gog runs the frames in the order the levels declare, the same order it uses on an axis (Data). A categorical column with no declared levels takes the order its values first appear in, which is the mistake the plot above showed.
Having an order is not on its own a reason to play a column. A sequence should move only when its frames hold the same things in different states. Then a reader can follow one of those things across the frames. The four frames above are that case: the same countries at four dates, and their points climb. The five continent frames above are not that case: each holds different countries, so nothing moves between them. The reader waits, and then has to remember what a facet would have shown at once. This needs saying plainly, because animation is the choice most people want to make.
How many values there are is a separate question, and the next section answers it. The gapminder years give twelve frames, and the glider flight in the next section gives 170. Both are worth animating, because in both the same things change from frame to frame. A long sequence takes more of the reader’s time without being harder to understand, and speed is there for that.

gog drew both of those sentences. It refuses neither, and it never will. A plot is refused for not being well formed, never for being a poor idea (Design laws). Which of the two says more about gliders is your judgment, not the engine’s. What the engine does instead is name the one cost it can measure. The message above counts the frames and reports how long one loop takes. It offers two answers: speed, or a column with fewer values.
Choose between the facet and the sequence before anyone else sees the plot. A reader needs one glance to see that a facet was the wrong choice. A sequence has to be watched for as long as the loop runs. If it then shows nothing new, the reader has waited for nothing.
The choice is easiest to see when the number of pieces is large. Imagine a year of hourly temperatures for New York, drawn as one curve for each day. As a facet that is 365 panels, and no fold leaves a curve large enough to read. As a sequence it is 365 frames, and a reader watches a year of weather pass. Below about ten pieces the panels usually read better, and Faceting shows ten of them wrapped and readable. Well above that the panels stop being readable, as the 170 glider panels did, and a sequence is the picture that still works.
A sequence can hold more pieces, and that alone does not make it the better picture. It loses the thing a facet does best: two pieces side by side, where a reader compares them instead of remembering them.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.4 What every frame shares
When a plot is cut into frames, can one frame still be compared with the next? Every scale, the color palette and every legend are fitted across the whole sequence at once, never per frame. That shared fitting is what makes a sequence worth trusting, and the fastest way to see why is to imagine a plot without it. If each frame fitted its own axis, 1952’s poorest countries and 2007’s would both be at the left edge. Even if incomes tripled, the points would not move from frame to frame. The only thing actually moving would be the axis, silently, with nothing on the page to say so. So free, which fits a scale to each panel, is refused on a played plot, as Faceting shows.
Because the frames share their scales, movement on the page is movement in the data. In the gapminder sequence this chapter opened with, the points genuinely move right and up, and a country whose point stays in place had no change in income or life expectancy.
The color palette is shared for a second reason. A reader follows a point by its color, so a palette that changed partway through would take away the one thing they are following. Every continent keeps its color in every frame, including frames where it happens to have no rows.
The statistics are not shared. A transform sees each frame’s rows as if they were the whole table, exactly as it sees a facet panel’s rows. That is the No Exceptions law, applied to frames. The gm_past60 table keeps the rows of gm_all where life expectancy is above 60 years:

title: 38  Play
text:
38.5 A layer with no frames
So far every layer in a plot has been cut into the same frames. A layer does not have to be. play is a channel, so it obeys the ordinary scope rule: written before any mark it reaches every layer, and written after one it binds that layer alone. A layer that never names it is drawn whole in every frame, which is how a fixed reference is drawn behind something that moves.

A play() written after one mark would pack that layer from one frame’s rows and the other layer from every row, so the names would land in the wrong regions. gog refuses that sentence and asks for play() before the marks.

One detail of the second table changes the number of frames, but not what the plot shows. thermal_marks calls its time column instant where thermals calls the same measurement second. The frames are gathered from every table that carries the played column, not only from the layer that bound play, on the same rule that gives the plot one scale rather than one per layer. If the marker had also called its column second, the route’s 170 samples would have set the frame count, and the sequence would have run 170 frames instead of 17.

title: 38  Play

38.6 How fast
Two sequences in this chapter have already carried speed = 3. A slow loop makes a reader wait for a pattern they have already seen. speed is a multiple of the normal pace, which shows a frame for 0.8 seconds. It is written inside the binding, the way scale and limits are written inside theirs, because it belongs to play and to nothing else:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + color(continent) +
  play(year, speed = 3)

  play(col.year, speed = 3))

  color(:continent) + play(:year, speed = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), play(col.year, { speed: 3 }))

“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, played by year at speed 3.”
These are the same twelve frames the chapter opened with, running three times as fast. speed = 0.5 would run them at half pace. speed exists for long sequences. The length of a loop is a default you did not choose, and the sentence does not show it. So when a sequence runs past thirty frames at the normal pace, gog reports how many seconds one loop takes.
When the played column holds numbers or dates, gog shows each frame for a time in proportion to the gap between its value and the next. Each sequence is timed against its own gaps: a frame whose gap is the middle one, when the gaps are put in order, shows for the normal 0.8 seconds. The gapminder years are all five years apart, so their frames all show for the same time. Here are the four years drawn as panels earlier, played by the number year instead of the category period:

  play(col.year))

“Given four of the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, played by year.”
Twenty years separate 1952 from 1972 and 1972 from 1992, so 1952 and 1972 show for 0.8 seconds. Only fifteen separate 1992 from 2007, so 1992 shows for 0.6. The last frame has no next value and shows for 0.8. Categories have an order but no distance between them, so the earlier play(period) shows every frame for the same time. A frame shows for at most four times the normal 0.8 seconds, so one long gap cannot make the sequence seem to stop. It shows for at least a quarter of 0.8 seconds, however short its gap.

Error:
! gog: `line` reads a function along `x`, but `year` both cuts the plot into frames and supplies `x` — so every frame holds a single `year`, and a line needs at least two positions to read between. Animate a different column — `play` is what the frames advance through, and `x(year)` is what the line draws along. Or use `point`, which places each row on its own and so needs no domain.

A line needs at least two positions to connect. If each frame holds one year, that frame has one position and no domain to draw across. Drawn anyway, the plot would be axes and a legend around an empty panel, with a frame strip counting up over it and nothing to say why. The refusal says why instead.
The engine refuses the same column split into panels, | facet(year), for the same reason: panels split the rows exactly as frames do. Marks that place each row on its own (point, bar, box) need no domain (no range of x) within a frame, so they draw in every frame:

title: 38  Play
text:
38.9 Frames in the cube
The gapminder table has a third measurement, population, and every country moves through the years. play does not depend on a flat plot. A frame is a subset of the rows, and the third position is a way of looking at whatever rows you have, so the two compose, and neither needed anything added for the other:

  color(col.continent) + play(col.year))

  z(:population) + color(:continent) + play(:year)

  z(col.population), color(col.continent), play(col.year))

“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, z is population, color by continent, played by year.”
Three of the kernel’s ideas meet in that sentence: the third position, the frames, and the selection. None of them was designed around the others, so they combine with no new rule. The sentence above uses two of them, and Selection adds the third to the same sentence.
The cube is fitted once across the whole sequence, exactly as a flat plot’s axes are. A box that resized itself per frame would move its own corners while the points stayed where they were, and every apparent motion would belong to the guide rather than to the countries. Fitted once, the height axis has room for 2007’s China from the first frame onward. That is why 1952 opens with the points low in the cube and only China and India far above the floor.
A transform inside the cube is the same transform. The floor is cut once from every frame’s rows and each frame then counts only its own into the cells, which is this chapter’s shared-cut rule read with a second axis present:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(life) + y(continent) + color(continent) +
  palette("okabe") + space() + play(year)

  palette("okabe") + space() + play(col.year))

  color(:continent) + palette("okabe") + space() + play(:year)

  color(col.continent), palette("okabe"), space(), play(col.year))

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 12, x is life, y is continent, color by continent, with the okabe palette, in the cube, played by year.”
Follow one continent’s row of bars rather than the whole floor. Each pile slides toward longer lives as the sequence runs, and it slides against cells that never move, so what you are watching is the countries changing which cell they fall in. color(continent) names the same column the y axis does, and it is there so that following one row is possible at all. A floor axis in a cube runs diagonally into the picture. Finding a row along that axis means tracing a receding edge while five rows of bars block the view. The legend names the row at once; the axis makes you trace it.
The sentence sets the palette by hand, and the cube is the reason for choosing the okabe set. A solid in space is shaded per face, so one category is already three tones before any two categories are compared. Shading has therefore narrowed the gap between hues before the reader looks, and a palette whose hues are close together narrows it again. Okabe and Ito’s eight are spaced for readers who cannot separate some hues at all, which is the same requirement as separating them once shading has removed a third of the light.
What the frames do not touch is the viewing angle. space(turn = , tilt = ) is a property of the space rather than of the data, so one angle serves the whole sequence and every frame is seen from the same place. That is a design choice, not something missing. A viewing angle that swung while the sequence played would add motion that no column asked for, and a reader would then have to separate it from the motion a column does explain. play moves the data, and the viewing angle stays fixed.
You can still turn the plot yourself while it runs, and that is not the same as a viewing angle that moves on its own. A reader who drags knows which motion is theirs, and can stop it. Turning matters more in this chapter than anywhere else in the book, because something is moving inside a solid shape. The only way to see what the near edge hides is to turn the cube and look from another side.
Panels and frames still compose in the cube. facet and play each split the rows by their own column, so crossing the two needs no new rule. Each panel draws its cube at whatever size its own rectangle allows.

  color(col.continent) + play(col.year) | facet(col.continent, wrap = 3))

  z(:population) + color(:continent) + play(:year) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  z(col.population), color(col.continent), play(col.year),
  across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))
