Wherever the flat plot is drawn, a drag selects only when it starts in its panel.
Alone, the cube has no other plot’s selection to show, so gog refuses its bare brush, as it refused brush(gdp) above. The message suggests two fixes: name the bound, or put the cube beside a brushed flat plot. A plot on a globe and a polar plot work the same way. Beside such a plot, a bare brush shows its selection, and alone it is refused.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.12 Changing the bound yourself
After the first one, every brushed plot in this chapter states where its selection starts. In the web edition, drag across a flat panel and your range replaces the sentence’s bound. The plot redraws as you drag. On a flow, a click on a slot moves the bound instead, as Selecting one place shows.
This changes nothing about the sentence, and the cube works the same way. space(turn =, tilt =) chooses the angle a plot starts at, and the pointer moves it from there. brush(gdp, at = ) chooses the bound a plot starts with, and the pointer replaces it from there. Drag to find a selection, read its two ends off the axis, and write them into the sentence.
In the PDF, each plot shows the bound its sentence asked for. That is why naming it matters even though a reader of the web edition can replace it: that reader starts from it too.
Like a bare brush, a brush that names a column but no at selects nothing until a reader drags. On a polar plot a drag never changes the selection. So there, as in the cube, a brush must name its bound, or show the selection of a flat plot beside it. Where the page cannot find a row explains why. A flow drawn in polar is the one exception, because a click on a slot selects.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.13 What the page adds
A flat brushed plot on a web page carries two lines of controls under it. None of them are in the sentence, and that is the rule rather than an omission. They report a selection, or they change how you look at one. Not one of them changes what the plot claims about the data, so none of them needs a word in the grammar. A plot in the cube follows the same rule: space() names the angle the plot starts at, and turning it needs no word. It carries two lines of controls, or three when it is brushed.
The first line is the one every plot carries:







Control
What it does




the magnifiers, − and +
Makes the picture smaller or larger


the frame button (four corners around a small square)
Returns to the whole picture


the camera
Saves what you are looking at as a picture file



It is first, directly under the picture, on a plain plot and a brushed one alike. This matters. A reader who has found the magnifiers once finds them in the same place under every plot in this book, rather than in a place that moves with whatever else the plot needed.
A plot that also plays carries three more buttons at the end of that same line, which pause the sequence and step through its frames. Play sets them out.
The second line is what a brush adds:



Control
What it does




drag: and its icons
Says what dragging the plot will do, and switches it: a rectangle, a free shape, or moving the picture. Absent on a flow, where a click on a slot selects. Absent also where no axis shows any column a brush names, because a drag there has no bound to change


40 of 142 selected
How many rows the current bound selects. On a played plot this counts every frame, not the one on screen. Plots composed with | or / share this count. When they read the same table, each row is counted once, and only if all their bounds select it


show rows
Opens a table of those rows; while the table is open the button reads hide rows. A long selection arrives ten at a time, with ‹ and › under the table


clear
Puts the selection back to what the sentence asked for


unstamp
Removes every stamp at once (Stamping a point explains stamps). With two or more, the button shows how many. Absent until you have made one



In the cube and on a polar plot, the line a brush adds holds only the count and show rows. In the cube it comes third, under the line that shows the angle. When a cube or a polar plot is beside a brushed flat plot, the arrangement carries the whole line, because a drag on the flat plot selects. With a cube, it is still the third line.
A control drawn as an icon names itself when the pointer rests on it. So do clear and unstamp, which say what they undo.

39.13.1 Dragging a box
A bound written in the sentence is a starting point, and a drag replaces it. Drag across the panel. A dotted box follows the pointer, and it shows exactly what is bound. On a plot with one brush the box spans the whole panel in the other direction, because that direction was not selected. On a plot with two, it is a rectangle. A box that narrowed an axis you never bound would claim a range you did not choose. The box disappears when you release the pointer, and from then on the dimming shows the bound.
Dragging in either direction gives the same bound, so you can start from any corner. A click on empty space empties the selection, so nothing is dimmed. A click that lands on a mark does something else, and Stamping a point is about that.


39.13.2 Drawing around a group
A rectangle is what a sentence can say. Some groups are not rectangles. The points of a scatter often form a shape: a narrow tail to one side, a curve, a group far from the rest. A box drawn around such a group includes points you did not mean.
The second icon beside drag: is the free shape. Choose it, then draw around the group with the pointer held down. The outline closes itself when you release the pointer, and everything inside it is selected. The count and the row table read exactly as they do for a box, because a shape and a bound ask the same question: which rows do you mean.
Nothing about the sentence changes. You do not type a shape, and the PDF still shows the bound the sentence named. Drawing one is a way of looking, like turning a cube, rather than a claim about the data.
That is also why the grammar has no word for it. Other tools call the gesture a lasso, and gog has no such word. Written down, a drawn shape is a long list of corner points, too long to type or read as part of a sentence. So you can draw the shape, but you cannot write it.
Two restrictions apply. A free shape needs two continuous axes, so where one axis is categorical the drag stays a rectangle. And clear removes a free shape and returns to the bound the sentence named. It cannot restore the shape, because no sentence can state a drawn shape.


39.13.3 Reading what you selected
The dimming shows where a group is, but not which rows are in it. The count says how many rows are selected, and show rows opens the row table. It lists the columns the sentence maps, not every column of your data, because the columns you did not plot are not what you are looking at. On a flow it also lists the columns named in flow(), so each row shows its place in each of them.
A long selection arrives ten rows at a time. The line under the table says which rows you are reading, as 11–20 of 40, and the two arrows beside it move you through the rest. Every row you selected is reachable, and none of them pushes the plot off the screen. A selection short enough to fit shows no arrows at all.
The row table lists every row you selected, with those columns, in one place, away from the picture. It shows country names only when the sentence maps country, as the labeled plot in Which one is that? does. Draw a bound tight around one point and the table lists that point alone.


39.13.4 Pointing at a mark
The row table shows which rows a group holds. Sometimes you want only the values behind one point. Rest the pointer on a mark, and a small card beside it shows the values of that mark’s row. The card lists the columns the sentence names, and nothing else from your table.
This needs no brush. The card appears on a point, a text label, a bar or a zone tile drawn with no transform. On a bar or a tile, it appears anywhere on the rectangle. Where the page cannot find a row lists the plots that show no card, and says why. Here is a scatter with no brush in its sentence. It uses the gapminder_2007 table, shown at the top of this chapter:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent))






                                                                                                                                                                                   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
In the web edition, rest the pointer on a point. The card shows that point’s continent, gdp and life. It does not name the country, because the sentence never names country. If the sentence sets how a number is written, as x(gdp, short = TRUE) does, the card writes it that way too (Writing the numbers). A date is written as a date, such as 2024-03-01, not as a number.
The card goes away when the pointer leaves the mark, and nothing stays on the picture. On a brushed plot, a click keeps the card on the picture, and the next section is about that. On a plot without brush, a click does nothing.


39.13.5 Stamping a point
The pointer shows one row’s values at a time, and they disappear as soon as you move away from the mark. That is right for a quick look and wrong for a comparison. Suppose three points on a scatter interest you. Reading them one after another means remembering the first two while you look at the third.
On a brushed plot, click a mark and its values stay. That is a stamp: a dot on the mark, a short line, and a small card saying what the pointer said. Click as many as you want to compare. The card is on the picture beside the mark it belongs to, which is the difference between a stamp and the row table. The row table names rows. A stamp labels the plot.
A card needs space on the picture. On a crowded scatter a card can cover the points you want to read. So drag a card and it goes where you put it. The line stretches to follow, and a long line ends in an arrowhead at the stamped point. Move four cards out to the edges and the picture underneath stays whole.
A card keeps the distance you gave it from its point. Zoom in, pan across, or drag a new bound, and the card moves with its point. Zoom far enough that the point leaves the picture on screen, and the whole stamp goes out of sight with it. It has nothing left to point at, and a card left over an unrelated corner would claim a point that is not there. Bring the point back and the card is where you left it.
A played plot works the same way, for the same reason. A row there is one country in one year, so a stamp made in 1972 names something the 1987 frame does not draw. The stamp is hidden while the other frames run, and it returns to its point when the sequence comes back to 1972. The card names the year it holds. Stamp the same country in three frames and each card appears in its own frame.
There are three ways to take a stamp off. The × in the corner of a card removes that card. Clicking the card itself does the same, as long as you did not move it: if the pointer moved between press and release, the click counted as a drag instead. unstamp removes every stamp at once.
clear does not remove the stamps, because a stamp is not a selection. A click on empty space does not remove them either. It empties the selection, so every point returns to full strength, and every stamp is still there. clear, unstamp and the frame button each undo one thing, which Three controls, three things sets out.
The camera saves the stamps too. Arrange the cards, press the camera, and the picture file carries the plot with your annotations on it, each card where you put it and each line pointing at its row. The camera saves what you are looking at, the same way it saves how far you have zoomed in and the angle a cube is turned to.
You do not type a stamp, and the PDF carries none.
A stamp is for deciding which points are worth naming. A plot with a name on every point is unreadable, and a plot with a name on the few that matter is the one you wanted. Stamping lets you try a few before you choose. Then put those rows in a small table of their own, give it to a text layer, and the picture carries the names itself, in the web edition and the PDF alike. A note is a layer shows how.
Arranging the cards by hand has a written form too. text * repel does the same job inside the sentence. Every label is placed outside its own dot, and one that moved far keeps a thin line back to the point it names. That is the stamp’s line again, written down rather than dragged. Stamp to decide what is worth naming, then write the labels down and let repel place them.
A stamp is for looking at the data. text is for telling a reader what it says.
Both can go into a presentation, and they are not the same there. A saved picture is fixed: it keeps one moment of one session and cannot be drawn again. A sentence with text in it draws again for anyone who has the data, in the PDF and on the page and in all four languages. Stamp and save to keep this one picture. Write the labels down to keep the plot itself.


39.13.6 Where the page cannot find a row
On a polar plot, the pointer shows no values, with a brush or without one. The reason is how the page finds the row under the pointer. From each row’s own values and the values at the ends of each axis, it computes where that row was drawn. That is exact when both axes are straight lines. A polar plot has no straight axes: it draws x as an angle and y as a distance from the center.
So the pointer shows nothing, rather than the values of the wrong row. Nothing can be stamped either. The page never reads positions from the picture itself. It only computes them.
The same reason applies to a drag. The page would read the box you drag as a range of values on a straight axis. On a polar plot, the rows in that range are drawn somewhere else, not under the box. So on a brushed polar plot, a drag never changes the selection.
The bound the sentence names still works: gog tests it against each row’s values, so the count and the dimmed marks agree. That is why gog accepts a brush with a bound on a polar plot, and no brush on a map. As in the cube, you choose the selection by naming the bound in the sentence, or by dragging across a flat plot beside the polar plot (A cube beside a flat plot). On a polar plot alone, a brush with no at would never select a row, so gog refuses it.
Here the medal bars from What can be brushed are bent into a circle. The bound in the sentence still selects China and Great Britain, as it did on straight axes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + polar() +
  brush(gold, at = c(20, 40))


(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + polar() +
  brush(col.gold, at = [20, 40]))


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + polar() +
  brush(:gold, at = [20, 40])


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), polar(),
  brush(col.gold, { at: [20, 40] }))






                            USA China Great Britain Russia Germany   10 20 30 40  Gold Country





“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, in polar, and let the reader select gold, starting from 20 to 40.”
In the web edition, drag across it: the selection does not change. A flow drawn in polar is the exception: a click on a slot selects, as Selecting a place in either column shows.
In the cube, as on a polar plot, the pointer shows no values, and nothing can be stamped. There the viewing angle moves every mark, so the page cannot compute where each row was drawn.
The pointer still shows values on a plot with a layer whose marks are not drawn at their rows’ values. jitter sets each point beside its value, repel moves each label away from the others, and a summary such as bin or mean draws one shape for many rows. As What can be brushed showed, a layer like that either refuses the brush or is drawn whole beside a layer that answers it. The pointer then reads that other layer, whose marks are drawn at their values. A flow is the exception. Its layers answer the brush, but none of its marks is drawn at a row’s value, so the pointer shows no values there.
Without a brush, the card passes the same test: it appears only on marks drawn at their own row’s values. A plot drawn only by a summary, such as bar * count or bar * mean, shows none, because each bar summarizes many rows. A line, a step, a path, an area or a box draws one shape through many rows, so it shows none either. A rule has one position, and the page needs two to find a row, so it shows none. Neither does a layer under jitter, dodge, stack or repel, because each of those moves a mark away from its own value. Add a layer that draws each mark at its row’s values, such as point, and the card appears on that layer’s marks. In polar, in the cube, on a map and on a globe, no layer shows it.
One more limit is size. A plot without brush whose table has more than 20,000 rows shows no card, because carrying all those rows would make the page much larger. Your data on the page says what the page carries.


39.13.7 Looking closer
A crowded corner is easier to read when it is larger. + and − magnify the picture, and the frame button returns to the whole of it. Zooming in switches the drag to panning, because a reader who has just looked closer usually wants to move around inside the picture. The frame button sets the drag back to selecting. You can switch by hand at any time with the icons beside drag:. The pointer also tells you which mode you are in: a crosshair to draw a box, an open hand to move the picture. A brushed polar plot has no drag: icons, because a drag there never selects. There, once you zoom in, a drag moves the picture.
A plot whose axes show no column a brush names has a third shape: a plain arrow. A drag there has no bound to change, so it draws no box. Resting the pointer on a point still shows its card, and a click still stamps it. Once you zoom in, a drag moves the picture, as on a polar plot.
This is a view, so it recomputes nothing. The bars are the same bars and the ticks are the same ticks, drawn larger. Zoom far enough into a histogram and you will see the same bins, not finer ones. If you want the statistics re-run over a narrower range, that is limits, the atom this chapter compared with brush.


39.13.8 Three controls, three things
Three of these controls undo something, and pressing the wrong one removes work you meant to keep. clear acts on the selection, unstamp acts on the stamps, and the frame button acts on the view. Each one undoes only its own thing, so pressing one never costs you the other two. The frame button is on the line above the other two, beside the magnifiers. It puts back the view they changed.
The × on a card is a fourth undo, and it is not under the plot at all. It belongs to the card rather than to the plot. A control under the picture acts on the whole plot: all the stamps, the whole selection or the whole view. A control on a card acts on that card alone.
The PDF has none of these controls, and it shows the bound the sentence named.


39.13.9 Your data on the page
Before you publish a plot on a web page, know what data it carries. Two kinds of plot in this chapter need the table in the page. The browser redraws a brushed plot as the reader drags, and it reads the rows of a plot that shows the card. In both, the page carries every row of the table, but only the columns the sentence names.
The rows are all there, though, each with its exact values in the columns the page carries. So check those values before you publish, the way you would check any file before sharing it. A plot without brush whose table has more than 20,000 rows carries none of its rows, and shows no card. Plots that carry the table lists every kind of plot that carries its table, and what a saved SVG file carries instead.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.14 In short
A selection runs after the axes and statistics are computed: it dims rows, removes none, and leaves the axes where they were. The column decides the reading, a range for numbers and a set for categories. A bound tests a column’s values rather than a panel, so the brushed plots of one table share one selection. Everything a brush needs is already inside the web page: every row of the table, but only the columns the sentence names.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.15 What comes next
Selection is the last atom this book teaches. The chapters so far started from the grammar; the cookbook starts from your data instead: one variable first, then two, then more.

title: The cookbook
text:
The 1446 book ends its explanations with a list: ninety-four everyday words, written out in the new letters. Persimmon, ice, tiger, star. It shows usage, not rules: the new letters could spell the words of daily life.
You have now met every word of gog, and every way of joining them into a sentence. What is left is practice on real questions. This part is gog’s version of the 1446 list. It is organized by your columns and your question, because you know those before you know a chart’s name. You will not find a chapter called “Histograms”. You will find a recipe called How is a measurement distributed?, and the sentence that answers it. (If you already know the chart’s name, the chart names appendix translates it into a sentence.)
The recipes use the book’s shared tables, which you can download from The book’s data. Each recipe chapter shows the first rows of every shared table before drawing from it. The recipes use only atoms taught in Parts I to III, and most link back to the chapters that own their atoms.
Almost every recipe has the same shape: the question, the sentence that answers it, the plot, and a line or two on why it works. Many then show what is one atom away: the same sentence with one small change, such as an atom swapped or one of its arguments changed. That is the real lesson. A cookbook of finished charts teaches you charts. This one teaches you that the recipes are connected: swap one atom in a recipe and you have another.
Most chapters are named for your columns: one variable, two, three or more, values over time, many groups. If you know your goal but not the chapter that answers it, start from the table below. Each row links to the recipes and chapters that answer it, in this part or an earlier one:

title: 40  One variable

40.1 How many of each?
You have one column. What can it tell you? Which question you can ask depends on the column’s type. With a categorical column you ask how many rows fall in each category. With a continuous column you ask how the values spread. When the table is small, there is a third question: whether to summarize the rows at all.

title: 40  One variable
section: 40.2 What share of the whole is each?
text:
40.2 What share of the whole is each?
In both count plots above, Africa has the longest bar: 52 countries. A count alone cannot say whether 52 is many or few. The table holds 142 countries in all, so Africa holds 52 of the 142, a share of about 0.37. When the question is each continent’s share of the whole, swap count for proportion. The counts become fractions that sum to one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent.”
One atom away. Swap proportion back to count for the counts themselves. The bars above follow the order the continents first appear in the table. To draw them in another order, use order(), which sorts them by the values in a column of the table: order(continent) sorts them alphabetically, by their own names. The transform writes the share into its own output, not into your table, so order(proportion) finds no column to sort by and is refused. Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length.” The gap near 2.5 cm is an empty bin. No flower in the table has a petal length between 1.9 and 3.0 cm. One species has much shorter petals than the other two, and the empty bin is part of the space between them.
One atom away. When the automatic choice makes the shape hard to read, give bin a number of bins or a bin width. bin(30) asks for thirty bins; bin(width = 0.5) asks for bins 0.5 cm wide:

The width 0.5 suits these lengths: they are recorded to one decimal place, so every bin holds exactly five possible values. Choosing a width explains how to pick a width for your own column.
A line * bin is the frequency polygon: a line through the same counts, placed at the center of each bin. Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

title: 40  One variable
text:
40.4 What is its smooth shape?
A histogram’s shape depends on the choice of bin edges. A reader can mistake that choice for a feature of the data. When the shape of the distribution itself is the answer, density draws a curve with no bin edges at all. Here is the histogram’s own column again, the petal lengths:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(col.petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(line, density), x(col.petal_length))






                               0 2 4 6 8   0.0 0.1 0.2  Density Petal Length





“Given the iris flowers: a line derived by density, x is petal length.” This answers the question the histogram answered, for the same column, with density in place of bin and a line to draw it. The two groups of petals are now two peaks, and the valley between them lies over the empty bin.
The curve starts below zero, although no petal is shorter than 1 cm. A density spreads each row into a small smooth bump, and the bumps of the shortest petals reach past zero.
The width of each bump is the bandwidth, and it sets how smooth the curve is. A number written alone multiplies the default bandwidth: density(0.5) is half as smooth as the default and density(2) is twice as smooth. density(bandwidth = 0.5) sets the bandwidth itself instead, in the column’s own unit, so here it is half a centimeter. Write one of the two forms, never both.
A histogram and a density curve can show a different number of peaks, because a wide bin or a wide bandwidth can merge two peaks into one. When the number of peaks matters, draw the histogram and the curve together. Put each in a plot of its own, and join the two plots with /, which places the first above the second:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length)) /
  (data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(petal_length))


((data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(col.petal_length)) /
  (data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(col.petal_length)))


(data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(:petal_length)) /
  (data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(:petal_length))


below(plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, bin), x(col.petal_length)),
  plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(line, density), x(col.petal_length)))






                                       0 10 20 30 40  Count


                            2 4 6   0.0 0.1 0.2  Density Petal Length






“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, above a line derived by density, x is petal length.”
The two plots read the same column, so they share one x axis. The curve’s two peaks are below the two groups of bars, so here the two groups are not an effect of the bins or of the bandwidth. Each plot keeps its own y axis. A bar counts the flowers in its bin, and the curve’s height is the share of flowers per centimeter of petal length.
In this arrangement, the curve is cut at the shortest and the longest petal. So it begins at 1 cm, high in its panel, rather than below zero. The marginal plot explains why a shared axis cuts it.
You might first try to draw the curve over the bars, in one panel. The tallest bar counts 44 flowers, and the curve never rises above 0.3, so on one axis the curve would lie flat along the bottom. gog refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + line * density + x(col.petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + line * density + x(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, bin), layer(line, density),
  x(col.petal_length))

40.5 How does the distribution look as a staircase?
The histogram drew bin with bar. step can draw it too, tracing the bin tops as a staircase outline with no fill. It is most useful when several distributions share one axis, as in Many groups, because unfilled outlines do not cover each other. This plot draws the histogram’s distribution again, so you can compare the two marks directly:

data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(col.petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(step, bin), x(col.petal_length))

“Given the iris flowers: a step outline derived by bin, x is petal length.”
This is the histogram’s sentence with one atom changed, step in place of bar. The bins are the same, the empty one included, and only the mark that draws them changed. With the line * bin named earlier, that is three marks on one transform. That is the No Exceptions law: a transform behaves the same on every mark. Owning chapters: Step, Transforms.

41.1 Are two measurements related?
You have two columns. What can they tell you together? The two kinds of column, continuous and categorical, decide which question you can ask. A category and a measurement ask about comparison: is the measurement larger in some groups than in others?

title: 41  Two variables
section: 41.2 What is the trend through the points?
text:
41.2 What is the trend through the points?
The first scatter in this chapter draws one dot for each of 142 countries. The dots show that life expectancy rises with GDP per person. Below $5,000, though, they spread from 40 to 74 years, so the typical value is hard to see. You want the trend, and you still want every country on the page. Layering a derived line over the points gives you both. + puts both marks in one panel, and * smooth fits one trend curve through all the points:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth))






                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
The curve climbs steeply on the left and much more slowly on the right. Most of its rise happens below $10,000 of GDP per person. At the far right the curve runs above the dots of the five richest countries. A smooth curve is least reliable at the edge of the data, where there are few points.
The positions are written before any mark, so both layers share them. color is written after point, so only the points are split into one group per continent. The curve is fitted to all 142 countries, not to any one continent. Owning chapters: Transforms for smooth, Encoding scope for that rule.
A curve shows the shape of a trend, but it does not give the trend as one number. On a log scale of GDP the dots lie close to a straight line, as the first recipe in this chapter showed. So a straight line is a good summary of them. * straight fits the least-squares line, and ribbon * straight_band adds the band that shows how precisely the line is known:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  ribbon * straight_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * straight


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  ribbon * straight_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * straight)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + point +
  color(:continent) + ribbon * straight_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * straight


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  point, color(col.continent), layer(ribbon, straight_band),
  style({ opacity: 0.3 }), layer(line, straight))






                                                                                                                                                                                 1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a ribbon derived by straight_band, and also a line derived by straight.”
The slope of the line gives the trend as one number: about 16.6 more years of life expectancy for each tenfold rise in GDP per person, such as from $1,000 to $10,000. The band is only a few years wide, because 142 countries are enough to know the line precisely. Even so, most countries lie outside it. The band describes the line, not the countries. Owning chapters: Transforms for straight and straight_band, Scales for why the line is fitted against the logarithm.

Sometimes the question is not whether sales rose but how large they were in each year. A line says where the value was; an area says how much there was. The fill is the quantity, so it starts from zero:

title: 41  Two variables
section: 41.4 What is the typical value per group?
text:
41.4 What is the typical value per group?
The last question in the opening was comparison, which pairs a category with a measurement. Each continent holds many countries, and each country has its own life expectancy. To compare the continents you need one number for each, so you summarize the measurement within each category. The transforms that summarize this way are the aggregation family: sum, mean, median, max, min and quantile. Each one groups the rows by the category and reduces the measurement to one value per group. Only quantile needs a number of its own, the probability: quantile(0.9) gives the 90th percentile of each group. Here is mean, the average life expectancy in each continent:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
Oceania’s countries average 81 years and Europe’s 78, while Africa’s average 55.
One atom away. A few very high or very low values can change a mean noticeably. They change a median much less. When that matters, swap mean for median:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, median), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by median, x is continent, y is life.”
Africa’s bar falls by about two years and Asia’s rises by about the same. The other three change by less than a year. Where the two bars differ, a few very high or very low values have moved the mean. In Africa, seven countries live 71 to 76 years, well above the other 45. Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

title: 41  Two variables
section: 41.5 What does every value per group look like?
text:
41.5 What does every value per group look like?
A bar * mean gives each continent one number. That number hides how much life expectancy differs among the continent’s countries. Sometimes you want to see every country, not the mean. The plot that shows every row is the strip plot. Its sentence differs from the bar * mean sentence in two places: * mean is gone, and point is written where bar was. Each row is one dot, at its own height in its category’s slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life))






                                                                                                                                                                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life.”
On each vertical line, dots with nearly the same value cover each other, and * jitter spreads them sideways. It moves them along the categorical axis only, so every dot keeps its exact height. gog never draws a point at a value that was not measured, not even to keep points from covering each other, so on two measured axes it refuses jitter. style() sets a value instead of mapping a column. Here it sets opacity to 0.6, below the default, so you can see where the dots overlap:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.6)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.6)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.6)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.6 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life.”
One atom away. Swap the positions and the strips run horizontally, which helps when the category names are long. Owning chapters: Point, Transforms, Setting vs mapping.

title: 41  Two variables
text:
41.7 What this section refuses
Every recipe in this chapter used at least one continuous column. Suppose both of your columns are categorical, a country and its continent. You write bar, with one column on each axis. A bar needs at least one continuous axis, because the value on that axis is what sets the length of the bar. Two categories give the bar nothing to measure. The one number you can still make from them is a count of rows, so the refusal names count:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(country) + y(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(:country) + y(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), bar, x(col.country), y(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bar` has categorical columns on both axes — `x(country)` and `y(continent)` — so there is nothing for it to measure. One axis must hold a continuous column: that is the length of the bar. To count the rows instead, count one column, `bar * count + x(country)` or `bar * count + x(continent)`, and `color()` splits each bar by the other. To keep both, `bar * count + x(country) + y(continent) + space()` draws one bar on each pair in the cube.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Adding * count to this sentence still refuses. bar * count draws its count along the axis that has no column, so on the flat page one axis must stay empty. To keep both, the message adds space(), which draws one bar on each pair in the cube. To count the countries in each continent, remove country and write bar * count + x(continent), the sentence of How many of each?.

title: 42  A third variable, and more
text:
42.1 Which plot fits which columns?
You have more columns than the flat page has positions. Where do the rest go? x and y are already taken. A further variable can go in one of four places. The first is a refining channel: color, size, shape, pattern or opacity. The second is the third position, z. The third is play, which gives the variable one frame per value, and the fourth is facet, which gives it one panel per value. This chapter uses all four. Each channel answers one kind of question, and a refining channel gets the legend that decodes it. When many measurements matter equally, there is a fifth place: x itself. Each value of each measurement becomes a row, and the measurement names become the categories on x.
The recipes in this chapter start from a question. If you start from your table instead, find the row below that describes your columns, and follow its links:
A table often has more columns than one plot can show. Choose the columns that answer your question, and leave the others out.

42.4 How big is each observation?
The last two recipes put a category on a channel. This one puts a measurement there, and it returns to the countries. Population is a third measurement of each country, and both positions are already taken by GDP per person and life expectancy. A magnitude is carried by size. That channel answers the question how much, so it accepts a continuous column and nothing else:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  size(population)

title: 42  A third variable, and more
text:
42.5 What if four variables matter?
The recipes so far bound color to the continent and size to the population, one column at a time. You may need both at once, to see which continent a country is in and how many people live there. Channels compose: any channel a mark accepts works beside any other channel it accepts. That rule is Orthogonality. GDP per person, life expectancy, population and continent in one sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + size(col.population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + size(:population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), size(col.population),
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007"))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  The health and wealth of nations, 2007 Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
Every channel keeps its own rule and its own legend; none of them changed meaning by being combined. Four variables are usually the most a single plot can carry. Beyond four, use panels instead of more channels.

section: 42.6 What if the third variable is continuous?
text:
42.6 What if the third variable is continuous?
Now return to three columns. A continuous third column does not have to go on size. Here population goes on color instead, so every dot keeps the same size and the color carries the number. color accepts either kind of column. A continuous column gets a sequential ramp, from light to dark, instead of a categorical palette. A skewed column reads better on a log ramp. On a linear ramp, China and India would be alone at the dark end, and almost every other country would get the same light shade:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population, { scale: "log" }))






                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Population         1.3B 16.2M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population on a log scale.”
The legend becomes a labeled ramp. The channel and its rule did not change; only the kind of column did. Scales owns the log scale.

title: 42  A third variable, and more
section: 42.7 What if three measurements matter equally?
text:
42.7 What if three measurements matter equally?
The iris flowers from the grayscale recipe above carry three measurements each, and none of them is less important than the others. color or size would make the third measurement a refinement, and the plot would still be about the other two. When three measurements matter equally, the third one is a position, not a refinement. Put one measurement on each of x, y and z, and the plot becomes a cube:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species)


(data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.sepal_width) + z(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species))


data(iris_flowers) + point + x(:sepal_length) + y(:sepal_width) +
  z(:petal_length) + color(:species)


plot(data(iris_flowers), point, x(col.sepal_length), y(col.sepal_width),
  z(col.petal_length), color(col.species))






                                                                                                                                                                               8 7 6 5 4 3 2 6 4 2 Sepal Length Sepal Width Petal Length   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal length, color by species.”
Setosa is separate from the others, near the bottom of the cube, because its petals are short. Versicolor and virginica are higher, and from this side they overlap.
One atom away. The viewing angle is a property of the space, not of the data. turn says which side of the cube you look at, and tilt says how high your eye is:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species) +
  space(turn = -50, tilt = 15)


(data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.sepal_width) + z(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) +
  space(turn = -50, tilt = 15))


data(iris_flowers) + point + x(:sepal_length) + y(:sepal_width) +
  z(:petal_length) + color(:species) + space(turn = -50, tilt = 15)


plot(data(iris_flowers), point, x(col.sepal_length), y(col.sepal_width),
  z(col.petal_length), color(col.species), space({ turn: -50, tilt: 15 }))






                                                                                                                                                                               8 7 6 5 4 3 2 6 4 2 Sepal Length Sepal Width Petal Length   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal length, color by species, turned -50, tilted 15.”
From this side versicolor and virginica overlap less. Space owns the third dimension.

title: 42  A third variable, and more
section: 42.8 What if four or more measurements matter equally?
text:
42.8 What if four or more measurements matter equally?
A cube has room for three measurements. The iris flowers have a fourth, petal width, and a table can have many more. A parallel coordinates plot gives each measurement a slot of its own on x, and draws each flower as one line through its values.
For that, the table needs one row for each flower and measurement, with the measurement’s name in one column and its value in another. Making that table is not gog’s job: gog never reshapes a table, as The table has to be tidy explains. You make it before you write the sentence, with the data manipulation tools of the language you are already using: tidyr::pivot_longer() in R, pandas.melt() in Python, DataFrames.stack() in Julia, or a short loop in JavaScript. iris_measurements holds the 150 flowers that way, in 600 rows:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
  line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3)


(data(iris_measurements) + x(col.measurement) + y(col.cm) + color(col.species) +
  line + group(col.flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3))


data(iris_measurements) + x(:measurement) + y(:cm) + color(:species) +
  line + group(:flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) + line * mean +
  style(size = 3)


plot(data(iris_measurements), x(col.measurement), y(col.cm),
  color(col.species), line, group(col.flower), style({ opacity: 0.2 }),
  layer(line, mean), style({ size: 3 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                           sepal length sepal width petal length petal width   0 2 4 6 8  Cm Measurement  Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris measurements: x is measurement, y is cm, color by species, lines grouped by flower, with opacity 0.2, and also lines derived by mean, with size 3.”
Each measurement is one slot on x, in the order it first appears in the table. The sentence has two line layers. In the first, group(flower) splits the 600 rows into 150 faint lines, and each line joins one flower’s four values. group(flower) is written after the first line, so it splits that layer alone. The second layer is line * mean. color(species) is written before both marks, so it splits both layers, and in each slot mean averages the flowers of each species. Each species gets one thick line through its four means, and the faint lines show how far each flower is from its species’ line. Each country and its continent’s mean or median uses the same two layers.
The three thick lines have three different shapes. Setosa’s line is low in both petal slots, far below the other two species. Virginica has the longest and widest petals, and versicolor’s petals are between those of setosa and virginica.
One atom away. Add polar(), and the slots are spread around a circle. Each flower’s line closes into a star. This is the radar chart from Line, drawn once for each flower instead of once through the continents’ means:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
  line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3) + polar()


(data(iris_measurements) + x(col.measurement) + y(col.cm) + color(col.species) +
  line + group(col.flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3) + polar())


data(iris_measurements) + x(:measurement) + y(:cm) + color(:species) +
  line + group(:flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) + line * mean +
  style(size = 3) + polar()


plot(data(iris_measurements), x(col.measurement), y(col.cm),
  color(col.species), line, group(col.flower), style({ opacity: 0.2 }),
  layer(line, mean), style({ size: 3 }), polar())






                                                                                                                                                                             sepal length sepal width petal length petal width   0 2 4 6 8  Cm Measurement  Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris measurements: x is measurement, y is cm, color by species, lines grouped by flower, with opacity 0.2, and also lines derived by mean, with size 3, in polar.”
The ring marked 0 is a small ring at the center, so each arm grows with the measurement in centimeters. Sepal length has the largest values, so every star is longest toward sepal length. The three thick stars, one for each species, have three shapes. Setosa’s star has very short petal arms. Virginica’s star is the largest toward every slot except sepal width.
All four measurements are in centimeters, so they share the y axis as they are. Every slot shares that one axis. So when the units differ, such as dollars and years, the measurement with the largest numbers sets the range of the axis, and the lines of the others look almost flat. In that case, standardize each measurement before you plot: subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation. Every measurement then has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Like the reshaping, this is a step for the data manipulation tools of your language, done before you write the sentence. The iris measurements need no such step, but standardizing them shows something new: 0 becomes the average in every slot. The standardized column holds the result:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(standardized) + color(species) +
  line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3)


(data(iris_measurements) + x(col.measurement) + y(col.standardized) + color(col.species) +
  line + group(col.flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3))


data(iris_measurements) + x(:measurement) + y(:standardized) +
  color(:species) + line + group(:flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) +
  line * mean + style(size = 3)


plot(data(iris_measurements), x(col.measurement), y(col.standardized),
  color(col.species), line, group(col.flower), style({ opacity: 0.2 }),
  layer(line, mean), style({ size: 3 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                       sepal length sepal width petal length petal width   -2 0 2  Standardized Measurement  Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris measurements: x is measurement, y is standardized, color by species, lines grouped by flower, with opacity 0.2, and also lines derived by mean, with size 3.”
The axis is no longer in centimeters. Its unit is the standard deviation, and 0 in each slot is the mean of that measurement over all 150 flowers. A line above 0 marks a flower larger than average on that measurement. Setosa’s thick line is the only one above 0 in the sepal width slot, and it is the lowest in both petal slots.

In the iris cube two sections above, each flower is its own dot, and the order of the rows means nothing. Sometimes the order is what matters. Here are the two gliders from Path again. Each row records where one glider was at one moment, and that glider’s next row is two seconds later. So the rows have to be joined in the order they were recorded. The mark that joins rows in table order is path:

data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) +
  color(col.glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + title("Two gliders, one thermal")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), title("Two gliders, one thermal"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude  Two gliders, one thermal  Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider.”
Each route rises because each glider gains altitude. Both gliders start at 900 meters and were recorded for the same 338 seconds. Bravo’s first point is drawn higher than Alpha’s, but only because it is at the back of the cube. In this view, the back is drawn higher on the page. By the end, Bravo has reached about 2,500 meters and Alpha about 2,100, so Bravo climbs faster.
Nothing in the sentence draws a spiral. The sentence asks path to connect the rows in order. Each glider moves in a circle while it rises, so the connected rows form a spiral. Look at the crossings as well. At each one the route nearer to the eye is drawn over the route behind it, and which route is nearer changes as the two gliders climb. Neither route is drawn entirely in front of the other: the pieces of both routes are sorted by depth together, as Path explains.
Turn the view, and the same two routes answer a different question. No binding changes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(glider) +
  space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) +
  color(col.glider) +
  space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), space({ turn: 20, tilt: 80 }),
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude  The same two routes, seen from overhead  Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider, turned 20, tilted 80.”
Seen from nearly overhead the climb is no longer visible, and you are looking down at two circles, one inside the other. Bravo’s circle is half as wide as Alpha’s. Together, the two views show that Bravo climbs faster and turns in a tighter circle.
These two plots raise one more question. line, step, area and ribbon also join their rows, so why is path the only one of the five that takes z? The answer is the difference that separates path from line on the flat page: the order in which each one joins its rows. A path joins rows in the table’s order. That order does not depend on any axis, so a third axis does not change it. A line sorts its rows by x. In the cube, x is one of three equal positions. At some angles it points straight into the page, and then you cannot see the order the line was sorted in. That is why a rising route is drawn with path, and why line refuses z rather than draw a stroke you cannot read:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + line + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider)


data(thermals) + line + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + color(col.glider)


data(thermals) + line + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider)


plot(data(thermals), line, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider))




Error:
! gog: `line` reads a *domain* left to right — it sorts by `x` and draws one value for each — and a cube has no left to right: `x` is one of three equal positions, and at some viewing angles it runs into the page and becomes depth. A `line` in space would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see, so this is refused rather than drawn. For a route through three dimensions use `path`, which is `line` with that sort removed: `path + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(altitude)`.

“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by magnitude.”
Color carries a fourth column here, the magnitude of each quake. The vertical axis is elevation, the height above sea level, so a quake 680 km down has the value −680. That is the deepest quake in the table.
The quakes are not scattered through the cube. They trace a sheet of ocean floor sinking into the earth. At this angle, east is on the left. The sheet begins near the surface at the eastern edge and dips west. About a third of the way from that edge, it is more than 600 km down. The shallower quakes farther west do not lie on this sheet. They form a separate group. That sheet lies in three dimensions, so drawing it takes three positions. Any two of them show it flattened onto the page.
Now cut the quakes into slices of depth and show the slices one after another. play(slab) steps through slab, a column that holds the depth in 90 km bands:

  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) + play(slab)

  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) + play(col.slab))

  z(col.elevation), space({ turn: 120, tilt: 20 }), play(col.slab))

The frames are not time here. play advances through the levels of an ordered column, and whether that column measures years or kilometers is a fact about the column, not about play. The same atom that steps through years steps through depths here.
In the PDF, only the first frame is drawn, the slice from 0 to 90 km, and the panels below replace the motion. They lay the same slices out across the page instead of showing them one after another in time:

“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, split into panel columns by slab, wrapped at 4.”
The eight panels share one set of scales. You compare two depths by looking from one panel to the next, not by remembering the frame that just played. Whether you choose panels or frames depends on your readers. Panels let them compare any two slices, and frames let them see the movement. Play owns that choice.

title: 42  A third variable, and more
section: 42.11 What if every column is categorical?
text:
42.11 What if every column is categorical?
Every recipe above had at least one measurement. Some tables have none, only categories. The storms on the globe in Play can be described this way. Each storm begins in one month and one hemisphere, and has one category on the Saffir-Simpson scale of strength, from 1, the weakest, to 5. Nothing can go on a continuous axis until you count the storms. The globe’s table has a row for every twelve hours of each storm, so gog’s count would count those positions, not storms. Making one row per storm and counting the storms is a step for the data manipulation tools of your language, like the reshaping for parallel coordinates. storm_seasons holds the counts for the 2,174 storms of hurricane strength from 1980 to 2025. Each storm is counted once: in the month and hemisphere where its track begins, and in the category of its strongest wind. category holds the digits 1 to 5 as names, so gog_table() needs its text argument for this table (Labels that look like numbers shows it in all four languages):



storm_seasons: first 5 of 98 rows


month
category

The two seasons fall in opposite halves of the year. In the Northern Hemisphere most storms begin from June to November, and September has the most, 378. In the Southern Hemisphere most begin from December to April, February has the most, 142, and no storm began in July or August. “Given the storm seasons: zones, x is month, y is category, color by storms, ordered by category, largest first, split into panel columns by hemisphere.”
Each tile is one count, and an empty cell is a month and category with no storm. The three darkest tiles are all in the north: category 1 in August and September, 116 and 111, and category 4 in September, 103. A shade is harder to compare than a length. So the rose shows the shape of each season more clearly, and the tiles give each count its own place, by month and category.
Two other charts are made for tables of categories. A mosaic gives each combination an area as large as its count. An alluvial diagram makes each column a stage, and carries each count from one stage to the next in a band.

The storm tiles had an order on both axes, months and categories. The nutrients table has none. It gives the amount of five nutrients in each of eight foods. The question is which foods resemble each other, and which nutrients are found in the same foods. As with the storms, the amount goes on color in a tile plot. How did a measurement change over time? Time is not a chart type in this grammar. It is a column like any other, and you decide where it goes. Most recipes here put it on x, which gives the familiar time series. One gives it to play instead, to show where earthquakes happened, one week at a time. The last section asks for one panel per year, which gog refuses.

A zone needs sides, and a year is a number, which has no width. bin(width = 5) gives the years their sides. In Iraq, it fell from 65.0 years in 1987 to 59.5 in 1992, and it was still below 65 in 2007. Owning chapters: Zone, Channels.

Scales owns the calendar’s rules.

Fifty-three frames: 52 full weeks, and a last one that holds only December 31. A typical week adds about 40 new earthquakes, most of them along the edges of the Pacific. The frame for the week of March 5 adds 335, and 303 of them lie off the coast of Japan. Twenty-six of them came in the two days before the magnitude 9.1 earthquake. The rest are the magnitude 9.1 earthquake itself and 276 aftershocks, the smaller earthquakes that follow a large one, in the 18 hours that remained in the week. The same preparation works for any event that should stay visible for several frames. Repeat its row once for each of those frames, and add a column that says how old each copy is. Owning chapters: Play, Globe.
One atom away. Swap globe(turn = 150, tilt = 15) for map(), and the whole earth shows at once, flattened. The earthquakes on the far side of this globe, in the Americas and along the middle of the Atlantic, then come into view. Map owns the flat version.

title: 43  Over time
text:
43.7 What this section refuses
The recipes so far put time on x or gave it to play. Suppose instead you want one scatter of GDP per person and life expectancy for each year, with the years side by side. One panel per year is what faceting does. A facet column names its panels, so it must be categorical, but year is a continuous column. gog refuses the sentence, and the message names two fixes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(year)


data(gapminder_asia) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) | facet(col.year)


data(gapminder_asia) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:year)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.year))




Error:
! gog: `facet(year)` splits on a continuous column, but a facet names its panels, so it needs a categorical column. Cut `year` into named groups first, such as small and large, or store it as text for one panel per value (it holds 12 different values, so that is 12 panels).
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The second fix turns year into text, and the message counts what that would draw here: 12 panels, one for each year. The gm_eras table already holds two of the years as text, in the column era. Many groups draws a plot split by era, with one row of panels for each of the two years.

title: 44  Many groups

44.1 How do the groups’ distributions compare?
How do several groups compare? There are two ways to separate the groups. You can split the marks inside one panel, with color or group. You can split the plot into panels, with | or /. The recipes below use both. Two of them also put the groups in an order you choose.
The first way is to split the marks. The iris_flowers table holds three species, and every row carries a petal length. The question is whether those lengths overlap or are separate. An overlaid histogram answers it: one histogram per species, drawn in one panel. bin cuts the axis into intervals, called bins, and it cuts one set of bins from all the rows, so every species is counted into the same bins. Nothing in the sentence below asks for transparency. The engine draws each species as a translucent fill under its own solid outline, so a fill that lies under another is still visible:

section: 44.2 What if the overlap gets worse?
text:
44.2 What if the overlap gets worse?
Three translucent fills are still readable. With more groups, or with groups closer together, the overlaps blend into one dark band, and you can no longer see where one fill ends. Remove the fills entirely: step * bin draws each group’s outline as an unfilled staircase. A thin outline hides almost nothing behind it:

data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(col.petal_length) + color(col.species)


data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(:petal_length) + color(:species)

  color(col.species))

“Given the iris flowers: step outlines derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species.”
Only the mark changed, from bar to step. Each group is now one outline rather than a filled area, so far less of the plot is covered. Near 5 cm, versicolor’s outline steps down where virginica’s steps up, and both lines stay visible. Step owns the staircase.

44.6 Which group is biggest?
The medals table lists five countries, and the question is which of them won the most gold. A comparison is easiest to read when it is sorted. gog draws the categories of a column of text in the order their rows appear in the table, and order() lets you choose another order:

                                   Germany Russia Great Britain China USA   0 10 20 30 40  Gold Country





“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, smallest first.”
The bars rise from left to right, from Germany’s 17 gold medals to the USA’s 46, so the country with the most gold comes last. order() names gold here, not the categorical column country. You name the column that holds the values, and the categories are sorted by those values.
One atom away. desc = TRUE puts the largest first. The table already lists the countries from most gold to least, so with desc = TRUE the bars keep the table’s own order. A sentence with no order() draws the same plot. Writing the order anyway keeps the plot sorted if a later version of the table lists the countries in a different order.
order() overrides a declared order as well. The next recipe uses it another way: it sorts by a column’s declared order, not by size.

title: 44  Many groups
section: 44.7 Where does a population pyramid come from?

44.7 Where does a population pyramid come from?
Two cities each have a population count in every age band, and the question is how the two age structures compare. The chart drawn for that question is the population pyramid. It is a named chart type, and no atom in the kernel carries that name. You never ask for a pyramid; you describe one.
The census table has three columns: an age band, a city (Busan or Seoul), and a population. age holds the band names as text, from 0 to 85, in a declared order from youngest to oldest. Each city has 18 bands, so the table holds 36 rows. The numbers are invented; the columns are the ones a census would hold.

The mirrored shape comes from one minus sign. Busan’s populations are negated, so Busan’s bars run to the left of zero. That is arithmetic, so it happens in the table, before the sentence:

mirrored <- census
mirrored$population <- ifelse(mirrored$city == "Busan",
                              -mirrored$population, mirrored$population)

The negation above is shown in R only; Python, Julia and JavaScript each negate a column in their own way. What follows is the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(mirrored) + bar + y(age) + x(population) + color(city) +
  order(age, desc = TRUE)


(data(mirrored) + bar + y(col.age) + x(col.population) + color(col.city) +
  order(col.age, desc = True))


data(mirrored) + bar + y(:age) + x(:population) + color(:city) +
  order(:age, desc = true)


plot(data(mirrored), bar, y(col.age), x(col.population), color(col.city),
  order(col.age, { desc: true }))






                                                                               -40K -20K 0 20K 40K   0 5 10 15 20 25 30 35 40 45 50 55 60 65 70 75 80 85  Age Population  City    Busan  Seoul 





“Given the mirrored table: bars, y is age, x is population, color by city, ordered by age, largest first.”
No new atom, and none was needed. The pyramid comes from three rules the grammar already states. First, the engine takes the orientation from the bindings, so a category on y makes the bars horizontal. Second, a bar runs from the zero baseline to its value, on whichever side of zero that value is, so a negative bar is not a special case. It is the same rectangle, extending the other way. Third, stack is something you ask for, never something the engine does on its own. This sentence does not ask for it, so the two bars in one slot are on opposite sides of zero. If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip() or matplotlib’s barh(), gog has no such word, because it would be a second way to say one thing.
order(age, desc = TRUE) is the atom from the medals recipe, used in a second way. There it named gold, a different column from the one on the axis. Here it names the categorical column itself, so it asks for that column’s own order: the declared order, youngest first. desc = TRUE reverses it. gog puts the first category at the top when the category is on y, so without desc = TRUE age 0 would be at the top. A pyramid needs its youngest band at the bottom.
Now look at the left half of the population axis. It reads -40K, not 40K.
Many versions of this chart replace each tick’s text with its absolute value. The minus sign that placed one city’s bars then disappears. gog keeps every tick showing the number at its own position, and this plot shows why. If the ticks were relabeled, the axis would carry two ticks reading 40K. Only a reader who knows the convention would know that the left 40K marks the position -40K. That reader could read -40K just as well, so the relabeling does not help. Any other reader gets bars whose positions no longer match the numbers on the axis. gog gives you no way to write your own tick text, and Coverage lists that among the capabilities with no decision recorded. These reasons argue against adding one.

title: 44  Many groups
text:
44.8 What this section refuses
Most recipes here separated groups with color, group or a panel. shape separates categories too, with one glyph per category on a point, and you might expect the same on a bar. A bar is a rectangle; it has no glyph to vary, so shape on a bar is refused outright:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + shape(country)


data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + shape(col.country)


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + shape(:country)


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), shape(col.country))




Error:
! gog: `shape` cannot be bound to `bar` — a bar has no shape feature. Remove the `country` mapping from `shape`, or use a mark that maps it: `point`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message says a bar has no shape feature, and tells you to remove shape or to use a mark that has one. point is the only mark that does. One rule table decides every pairing of a mark and a channel, and it makes no exception for any mark. The companion grid prints all of it.

title: 45  Comparing categories
text:
45.1 Which country lives longest?
How do many categories compare, and how did their order change over time? Many groups splits one plot by a few groups, with color or with panels. This chapter compares one value for each of many categories. A ranked bar chart answers the first question, and the chapter starts from that chart and changes a few atoms at a time. Each change draws a chart that has a name of its own: the Cleveland dot plot, the lollipop chart, the dumbbell chart, the slope chart and the bump chart. All of them show twelve countries of East, Southeast and South Asia, and how long their people lived, from the gapminder data.
The question is which of the twelve countries had the longest life expectancy in 2007. The ranked bar chart is the usual answer, and Which group is biggest? shows how order() sorts the bars. gm_twelve_2007 holds the twelve countries’ life expectancy in 2007, one row per country:

  title("Life expectancy in 2007")

  title("Life expectancy in 2007"))


data(gm_twelve_2007) + bar + y(:country) + x(:life) +
  order(:life, desc = true) + title("Life expectancy in 2007")


plot(data(gm_twelve_2007), bar, y(col.country), x(col.life),
  order(col.life, { desc: true }), title("Life expectancy in 2007"))
