RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(actuals, name = "series") + x(year) + y(sales) + line +
  data(forecast, name = "series") + point


(data(actuals, name = "series") + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + line +
  data(forecast, name = "series") + point)


data(actuals, name = "series") + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line +
  data(forecast, name = "series") + point


plot(data(actuals, { name: "series" }), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line,
  data(forecast, { name: "series" }), point)




Error:
! gog: two different tables are both called `series` — a layer resolves its bare columns against the nearest table by name, so one of these can never be reached. Give them distinct names: `data(name = "...")`.


Without that refusal the plot would draw the first table twice and report the second table’s columns as misspellings. You would have spelled the columns correctly, and gog would have checked them against the wrong table. Two %>% tables do not cause this refusal. gog calls them data and data2, warns once for each, and draws the plot. Naming the tables yourself removes both warnings.

title: 49  R
section: 49.4 What the pipe does not change
text:
49.4 What the pipe does not change
The pipe supplies the table that data() names. It does not replace +, and there is no piped form of the rest of the sentence. Marks, channels, and transforms compose with + and * as they do everywhere else in this book. gog has no pipe of its own, because R already has two.
The pipe question is R’s alone. Julia has a |>, but Julia’s data() never reads a table’s name from your code, so its pipe changes nothing. Neither Python nor JavaScript has a pipe operator. The other three chapters do not raise it.

title: 49  R
text:
49.5 The operators, and their precedence
That was the first question. The second is how R groups the four operators of a sentence. The pipe section used one case of precedence: |> groups before * and +. Among gog’s operators, R groups * and / first, then +, then |. That order is R’s, not gog’s, so it applies to every sentence you write (What groups first).
In that order, one plot needs no parentheses, even with a facet. An arrangement, two plots joined by | or /, is different, because R groups / before + and | after it. gog draws an arrangement written with | and no parentheses, because | groups last, after both plots are complete. It refuses the same arrangement written with /, because / joins the first plot’s last atom to the second plot’s data(). Inside an arrangement, / also groups before |, so a | b / c is read as a | (b / c). And a theme() added after an arrangement with no parentheses around it goes to the second plot, not to the arrangement, because + groups before |.
So in an arrangement, write each plot inside its own parentheses, whichever operator joins them. When one arrangement holds another, put the inner one in parentheses too. Put the whole arrangement in parentheses before a theme() for it. The arrangement then means the same thing in all three languages, including Julia, which groups | together with + (Parentheses in an arrangement).

title: 49  R
text:
49.6 Showing the plot
The third question is where a plot appears once you have written its sentence. You do not call anything to show it: R shows a plot as soon as you run its sentence, and where it appears depends on where you work:

At the console, it opens in the viewer pane of RStudio or Positron. Without a viewer pane, it opens in your web browser.
In a Quarto or R Markdown document, it is drawn under the chunk, as every plot in this book is.
In a Jupyter notebook with the R kernel, it appears under the cell. print() shows it too, so a loop can show several plots one after another.

To keep the drawing itself, render_svg() returns it as text.

title: 49  R
text:
49.7 Twenty names R already uses
The fourth question is which of gog’s words are already R’s. Twenty of the names gog provides are also names in the packages R loads when it starts, and library(gog) lists twelve of them. Here are all twenty:



from
names




stats
density line median quantile smooth step


graphics
box layout text title


grDevices
palette


utils
data stack


base
jitter max mean min order range sum



Eight of the twenty cannot affect an ordinary call, and library(gog) leaves those eight out of its message. A rule in R itself is the reason. A mark that takes no argument is an object rather than a function, and so is a transform that takes no argument. When R evaluates a call, it looks for a function of that name and skips any object of that name that is not a function. So a call still reaches base R’s mean, even though library(gog) attached its own:

is.function(mean)   # gog's `mean` is an object, so a call cannot reach it

[1] FALSE

mean(1:10)          # and base R's function answers anyway

[1] 5.5


The same is usually true when you pass mean to another function, because most functions look the name up the same way; the exceptions come later in this chapter:

sapply(gapminder_2007["life"], mean)

    life 
67.00742 


The other twelve are functions, and a call does reach gog’s: box, data, density, jitter, layout, order, palette, quantile, range, smooth, stack and title. To choose one, give it a prefix: the package’s name and ::, as in base::order. Both remain available:








you write
you get
for R’s own, write




order(population)
the plot’s sort order
base::order(df$population)


data(gapminder_2007)
the plot’s table
utils::data(mtcars)


density(2)
the density transform
stats::density(x)


jitter(0.5)
the offset transform
base::jitter(x)


layout(exporter, importer)
the layout transform
graphics::layout(mat)


quantile(0.9)
the 90th percentile transform
stats::quantile(df$gdp)


range(0.25, 0.75)
the band transform
base::range(df$gdp)


smooth(places = 200)
the fitted-curve transform
stats::smooth(x)


stack(share = TRUE)
the piling transform
utils::stack(df)


palette("soft")
the plot’s colors
grDevices::palette()


title("Life expectancy")
the plot’s title
graphics::title(main = "…")


box()
the box-and-whisker mark
graphics::box()



gog’s range takes two numbers, so it is a function rather than an object, and R does not skip past it. Writing range(0.25, 0.75) therefore reaches gog’s range and never base R’s. gog then reads the argument you passed. If you pass a vector where gog expects two numbers between 0 and 1, you meant base R’s range, and gog’s refusal says so:

range(c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5))

Error:
! gog: `range()` takes the band's two ends, each one number between 0 and 1, e.g. `range(0.25, 0.75)`. It was given 5 numbers. For the smallest and largest of a vector, gog masks that name: use `base::range()`.


Of the twelve, order causes the most errors, because you often sort a table while you are making plots. gog’s order returns an atom, not the row positions that [ expects. Without a refusal, R would stop with invalid subscript type 'list', which names neither order nor gog. So whenever the argument is not a bare name, the refusal says which function you reached and how to reach the other one:

gapminder_2007[order(gapminder_2007$population), ]

Error:
! gog: `order(gapminder_2007$population)` is not a column name. gog's `order()` takes a bare column, as in `order(population, desc = TRUE)`. To sort a vector, the base function is still there as `base::order(gapminder_2007$population)`.


With the prefix, it sorts:

ranked <- gapminder_2007[base::order(-gapminder_2007$population), ]
head(ranked[c("country", "population")], 3)

          country population
25          China 1318683096
59          India 1110396331
135 United States  301139947


Several other chapters write base::order for exactly this reason.
Three of the twelve refuse nothing, because gog cannot tell from the argument which function you meant. data(mtcars) is well formed for both. It starts a plot and raises no complaint, so write utils::data() when you mean to load a dataset. title("...") is the same case: a string is what both want. So is box(), which both accept with no argument at all. Seven of the others report the mistake, because what R’s function usually takes, a vector, a matrix or a table, is an argument gog refuses. The last two catch only part of it. order reports order(df$population) but not order(pop), where pop is a bare name holding a vector. palette reports palette() but not palette("R4"), because a palette name is what both want.
The names stay as they are, because renaming order to sort_by would replace a word every reader knows with one that only gog uses. The grammar chapter gives the full reason and compares how each language handles a name it already uses. R’s own packages are not the only source of a collision. Another package may define a name gog also defines. Load gog with library(gog) after that package, so R finds gog’s name first, or write the name with the prefix gog::.

title: 49  R
section: 49.8 Five calls that still need a prefix
text:
49.8 Five calls that still need a prefix
The eight words that are objects in gog, such as mean, are safe in ordinary code, and sapply() was only one example: lapply(), tapply(), mapply(), Map(), Reduce() and apply() are all safe for the same reason.
Five ways of writing a call still fail, for two different reasons. The first is a name that one function passes to a second function before R looks it up:

aggregate(life ~ continent, gapminder_2007, mean)

Error in `get()`:
! object 'FUN' of mode 'function' was not found


When R finally looks the name up, it is looking for FUN, the name aggregate() gave the function you passed, and not for mean. So the message names neither mean nor gog. by() and ave(..., FUN = mean) fail the same way. Writing base::mean fixes all three. The data frame form of aggregate() looks the name up one step earlier, so aggregate(gapminder_2007["life"], gapminder_2007["continent"], mean) works unchanged.
The second reason is a name used as a value rather than called. do.call(sum, list(x)) wants a function and receives an object, so write do.call("sum", list(x)) or do.call(base::sum, list(x)). And f <- mean copies the object, so f(x) reports that it could not find a function called f.
That is the whole cost, and one habit avoids all five failures: when you pass one of those eight words to another function, or store it in a variable, write it with its prefix, as in base::mean. The functions listed above work without the prefix, but the prefixed name works everywhere. Only four of the eight are base R’s own: max, mean, min and sum. line, median and step belong to stats, and text belongs to graphics, so write stats::median; base::median is itself an error.

title: 49  R
section: 49.9 Two kinds of value gog refuses
text:
49.9 Two kinds of value gog refuses
The fifth question is which values in a data frame gog cannot draw. R has two kinds of value that are stored as numbers, and no scale can place either of them.
The first is an infinite number. log10(0) is -Inf, and 1 / 0 is Inf. An infinite value is not a missing one, so gog does not drop its row. It refuses the plot and names the column:

growth <- data.frame(day = c(1, 2, 3, 4), cells = c(0, 12, 150, 1900))
growth$log_cells <- log10(growth$cells)
data(growth) + point + x(day) + y(log_cells)

Error:
! gog: column `log_cells` of `growth` holds -Inf, which is not a number a scale can place. Use `NA` for a missing value.


If a row with an infinite value should be left out, write NA in its place: growth$log_cells[is.infinite(growth$log_cells)] <- NA. gog then drops that row and says so, as Missing values shows.
The second is a length of time. Subtracting one date or date-time from another gives a difftime, R’s type for a duration, and so does as.difftime(). gog has no scale for a duration, and one duration can be shown in minutes, hours or days. gog does not choose the unit for you. travel holds how many minutes the trip to work took on five days. gog refuses the plot and names the column, and the message gives the code that makes it a number:

travel <- data.frame(
  day  = as.Date("2024-05-06") + 0:4,
  time = as.difftime(c(42, 38, 55, 40, 47), units = "mins")
)
data(travel) + line + point + x(day) + y(time)

Error:
! gog: column `time` of `travel` holds lengths of time, and gog has no scale for a duration. Make it a number in the unit you mean, such as hours: `as.numeric(travel$time, units = "hours")`.


Choose the unit you want to read on the axis. Here it is minutes:

travel$minutes <- as.numeric(travel$time, units = "mins")
data(travel) + line + point + x(day) + y(minutes)



                                         May 6 May 7 May 8 May 9 May 10   40 45 50 55  Minutes Day





“Given the travel table: a line and also points, x is day, y is minutes.”
gog checks for both kinds of value only in the columns the sentence names. travel still holds time, and this plot draws, because it never reads that column. A missing value in a column the sentence never names changes nothing either.

title: 49  R
section: 49.10 A small table inside the sentence
text:
49.10 A small table inside the sentence
The sixth question is how to draw from a table of one or two rows, such as the value for a reference line. A table that small does not need a file or a name of its own. Write it inside the sentence with data.frame():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(data.frame(life = 67.0)) + rule


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data({"life": [67.0]}, name='data.frame(life = 67.0)') + rule)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data((life = [67],)) +
  rule


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data({ life: [67] }), rule)






                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with life 67: a rule.”
The line is drawn at 67.0 years, the mean life expectancy in 2007. data() takes the table’s name from the expression you wrote, as it does for a filtered table in If your code uses %>%, so this table is called data.frame(life = 67). Two rows draw two lines, and a second column can name each one for color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(data.frame(life = c(60, 70), band = c("Low", "Middle"))) +
  rule + color(band)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data({"life": [60, 70], "band": ["Low", "Middle"]}, name='data.frame(life = c(60, 70), band = c("Low", "Middle"))') +
  rule + color(col.band))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  data((life = [60, 70], band = ["Low", "Middle"],)) + rule + color(:band)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data({ life: [60, 70], band: ["Low", "Middle"] }), rule,
  color(col.band))






                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Band    Low  Middle 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given two rows with life 60 and 70: rules, colored by band.”
A table written this way needs no name =. Other chapters give one anyway, as in data(data.frame(life = 67.0), name = "life_mean"), so that the table has a short name. The plot is the same either way.

title: 49  R
text:
49.11 Reading from a database
The seventh question is how a table in a database reaches a plot. query() runs a query on a database, and it takes a DBI connection. DBI is R’s database standard, so the same call reaches SQLite, Postgres, MariaDB, BigQuery, and anything with an ODBC driver.
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "sales.db")

query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(status) + y(revenue)
DBI and the drivers are optional: gog’s DESCRIPTION file lists DBI and RSQLite under Suggests, R’s field for optional packages, so installing gog does not install them. If you never write SQL, you need neither. If you do, install DBI and the one driver your database needs:
install.packages(c("DBI", "RSQLite"))    # or RPostgres, RMariaDB, odbc, bigrquery
You open the connection with DBI yourself, as the example above does, and pass it to query(). gog never opens one and never stores a password. Data covers what query() sends and how much data comes back.

title: 49  R
text:
49.12 Installing gog
The last question is how you install gog. Every plot is drawn by the engine, a separate program written in Rust, so the R package has to be able to find it. An installed copy of the package carries its own engine. The package’s configure script, which runs during the install, puts the engine inside the package, and it stops the install rather than leave you a package that cannot draw.
install.packages("gog", repos = c("https://psychometrician.r-universe.dev",
                                  "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
gog is published on r-universe. For the current version of R and the one before it, r-universe builds a ready-to-install copy of the package for macOS and Windows, with the engine already inside it, so installing needs no Rust toolchain. With an older version of R, the command installs from source, as it does on Linux.
On Linux the same command installs from source, and the source build compiles the engine. That needs Rust 1.75 or newer and a network connection. If the machine has no Rust, or only an older version, install the latest version first:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
Then install gog with the install.packages() call at the start of this section. The build runs once, while the package installs.
The build also needs memory. On a machine with little memory, such as some Posit Cloud projects, the compiler may need more memory than the machine has. The operating system then stops the compiler, and the install stops with a message that says so. The message also gives the R code that downloads the engine already built, so nothing has to be compiled. Run that code, then install gog again in the same session.
The repos argument names two addresses because gog is not on CRAN. The first address is the r-universe repository that holds gog. The second is an ordinary CRAN mirror. It is there for jsonlite, the one package gog needs that r-universe does not hold.
You can also work from a checkout, a copy of gog’s source repository on your own computer; that is how you change gog itself. Besides the packages that come with R, gog needs one package, jsonlite, which turns the sentence you write into the JSON that the engine reads. install.packages() installs it along with gog. Loading from a checkout needs pkgload as well, which loads a package from a folder instead of from a library. Working from a checkout installs neither, so install both if you do not have them:
install.packages(c("jsonlite", "pkgload"))
If one is missing, the step that needs it stops immediately, and the message names the missing package.
Then, from the checkout’s top folder, build the engine once (this needs Rust) and load the package from its folder:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
pkgload::load_all("r-pkg/gog")
If you change gog’s source, installing from the checkout checks more than loading it does, because the install runs configure, which puts the engine inside the installed package:
R CMD INSTALL r-pkg/gog
The R package looks for the engine in five places. In order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, a target/ build in a surrounding checkout, the copy inside the installed package, gog-cli on your PATH, and last a search upward from the working directory. A checkout is searched before the bundled copy on purpose. Inside a checkout the bundled engine is a copy an earlier install left behind. Using it would draw with an old engine while you are changing the engine’s source. If GOG_CLI_PATH names no file, gog refuses to draw and says which path it was given, and R CMD INSTALL stops for the same reason. Neither moves on to the next place, because a mistyped path would then draw with an engine you did not choose.

title: 49  R
text:
49.13 What comes next
R’s sentence is the one every chapter before this has written. Python writes the same sentence with col.gdp where R writes a bare name, and draws the same picture, byte for byte.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.1 A column is written col.gdp
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in Python as it is in R. What differs is short enough to state in one chapter. The sections below cover how a column is named, how a sentence is written over several lines, how values are written, and what counts as a table. Then come computed columns, showing a plot, and the six names Python already uses. After them comes the operators section. Python groups the operators in the same order as R, and an arrangement, two plots joined by | or /, needs two kinds of parentheses. The vocabulary and the refusals follow, and they do not change. Reading from a database and installing the package come last.
Every Python block on this page was run when the page was built, through the same engine every other chapter uses. Each block runs after from gog import *, and after gapminder_2007 is read as the section The table shows. The blocks leave those lines out. The database and install commands at the end are shown, not run.
In Python, gog marks each column with four characters, col., so that a column is never mistaken for a value. R writes a column as a bare name and Julia as a symbol. Python writes it through col, a small object called an accessor: col.gdp names the column gdp:

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale='log') + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
This is the sentence from A first plot, without its title and with col. in front of each column. The four characters are needed because R and Python pass an argument differently. In R, the call x(gdp) receives the word gdp itself, not a value. Python always passes values, so a bare gdp would have to be a variable you defined earlier. In this grammar, a plain string is how you spell a value: style(color="tomato"), title("…"), palette("okabe"). Without the accessor, a column and a value would both be plain strings, and gog could not tell which one you meant.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x('gdp') + y(col.life)
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. In Python, a bare name is a variable, so a column is written with the accessor: `x(col.gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.
The message names the column spelling, x(col.gdp). Where one name is both a channel and a setting, such as color, the message gives both spellings, because the two do different things. A channel maps a column and the plot gets a legend for it; a setting sets one value and gets none (Setting vs mapping). The opposite mistake, a column where a value belongs, is refused the same way:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color=col.continent)
gog: `style(color=)` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `col.continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(col.continent)`.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.1.1 Names that need brackets
After col., Python accepts only an identifier: a name made of letters, digits and underscores that does not start with a digit. Any other name is written in square brackets instead: col["life exp"], col["gdp.2007"], col["2007"]. Inside the brackets the name is a string, but col still marks it as a column. Be careful with a hyphen: Python reads col.life-exp as col.life minus a variable named exp, so write col["life-exp"].
Python also keeps some words for its own syntax, such as class, from and global. These reserved words need brackets too: col["class"]. If you write col.class, Python stops with SyntaxError: invalid syntax before any gog code runs. Unlike gog’s messages above, this message comes from Python, so it cannot tell you to write col["class"]. help("keywords") prints the full list.
A name in another writing system needs no brackets: col.국가 (country) works with the dot. Python accepts letters from any writing system in a name. The bracket form works for any name.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.2 A sentence over several lines
The second thing you type differently is about lines rather than names. R continues a line that ends in +. Python ends the statement there, so a sentence spanning several lines is wrapped in parentheses:


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale='log') + y(col.life)
 + color(col.continent) + size(col.population)
 + title('Wealth and life expectancy, 2007'))


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Wealth and life expectancy, 2007 Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
That is Python’s rule about lines, not a rule of gog’s. Those parentheses and the accessor are nearly the only things you will type differently. The rest is as in R, except that values take Python’s spelling.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.3 How values are written
In the other chapters, a code block that is a sentence has a tab for each language. Code written inside the text has none, so it is written in R, as in x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)). Most of it reads the same in Python once col. is written before each column. The values are what change. R writes several values inside c(), and Python writes them in a list, inside square brackets. The table gives the Python spelling of each kind of value the book uses:








Kind of value
R
Python




true or false
TRUE, FALSE
True, False


several numbers
c(37.5, 87.5)
[37.5, 87.5]


several strings, such as colors
c("tomato", "steelblue")
["tomato", "steelblue"]


a color for each category
c(Asia = "tomato", Europe = "steelblue")
{"Asia": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue"}


a missing value
NA
None


the number e
exp(1)
math.e, after import math


a declared order
factor(values, levels = c("Low", "High"))
pd.Categorical(values, categories=["Low", "High"]), after import pandas as pd



So x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) in the text is x(col.life, limits=[37.5, 87.5]) in Python. A tuple works too: limits=(37.5, 87.5). A missing value leaves that end of an axis open, so the data decides it: y(sales, limits = c(100, NA)) in the text is y(col.sales, limits=[100, None]) in Python. A named argument is written as in R, because Python has named arguments of its own: legend = FALSE is legend=False. A pandas Categorical declares the order of a column’s categories, as R’s factor() does. The next section says more about it, and about the other column types that carry an order.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.4 The table
The simplest table is a dict of columns, so a first plot needs no package besides gog:


data({'level': ['Low', 'Medium', 'High'], 'count': [30.0, 20.0, 10.0]},
     name='small') + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count)


                            Low Medium High   0 10 20 30  Count Level




“Given the small table: bars, x is level, y is count.”
Any object with a .columns attribute that you can index by column name is also a table, which covers pandas and polars. The binding imports neither one, so neither is a dependency. You read a file the way you already do. GAPMINDER_CSV here is the path to the book’s gapminder_2007.csv, and The book’s data says where to get that file:


import pandas as pd

gapminder_2007 = pd.read_csv(GAPMINDER_CSV)
print(gapminder_2007.shape, list(gapminder_2007.columns))
(142, 6) ['country', 'continent', 'year', 'life', 'population', 'gdp']


Apart from the small bar plot above, every plot on this page draws from this table or from a table computed from it.
The column kinds follow the Python types. A column of numbers is read as continuous, and a column of text as categorical. A column of datetime64, date or datetime values is drawn on a calendar axis. NaN and None are missing values. A row with one in a column the plot maps is left out, and the engine says how many rows it left out. A pandas Categorical keeps its declared order when the engine reads it. It is the pandas counterpart of R’s factor(x, levels = …). It can be a column of a pandas DataFrame, or a column of a plain dict of lists: pd.Categorical(values, categories=levels), as the Data chapter shows. A polars Enum column keeps its order in the same way. gog has no function of its own for this in Python, because these types already declare an order. A column with a declared order is categorical even when its values are numbers, such as years.
A pyarrow Table is a table too. A dictionary-encoded column, pyarrow’s form of a category, keeps the order of its categories, as a pandas Categorical does. A polars LazyFrame is a query that has not been run yet, so it holds no rows. gog refuses it and names the call that runs it, frame.collect().
Two kinds of value are refused rather than drawn. The first is an infinite number. numpy.log10(0) is -inf, and an infinite value is not a missing one, so gog does not drop its row. The first value of log_cells is -inf:


import numpy as np

growth = {'day': [1, 2, 3, 4], 'log_cells': np.log10([0, 12, 150, 1900])}
print(growth['log_cells'])
[      -inf 1.07918125 2.17609126 3.2787536 ]


gog refuses the plot and names the column:


data(growth) + point + x(col.day) + y(col.log_cells)
gog: column `log_cells` of `growth` holds -inf, which is not a number a scale can place. Use `None` for a missing value.


If a row with an infinite value should be left out, write None in its place, and gog drops that row and says so.
The second is a length of time. A timedelta, or a pandas, polars or numpy column of them, can be shown in minutes, hours or days. gog does not choose the unit for you. travel holds how many minutes the trip to work took on five days:


travel = pd.DataFrame({
    'day': pd.date_range('2024-05-06', periods=5),
    'time': pd.to_timedelta([42, 38, 55, 40, 47], unit='min'),
})


gog refuses the plot and names the column, and the message gives the code that makes it a number:


data(travel) + line + point + x(col.day) + y(col.time)
gog: column `time` of `travel` holds lengths of time, and gog has no scale for a duration. Make it a number in the unit you mean, such as hours: `travel['time'].dt.total_seconds() / 3600` for a pandas column, or `td.total_seconds() / 3600` for each `timedelta`.


Choose the unit you want to read on the axis. Here it is minutes:


travel['minutes'] = travel['time'].dt.total_seconds() / 60
print(travel['minutes'].tolist())
[42.0, 38.0, 55.0, 40.0, 47.0]




data(travel) + line + point + x(col.day) + y(col.minutes)


                                        May 6 May 7 May 8 May 9 May 10   40 45 50 55  Minutes Day




“Given the travel table: a line and also points, x is day, y is minutes.”
gog checks for both kinds of value only in the columns the plot maps. travel still holds time, and this plot draws, because it never reads that column.

50.4.1 A small table inside the sentence
A table of one or two rows, such as the value for a reference line, needs no file and no variable. Write it inside the sentence as a dict, as the small bar plot above did, and give it a name with name=:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data({'life': [67.0]}, name='life_mean') + rule


                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with life 67: a rule.”
The line is drawn at 67.0 years, the mean life expectancy in 2007. Python takes a table’s name from the variable you pass, and a dict written in the call has none. Without name=, gog calls the table data and warns that it did. Two rows draw two lines, and a second column can name each one for color:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data({'life': [60, 70], 'band': ['Low', 'Middle']}, name='bands') +
  rule + color(col.band)


                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Band    Low  Middle 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given two rows with life 60 and 70: rules, colored by band.”
Each column is a list, even when it holds one value. A bare value is refused, and the message gives the list:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data({'life': 67.0}, name='life_mean') + rule
gog: column `life` of `life_mean` is not a column — a column is a list of values, one per row. A single value is a length-1 list: `{'life': [67.0]}`.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.5 Computing a column first
A channel takes a column name and never an expression. That rule is the same in all four languages. There is no x(log(col.gdp)), and gog has no language of its own for deriving values, because Python already has one. So compute the column first, then bind it by name.
Dividing a column inside the channel is a natural thing to try. gog refuses it, and says where the computation belongs:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp / 1000) + y(col.life)
gog: a channel takes a column name, not an expression — gog has no computed channels. Compute the column in Python first and bind the result: `df['ratio'] = df['a'] / df['b']`, then `col.ratio` where the expression was.




europe = gapminder_2007[gapminder_2007.continent == 'Europe'].copy()
europe['gdp_thousands'] = europe.gdp / 1000
europe = europe.sort_values('life', ascending=False)
print(europe[['country', 'gdp_thousands', 'life']].head(3).to_string(index=False))
country  gdp_thousands   life
    Iceland      36.180789 81.757
Switzerland      37.506419 81.701
      Spain      28.821064 80.941


That result is a table like any other, and the sentence that draws from it is one you already know:


(data(europe) + point + x(col.gdp_thousands) + y(col.life)
 + size(col.population) + style(color='steelblue')
 + x_label('GDP per person (thousands)')
 + title('Europe, 2007'))


                                                                  10 20 30 40 50   72 74 76 78 80 82  Europe, 2007 Life GDP per person (thousands)  Population    301.9K  41.4M  82.4M 




“Given the europe table: points, x is gdp thousands, y is life, size by population, colored steelblue.”
You did the division in pandas, in a line of your own code that you can check. The plot then names a column that exists. Keeping the computing and the plotting apart is deliberate rather than a missing feature. A plot is a mapping from a table (Data), so a channel names one of its columns. Anything you want to compute is computed before you write the sentence.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.6 Showing the plot
The plots above appear on this page because the book drew each one when it was built. In your own session, where a plot appears depends on how you are running Python. In a Jupyter notebook, a plot on the last line of a cell is drawn below that cell, as the R console draws a plot you type. A script displays nothing on its own, so you ask for the picture yourself:


plot = data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
print(plot)
print(save_svg(plot, '/tmp/life.svg'))
<gog plot: point on gapminder_2007>
/tmp/life.svg


Printing a plot gives one line, naming its mark and its table. It does not give the picture. save_svg() writes the SVG to a file and returns its path, which is the second line printed above. plot.show() opens the SVG in a browser, and render_svg(plot) returns it as a string. R’s print() draws the picture, and Python’s does not. Each language is following the convention it already has.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.7 Six names Python already uses
Six of gog’s names are also Python builtins, the functions Python provides without any import: bin, map, max, min, range and sum. After from gog import *, those six names mean gog’s atoms, not Python’s builtins, for the rest of the file or notebook. gog’s R package shares names with R as well, and max, min, range and sum are four of them. gog does not rename an atom to avoid a name the language already uses. If you call sum, min, max or map as you would call Python’s builtin, gog refuses the call. So does range with whole numbers outside 0 to 1. The message says the name is gog’s, and how to reach Python’s builtin:


try:
    range(10)
except GogError as error:
    print(error)
gog: `range()` takes the band's two ends, each one number between 0 and 1, e.g. `range(0.25, 0.75)`. For a sequence of integers, gog shadows that name: use `builtins.range` for Python's.


That is range’s message. Its word for this is shadows: after the import, the name reaches gog’s atom instead of Python’s builtin. sum, min, max and map share a different message, which lists all six names and says how to reach Python’s builtin.
One name, bin, gives no message at all. bin(5) is also how you ask gog for five bins, so it returns a transform instead of Python’s string '0b101'.
If a file needs Python’s builtins as well as gog, write import gog and then gog.point, or restore one builtin with from builtins import sum.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.8 The operators, and their precedence
The four operators do not change from R to Python, and neither does their precedence, the order in which they group. * and / group first, then +, then |. That order is Python’s own, and R’s is the same. So bar * mean below becomes one compound mark before any + joins it, exactly as in Operators:


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
 + order(col.life, desc=True)
 + title('Mean life expectancy, highest first'))


                                  Oceania Europe Americas Asia Africa   0 20 40 60 80  Mean life expectancy, highest first Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, ordered by life, largest first.”
The same order decides where an arrangement needs parentheses. In an arrangement, Python has two kinds of parentheses, and they do different jobs. The outer pair, around the whole sentence, lets it continue on the next line (A sentence over several lines). It groups nothing inside the sentence. So an arrangement with only the outer pair is still refused when / joins its plots. / groups before +, so it joins the first plot’s last atom to the second plot’s data():


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) /
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))
gog: `/` places one plot below another, and it groups before `+`, so here it joined `y()` to the plot after it. Put each plot in parentheses: `(data(df) + point + ...) / (data(df) + bar + ...)`.


The inner pairs, one around each plot, are the ones that group. Each plot is then complete before / joins it. This book writes both kinds whenever it composes plots:


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, above bars derived by count, x is continent.”
With | between the plots, gog draws the arrangement without the inner pairs, because | groups after +. Write them anyway. The arrangement then means the same thing with either operator, and the same as in Julia, which groups | together with +. An arrangement inside an arrangement needs a pair of its own too, and so does a whole arrangement before a theme() for it. Inside an arrangement, / groups before |, so a | b / c is read as a | (b / c). Without the pair around a whole arrangement, + groups before |, and the theme() goes to the second plot (Parentheses in an arrangement).

title: 50  Python
section: 50.9 The same vocabulary and the same refusals
text:
50.9 The same vocabulary and the same refusals
Like the operators, the vocabulary does not change: every mark, transform, channel, setting and plot-level atom in the kernel card keeps its name in Python. An engine refusal does not change either. The engine does not know which binding asked, so it sends you the same words it sends an R user:


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.continent)
gog: `bar` needs `y()` but none is set. Add `y(<column>)` — a bar cannot be drawn without it. To count the rows in each slot instead, write `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The refusals that differ are the binding’s own, like the two about the accessor. Each of those has to teach the spelling of the language you are writing in.
This chapter’s examples are only a small sample. On every change to the project, its automated tests translate the book’s sentences into Python and draw them again. How far the two spellings differ was measured that way, sentence by sentence. Of the book’s 926 sentences, eleven have no Python spelling at all. Nine are in the R chapter and use R’s own syntax, such as the pipe. Two are the GIF exports in the Play chapter. Every one of the rest was translated by rule and run through the Python binding. Of those, 708 drew the same plot, byte for byte, and 187 gave the same refusal, word for word. The other 20 were refused in both languages, in a message worded for each one. Two rewrites do nearly all of the translating. The accessor is needed in 909 sentences, and the parentheses in 635.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.10 Reading from a database
Your table may be stored in a database rather than held in your session. Python’s database standard is DB-API, also called PEP 249, and query() reads any connection that follows it. It also reads a Spark session, because many Python users reach their data through Spark.
Any connection with a .cursor() method works: sqlite3 from Python’s standard library, DuckDB, psycopg, pyodbc, Snowflake’s connector, and the Databricks SQL connector.
import sqlite3
from gog import query, bar, x, y, col, save_svg

con = sqlite3.connect("sales.db")
plot = query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(col.status) + y(col.revenue)
save_svg(plot, "orders.svg")
Pass the Spark session itself to query(). In the SQL, write the table’s full name as Spark lists it, such as main.sales.orders. This is how you read a Databricks table:
plot = query(spark, "SELECT status, revenue FROM main.sales.orders") + bar + x(col.status) + y(col.revenue)
In a Databricks notebook the session is already there, under the name spark, and %pip install gog is the only setup step.
Neither way adds a dependency to gog. You open the connection, and gog only reads rows from it.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.11 Installing gog
A plot is drawn by the engine, which is a compiled Rust binary, so the Python package has to be able to find one. The released package carries it. A Python package is released as wheels, ready-built files for one platform each, and each wheel holds the engine built for its platform. So installing needs no Rust toolchain.
pip install gog
That command works. gog is on PyPI as five wheels. They cover macOS on Intel and ARM processors, Linux on Intel, AMD and ARM processors, and Windows on Intel and AMD processors. On any other platform, pip install gog stops with an error, because there is no wheel for it. The other three bindings install from their own registries, and the preface lists all four commands.
To work from a checkout instead, a copy of gog’s source repository, build the engine once. Then start Python in the repository’s top folder and import the package from there:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "py-pkg/gog")

from gog import *
The engine is looked for in four places, in this order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, the copy inside the installed package, gog-cli on your PATH, and a local target/release build. Only a checkout has the fourth, which also accepts a target/debug build. This page used the first: the book sets GOG_CLI_PATH to a local build before any Python runs. If GOG_CLI_PATH names no file, gog refuses to draw and says which path it was given. It does not move on to the next place, because a mistyped path would then draw with an engine you did not choose.

title: 50  Python
text:
50.12 What comes next
Python’s differences are spelling rather than grammar. Julia has four differences of its own. A column is a symbol, | has a different precedence, nine names need one extra import line, and the package has a different name.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.1 A column is a symbol
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in Julia as it is in R.
Of the three languages that are not R, Julia asks for the fewest changes to the sentence you already know. Like R and Python, it lets a package give +, *, | and / new meanings. Like R, it also keeps a column apart from a value in the syntax itself. So the sentence below differs from the R version only by a colon in front of each column:
The first sections cover how a column is written, how to break a sentence across lines, and how values are written. The next one shows where Julia groups the operators differently from R. Then come the tables Julia accepts, showing a plot, the nine names gog shares with Base, reading from a database, and installing the package.
Every Julia block on this page that shows a plot, a refusal or printed output ran when the page was built, through the same engine every other chapter uses. The other blocks are shown but not run. Each block ran after gapminder_2007 was fetched as The table shows, and after these two lines, which Nine names Julia already uses explains:
The colon is the main change to the sentence, so this section shows it in a plot. R writes a column as a bare name, Python as col.gdp, and Julia as a symbol, a name written after a colon, such as :gdp:
gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows


country
continent
year
life
population
gdp




Afghanistan
Asia
2007
43.828
31889923
974.5803


Albania
Europe

                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
That is the sentence from A first plot, without its title and with a colon in front of each column. In this grammar a plain string spells a value, as in style(color = "tomato") or palette("okabe"). A symbol is visibly not a string, so the colon does the same work as R’s bare name and Python’s col. accessor. A channel takes a column and never a value. Because a symbol and a string look different, both you and the package can see when a value is written where a column belongs.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y(:life)
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. In Julia a column is a symbol, which is what keeps the two apart: `x(:gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.
The opposite mistake, a column where a value belongs, is refused the same way and for the same reason (Setting vs mapping):
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + style(color = :continent)
gog: `style(color = )` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `:continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(:continent)`.
A column name with a space or a dot in it is written Symbol("life exp"). A name in another writing system needs no Symbol(): :지역 (region) is an ordinary symbol. Julia accepts letters from any writing system in a name.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.2 A sentence over several lines
A long sentence can be broken across lines, and Julia asks for nothing extra. Like R, it continues a line that ends in +:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
    color(:continent) +
    size(:population)


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
What does not work is the opposite: a line that starts with the operator. Julia ends the statement at the line break and reads the next line on its own, so it reports an error about + instead of drawing. To write a sentence that way, put the whole sentence inside parentheses. The Python chapter writes every multi-line sentence this way (Python), and inside parentheses a line may begin with + in Julia too. Values also take Julia’s spelling, as the next section shows.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.3 How values are written
In the other chapters, a code block that is a sentence has a tab for each language. Code written inside the text has none, so it is written in R, as in x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)). Most of it reads the same in Julia once each column is a symbol. The values are what change. R writes several values inside c(), and Julia writes them in a vector, inside square brackets. The table gives the Julia spelling of each kind of value the book uses:








Kind of value
R
Julia




true or false
TRUE, FALSE
true, false


several numbers
c(37.5, 87.5)
[37.5, 87.5]


several strings, such as colors
c("tomato", "steelblue")
["tomato", "steelblue"]


a color for each category
c(Asia = "tomato", Europe = "steelblue")
["Asia" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue"]


a missing value
NA
missing


the number e
exp(1)
exp(1), or ℯ


a declared order
factor(values, levels = c("Low", "High"))
CategoricalArray(values; levels = ["Low", "High"]), after using CategoricalArrays



So x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) in the text is x(:life, limits = [37.5, 87.5]) in Julia. Write several values in square brackets. A tuple in parentheses also works for limits, but palette() does not accept one. A missing value leaves that end of an axis open, so the data decides it: y(sales, limits = c(100, NA)) in the text is y(:sales, limits = [100, missing]) in Julia. A named argument is written as in R, because Julia has named arguments of its own: legend = FALSE is legend = false. A CategoricalArray declares the order of a column’s categories, as R’s factor() does, and the next section says more about it.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.4 The operators, and their precedence
A sentence can use up to four operators, so it matters which one Julia groups first. That order is called precedence, and Julia’s is not R’s. R and Python group | after +, and Julia groups | together with +, from left to right. That difference could change how a sentence is grouped, so the table compares four expressions in the three languages:



Written
Julia reads it as
R and Python read it as




a + b + c | d
(a + b + c) | d
the same


a | b / c
a | (b / c)
the same


a * b + c
(a * b) + c
the same


a | b + c
(a | b) + c
a | (b + c)



The first three rows are read the same way in all three languages. In the first, Julia groups | together with +, from left to right, so everything left of the | is joined first. In the second and third, * and / group first in every language. Only the last row differs, because it is the only one with a + after the |. When b is a facet and c an atom such as title(), the difference does not change the plot. R joins the atom to the facet first, and Julia joins it to the plot directly. Both draw the same plot as a sentence with the atom written before the facet.
Faceting therefore reads exactly as it does in R:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                      1K 10K                                                                              1K 10K                                                   1K 10K                            1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
A transform joins its mark first, as in R, because * groups before + in both languages:


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)


                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
The last row of the table matters in an arrangement, two plots joined by | or /. The plot on the right of | starts with its own data(), and its other atoms follow with +. So an arrangement written in full has a + after the |. Without parentheses, Julia groups the first plot with that data() alone, and gog refuses an arrangement that it draws in R and Python:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) |
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent)
gog: `|` places one plot beside another, and the plot beside it holds nothing but its table. Julia groups `|` with `+`, from left to right, so `|` joined that table before `+` could add the rest of its plot. Put each plot in parentheses: `(data(df) + point + ...) | (data(df) + bar + ...)`.


So in an arrangement, put each plot inside its own parentheses, with | as well as with /, which groups before + in all three languages. Each plot is then complete before | joins it, and the arrangement draws as it does in R:


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The same row decides where a theme() for the whole arrangement goes. Written after an arrangement with no parentheses around it, the theme() goes to the arrangement in Julia, and to the second plot in R and Python. Put parentheses around the arrangement before the theme(), as in ((…) | (…)) + theme(height = 260). Then the theme() goes to the arrangement in all three languages (Parentheses in an arrangement).

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.5 The table
Every sentence starts from a table. The simplest table in Julia is a named tuple of columns, which the language provides, so a first plot needs nothing installed:


data((person = ["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"], cm = [160.0, 172.0, 181.0]),
     name = "heights") + bar + x(:person) + y(:cm)


                            Ada Alan Grace   0 50 100 150  Cm Person




“Given the heights table: bars, x is person, y is cm.”
The table holds three people and their heights, written directly inside the call. A Dict of columns works too. So does any object that supports names(table) and table[!, col], as a DataFrame does. The package never imports DataFrames, so if you do not use one, you install nothing extra. A CategoricalArray, from the CategoricalArrays package, is drawn in the order of its declared levels, as R’s factor is. gog has no function of its own for this in Julia, because that type already declares an order. gog does not install CategoricalArrays, so add it yourself. Put the CategoricalArray in the table when you build it, or assign it into a Dict{String,Any}, the type gog_table() returns. A Dict built from plain vectors, such as Dict("level" => ["High", "Low"], "count" => [30.0, 10.0]), has a narrower type than Dict{String,Any}. Julia turns a CategoricalArray assigned into it back into a plain vector, and the order is lost before gog sees the table.
The other plots use gapminder_2007, one of the book’s shared tables, and gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007") fetches it. gog_table() fetches any of the shared tables by name, as it does in the other three languages (The book’s data).
Julia has both a Date and a DateTime. R and Python each have the same pair of types under their own names. A Date column never gets clock ticks, and a DateTime column can, because it stores a time of day (Scales). The package tells the two apart by type, so nothing is guessed.
In R, data() reads a table’s name from the expression you wrote. In Julia, data() receives only the table itself, so an unnamed table gets a generated name instead: data, then data2. Some messages name the table they are about, such as the warning about missing values, so write data(df, name = "notes") when you want that message to say notes (Data).
A column of lengths of time is refused. A Period from Dates, such as Minute(42), can be shown in minutes, hours or days, and gog does not choose the unit for you. travel holds how many minutes the trip to work took on five days:


using Dates

travel = (day = Date(2024, 5, 6) .+ Day.(0:4),
          time = Minute.([42, 38, 55, 40, 47]))


gog refuses the plot and names the column, and the message gives the code that makes it a number. That code uses the table’s name, so the sentence below gives the table one. Without it, the message would write data.time, which is not your variable:


data(travel, name = "travel") + line + point + x(:day) + y(:time)
gog: column `time` of `travel` holds lengths of time, and gog has no scale for a duration. Make it a number in the unit you mean, such as hours: `Dates.value.(Dates.Second.(travel.time)) ./ 3600`.


Choose the unit you want to read on the axis. Here it is minutes:


travel = merge(travel,
               (minutes = Dates.value.(Dates.Second.(travel.time)) ./ 60,))
println(travel.minutes)
[42.0, 38.0, 55.0, 40.0, 47.0]




data(travel, name = "travel") + line + point + x(:day) + y(:minutes)


                                        May 6 May 7 May 8 May 9 May 10   40 45 50 55  Minutes Day




“Given the travel table: a line and also points, x is day, y is minutes.”
travel still holds time, and this plot draws, because gog checks only the columns the sentence names.

51.5.1 A small table inside the sentence
A table of one or two rows, such as the value for a reference line, needs no file and no variable. Write it inside the sentence as a named tuple, as the heights table above was:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  data((life = [67.0],)) + rule


                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with life 67: a rule.”
The line is drawn at 67.0 years, the mean life expectancy in 2007. A named tuple with one column needs the comma before its closing parenthesis: (life = [67.0],). Without it, Julia reads data((life = [67.0])) as a named argument life passed to data(), and gog refuses the call with the comma in its message:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  data((life = [67.0])) + rule
gog: `data()` was given `life` as a named argument, not a table. A table written in place is a named tuple, and a named tuple of one column needs a comma before its closing parenthesis: `data((life = [67.0],))`. Without the comma, Julia reads the parentheses as named arguments to `data()`.


Each column is a vector, even when it holds one value. Two rows draw two lines, and a second column can name each one for color:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  data((life = [60, 70], band = ["Low", "Middle"])) + rule + color(:band)


                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Band    Low  Middle 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given two rows with life 60 and 70: rules, colored by band.”
The table gets a generated name, as any unnamed table does, and name = "life_mean" gives it one of your own. A column called end is written var"end", because end is a word Julia reserves: (start = [0], var"end" = [5000],). The same escape names the last argument of bounds(), which is written by name: bounds(:lower, :upper, start = :start, var"end" = :end).

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.6 Showing the plot
The plots on this page appear under their code. In your own session, where a plot appears depends on where you run it. In a notebook, such as Jupyter or Pluto, the notebook asks the package for a picture, and the plot is drawn under the cell. At the REPL, Julia’s prompt in a terminal, a plot prints as one line of text, such as <gog plot: bar on heights> for the heights plot in The table. To see the picture, assign the plot to a variable such as p, write it to a file with save_svg(p, "plot.svg"), and open that file in a web browser. render_svg(p) returns the same drawing as text.
Julia also exports three functions that R and Python do not. You need them only to build a tool with gog, such as a web server, and never to write a sentence. svg_block(svg) puts the text from render_svg() in centered HTML for a web page. Given the plot too, svg_block(svg, p) adds its controls. find_gog_cli() returns the path of the engine the package found (Installing gog). to_wire(table, name) returns the table as gog sends it to the engine, before it becomes JSON; name labels its messages. JavaScript exports the same three.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.7 Nine names Julia already uses
Every plot above ran after two lines that its block leaves out, and this section explains them. Nine of the kernel’s words are also names in Base: count, sum, min, max, range, size, step, stack and map. Julia will not choose between two modules that export the same name, and the rule is the language’s own. Writing one of these nine without an import stops with an UndefVarError and a hint, rather than quietly calling the wrong function. The fix is one more import line:
using GrammarOfGraphics
using GrammarOfGraphics: count, sum, min, max, range, size, step, stack, map
With them, a bare sum is gog’s transform, and Base.sum still adds numbers:


println(sum)
println(Base.sum([1, 2, 3]))
<gog sum>
6


bin is not in the import line, because Base.bin is not exported, so there is no second bin to choose between.
The import line treats the nine names alike, but your existing code does not use them equally. map and size appear in ordinary Julia code constantly. After the import, a call such as map(f, xs) or size(A) in that code reaches gog’s word instead, and the error appears on a line you did not change. Write Base.map or Base.size there, and the same prefix works for any of the nine.
R, Python and Julia all have this problem, and each one solves it in its own way. R’s range, sum and min belong to base R, Python’s bin, sum and max are builtins, and Julia’s belong to Base. A grammar keeps its own vocabulary; what changes is how each language asks you to say which one you meant.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.8 Reading from a database
Your table may be stored in a database rather than in your session. query() runs a SQL query on that database, and it takes a DBInterface.jl connection. DBInterface.jl is Julia’s database standard, and SQLite.jl, LibPQ.jl, MySQL.jl and DuckDB.jl all implement it.
using DBInterface, SQLite, GrammarOfGraphics

con = SQLite.DB("sales.db")
query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(:status) + y(:revenue)
GrammarOfGraphics does not depend on DBInterface. Every dependency the package declares is a Julia standard library, and many readers never write SQL, so none of them should have to install a database package. Instead, the package uses the DBInterface that your driver loads. If no driver is loaded, drawing the plot stops with a message that names DBInterface and the line that loads it.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.9 Installing gog
The Julia package is named GrammarOfGraphics. The name is longer than the one R and Python use, and the registry is the reason. Julia’s registry checks a new name automatically. The name must be at least five letters long and must start with a capital. A lowercase gog is too short and has no capital.
Every plot is drawn by the engine, a separate program written in Rust, so the Julia package has to be able to find it. Python and JavaScript each publish the engine built for every common platform, and the install picks the one for your computer. R builds it during the install, or installs one already built. Julia fetches it as an artifact, which is how a Julia package distributes a program it needs. Pkg downloads the copy of the engine built for your computer along with the package, so one call to Pkg.add installs everything:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("GrammarOfGraphics")
To work from a checkout, a copy of gog’s source repository on your own computer, first build the engine once from the checkout’s top folder (this needs Rust):
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
Then run Pkg.develop from the same folder:
using Pkg
Pkg.develop(path = "jl-pkg/GrammarOfGraphics")

using GrammarOfGraphics
The Julia package looks for the engine in six places. In order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, a build in the checkout that holds the package, the artifact the install fetched, a copy you placed inside the package yourself, gog-cli on your PATH, and last a build found by searching upward from the working directory. The search stops at the first place that holds the engine. An installed copy is not inside a checkout, so it uses the artifact. Inside a checkout, your own build is searched before the artifact on purpose. The artifact is the engine of the last release, and using it would draw with an old engine while you are changing the engine’s source. If GOG_CLI_PATH names no file, gog refuses to draw and says which path it was given. It does not move on to the next place, because a mistyped path would then draw with an engine you did not choose.

title: 51  Julia
text:
51.10 What comes next
R, Python and Julia write one sentence three ways, and the main difference is how a column is named. JavaScript reads differently, because it cannot give + * | / new meanings, so it spells them as words.

title: 52  JavaScript
text:
52.1 The comma is +
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in JavaScript as it is in R.
The sentence is spelled differently here, and the operators are the reason. Every other binding joins the same words with the same four operators. JavaScript cannot join words that way, because +, *, | and / cannot be given a meaning on objects. For two objects a and b, a + b joins them into one piece of text, a * b is NaN, and a | b is the number 0. There is no version of the language in which data(gm) + point builds a plot.
So JavaScript spells the four operators as six words: plot(), layer(), across(), down(), beside() and below(). That is the change this chapter starts from. Read the two lines together, the R first and the JavaScript under it:
Every JavaScript block with a plot, a message or a printed line under it was run when the page was built, through the same engine every other chapter uses. The database and install commands are shown, not run. In your own code, import the words you use, such as import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "grammar-of-graphics". The blocks on this page leave that line out, and also the line that reads the table: const gapminder_2007 = await gog_table("gapminder_2007");.
JavaScript brings in only the names you list, and none of gog’s names is already a name in the language. So, unlike the R, Python and Julia chapters, this one has no section on names the language already uses. If a gog word matches a name your own script uses, such as path beside Node.js’s node:path, import it under another name with as. The sections below take the four operators first. Then come how a column, a named argument and a table are written, a plot for a web page, reading from a database, and installing the package.
A gog sentence is a list of words, and in JavaScript it is a list of arguments. A comma means nothing on its own. Inside plot(), the commas join the words, exactly as + joins them in R. A named argument is written differently: it goes into an object at the end of the call. The section on named arguments, below, sets that out in full.
