Those are the words of A first plot without its title, in the same order, reading the same way. Where you write a word still decides its scope (Encoding scope). A channel written after a mark belongs to that mark, and one written before any mark belongs to the plot. The commas change nothing about that; they are the + signs.

title: 52  JavaScript
text:
52.2 layer() is *
The commas replaced +. * cannot become a comma, because R groups * before +. That order is called precedence, and it is how bar * bin + x(life) reads as a binned bar rather than a bar plus a bin. JavaScript writes function calls rather than operators here, so there is no precedence to use. Nesting does the same work:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.life))


                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
Nesting is clearer than precedence. A reader who does not know that * groups before + has to be told. A reader looking at layer(bar, mean) can see it.
Just over half the sentences in this book need no layer() at all, because they are a flat list of words. Where one is needed, it usually holds two words:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent), style({ color: 'steelblue' }))


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The two words are a mark and the transform that derives it. The color here is a setting, written as an object inside style().

title: 52  JavaScript
text:
52.3 across() and down() are | and /
Two operators are left, | and /. With facet() on their right, both split one plot into panels. Faceting in R is plot | facet(era), panels side by side, or plot / facet(era), panels stacked. In R, facet() means nothing on its own: it always follows a | or a /. JavaScript writes that whole phrase as one word:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log' }), y(col.life), across(col.continent))


                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                      1K 10K                                                                              1K 10K                                                   1K 10K                            1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
down() stacks the panels instead. Writing both gives a grid: one panel column per value of the column in across(), and one panel row per value of the column in down(). That is what plot | facet(a) / facet(b) does in R.
Because the operator and facet() are one word here, there is no separate facet() to write. Writing facet(), as the other three languages do, is refused, and the message names the two words to use instead:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), facet(col.continent))
gog: JavaScript has no `facet()`, because it has no `|` or `/` to join it with — the pair is one word here. Panels side by side: `across(col.continent)`. Panels stacked: `down(col.continent)`.

title: 52  JavaScript
section: 52.4 Composing two plots: beside() and below()
text:
52.4 Composing two plots: beside() and below()
The | you have just replaced had a second job in R. What is on its right decides which job it does: plot | facet(g) splits one plot into panels, and plot_a | plot_b places two plots in one arrangement. JavaScript cannot overload |, so the two meanings never share a symbol. The second one gets its own word, beside(), and below() for /:


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp), theme({ height: 130 })), plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)))


                                         0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, above points, x is gdp, y is life.”
The two words come from an algebra of pictures published in 1982. Henderson’s Functional Geometry (Henderson, 1982) combines pictures with beside and above. His above(a, b) and gog’s below(a, b) draw the same picture, with a on top and b under it. Composition gives the history. Both words also take an arrangement, the result of an earlier beside() or below(), so one arrangement can hold another. below(top, beside(main, right)) is the marginal plot, exactly as top / (main | right) is in R: a histogram above a scatter, and another to its right. The spelling does not decide what two composed plots share; the engine does. Plots one above the other align their x axes, and plots side by side align their y axes. When both plots put the same column on that aligned axis, and read it the same way, it becomes one axis: one scale, both panels the same length along it, drawn once.
That marginal plot, below(top, beside(main, right)), needs no parentheses beyond the calls themselves. In an arrangement written in R, Python or Julia, this book puts each plot inside its own parentheses. Without them, precedence can group parts of two plots together (Parentheses in an arrangement). JavaScript needs none of those parentheses. Each plot is already one plot() call, and beside() and below() take whole plots and arrangements as their arguments, so the nesting shows the grouping. This book writes a theme() for the whole arrangement as the last argument of beside() or below():


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)), plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)), theme({ height: 260 }))


                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
In R, Python and Julia, a theme() for the whole arrangement follows parentheses around the arrangement, as in ((…) | (…)) + theme(height = 260). In JavaScript, the theme() goes inside the call that makes the arrangement, so no extra parentheses are needed.

title: 52  JavaScript
text:
52.5 A column is written col.gdp
The operators are the largest change JavaScript makes to a sentence. Three smaller ones are left, and the first is how a column is named. R writes a column as a bare name and Julia as a symbol. Python and JavaScript write it through col, a small object called an accessor: col.gdp names the column gdp. Both languages make that choice for the same reason. In this grammar a plain string is how you spell a value, as in style({ color: "tomato" }), title("…"), palette("okabe"). Without the accessor, a column and a value would both be plain strings, and gog could not tell which one you meant.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x('gdp'), y(col.life))
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. In JavaScript, a bare name is a variable, so a column is written with the accessor: `x(col.gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.


The message names the column spelling, x(col.gdp). A channel takes a column, and a string is a value (Setting vs mapping). The opposite mistake, a column where a value belongs, is refused the same way:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), style({ color: col.continent }))
gog: `style({ color: … })` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `col.continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(col.continent)`.


A column name with a space or a dot in it is not a JavaScript identifier, the kind of name that can follow a dot. Write it in the bracket form instead: col["life exp"]. A name in another writing system needs no brackets. JavaScript accepts letters from any writing system in an identifier, so col.지역 (region) works.

title: 52  JavaScript
section: 52.6 A named argument is one trailing object
text:
52.6 A named argument is one trailing object
That was the first of the smaller differences. The second is how a named argument is written. R writes x(gdp, scale = "log"). JavaScript has no syntax for a named argument. You put the named ones into a single object at the end, and the positional ones stay where they are:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log', base: 2 }), y(col.life), title('Doublings of income'))


                                                                                                                                                                                      256 512 1024 2048 4096 8192 16384 32768   40 50 60 70 80  Doublings of income Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale in base 2, y is life.”
style() is the case where every argument is named, so it is written as one object throughout the book: style({ color: "tomato", size: 3 }).

52.6.1 How values are written
In the other chapters, a code block that is a sentence has a tab for each language. Code written inside the text has none, so it is written in R, as in x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)). In JavaScript, limits goes into the trailing object, and its value takes JavaScript’s spelling. R writes several values inside c(), and JavaScript writes them in an array, inside square brackets. The table gives the JavaScript spelling of each kind of value the book uses:








Kind of value
R
JavaScript




true or false
TRUE, FALSE
true, false


several numbers
c(37.5, 87.5)
[37.5, 87.5]


several strings, such as colors
c("tomato", "steelblue")
["tomato", "steelblue"]


a color for each category
c(Asia = "tomato", Europe = "steelblue")
{ Asia: "tomato", Europe: "steelblue" }


a missing value
NA
null


the number e
exp(1)
Math.E


a declared order
factor(values, levels = c("Low", "High"))
ordered(values, ["Low", "High"])



So x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) in the text is x(col.life, { limits: [37.5, 87.5] }) in JavaScript, and legend = FALSE is { legend: false }. A missing value leaves that end of an axis open, so the data decides it: y(sales, limits = c(100, NA)) in the text is y(col.sales, { limits: [100, null] }) in JavaScript. ordered() declares the order of a column’s categories, as R’s factor() does, and the Data chapter describes it. JavaScript is the one binding with this function, because JavaScript and its common table packages have no type for a category.

title: 52  JavaScript
text:
52.7 The table, and its name
The third difference is how a table gets its name. A table is an object of columns, or an array of rows, one object per row. Neither needs a package besides gog, and this one is written in place:
const heights = { person: ["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"], cm: [160, 172, 181] };


plot(data(heights), bar, x(col.person), y(col.cm))


                            Ada Alan Grace   0 50 100 150  Cm Person




“Given the heights table: bars, x is person, y is cm.”
R reads the table’s name from the expression you wrote, and Python from the variable you passed. JavaScript can do neither. The name matters, because a layer looks up its columns in the nearest table, and it finds that table by name (Data). So an unnamed table gets a generated name instead, such as data or data2, which is enough to tell two tables in one sentence apart. Some messages name the table they are about, such as the warning about missing values. Write data(df, { name: "notes" }) when you want such a message to say notes.
A column of Date values is drawn on a calendar axis. gog reads each Date in local time, the time shown by the clock of the computer that runs your code. So new Date(2024, 0, 1, 12), noon on January 1, is drawn at 12:00. JavaScript’s Date type holds both a date and a date-time, so gog distinguishes the two by their values. If every value in a column is midnight in local time, as new Date(2024, 0, 1) is, gog reads the column as dates and never gives it clock ticks. JavaScript reads the text in new Date("2024-01-01") as midnight in UTC, the time every time zone is counted from. On a computer in New York, gog draws that value at 19:00 on December 31, 2023. On a computer in Seoul it is 09:00 on January 1: the right day, but not midnight, so the column is read as date-times. To get midnight in every time zone, write a time after the date: new Date("2024-01-01T00:00") is midnight in local time.
Three more things have a JavaScript spelling. A missing value is null, undefined or NaN: a row with one in a column the plot maps is left out, and gog says how many rows it left out. ordered(values, levels) declares the order of a column’s categories, which the Data chapter describes. And the book’s own tables come from gog_table(), which fetches them over the network. It returns a Promise, JavaScript’s object for a value that arrives later, so you write await before it, as The book’s data shows.
A column can also be a typed array, such as a Float64Array or an Int32Array, which numeric libraries often return. A BigInt is JavaScript’s type for a whole number of any size, written with a final n, as in 1204n. Some database drivers return one, and gog reads it as a number:
const sales = { year: Int32Array.of(2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023), units: [1204n, 1350n, 1288n, 1523n, 1689n] };


plot(data(sales), line, point, x(col.year), y(col.units))


                                            2019 2020 2021 2022 2023   1200 1300 1400 1500 1600 1700  Units Year




“Given the sales table: a line and also points, x is year, y is units.”
JavaScript’s Number type holds every whole number exactly only up to 253, about 9 × 1015. Above that, gog refuses a BigInt that a Number cannot hold exactly, in a column the sentence names, rather than draw it in the wrong place.

52.7.1 A second table
A sentence can also draw from a second table. In JavaScript a later data() is one more argument, and as in every language it applies only to the mark written directly after it (Data). So two marks that read the second table each take their own data(). Here the line reads actuals, and the points and the area both read forecast:



actuals: all 5 rows


year
sales




2019
120


2020
135


2021
128


2022
152


2023
168






forecast: all 3 rows


year
sales




2024
180


2025
195


2026
210







plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  line,
  data(forecast), point,
  data(forecast), area)


                                     2020 2022 2024 2026   0 100 200  Sales Year




“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line; then given the forecast: points; then given the forecast: an area.”
You might try to give the second table to both marks at once, by putting them in a plot() of their own inside the first one. A plot() cannot be an argument to another plot(), so gog refuses the sentence:


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, plot(data(forecast), point, area))
gog: a plot cannot be an argument to another plot, so everything inside it would be dropped. Write the atoms in sequence instead, and repeat `data()` before each mark that reads that table: `plot(data(a), line, data(b), point, data(b), area)`. To arrange two plots, use `beside()` or `below()`.


The message gives the sentence above. It is the same mistake as + (data(forecast) + point + area) in R, Python and Julia (What parentheses may group).


52.7.2 A small table inside the sentence
A table of one or two rows, such as the value for a reference line, needs no file and no variable. Write it inside the sentence as an object of columns:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data({ life: [67] }), rule)


                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with life 67: a rule.”
The line is drawn at 67 years, the mean life expectancy in 2007. Two rows draw two lines, and a second column can name each one for color:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data({ life: [60, 70], band: ['Low', 'Middle'] }), rule, color(col.band))


                                                                                                                                                                                      0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Band    Low  Middle 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given two rows with life 60 and 70: rules, colored by band.”
Each column is an array, even when it holds one value. A bare value is refused, and the message gives the array:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data({ life: 67 }), rule)
gog: column `life` is not a column — a column is an array of values, one per row. A single value is a length-1 array: `{ life: [67] }`.


The table gets a generated name, as any unnamed table does, and data({ life: [67] }, { name: "life_mean" }) gives it one of your own.

title: 52  JavaScript
52  JavaScript
section: 52.9 A plot for a web page: html_block()

title: 52  JavaScript
52  JavaScript
text:
52.11 Installing gog
Every plot is drawn by the engine, a separate program written in Rust, so the npm package has to be able to find it.
npm install grammar-of-graphics
That command works. The package is on npm, and the name is written in full because npm already had a package called gog. The registry also forbids capital letters in a new name, so this is Julia’s GrammarOfGraphics written the way npm writes names.
The engine is installed with it. There are five more packages on npm, one per platform, each holding the engine compiled for that platform. The main package lists all five as optional dependencies. The install takes the one that matches your computer and skips the other four. So there is nothing to put on your PATH, nothing to build, and no Rust toolchain to install. The five cover macOS on Intel and ARM processors, Linux on Intel, AMD and ARM processors, and Windows on Intel and AMD processors. On any other computer the install still succeeds, and the first plot stops with an error that says no engine is published for that computer.
The binding itself only builds the specification and hands it to that engine, and it depends on nothing else:
import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "grammar-of-graphics";

const gm = { gdp: [1000, 2000, 3000], life: [60, 70, 80] };
console.log(render_svg(plot(data(gm), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life))));
The package runs in Node.js and not in a browser, because it starts the engine as a separate program. On a server, you send the SVG string as the response, and the page puts it straight into its DOM. Nothing has to open a viewer window, and nothing has to be turned into pixels first. What the engine returns is already the finished picture.
To work from a checkout instead, a copy of gog’s source repository, build the engine once. Then import the package by its path, from the repository’s top folder:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "./js-pkg/gog/src/index.js";
The engine is looked for in four places, in this order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, the platform package installed beside the main one, gog-cli on your PATH, and a target/release build in a surrounding checkout. The search stops at the first place that holds the engine, so an installed copy normally stops at the platform package. GOG_CLI_PATH is how this page was rendered. If GOG_CLI_PATH names no file, gog refuses to draw and says which path it was given. It does not move on to the next place, because a mistyped path would then draw with an engine you did not choose.

title: 52  JavaScript
text:
52.12 What comes next
These four chapters are about spelling, and none of them changes what a sentence means. The afterword closes the book with the ten-day challenge, and the one goal that remains.




Henderson, P. (1982). Functional geometry. In D. P. Friedman & D. S. Wise (Eds.), Conference record of the 1982 ACM symposium on lisp and functional programming (pp. 179–187). ACM Press.

title: Afterword
text:
The ten-day challenge
The 1446 book closed with a postface, and it made two claims for its little alphabet. The first was that a wise man could learn it before the morning was over, and a slow one within ten days. The second was that it could write down any sound at all: the wind, the cry of a crane, the crowing of a cock, the barking of a dog. This book closes by restating both, because they are its own measures of success.
The first claim was about speed, and the preface restated it for this book: read the whole grammar in a morning, and write it fluently within ten days. You have done the reading. Here is the rest of the promise. For the next ten days, ask one question a day of your own data, not of the book’s cast of tables, and answer it in one sentence. Start where the cookbook starts: with your columns and your question. By day three the recipes will read as ordinary sentences, because you will have written sentences like them yourself. By day ten you should be writing sentences this book never showed you. That is the one outcome that proves you learned the grammar and not the examples.
During those ten days, report two kinds of result: a sentence that renders when you expected a refusal, and a refusal whose direction you disagree with. Reports like these are how the grammar’s mistakes are found.

title: Afterword
text:
Growth without new words
The second claim was about what the letters could write: any sound at all. gog has the same goal for plots, but it does not promise that every plot is possible. The kernel you learned is its whole vocabulary. The engine draws every word in it, though not every pairing of words. Combinations shows which pairs it draws and which it refuses.
A new kind of plot does not need a new word. The choropleth is an example of that. It is a map that shades each country by a value, and no atom was added for it. What it needed was a different kind of table: one row for every point along a country’s border, so that many rows make up one country. A zone is a filled region, and several things can decide its sides. One of them is a boundary, the outline those rows trace, and group already says which rows belong to one country. Map shows the choropleth drawn with the words the kernel already had.
The vocabulary is also the same in all four languages. Whatever sentence you write, all four bindings build the same specification from its words. The main difference is how each binding names a column. JavaScript also cannot give the operators new meanings, so it spells them as words. Each language has a chapter of its own, listing what differs: R, Python, Julia, JavaScript. Here is one sentence from A first plot in all four:
# R
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
# Python
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
  + color(col.continent))
# Julia
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)
// JavaScript
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent))
All four draw the same plot, byte for byte.

title: Afterword
text:
One goal left
Those four spellings are finished work. One thing this project planned to do is not finished, and it is written down here so you can check later whether the project did it. Half of it already works: the engine itself runs inside the page, which is how a 3-D plot turns when you drag it in the web edition. The other half is making every example in this book editable on the page. You could then change color(continent) to shape(continent) and watch the plot redraw. This book is ready for editable examples, because no plot in it is a screenshot: the engine draws every one from its specification.

title: Afterword
section: Writing quickly is not writing well
text:
Writing quickly is not writing well
Both claims of 1446 are about the letters: how fast they can be learned, and what they can write. Neither says how well anyone will write with them.
I think Hangeul (한글) is the best writing system in the world. I should admit that I may be biased, because it is the alphabet I write with. Most people agree that it is quick to learn, to read and to write.
Writing quickly is not the same as writing well. Good writing cannot be learned quickly: you read good writing, and you practice. Visualization is no different. This tool is new and still has problems, but I hope it is already a good tool to practice with.
The 1446 story makes the same distinction, between making a writing system and writing with it. King Sejong made the alphabet. Other people wrote most of the books that used it. I designed gog, but I am not a great author of plots. What I do have is many years as a user of visualization tools, watching and listening and reading. The design comes from that experience, and the result is a tool that is easy to learn and easy to use.
I hope you do good work with it.

title: Afterword
text:
The gap
A specification is a sentence written before the picture exists. Between writing it and the moment the engine shows you what you said, there is a gap, and everyone who writes a specification waits in it. The package is gog. The state you are in while you wait is agog: eager to see what comes next. I hope the book kept you agog.

Be agog. Use gog.

title: Appendix A — The kernel card
text:
The whole grammar, on one page. The table below is the kernel, the list of every word in the grammar. Each word is an atom, and the operators join atoms into a sentence that describes a plot. The table is copied from The kernel each time the book is built, so it always matches that chapter. Functions you never write into a sentence, such as render_svg(), are in Functions around the grammar.







Kind
The words




Sources
data query


Marks
point line area bar step interval box ribbon text path rule zone surface edge


Channels
x y z color size shape pattern opacity group label play


Transforms
bin smooth straight count density proportion sum mean median max min quantile cumulative range confidence deviation smooth_band straight_band bounds partition flow layout cluster, and the four collision modifiers, dodge stack jitter repel


Operators
+ layers, * derives, | and / arrange


Scales
linear log time category order


Spaces
flat space polar nest map globe network


Settings
style theme palette


Labels
title subtitle caption x_label y_label z_label


Facets
facet


Selections
brush



The minimum sentence is a source, a mark, and the position channels that mark needs:
data(table) + mark + x(column) + y(column)
The order of + matters in a few places only. Each mark starts a layer: the mark, and the channels and settings that apply to it. In a plot with one mark, the mark and its channels may be written in any order. This book usually writes a sentence as data, mark, positions, refinements, where the refinements are the optional parts, such as color and title. Only two parts of the order are rules. A sentence must start with a source (data() or query()), and a style() needs a mark before it. The engine refuses a sentence that breaks either rule.
What the order does change is which marks each channel or table applies to, and which mark is drawn on top. A channel written before any mark applies to every layer that can accept it, and this book writes a channel there when every layer should use it. A channel such as color, written after a mark, belongs to that mark alone. Positions are the exception: a mark with no x or y of its own reads the first ones written. Each later data() applies to the mark written directly after it, and a style() styles the nearest mark before it. Two marks draw in the order you wrote them, so the second is drawn on top of the first. Which orders matter and Encoding scope have the rules in full.
Deriving is what * does: it joins a transform to a mark, and the mark is always on the left. More than one transform can follow one mark: bar * bin * mean cuts the x axis into bands, then averages y inside each band. Transforms on one mark must each do a different job, and each job is done at its own step. So the order you write them in does not change the picture, and writing them in the order they happen is the convention. Chaining transforms names the four jobs.
Precedence is the order in which a language groups its operators. In R and Python, * and / group first, then +, then |. Julia groups | together with +, from left to right. JavaScript spells the operators as words, so it has no precedence to remember. In every language, one plot needs no parentheses, even with a facet: data(table) + bar * bin + x(a) | facet(g).
Two whole plots joined by | or / make an arrangement. In an arrangement, put each plot inside its own parentheses: (…) / (…). Without them, / groups before + and joins the first plot’s last atom to the second plot’s data(), and gog refuses that sentence. Put parentheses around an arrangement inside an arrangement too: ((…) | (…)) / (…). Put them around a whole arrangement before you add a theme() to it. What groups first gives the order in each language, and Parentheses in an arrangement shows what that order does to an arrangement.
When gog refuses, the message names the rule, and says what to write instead. Illegal means the grammar forbids the sentence you wrote: rewrite it. Unsupported means the grammar allows it and this engine does not draw it: remove the atom the message names, or use one this engine draws. Illegal is not the same as unsupported has the rule, and a refusal of each kind, printed by the engine when the book is built.
When gog assumes instead of refusing, the plot still draws. The message is an Assumption: it says what gog decided for you. Read it, and check that the decision was what you meant.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.1 render_svg()
Every word in the kernel belongs to a sentence. point is a mark, x is a channel, bin is a transform, and none of them means anything on its own. They are words, and a word needs a sentence.
The functions in this appendix are not words. Five of them take a finished plot and act on it. The sixth gives you a table that your sentence can name. None of them can be written into a sentence with + or *, and none of them is part of the grammar.
The name alone will not tell you whether a function is a word of the grammar. x_label is a word of the grammar, and its name joins two parts with an underscore, exactly as render_svg does. What separates them is where each one is written. A word of the grammar is written inside a sentence. The six functions below are always written outside one, which is why none of them appears in The kernel card.
Each function has a section below, in the same order as the rows above. The first turns a finished plot into text. The last section lists the buttons under each plot in the web edition. They are neither words nor functions.
A plot is a specification until the engine draws it. Sometimes you want the drawing itself: to save it as a file, or to put it in a web page of your own. render_svg() draws the plot and gives you the drawing as ordinary text. It takes the plot as its only argument, and it has the same name in all four languages:

println(length(picture), " characters")

console.log(picture.slice(0, 51));

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="800"
14710 characters
The first line of output shows where that text begins. The second line gives its whole length. So every plot in this book is also a piece of text. It starts with <svg and gives the width of the picture. After that it gives the position of every point, every tick and every label.
That text is the whole picture. A notebook displays it, and so does this book. Write it to a file whose name ends in .svg, and any web browser can open that file as a picture. A vector drawing program, such as Inkscape, can edit it too, because the file describes shapes rather than a grid of colored dots.
save_svg() writes that file for you, in all four languages.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.1.1 What the file carries
An SVG file is text, so anyone who opens it in a text editor can read everything in it. The file carries the drawing and nothing else, but the drawing itself can show private values. If your table holds something private, open the file and read it yourself before you publish.
A plot uses only the columns its sentence names. Columns the sentence never names are absent from the file, and so are their names:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


patients <- data.frame(
  patient = c("A. Smith", "B. Jones", "C. Brown", "D. Taylor"),
  email   = c("as@ex.com", "bj@ex.com", "cb@ex.com", "dt@ex.com"),
  weight  = c(61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68.0)
)

picture <- render_svg(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(weight))
sapply(c("A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"), grepl, x = picture, fixed = TRUE)
A. Smith    email   ex.com     61.2 
   FALSE    FALSE    FALSE    FALSE


patients = {
  "patient": ["A. Smith", "B. Jones", "C. Brown", "D. Taylor"],
  "email": ["as@ex.com", "bj@ex.com", "cb@ex.com", "dt@ex.com"],
  "weight": [61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68.0],
}

picture = render_svg(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(col.weight))
for text in ["A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"]:
    print(text + ":", text in picture)
A. Smith: False
email: False
ex.com: False
61.2: False


patients = (
  patient = ["A. Smith", "B. Jones", "C. Brown", "D. Taylor"],
  email = ["as@ex.com", "bj@ex.com", "cb@ex.com", "dt@ex.com"],
  weight = [61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68.0],
)

picture = render_svg(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(:weight))
for text in ["A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"]
    println(text, ": ", occursin(text, picture))
end
A. Smith: false
email: false
ex.com: false
61.2: false


const patients = {
  patient: ["A. Smith", "B. Jones", "C. Brown", "D. Taylor"],
  email: ["as@ex.com", "bj@ex.com", "cb@ex.com", "dt@ex.com"],
  weight: [61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68],
};

const picture = render_svg(plot(data(patients), layer(bar, bin), x(col.weight)));
for (const text of ["A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"]) {
  console.log(text + ":", picture.includes(text));
}
A. Smith: false
email: false
ex.com: false
61.2: false





None of the four searches finds anything. The sentence names one column, so the drawing uses one column. Even the weights are gone: bin cuts the weights into intervals and counts the rows in each, so the bars show only the counts.
The weights are absent because of the transform, not because a plot never carries values. A point with no transform draws one glyph per row, and each glyph is placed from one value:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


picture <- render_svg(data(patients) + point + x(weight) + y(patient))
lengths(gregexpr("<circle", picture))
[1] 4


picture = render_svg(data(patients) + point + x(col.weight) + y(col.patient))
print(picture.count("<circle"))
4


picture = render_svg(data(patients) + point + x(:weight) + y(:patient))
println(length(findall("<circle", picture)))
4


const picture = render_svg(plot(data(patients), point, x(col.weight), y(col.patient)));
console.log(picture.split("<circle").length - 1);
4





The four rows are drawn as four circles, and the four patient names are printed along the axis. This is not special to gog: a scatterplot in any plotting tool draws a point for every row you give it.
The weights are not written in the file as numbers. But each circle is placed by its weight, so a reader who measures the drawing can recover every weight.
So the rule is not that the file is safe. It is narrower: what your sentence names is what you publish. That includes a column named only in facet(), whose values are printed as panel labels. A column the sentence never names cannot be recovered from the file, so it stays private.


B.1.2 Plots that carry the table
A saved SVG file carries only the drawing. A web page can carry more, and that includes a page that a notebook or Quarto makes for you. You should know what it carries before you publish it.
Some plots are drawn twice. The engine makes the first drawing. The reader’s browser makes the second, because the reader can move a selection or turn the view. Three kinds of plot do this: one that binds brush(), one in the cube, and one on the globe. A network in the cube is one of them. The second drawing needs the numbers, so the web page also holds a copy of the table. That copy is in the page’s code: the screen does not show it, but anyone who opens the page’s code can read it.
One more kind of plot carries the table, although the browser never draws it again. It is a plot that draws each mark at its own row’s values, such as a scatter. Resting the pointer on a mark shows the values of the mark’s row, as Pointing at a mark explains, so the page needs the rows. A plot without brush whose table has more than 20,000 rows carries no copy, and its marks show no values.
Where the page holds a copy, it holds every row of the table, but only the columns the sentence names. As in a saved SVG file, a column the sentence never names is not in the page. The difference is in the values: the page holds each row’s exact numbers, and the file holds only a drawing of them. Here is patients again, with a brush:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(patients) + point + x(weight) + y(patient) + brush(weight)


data(patients) + point + x(col.weight) + y(col.patient) + brush(col.weight)


data(patients) + point + x(:weight) + y(:patient) + brush(:weight)


plot(data(patients), point, x(col.weight), y(col.patient),
  brush(col.weight))






                                     55 60 65 70 75   D. Taylor C. Brown B. Jones A. Smith  Patient Weight





“Given the patients: points, x is weight, y is patient, and let the reader select weight.”
That sentence names a brush and draws one point for each row. Either one is enough for the web edition of this page to carry a copy of the table. The copy has two columns, weight and patient, because the sentence names those two. The email column is not in that copy at all. In the web version, the plot has a show rows button under it, which Selection explains. The table that button opens lists the same two columns.
An SVG file never carries the table, even when its sentence names a brush. render_svg() returns only the picture.


B.1.3 What “byte for byte” means
This book says in several places that the four languages draw the same picture byte for byte. That claim is about the text that render_svg() returns.
A plot looks like a picture on your screen, and that picture is drawn from this text. A byte is the unit a computer stores text in: one English letter, digit or space takes one byte. Two plots are the same when their text is the same, byte for byte. Text that is only similar does not count, even when the two pictures look the same.
That is how gog checks that the four languages draw the same picture. Nearly every sentence in this book is written in R, in Python, in Julia and in JavaScript. Each one that draws is turned into its text, and the text from Python, Julia and JavaScript is compared with R’s, byte for byte. One wrong byte counts as a disagreement, and one disagreement makes the whole check fail.
A test that allowed small differences would accept pictures that are not the same. The pictures are not compared by eye, because a person cannot see a bar that is half a pixel too wide, or a color that is slightly wrong. Comparing the text finds both differences, and it works the same way every time.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.2 save_svg()
save_svg() draws the plot and writes the drawing to a file. It takes the plot and a path that ends in .svg, and it has the same name in all four languages:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


path <- file.path(tempdir(), "life.svg")
save_svg(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life), path)
cat(basename(path), file.size(path), "bytes\n")
life.svg 14710 bytes


import os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "life.svg")
save_svg(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life), path)
print(os.path.basename(path), os.path.getsize(path), "bytes")
life.svg 14710 bytes


path = joinpath(tempdir(), "life.svg")
save_svg(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life), path)
println(basename(path), " ", filesize(path), " bytes")
life.svg 14710 bytes


import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join, basename } from "node:path";
import { statSync } from "node:fs";

const path = join(tmpdir(), "life.svg");
save_svg(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)), path);
console.log(basename(path), statSync(path).size, "bytes");
life.svg 14710 bytes





The output names the file that was written and its size. The file holds the text that render_svg() returns, byte for byte, so the same plot gives the same file in every language. For a plot p, the call is the same in all four:



R
save_svg(p, "life.svg")


Python
save_svg(p, "life.svg")


Julia
save_svg(p, "life.svg")


JavaScript
save_svg(p, "life.svg")



A path that does not end in .svg is refused, and the message repeats the path with the right ending. gog draws the plot before it writes anything. So when gog refuses the plot, a file already at that path stays unchanged.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar

B.3 save_gif()
A plot that binds play() is a sequence of pictures rather than one. It moves in a browser, because the SVG carries its own timing. A chat message, a slide in a talk and a post on a social site cannot show that movement. save_gif() writes the same sequence as a file that those places do play:

import { join, basename } from "node:path";

const ring = join(tmpdir(), "ring.gif");

              polar(), play(col.year)),
         ring, { scale: 2 });
console.log(basename(ring), Math.round(statSync(ring).size / 1024), "KB");
ring.gif 708 KB





The output names the file that was written and its size. The engine writes the GIF itself, so no other program has to be installed.
scale multiplies the width and the height of the picture. A plot is 800 by 600 pixels unless its theme says otherwise, so scale = 2 writes a GIF of 1600 by 1200 pixels.
Three of the four languages take scale as a named argument. JavaScript has no named arguments, so it takes scale in an object at the end of the call:



R
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", scale = 2)


Python
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", scale=2)


Julia
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", scale = 2)


JavaScript
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", { scale: 2 })



A plot with no play() is refused rather than written as a file of one frame. The Play chapter shows that refusal. It also explains why gog writes no video.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.4 save_png()
An SVG stays sharp at any size, because it is text that is drawn again each time it is shown. Some places accept only a picture made of pixels, such as an older word processor, some slide programs and most chat messages. save_png() saves the plot as a PNG file, which all of them accept. It takes the plot and a path that ends in .png, and it has the same name in all four languages:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


path <- file.path(tempdir(), "life.png")
save_png(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent), path)
cat(basename(path), round(file.size(path) / 1024), "KB\n")
life.png 230 KB


import os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "life.png")
save_png(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent), path)
print(os.path.basename(path), round(os.path.getsize(path) / 1024), "KB")
life.png 230 KB


path = joinpath(tempdir(), "life.png")
save_png(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent), path)
println(basename(path), " ", round(Int, filesize(path) / 1024), " KB")
life.png 230 KB


import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join, basename } from "node:path";
import { statSync } from "node:fs";

const path = join(tmpdir(), "life.png");
save_png(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent)), path);
console.log(basename(path), Math.round(statSync(path).size / 1024), "KB");
life.png 230 KB





The output names the file that was written and its size. As with save_gif(), the engine writes the picture itself, so no other program has to be installed.
A plot is 800 by 600 pixels unless its theme says otherwise. scale multiplies the width and the height, and it is 2 if you leave it out, so the picture above is 1600 by 1200 pixels. That is sharp enough for a document or a slide on most screens. scale = 1 saves the plot at 800 by 600, and scale = 3 at 2400 by 1800. JavaScript takes scale in an object at the end of the call, as it does for save_gif():



R
save_png(p, "life.png", scale = 3)


Python
save_png(p, "life.png", scale=3)


Julia
save_png(p, "life.png", scale = 3)


JavaScript
save_png(p, "life.png", { scale: 3 })



A PNG holds one picture, so a plot that plays more than one frame is refused. Saving only its first frame would drop every other frame, and nothing would tell you. The message names save_gif(), which writes every frame:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


moving <- data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + play(year)
save_png(moving, "life.png")
Error:
! gog: a PNG holds one picture, and this plot plays 12 frames of `year`, so every frame but the first would be left out. `save_gif()` writes every frame. To save one frame as a still, keep only that frame's rows in the table.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


moving = data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + play(col.year)
save_png(moving, "life.png")
gog: a PNG holds one picture, and this plot plays 12 frames of `year`, so every frame but the first would be left out. `save_gif()` writes every frame. To save one frame as a still, keep only that frame's rows in the table.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


moving = data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + play(:year)
save_png(moving, "life.png")
gog: a PNG holds one picture, and this plot plays 12 frames of `year`, so every frame but the first would be left out. `save_gif()` writes every frame. To save one frame as a still, keep only that frame's rows in the table.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


const moving = plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), play(col.year));
save_png(moving, "life.png");
gog: a PNG holds one picture, and this plot plays 12 frames of `year`, so every frame but the first would be left out. `save_gif()` writes every frame. To save one frame as a still, keep only that frame's rows in the table.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.





An arrangement of plots is saved as one picture. As with save_svg(), a path that does not end in .png is refused, and a file already at the path stays unchanged when gog refuses the plot.
A PNG is pixels, so its text becomes blurred when a reader zooms in. Its letters are drawn with the fonts installed on the computer that saves it, so the same plot saved on two computers can give two slightly different pictures. A computer with no fonts at all, such as a bare server, gives a picture with no text, and gog says so when it saves one. For a web page, use the SVG, whose text stays sharp at any zoom.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.5 save_json()
When a plot is drawn wrong, the person who fixes it has to draw the same plot. Your code alone cannot do that, because it reads a table that only you have.
Every language turns your sentence into one request for the engine. The request holds the sentence and every column the sentence names, and the engine draws the plot from that request alone. save_json() writes the request to a file. The file is in JSON, a plain-text format for structured data, so any text editor can open it. Like save_svg(), it takes the plot and a path, and the path ends in .json.
The code below saves the histogram of patients from What the file carries. Then it searches the file for the same four pieces of text as that section:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


path <- file.path(tempdir(), "weights.json")
save_json(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(weight), path)
request <- readLines(path)
sapply(c("A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"), grepl, x = request, fixed = TRUE)
A. Smith    email   ex.com     61.2 
   FALSE    FALSE    FALSE     TRUE


import os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "weights.json")
save_json(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(col.weight), path)
request = open(path).read()
for text in ["A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"]:
    print(text + ":", text in request)
A. Smith: False
email: False
ex.com: False
61.2: True


path = joinpath(tempdir(), "weights.json")
save_json(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(:weight), path)
request = read(path, String)
for text in ["A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"]
    println(text, ": ", occursin(text, request))
end
A. Smith: false
email: false
ex.com: false
61.2: true


import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const path = join(tmpdir(), "weights.json");
save_json(plot(data(patients), layer(bar, bin), x(col.weight)), path);
const request = readFileSync(path, "utf8");
for (const text of ["A. Smith", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"]) {
  console.log(text + ":", request.includes(text));
}
A. Smith: false
email: false
ex.com: false
61.2: true





The file leaves out the patient and email columns, their values and their names, because the sentence never names them. But it holds 61.2, the first patient’s weight, which the SVG file did not hold. The SVG file shows only the counts that bin made. The request holds every value of each column the sentence names, because the engine needs those values to draw the plot.
So read the file before you share it. If a column the sentence names holds something private, replace its values in your table with invented ones. Draw the plot again and check that it still shows the problem, then save the file again.
This file is what to attach to a bug report. From the file alone, the engine draws the plot you saw, byte for byte, without your code and without the rest of your table. Unlike save_svg(), save_json() writes the file even when gog refuses the plot, because a refusal you think is wrong is also worth reporting. A path that does not end in .json is refused, and the message repeats the path with the right ending.
In R, the reprex package (Bryan et al., 2024) turns your code into a reproducible example, called a reprex. It has the same aim as this file: give the person who fixes a problem everything they need to draw it again. The difference is in what each one holds. A reprex runs your code in a new, empty session, so your code must first build a few rows of data itself, and you choose which rows. The file from save_json() already holds the data the plot needs, which is why you read it before you share it. All four languages write this file, and the engine draws the same plot from each one.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.6 gog_table()
Every example in this book starts from a table. The examples draw from a set of shared tables, such as gapminder_2007, and each one is published with the book as a CSV file. gog_table() reads one by its name, so you can run any example without finding and saving the file yourself. Unlike the other four, this function comes before the plot rather than after it:
gapminder_2007 <- gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
No plot appears under that block, because the book does not run it. The call reads the table over the network, and running it here would mean the book could be built only with a network connection.
gog_table() is there so that you can run this book’s examples, not for your own work. When the data is yours, bind it with data() and skip gog_table() entirely.
gog_table() takes a second argument, text. A CSV file records each value but never what kind of value it is. A column of 01, 02, 03 looks like numbers, so it is read as 1, 2, 3, and the leading zeros are lost. To keep such a column as text, list it in text. Labels that look like numbers names the three columns in the book’s tables that need it.
The book’s data explains this function in full. It lists every shared table in the book and shows the call in each of the four languages.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
section: B.7 The buttons under a plot
text:
B.7 The buttons under a plot
In the web edition, a line of buttons is under every plot. Each one changes how you look at the plot, or saves what you see, and none changes its sentence. So none of them is a word of the grammar:







Button
What it does




the magnifiers, − and +
Make the picture smaller or larger


the frame button (four corners around a small square)
Returns to the whole picture


the camera
Saves what you are looking at as a PNG file, large enough for a slide or a journal figure



A plot that plays adds three buttons to the same line: they pause the sequence and step through its frames (Play). A brushed plot adds a line of controls for its selection (Selection), and a plot in the cube adds a line for its viewing angle (Space). The buttons under every plot introduces this line.

title: Appendix C — Combinations
text:
C.1 Marks and channels
This page holds the whole of what the grammar lets you combine, in four crossings. The first is what a mark lets you map, which is the channels. The second is what a mark lets you derive, which is the transforms. The third is which two transforms can be chained on one mark. The fourth is where a mark can be drawn, which is the coordinate spaces. Three of them show what a mark takes, what it does not, and the surprising pairings that are legal anyway. The third asks the same question of two transforms.
These grids are the orthogonality law made visible. Law 1 says every compatible atom combines with every other; a table is that promise enumerated, one cell at a time. It is the direct analog of the letter chart a Hangeul (한글) learner reads, with the consonants down one side and the vowels across the top. A syllable block is what those letters assemble into. This book has used that pairing from the start: a mark is a consonant and a position is a vowel, and neither draws alone. Every syllable the grammar can form appears somewhere in these grids.
Legal is not the same as useful. Law 8, Pronounceable ≠ Usable, guarantees only that the engine draws what a ✓︎ cell allows. Whether it should be drawn is your judgment. A cell the engine refuses teaches as much as one it draws. It records a real limit of the geometry, a ruling, or a part of the engine that is not built, and never an oversight.
Every crossing here is generated live from the engine’s own rule table, each time the book is built. That is the same table the engine consults to accept or refuse your plot. A grid written by hand can stop matching the code; a grid generated from it cannot. Add a mark, a channel, a transform or a space, and this page gains the row or the column by itself.
Start with the channels. The marks run down the side and the channels across the top, and each cell says whether you may map a column to that channel on that mark.
Reading the five glyphs:
With the glyphs read, the grid itself shows five patterns:

● must: a required channel. The mark does not render without it. A point needs an x and a y; a text needs its label.
✓︎ maps: bind a column of your table here and the engine draws it. This is the ordinary case: the channel shows the column. A column that a transform writes is checked the same way, and a few of those are not drawn yet (Other columns a transform writes).
○ set: the mark has this feature, but not row by row. A line is one stroke, so its size and opacity are a single value for the whole layer, fixed with style() rather than mapped. Those constants have their own settings grid. Nine of them never appear on the channel grid at all: border_color, border_size, caps, center, nudge, angle, arrow, reach and gap are settings and nothing else. Two questions, not one shows in one table where each of five properties can be mapped and where it can only be set.
◌ not drawn: the engine refuses this pairing and gives you a direction instead of a wrong picture. Three cells are marked this way. Two are z on rule and on zone. Their 3-D forms are a plane and a slab with no single depth to sort by (Space). Drawing one means working out what hides what, and the engine does not do that. The third is play on edge. An edge is always placed by layout, and the engine does not play a network yet. The message points to | facet(): every panel shares one layout, so each node keeps its place.

Either binding means nothing, and the engine says so. Decided: z on line, step, area and ribbon. These marks sort by x, and in a cube x can point into the page, so the order cannot be seen. The refusal points to path instead, which for an area or a ribbon draws only the edge.



group splits a line, not a bar. Read down the group column: ✓︎ on every mark that builds one shape out of many rows. point, bar and text draw one shape or one label per row, and on them group splits only what a statistic or dodge acts on (and on a bar, stack). A bare group there has no line to divide, and is refused. rule and edge take no group at all.
label belongs to text alone. Its column is ● on text and — everywhere else. A labeled scatter is two layers, point + text, never a label given to the point.
Categories on x and on y. A category on x reaches every mark that has positions except surface, and on y it reaches fewer of them. Read the x and y columns against each other. Which types each accepts is in Channels, and the split divides the other marks with positions in two. The marks drawn at one place (point, text) and the marks drawn in a slot, which measure along the other axis (bar, interval, box), take either type on both positions. A point’s or a label’s two axes are the same kind, which is why it takes either type on both. That one rule is where a strip plot, a horizontal bar and a categorical box all come from. Three more marks do the same. A path sorts nothing, so it has no domain. A rule measures nothing on either axis. A zone measures nothing by length, and that is what makes a heatmap cell a zone rather than a second kind of bar. The stroke and region marks (line, step, area, ribbon) take either type on x alone. Their x is the domain the mark is read along, and their y is the quantity it traces. Those are two different kinds of axis. surface is outside the split, because both of its positions measure. A sheet is a height, and the two positions say where that height is read.
Three rows have no ● at all. rule and zone show ✓︎ on both positions and ● on neither, because no single cell can state what they need. A rule needs exactly one of the two, and the panel supplies the other (Rule). A zone has no fixed need: a categorical position, bounds, bin, density or a boundary on a map can each give it its sides (Zone). edge is the third, and it takes no position at all. Those obligations are stated once in the engine instead.
zone and surface take either type on color. Of the five filled regions, zone is the only one that takes a number: bar, box, area and ribbon take a category only. surface, a sheet rather than a region, takes a number as well, and both read the ramp.

C.2 Marks and transforms
The second crossing: not what a mark maps, but what it derives. A transform enters through * (bar * bin, interval * range, point * jitter), and which transform a mark takes is decided by the mark’s geometry against the transform’s kind. There are three kinds, and each has its own grid below.
Each cell holds one of three glyphs:

✓︎ combines: the transform applies to this mark and renders.
● required: on interval, ribbon and edge, the mark does not draw until one of its ● transforms is present, so that transform is part of its minimum syllable. The ● cells in a row are a choice, not a list: pick one. A zone is the exception. Each ● is one way to give it its sides, and a categorical position is another, so a zone can draw with no transform at all.
— none: the mark has no use for this kind of transform, and the engine refuses it with a direction toward the transform its geometry does want.


C.2.1 Statistics: a value per group
The first of the three kinds is also the largest. Most summarizing transforms reduce the data to one value at each x: a bin’s count, a group’s mean, a smoothed height. Any mark that draws a value at each x can draw that summary, so those marks are ✓︎ under every summary. That is why a distribution has several spellings rather than one histogram with a shape option: bar * bin is the histogram, line * bin is the frequency polygon, and step * bin is the staircase.

C.2.3 Collision modifiers: an offset, not a statistic
When marks collide at one position, four offsets separate them, and which one a mark takes is decided by its geometry and by the axis the collision is on. dodge sets groups side by side within a category’s slot. On the marks that have a width (bar, box, interval), it subdivides that width among the groups. A point has no width to subdivide, so dodge gives each group a part of the slot. It then moves each point within that part, only as far as it must to touch no other point. With one group in each slot, that is the beeswarm. stack piles marks along the measure axis. A bar or an area piles as lengths. A point has no length of its own, so it piles as dots, which is the dot plot. jitter also moves a point along a categorical axis, by a small amount that varies from point to point, and it serves point alone. Which marks take repel is decided by a different question: not what geometry a mark has, but what it is made of. A label is as wide as the word it draws, so two labels overlap where their points do not, and text is the only mark made of words.

title: Appendix C — Combinations
text:
C.3 Transforms and transforms
The third crossing is the only one where a mark does not appear. Two transforms can follow one mark: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each. Which pairs can do that is decided by the transforms alone, and by one rule.
A transform has a job. There are four of them, and every transform in gog fills at least one, except repel:








job
the question it answers
the transforms that answer it




extent
where are the cells?
bin, density, smooth, straight, smooth_band, straight_band, partition, and bounds on a zone


measure
what is in them?
count, sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, range, confidence, deviation, bounds


scale
what scale is the answer read on?
proportion, cumulative, and stack(share = TRUE)


position
where are the marks drawn?
dodge, stack, jitter


all four at once
what is the whole picture?
flow, layout, cluster



cumulative fills the scale job as well: it keeps the measurement, and reads it as a total so far. So it contradicts proportion and stack(share = TRUE).
repel fills no job at all. It moves a label after every job has run, so it contradicts nothing. Its row in the grid below is the only one with no refused pair, not even under the other three offsets. flow, layout and cluster fill all four jobs at once. Each computes the whole picture, so repel is the only transform that composes with one. No mark takes cluster and repel together, though.
Two transforms compose when they do different jobs, and contradict when they do the same one. Each cell a transform computes (a bin, a group, a point on a curve) holds one extent, one measure, one scale and one position. So a second transform doing a job the first already did leaves the engine no reading that keeps both, and it refuses rather than drawing one and discarding the other.
One transform is the exception, and it is the exception that makes chaining useful. bin does two jobs: it cuts the axis, and it counts what lands in each band. The count is a by-product of the cut, so bin does not have to keep it. It hands the measure job to a transform that reduces a column you named, such as mean. The other extent transforms do two jobs as well, and none of them can hand one over. A density or a smooth cell is a point on an estimated curve, which is between the rows rather than holding any of them, so there is nothing inside it to reduce. That is why bar * bin * mean composes: bin supplies the cells and mean supplies their value. And it is why bar * bin * count does not, since count was never handed a column to reduce.

A ∅ marks a pair that composes but that no mark takes together, so the engine refuses every sentence that writes both. range is drawn by a line, a step, an interval or a ribbon. stack piles a bar, an area, a point or a text. So on a bar the engine refuses range, and on a line it refuses stack.
The grid is symmetric, and the rule is the reason. Whether two transforms contradict is a fact about their jobs, and it has nothing to do with which one you typed first. So the order is yours to choose. Each job has its own step in the engine, extent first and position last. Write the transforms in that order, and the sentence reads the way it runs. The · on the diagonal pairs a transform with itself. Written twice, a transform repeats its own job, and the engine refuses it like any other repeat. repel has no job to repeat, so it is the one transform the engine lets you write twice.
Eleven transforms measure, so no two of them combine: read their rows against each other, and every cell between two of them is —. That is why chains such as bar * count * mean, bar * mean * sum and interval * range * confidence are refused. Now compare bin’s row with smooth’s, straight’s and density’s. Those three chain with no measure transform at all. bin chains with nine of the eleven. The two it refuses are count and bounds. count was never handed a column. bounds reads two columns but reduces neither: it draws each row’s own low and high, so a bin would hold many pairs and no one value. That is the exception above, written out in the grid.
Three more rules refuse a pair whose jobs differ. A share and a running total each add up one number per cell. range computes two, a low and a high, and the points of a curve such as density are where it was computed, not parts of a whole. So proportion and cumulative refuse both. stack and dodge move marks that share one position. density, smooth, straight, smooth_band and straight_band compute each group’s curve or line at points along that group’s own range, and the groups’ points do not line up. That is why stack and dodge refuse all five. And jitter spreads points within a category’s slot. bin, density, smooth, straight, smooth_band and straight_band each compute a value along a continuous axis, so there is no slot to spread in.
One contradiction does not fit the grid, because it depends on something outside the pair. stack(share = TRUE) divides each pile by its own total, which is a scale. proportion divides again, and a number divided twice is not a share of anything. The engine refuses it, and the grid shows the common case: stack without share.
A chain fills at most four jobs, and the number was not chosen. There are four jobs and each takes at most one transform, so a fifth transform that fills a job has to repeat one. Repeating one is the contradiction this whole section is about. repel fills no job, so it can still follow a chain of four: text * bin * mean * proportion * dodge * repel draws.

C.3.1 The shapes a long chain can take
The rule above allows chains of three and four, so the next question is how many there are. The answer is a short list. Once each job is filled at most once, and the marks are asked which transforms they take, every chain of three or four takes one of the shapes below. Two slots stand for a family rather than a transform: <aggregation> is any of sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, and <collision modifier> is dodge, stack, jitter or repel, whichever the mark takes.

That leaves the aggregation, which is free among six, and the offset, which the mark narrows to one or two. So chains of four exist, but few of them.
The shapes say what the transforms allow. A mark can still refuse a chain whose every pair is ✓︎, for a reason about its own geometry, and no grid shows it. point * proportion * stack is the clearest case. A dot plot piles one whole dot per observation, and a share is less than one dot. So the chain is refused on point and drawn on bar.

C.4 Marks and spaces
The fourth crossing is not about the mark itself. It is the coordinate space the whole plot is drawn in, and it asks a different question of every mark. Once the plane is bent, or extended into a cube, can this geometry still be drawn? A polar() bar is a wedge, a polar() line runs around the center, and a scatter with a z is drawn in a cube, all from the same sentences that draw them flat.
Two glyphs here, not five. Either the engine draws this mark in this space, or it does not and says so:

✓︎ drawn: the mark renders in this space.
— not drawn: refused, with a message that says what to write instead, never half-drawn. A — in the space column has one of two reasons, blocked or decided. On the channel grid a blocked cell shows as ◌ and a decided one as —. Every other blank is simpler: the mark needs what the space lacks, as a surface needs the cube. The paragraphs under the table say why each column’s blanks are blank.
